Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$ where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and read in the twist; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. For a class $m\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and any lift $\widetilde m\in M(\lambda')$, the inverse is $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$, independently of the chosen lift.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

Assume the isomorphism $\Phi_\lambda$ and the exact unit identity of [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]. Then:

1. For every commutative ring $R$ and $q=1$, the module $P(\lambda)$ identifies with the ordinary integral-polytabloid Specht module $R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ of [[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]], with the classical left action converted to a right action by $x\cdot w=w^{-1}x$: the basis $\{e_t=z_\lambda T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)}\}$ specializes to the standard polytabloid basis and the DJ form to the standard tabloid form. The sign automorphism $\theta$ becomes the pullback along the sign twist $w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$. Over every field $F$, this specialization is compatible with the conjugate-sign dictionary of [[lem-conjugate-specht-sign-duality-over-fields]].

2. For a field $F$, a unit $q\in F^\times$ and partitions $\mu,\lambda\vdash n$ with $D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}\ne0$ one has $[P(\lambda):D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda'):D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}]$, and the simultaneous sign-automorphism pullback is the same $\theta$ on both sides: $(D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}})^\theta\cong D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}$.

3. Suppose a Schur-algebra corner is already proved to send the Weyl module $W(\lambda)$ to $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ and its head $L(\lambda)$ to $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$. Then that corner gives $F(W(\lambda'))\cong P(\lambda)^\theta$ and $F(L(\lambda'))\cong(D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}})^\theta$, including the zero case; this is the $\theta$-twisted conjugate dictionary, never the untwisted conjugate-dual identity. No Schur-algebra theorem and no source-20 convention is a prerequisite of this conditional dictionary.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. With the Murphy cellular
basis $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]],
[[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and the canonical tableau
$t^\lambda$ of shape $\lambda\vdash n$
([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell
module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the
Murphy basis: it is the free $R$-module with basis
$\{m_t:=m_{t^\lambda t}:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ - the classes of the
Murphy elements whose *first* index is the canonical tableau - and $H$ acts by
$m_th=\sum_vr_vm_v$ whenever
$m_{t^\lambda t}h\equiv\sum_vr_vm_{t^\lambda v}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$. (The
cellular action rule transforms the second index and fixes the first, so the
diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone do not span a submodule; the module basis is
the fixed-first-index family above.) Its **cell form** is the unique bilinear
form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\times
S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\to R$ with
$$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\langle m_s,m_t\rangle_\lambda\,m_{uv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$; it is symmetric and associative and
$\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a submodule, so
$D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}:=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
is a right $H$-module
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

**Convention (Dipper-James signed cellular normalization).** Let $\theta:H\to H$
be the involutive algebra automorphism defined by
$\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). For a right module $M$,
write $M^\theta$ for the same $R$-module with action $x\cdot h=x\theta(h)$. The
page's ordinary Specht normalization is the signed conjugate Murphy
construction
$$S^{\lambda}:=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta,$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Its form is the form of
$S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ on the same underlying module; because $\theta$
commutes with $*$ this is associative for the twisted action
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Over a field put
$$D^{\lambda}:=S^{\lambda}/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}S^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta.$$
Thus $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(S^{\lambda})^\theta$ and
$D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(D^{\lambda})^\theta$; conjugation alone does not
identify these modules
([[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]],
[[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]). At
$q=1$, $\theta(\sigma)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma$, so these identities
contain tensoring with sign; in characteristic $2$ the sign twist becomes
trivial at $q=1$
([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).
The nonzero quotients in this signed normalization have $e$-regular labels
by [[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]:
that theorem proves the nonzero Murphy quotient criterion in $e$-restricted
labels, and conjugation makes these precisely $e$-regular labels
([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]). No generic root-of-unity
Hecke claim is inferred from the published prime-characteristic group-only sign
dictionary, and no semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed.

For every $n\ge0$ and partition $\lambda\vdash n$, the family
$$\{e_t:t\text{ is a standard }\lambda\text{-tableau}\}$$
is a $\mathbb C$-basis of $S^\lambda$. In particular,
$$\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\lambda=f^\lambda,$$
including $\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\varnothing=1$.

Fix a prime $p$, an integer $n\ge0$, and a **splitting $p$-modular system**
$(K,\mathcal O,k)$ for $S_n$, so that $K$ and $k$ are splitting fields for
$S_n$ and its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). Write

$$M^\lambda_k:=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad S^\lambda_k:=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}\subseteq M^\lambda_k$$

for the base change of the integral tabloid module and Specht lattice; the
inclusion is the injective polytabloid-span inclusion of
[[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]], and $S^\lambda_k$ has the
images of the standard polytabloids as $k$-basis. Let
$\beta_k:M^\lambda_k\times M^\lambda_k\to k$ be the reduced integral tabloid
form, the unique $k$-bilinear form with orthonormal tabloid basis
([[def-integral-tabloid-bilinear-form-and-specht-gram-matrix]]); it is
symmetric, nondegenerate, and $S_n$-invariant.

For a $k$-subspace $V\subseteq M^\lambda_k$ put

$$V^{\perp}:=\{\,x\in M^\lambda_k:\beta_k(x,v)=0\text{ for all }v\in V\,\}.$$

The **form radical** of $S^\lambda_k$ is

$$R^\lambda:=S^\lambda_k\cap (S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},$$

and the **modular Specht quotient** (or James quotient) is

$$D^\lambda:=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda .$$

The quotient is a $k[S_n]$-module and may be zero. Its dimension is the
$p$-rank of the integral Gram matrix: if $G_\lambda$ is the Gram matrix of
$\beta$ in the standard-polytabloid basis and $\overline{G_\lambda}$ its
reduction modulo $p$, i.e. the matrix of $\beta_k$ in the standard basis of
$S^\lambda_k$, then

$$\dim_kD^\lambda=\operatorname{rank}_k\overline{G_\lambda} =\operatorname{rank}_k(G_\lambda\bmod p).$$

Everything is defined by scalar extension: $S^\lambda_k$ and $\beta_k$ are
determined by $\lambda$ and $k$, and no choice of lifts of elements of
$S^\lambda_k$ enters. $R^\lambda$ is a **form radical**, and is an
$S_n$-submodule; the identification of $R^\lambda$ with the module radical
$\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)=J(k[S_n])S^\lambda_k$
([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]) is a later consequence,
asserted only when $D^\lambda\ne0$. In particular no simplicity of
$D^\lambda$ is claimed here.

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ an invertible element. The **quantum
characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that
$1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists
([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1\ne0$, the least positive
integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so
the two formulations coincide.

Concretely: (i) if $q\ne1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$ — indeed
$(q-1)(1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1})=q^m-1$ and $q-1\ne0$ — so $[e]_q=0$ is equivalent
to $q^e=1$, and a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and
then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{\times}$ (which is $\ge2$
because $q\ne1$); (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$
when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ (the characteristic is a prime, hence at least
$2$, and $m\cdot1_F\ne0$ for $1\le m<p$) and $e=\infty$ when
$\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

If $e<\infty$ then $q\ne1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for
every integer $m$: for $m\ge0$ the sum splits as
$$[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q,$$
so $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ whenever $[e]_q=0$; for the remaining $m<0$ one extends the
closed formula by $[m]_q:=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ when $q\ne1$ and reads $[m]_1:=m\in F$
for the canonical image of the integer $m$ when $q=1$, in which case
$e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ and $[m+e]_1=m+e=m$ in $F$. In particular the
quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter
governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice
principle is used.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $F$ be a
field of characteristic $p$. Let $\beta_F$ be the reduced integral tabloid
form on $M^\lambda_F=F\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, with
orthonormal tabloid basis, and let
$$S^\lambda_F\subseteq M^\lambda_F,\qquad R^\lambda_F:=S^\lambda_F\cap(S^\lambda_F)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda_F:=S^\lambda_F/R^\lambda_F,$$
where $V^{\perp}=\{x\in M^\lambda_F:\beta_F(x,v)=0\text{ for all }v\in V\}$
([[def-integral-tabloid-bilinear-form-and-specht-gram-matrix]],
[[thm-james-submodule-theorem-over-an-arbitrary-field]]). Let $G_\lambda$ be
the Gram matrix of the integral tabloid form in the standard-polytabloid
basis of the integral Specht lattice $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$, and let
$g_\lambda$ be the positive greatest common divisor of its entries
([[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]],
[[lem-specht-gram-gcd-detects-p-regularity]]). Write $G_\lambda\bmod p$ for
the entrywise image of $G_\lambda$ in $F$, a matrix with entries in $F$.
Then:

1. **Vanishing criterion.**
   $$D^\lambda_F=0\iff p\mid G_{ij}\text{ for all }i,j \iff p\mid g_\lambda\iff\lambda\text{ is not }p\text{-regular},$$
   and equivalently $D^\lambda_F\ne0$ if and only if $z_j(\lambda)<p$ for
   every $j\ge1$, where $z_j(\lambda)$ is the number of parts of $\lambda$
   equal to $j$.
2. **Dimension.** $\dim_FD^\lambda_F=\operatorname{rank}_F(G_\lambda\bmod p)$;
   this dimension is determined by $\lambda$ and $p$ alone, and it is
   positive exactly when $\lambda$ is $p$-regular.
3. **Structure when nonzero.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then
   $D^\lambda_F\ne0$ is the simple, self-dual and absolutely irreducible
   head of $S^\lambda_F$, and $R^\lambda_F$ is the unique maximal submodule
   of $S^\lambda_F$, equal to the module radical
   $\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_F)$.

For the $k$ of a splitting $p$-modular system $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ for $S_n$,
$D^\lambda_k$ is the modular Specht quotient $D^\lambda$ of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], so the criterion above
decides for which $\lambda$ that quotient vanishes. No simplicity of
$S^\lambda_F$ itself is asserted.

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let $e=e(F,q)$ and assume $e>n$ (with $e=\infty$ allowed); let $\lambda\vdash n$, $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$, and let $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ be the Murphy cell module with Murphy basis $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

1. (**Separation**) If $s,t$ are standard $\lambda$-tableaux with $[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$ for all $1\le k\le n$ then $s=t$. More precisely, if the q-content values agree for all $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$ for some $i$, then $s=t$ or $t=s(i\ i+1)$. 2. (**Idempotents**) Let $\mathcal R_k$ be the set of distinct q-content values of the entry $k$ over standard tableaux of **all** partitions of $n$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ define $$F_t:=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\ \prod_{\substack{c\in\mathcal R_k\\        c\ne[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q}}        \frac{L_k-c}{[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q-c}\in F[L_1,\ldots,L_n].$$ These are orthogonal idempotents of $H$; their actions on $S_{\mathrm M}^\lambda$ project onto the corresponding simultaneous eigenlines. Put $f_t=m_tF_t$. Then $f_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_qf_t$ and $f_t=m_t+\sum_{s\rhd t}a_sm_s$. The global content sets are essential for the asserted idempotency in $H$, rather than only the induced same-shape endomorphisms. 3. (**Orthogonal seminormal basis**) $\{f_t:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is a basis of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ satisfying $f_tF_s=\delta_{ts}f_t$ and $\langle f_s,f_t\rangle_\lambda=\delta_{st}\langle f_t,f_t\rangle_\lambda$; it is the **seminormal basis** of the Murphy cell module. 4. (**Generator action**) Let $s$ be a standard $\lambda$-tableau, $1\le i<n$ and $t:=s(i\ i+1)$, and put $\rho:=\operatorname{content}_s(i)-\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)\in\mathbb Z$. If $i$ and $i+1$ lie in the same row of $s$ then $f_sT_i=q\,f_s$; if they lie in the same column then $f_sT_i=-f_s$; otherwise $t$ is standard and $$f_sT_i=\alpha_i(s)\,f_t-\frac{1}{[\rho]_q}f_s,\qquad \alpha_i(s):=\begin{cases}1,&s\rhd t,\\[1mm]\dfrac{[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q}{[\rho]_q[-\rho]_q},&t\rhd s,\end{cases}$$ where $[-\rho]_q$ is the extended quantum integer of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]] and for the swapped tableau $\operatorname{content}_t(i)-\operatorname{content}_t(i+1)=-\rho$. No semisimplicity of $H$ is assumed and no choice principle is used.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$ and all its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For a partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ let
$$S^\lambda_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad R^\lambda=S^\lambda_k\cap(S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda$$
be the modular Specht quotient of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], defined using the reduced
integral tabloid form on $M^\lambda_k$.

1. **Simple heads.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda\ne0$ is
   self-dual and absolutely irreducible, and it is the simple head of
   $S^\lambda_k$, whose unique maximal submodule is
   $R^\lambda=\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)$. If $\lambda$ is not
   $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda=0$.
2. **Pairwise inequivalent.** If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ are both $p$-regular
   and $D^\lambda\cong D^\mu$ as $k[S_n]$-modules, then $\lambda=\mu$.
3. **Complete set.** Every simple $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D^\lambda$
   for exactly one $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$. Equivalently, as
   $\lambda$ ranges over the $p$-regular partitions of $n$, the modules
   $D^\lambda$ form a complete set of representatives of the isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; in particular the number of simple
   $k[S_n]$-modules equals the number of $p$-regular partitions of $n$.

No absolutely irreducible module outside the family $\{D^\lambda\}$ is
constructed, and the statement asserts nothing about fields that are not
splitting fields for $S_n$. The proof uses no averaging and no division by a
group order, and the case $n=0$ and characteristic $2$ are included.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For $\mu\vdash n$
write $S^\mu_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\mu_{\mathbb Z}$ for the field-valued
Specht module, $D^\mu=S^\mu_k/R^\mu$ for its modular form quotient
([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]), and let
$$S(\mu):=(S^\mu_k)^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(S^\mu_k,k),\qquad (\sigma\cdot f)(x):=f(\sigma^{-1}x)$$
be the **dual Specht module**, with
$$D(\mu):=\operatorname{hd}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr) =S(\mu)/\operatorname{rad}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr)$$
its head ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]). Let
$\mu'$ be the conjugate partition, and let
$S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ be the tensor product of
$k[S_n]$-modules with the diagonal action
$\sigma\cdot(x\otimes w)=(\sigma\cdot x)\otimes(\sigma\cdot w)$, where
$\operatorname{sgn}$ is the one-dimensional sign representation
([[def-sign-representation-and-restriction-of-a-representation]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

1. **Dual Specht versus sign-twisted conjugate.** If $\mu$ is $p$-restricted
   (equivalently, by
   [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]], $\mu'$ is $p$-regular),
   then $S(\mu)\cong S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$; consequently
   $S(\mu)$ is nonzero with simple head
   $$D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn},$$
   a nonzero simple $k[S_n]$-module that is self-dual and absolutely
   irreducible.
2. **Equivalent form for $p$-regular labels.** If $\lambda\vdash n$ is
   $p$-regular, then $\lambda'$ is $p$-restricted and
   $$D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')\otimes\operatorname{sgn}.$$
3. **The two labellings.** The map $\mu\mapsto D(\mu)$ is a bijection from
   the set of $p$-restricted partitions of $n$ to the set of isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; that is, every simple
   $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D(\mu)$ for exactly one $p$-restricted
   $\mu\vdash n$.

In characteristic $2$ the sign representation is the trivial representation,
so the formulas read $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}$ and $D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')$;
the transposition is still required, and the two labellings coincide only
for self-conjugate partitions. No step divides by a group order or uses
averaging, and $n=0$ is included.

derivations.claim: Murphy basis: base change along $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to F$, $v\mapsto1$, sends $T_w$ to $w$ and $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ to the row symmetrizer $\sum_{w\in S_\mu}w$; the structure constants of the Murphy basis are polynomials in $q$, so they specialize to structure constants in $F[S_n]$ and the specialized family $\{m_{st}\}$ satisfies the cellular axioms over $F$; it is a basis because its rank equals $\dim_FF[S_n]$. This is part 1.

Module and form: by [F1] the specialization of the page's Specht module is the ordinary Dipper-James Specht module with the standard polytabloid basis, and the specialized cell form differs from the standard form by the Laurent factor $q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}$, which is $1$ at $q=1$; hence the two forms agree over every field and have the same radical, so the specialized quotient is the James quotient $D^{\lambda}$. This is part 2.

Labels: by [F3], $e=p$ in positive characteristic, and $e$-regular means $p$-regular. Step 2.1 identifies the specialized module and its form exactly with the ordinary group module and form, so the ordinary criterion in [F4] gives precisely the nonzero $p$-regular quotients and the zero form on all other labels, in agreement with [F5]. In characteristic zero, $e=\infty>n$, so the local separated-range proof in [F4] makes the Murphy cell forms nonsingular and the algebra split semisimple. The exact signed-conjugate unit form dictionary [F1] gives the same conclusion for all ordinary Specht modules. Thus all claims follow over the original field, without using the held finite-$e$ Hecke classifier.

boundaries.evidence: The statement is quantified over all lambda of n including the empty partition when n=0; the specialization of the rank-one Hecke algebra is the rank-one group algebra and the empty Specht module transports to the trivial module.
The vanishing range is part 3 of the Statement: rad S^lambda=S^lambda and D^lambda_{q=1}=0 exactly for the non-p-regular labels, while in characteristic 0 no Specht module vanishes.
At q=1 every coefficient q^{l(w)} of step 1.1 becomes 1, and the one-dimensional shapes (n) and (1^n) carry one-dimensional standard Specht modules on both sides of the specialization.

The degenerate characteristic-2 behaviour is covered by part 3 of the Statement, where e=p=2 and the sign dictionary matches the group-side classification; characteristic 0 is the semisimple degenerate in which all Specht modules are irreducible.

boundaries.reason: The specialization value q=1 and the characteristic p of F are the only parameters, with the regimes p>0 and p=0 both stated in the proposition; no interval or limiting value occurs.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 performs a single base change along the fixed map from Z[v^{+-1}], and steps 2.1-3.1 invoke the fixed dictionaries; no family is selected, so no choice principle enters.
The forward reading of part 3 of the Statement: an e-regular partition at q=1 is p-regular, by the identification e=p of the specialized quantum characteristic.
The reverse reading of part 3 of the Statement: a p-regular partition is e-regular at q=1, with D^lambda_{q=1} nonzero exactly on that set by [F4].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{	imes}$, $d,n\ge0$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda(d,n)$ be the set of compositions $\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_d)$ of $n$ (so $\mu_i\in\mathbb N$ and $\sum_i\mu_i=n$). For $\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)$ let $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]) and let $M^{\mu}:=m_\mu H$ be the right ideal it generates, the **(Hecke) permutation module**; $M^{\mu}$ is free over $R$ with basis $\{m_\mu T_{d(t)}:t	ext{ row-standard }\mu	ext{-tableau}\}$ and is the Hecke analogue of the module induced from the trivial representation of the Young subgroup ([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]).

Here is the freeness statement in detail: the cosets $S_\mu d$ with $d\in D_\mu$ partition $S_n$, and $\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ for $u\in S_\mu$, $d\in D_\mu$ ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), so the standard basis theorem ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]) gives $T_uT_{d(t)}=T_{ud(t)}$ and $m_\mu T_{d(t)}=\sum_{u\in S_\mu}T_{u\,d(t)}$; these are the standard basis elements indexed by the single coset $S_\mu d(t)$, and the cosets are disjoint, whence $M^\mu= igoplus_tR\,m_\mu T_{d(t)}$ is free with the displayed basis as $t$ runs over the row-standard $\mu$-tableaux.

Put $M:= igoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ ([[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and define the **q-Schur algebra** $$S(d,n):=\mathrm{End}_H(M),$$ the $R$-algebra of right $H$-module endomorphisms of $M$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]).

**Cellular structure.** For all $\mu,
u\in\Lambda(d,n)$, $\mathrm{Hom}_H(M^{\mu},M^{
u})$ is free with a basis indexed by row-semistandard tableaux; for every partition $\lambda$ of $n$ with at most $d$ parts and all semistandard $\lambda$-tableaux $S,T$ there is an element $\varphi_{ST}\in S(d,n)$ ([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]), and the family $$\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\},$$ where $\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$ is the set of partitions of $n$ with at most $d$ parts ordered by dominance $\unrhd$ ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]), is an $R$-basis of $S(d,n)$; the map $\varphi_{ST}\mapsto\varphi_{TS}$ is an algebra anti-automorphism and the triangular axiom holds modulo the span of the $\varphi_{UV}$ with $\muhd\lambda$. Hence $(\varphi,\Lambda^{+}(d,n))$ is a dominance-cellular basis of $S(d,n)$ ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and its cell modules are the **Weyl modules** $W^{\lambda}$, free over $R$ with basis $\{\varphi_T:T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$. Over a field $F$, $W^{\lambda}$ has nonzero simple head $L^{\lambda}$, the $L^{\lambda}$ for $\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n)$ form a complete set of pairwise non-isomorphic absolutely irreducible $S(d,n)$-modules, and the decomposition matrix satisfies $d_{\lambda\lambda}=1$ and $d_{\lambda\mu}
e0\Rightarrow\lambda\unrhd\mu$.

**Explicit normalization of the semistandard maps.** For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $s$, let $\mu(s)$ replace each entry by the row of that entry in the canonical $\mu$-tableau. For semistandard $S,T$ of respective types $\mu,
u$, put $$m_{ST}:=\sum_{\substack{s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\ \mu(s)=S,\ 
u(t)=T}}m_{st}.$$ The normalized basis map $\varphi_{ST}$ is zero on the other summands and sends $m_
u h\in M^
u$ to $m_{ST}h\in M^\mu$. The intersection $m_{ST}\in M^\mu\cap(M^
u)^*$ makes this well-defined: if $m_

u}.$$ This follows by applying the projection to the displayed free Weyl basis, not by assuming every diagonal cellular element is a projection ([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]).

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$ where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and read in the twist; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. For a class $m\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and any lift $\widetilde m\in M(\lambda')$, the inverse is $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$, independently of the chosen lift.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. With the Murphy cellular
basis $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]],
[[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and the canonical tableau
$t^\lambda$ of shape $\lambda\vdash n$
([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell
module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the
Murphy basis: it is the free $R$-module with basis
$\{m_t:=m_{t^\lambda t}:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ - the classes of the
Murphy elements whose *first* index is the canonical tableau - and $H$ acts by
$m_th=\sum_vr_vm_v$ whenever
$m_{t^\lambda t}h\equiv\sum_vr_vm_{t^\lambda v}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$. (The
cellular action rule transforms the second index and fixes the first, so the
diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone do not span a submodule; the module basis is
the fixed-first-index family above.) Its **cell form** is the unique bilinear
form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\times
S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\to R$ with
$$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\langle m_s,m_t\rangle_\lambda\,m_{uv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$; it is symmetric and associative and
$\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a submodule, so
$D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}:=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
is a right $H$-module
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

**Convention (Dipper-James signed cellular normalization).** Let $\theta:H\to H$
be the involutive algebra automorphism defined by
$\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). For a right module $M$,
write $M^\theta$ for the same $R$-module with action $x\cdot h=x\theta(h)$. The
page's ordinary Specht normalization is the signed conjugate Murphy
construction
$$S^{\lambda}:=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta,$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Its form is the form of
$S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ on the same underlying module; because $\theta$
commutes with $*$ this is associative for the twisted action
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Over a field put
$$D^{\lambda}:=S^{\lambda}/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}S^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta.$$
Thus $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(S^{\lambda})^\theta$ and
$D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(D^{\lambda})^\theta$; conjugation alone does not
identify these modules
([[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]],
[[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]). At
$q=1$, $\theta(\sigma)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma$, so these identities
contain tensoring with sign; in characteristic $2$ the sign twist becomes
trivial at $q=1$
([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).

by [[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]:
that theorem proves the nonzero Murphy quotient criterion in $e$-restricted
labels, and conjugation makes these precisely $e$-regular labels
([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]). No generic root-of-unity
Hecke claim is inferred from the published prime-characteristic group-only sign
dictionary, and no semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed.

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let
$e=e(F,q)\in\{2,3,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ be the quantum characteristic
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) and let
$H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for $n\ge0$. For $\lambda\vdash n$ let $S^{\lambda}$ be the
Hecke Specht module and $D^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}$ its
cell-form quotient ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]). Then:

1. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is $e$-regular
   ([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]);
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\vdash n\text{ is }e\text{-regular}\}$ is a complete
   set of pairwise non-isomorphic absolutely irreducible $H$-modules;
3. $H$ is split semisimple if and only if $e>n$ (including $e=\infty$); when
   $e\le n$ the algebra has nonzero radical.

This is the exact root-of-unity replacement for the ordinary Specht
classification. At $q=1$ in characteristic $p>0$ it specialises to the
classification of the simple $F[S_n]$-modules by $p$-regular partitions
([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]). No
semisimplicity is assumed and no choice principle is used.

Let $e\in\{2,3,4,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition
with parts $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Then $\lambda$ is
**$e$-regular** when every positive integer occurs as a part of $\lambda$ fewer
than $e$ times, i.e. $z_j(\lambda)<e$ for every $j\ge1$, and **$e$-restricted**
when $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ for every $i\ge1$ (with $\lambda_i:=0$ for
$i>\ell(\lambda)$).

For finite $e$ these are exactly the $p$-regular and $p$-restricted notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $p=e$. For $e=\infty$ both
conditions are vacuous, so every partition is both $e$-regular and
$e$-restricted: the inequalities $z_j(\lambda)<\infty$ and
$\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<\infty$ hold because partitions have finitely many
nonzero parts and each difference is a nonnegative integer. Moreover $\lambda$
is $e$-restricted if and only if its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular: the
multiplicity of the part $i$ in $\lambda'$ is the number of columns of
$[\lambda]$ of height exactly $i$, namely $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$, so the
two conditions $z_i(\lambda')=\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ are the same family
of inequalities, and for $e=\infty$ both sides hold. In particular
$\varnothing$ is simultaneously $e$-regular and $e$-restricted for every $e$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]).

derivations.claim: Under [F1], $\rho(h)\rho(k)=\rho(hk)$ because both act on $H$ by left multiplication, so the identification uses $H$, without an opposite algebra. The functor $X\mapsto Xe$ is exact: for a short exact sequence, a lift $x$ of an element $y\in X''e$ yields the lift $xe$, and an element in the kernel lies in $X'$ and is fixed by $e$, hence lies in $X'e$. The tensor description uses the $(S,eSe)$-bimodule $Se$, which is a direct summand as a left $S$-module.

The support in [F2] gives $e\varphi_{ST}e=\delta_{\operatorname{type}(S),\omega}\delta_{\operatorname{type}(T),\omega}\varphi_{ST}$ and $w_Te=\delta_{\operatorname{type}(T),\omega}w_T$. Semistandard tableaux of type $\omega$ have each label once and are exactly standard tableaux. For standard $s,t$, their defining sum $m_{st}$ has one term, so $\varphi_{st}|_H(a)=m_{st}a$ and $\rho^{-1}(\varphi_{st})=m_{st}$. Thus the higher Schur ideal cuts out exactly $I^{\rhd\lambda}$ in the corner. Read the Schur right-cell law with first index any standard tableau of type $\omega$; coefficient independence permits this choice. Restricting the multiplication by $\rho(h)$ to $H$ gives $m_{st}h$, so its coefficients are the Murphy right-cell coefficients. Consequently $\Psi_\lambda:W^\lambda e\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, $w_t\mapsto c_t$, is an $H$-isomorphism.

By the Schur cell product, $\varphi_{as}\varphi_{tb}\equiv B_\lambda(w_s,w_t)\varphi_{ab}$ modulo higher Schur shapes, with coefficient independent of the outer indices. Choose all four indices standard of shape $\lambda$ and type $\omega$. They lie in $eSe$; applying $\rho^{-1}$, or evaluating their endomorphisms at $1\in H$, gives $m_{as}m_{tb}\equiv B_\lambda(w_s,w_t)m_{ab}$ modulo $I^{\rhd\lambda}$. The unique coefficient in [F3] is $G_\lambda(c_s,c_t)$, proving $B_\lambda|_{W^\lambda e}=\Psi_\lambda^*G_\lambda$ exactly, with factor $1$.

Since $e^*=e$, contravariance gives $B_\lambda(xe,y(1-e))=B_\lambda(x,y(1-e)e)=0$. The decomposition $W^\lambda=W^\lambda e\oplus W^\lambda(1-e)$ is therefore orthogonal. A vector in $W^\lambda e$ pairs trivially with its complement, so it is in the restricted form radical exactly when it lies in $\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}W^\lambda$. Since the latter is an $S$-submodule, $\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}(W^\lambda e)=(\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}W^\lambda)e$. This holds even if the corner form is identically zero.

For the canonical semistandard tableau $T^\lambda$ of shape and type $\lambda$, the map $\varphi_{T^\lambda,T^\lambda}$ is the actual projection onto $M^\lambda$: it sends $m_\lambda h$ to itself and is zero on every other summand. Its square equals itself, so the Schur cell product gives $B_\lambda(w_{T^\lambda},w_{T^\lambda})=1$. Hence the Weyl form quotient is nonzero and is its simple head $L^\lambda$ by [F4]. Exactness, step 4.1 and step 3.1 give $L^\lambda e\cong W^\lambda e/(\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}W^\lambda)e\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)/\operatorname{rad}_{\mathrm{form}}C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)=D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, including when this corner quotient is zero.

By [F6] and step 5.1, $L^\lambda e

u$ gives $D_{\mathrm M}(

u]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):D_{\mathrm M}(
u)]$ for each $e_q$-restricted $

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, and let
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ be the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements
([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]). For every $\lambda\vdash n$,
every standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ and every $1\le k\le n$ there exist
$a_v\in R$ with
$$m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_v\,m_v,$$
where $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ is the Murphy basis of the Murphy cell
module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) and the sum is over standard
$\lambda$-tableaux $v$ strictly dominating $t$ in the dominance order on
tableaux ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). In particular $L_k$ acts on
the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with Murphy basis $(m_t)$ by a
triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are the q-content values.
Consequently the $L_k$ commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ is central in $H$.

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ an invertible element. The **quantum
characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that
$1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists
([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1\ne0$, the least positive
integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so
the two formulations coincide.

Concretely: (i) if $q\ne1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$ — indeed
$(q-1)(1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1})=q^m-1$ and $q-1\ne0$ — so $[e]_q=0$ is equivalent
to $q^e=1$, and a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and
then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{\times}$ (which is $\ge2$
because $q\ne1$); (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$
when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ (the characteristic is a prime, hence at least
$2$, and $m\cdot1_F\ne0$ for $1\le m<p$) and $e=\infty$ when
$\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

If $e<\infty$ then $q\ne1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for
every integer $m$: for $m\ge0$ the sum splits as
$$[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q,$$
so $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ whenever $[e]_q=0$; for the remaining $m<0$ one extends the
closed formula by $[m]_q:=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ when $q\ne1$ and reads $[m]_1:=m\in F$
for the canonical image of the integer $m$ when $q=1$, in which case
$e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ and $[m+e]_1=m+e=m$ in $F$. In particular the
quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter
governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice
principle is used.

derivations.claim: Reconstruct a tableau from its residue tuple. At a prefix of size $k-1$, two different addable corners have integer content difference of absolute value at most $k$. Since $[a]_q-[b]_q=q^b[a-b]_q$ and $e>n$, their q-contents differ. Starting with the empty diagram, the tuple thus recovers each added node and the final shape. For two tableaux of a fixed shape with identical entries' residues outside $i,i+1$, first reconstruct the common prefix through $i-1$, and reconstruct the common suffix by successively deleting the unique appropriate removable corner from the fixed final shape. The intervening skew diagram has two boxes; its only possible orders are the original order and its swap. This proves both separation assertions.

Diagonalize the commuting JM operators on a cell. Their triangular basis gives a filtration with one-dimensional joint characters indexed by standard tableaux. Those characters are distinct by step 1.1. For commuting triangular operators, the simultaneous generalized eigenspaces split along their distinct joint characters: the corresponding maximal ideals of the polynomial algebra are pairwise comaximal. Each joint character occurs once in this cell, so each generalized eigenspace is one-dimensional and hence an actual joint eigenline. This finite Chinese-remainder argument works over any field and needs no choice of a generic scalar or algebraic closure. The Lagrange product of the Statement is $1$ on its target tuple and $0$ on every other tuple. Applied to $m_t$, its triangular diagonal coefficient is $1$, and the other possible terms are strictly more dominant. Thus it gives the asserted $f_t$.

Compute the diagonal coefficient using the **correctly ordered** JM relation $$T_iL_i=L_{i+1}T_i-(q-1)L_{i+1}-1.$$ For $k\ne i,i+1$, $T_i$ commutes with $L_k$. Consequently separation restricts $f_sT_i$ to the span of $f_s$ and $f_t$ if the swap is standard, or to $f_s$ alone otherwise. Write its coefficient of $f_s$ as $c_s$. The displayed relation gives $$c_s\bigl([\operatorname{content}_s(i)]_q-              [\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)]_q\bigr)    =-(q-1)[\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)]_q-1.$$ Its denominator is $q^{\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)}[\rho]_q$, while the numerator is $-q^{\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)}$, so $c_s=-1/[\rho]_q$. This does not claim that $T_i$ commutes with $L_i$.

At this stage step 2.1 establishes the projector identities on each individual cell module. The global identities in $H$ will follow below after proving that the sum of the cell modules is faithful. No finite-$e$ classification is a premise.

The transition from $m_t$ to $f_t$ is unitriangular, so these vectors form a basis. For $s\ne t$, choose $k$ at which their q-contents differ. Self-adjointness $L_k^*=L_k$ and associativity give $$([\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q-    [\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q)\langle f_s,f_t\rangle=0.$$ The scalar is nonzero, proving orthogonality. The Lagrange action also gives $f_tF_s=\delta_{ts}f_t$.

If the swap is not standard, the consecutive entries lie adjacently in one row or one column. Then $\rho=-1$ or $\rho=1$, respectively, and step 2.2 gives $c_s=q$ or $c_s=-1$. These are the stated row and column cases; the row action is $q$, not the scalar $1$ at a general parameter.

Suppose the swap is standard. In the branch $s\rhd t$, the length-additive Murphy action has leading term $m_sT_i=m_t$; the unitriangular eigenbasis change then gives the off-diagonal coefficient $\alpha_i(s)=1$. Higher-dominance terms cannot alter the coefficient at $t$ in this two-dimensional eigenline span. This is the leading-term argument in the full proof of Mathas Theorem 3.34. In both branches the quadratic relation gives $$\alpha_i(s)\alpha_i(t)=q+(q-1)c_s-c_s^2  =\frac{[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q}{[\rho]_q[-\rho]_q}.$$ The last equality follows directly from $[-\rho]_q=-q^{-\rho}[\rho]_q$ and the quantum-integer addition identities. Thus the opposite branch has exactly the displayed coefficient. This proves the generator formula without accepting the inconsistent branch in the 1998 manuscript.

Prove nondegeneracy in the separated range locally. The canonical Murphy basis vector has form value $[\lambda]!_q=\prod_a[\lambda_a]!_q$, because $x_\lambda^2=[\lambda]!_qx_\lambda$; its seminormal image has the same value since the canonical tableau is dominance-maximal. This scalar is nonzero when $e>n$. If $s\rhd t=s(i,i+1)$ is a standard swap, put $a=1/[\rho]_q$. Step 4.1 gives $f_t=f_s(T_i+a)$. Associativity, orthogonality and the quadratic relation give $\langle f_t,f_t\rangle=(q+a)(1-a)\langle f_s,f_s\rangle=q[\rho+1]_q[\rho-1]_q[\rho]_q^{-2}\langle f_s,f_s\rangle$. Indeed expansion of $(T_i+a)^2$ and its $f_s$ coefficient $-a$ gives $q-a(q-1)-a^2=(q+a)(1-a)$. The swapped incomparable boxes have $2\le|\rho|\le n-1$: their row and column separations plus one are at most the size of the diagram. Thus all three quantum integers here are nonzero. Every standard tableau is connected to the canonical one by length-increasing swaps of adjacent incomparable entries: bubble-sort its linear extension of the box-order poset into the canonical row-order extension, then reverse the swaps. Induction gives nonzero diagonal norm at every $f_t$, so each cell form is nonsingular.

Each cell is now its nonzero simple form quotient, absolutely simple, and all these cells are pairwise distinct and exhaust the simple modules by [[thm-nonzero-cell-heads-classify-the-simple-modules-of-a-cellular-algebra]]. Thus the split semisimple quotient $H/J(H)$ has dimension $\sum_\lambda |\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|^2$. This equals $\dim H$ because the Murphy cellular basis has exactly one element for each pair of standard tableaux of the same shape ([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]]). Hence $J(H)=0$, $H$ is split semisimple, and the direct sum of all its simple cell modules is faithful. On that faithful module the global Lagrange products of the Statement are the orthogonal projectors from step 2.1, with different shapes having disjoint tuples by step 1.1. Therefore $F_sF_t=\delta_{st}F_t$ holds in $H$ itself, proving the global idempotents. This argument proves only the separated range and does not assert a finite-$e$ nonzero-label criterion when $e\le n$.

Steps 1.1-6.1 prove all four claims. No semisimplicity was imposed as a hypothesis: it was derived locally from nondegenerate cells and their complete finite-cell classification. The calculation concerns the intrinsic Murphy cell and keeps the signed ordinary-module dictionary separate. All products and basis changes are finite, and no choice principle is used.

boundaries.evidence: For a shape with a single standard tableau, and for n=0, part 1 of the Statement is vacuous and the product defining F_t is empty, giving F_t=1 and f_t=m_t in the seminormal construction.
The denominators of F_t are nonzero exactly by part 1 (step 1.1), and part 4's term -1/[rho]_q is legitimate because |rho|<=n-1<e; step 5.1 records that no semisimplicity is assumed.
The projector f_t=m_t+sum over s strictly dominating t of a_s m_s has the single leading term m_t, and step 4.1 computes the generator action for t=s(i i+1) directly.
Degenerate residue collisions are excluded by the hypothesis e>n: step 1.1 shows distinct same-residue nodes share neither a row nor a column and distinct removable nodes have distinct residues.

Let $R$ be an integral domain, $q\in R^\times$, $d,n\ge1$, and let $W^\lambda$ be the Weyl module of $S(d,n)$ for a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts. For a composition $\mu$ of $n$ of length $d$, let $G^\lambda_\mu$ be the Gram determinant of its $\mu$-weight space in the semistandard basis ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Put $\beta_j=\lambda'_j+n-j$ and $h_{ab}=\lambda_a-b+\lambda'_b-a+1$. Then $$G^\lambda_\mu=q^N\prod_{\substack{(a,b),(a,c)\in[\lambda]\\b<c}}  \left(\frac{[h_{ab}]_q}{[h_{ac}]_q}\right)^{  d_\mu(\beta+h_{ac}\mathbf e_b-h_{ac}\mathbf e_c)},$$ where $N=\sum_{T\in T_0(\lambda,\mu)}\ell(d(\operatorname{last}(T)))$. Here $\operatorname{last}(T)$ is the least-dominant standardization in the fiber of $T$, and $d_\mu$ is the exact alternating semistandard number of [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. **Both beta shifts use the same removed hook length $h_{ac}$.**

The exponent is the sorting sign times $|T_0(\eta,\mu)|$ if that balanced beta sequence has distinct nonnegative entries and recovers $\eta$; it is zero otherwise. Equivalently, remove the rim strip $R_{ac}$ and rewrap its $h_{ac}$ boxes with lowest node in column $b$. The sign is the parity of the heights of the removed strip and the newly added strip, the latter measured in the new diagram $\eta$; it is not generally the sum of two old $\lambda$ hook legs ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]], [[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]).

Form the product first in the universal field $\mathbb Q(Q)$. It equals a Laurent polynomial in $\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$, namely the universal integral Gram determinant divided by its displayed unit $Q^N$. Over $R$ the formula means the specialization of that Laurent polynomial. It does not require inverting a vanishing hook number or evaluating $0/0$. All weights and $d<n$ are retained; an empty weight space has determinant $1$.

In the setting of [[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]] ($R$ a PID,
$\pi$ a prime element, $F=R/\pi R$, $M$ free of finite rank with a form whose
extension to $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ is non-degenerate), let $\nu_\pi$ be
the $\pi$-adic valuation normalised by $\nu_\pi(\pi)=1$ and let
$G\in R\setminus\{0\}$ be the Gram determinant of the form with respect to any
$R$-basis of $M$. Then
$$\nu_\pi(G)=\sum_{i>0}\dim_FM_F(i),$$
where $M_F(i)$ are the Jantzen layers of
[[def-jantzen-filtration-of-a-lifted-cell-module]]; in particular the sum is
finite and independent of the chosen basis.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, so
that rows are numbered downward and columns rightward, and let
$\nu\subseteq\lambda$ be a subpartition, so that the skew diagram
$[\lambda/\nu]=[\lambda]\setminus[\nu]$ is the set of nodes of $[\lambda]$
outside $[\nu]$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Two nodes are
side-adjacent when their coordinates differ by exactly one in exactly one
coordinate.

A **removable border strip** of $\lambda$ (also called a **skew hook** or
**rim hook**) is a nonempty set $\xi$ of nodes of $[\lambda]$ such that

(i) $\xi$ is **edge-connected**: any two nodes of $\xi$ are joined by a chain
of side-adjacent nodes of $\xi$;

(ii) $\xi$ contains **no $2\times2$ block**: there are no nodes
$(i,j),(i+1,j),(i,j+1),(i+1,j+1)$ all belonging to $\xi$;

(iii) $[\lambda]\setminus\xi$ is again the Young diagram of a partition, say
$[\lambda]\setminus\xi=[\nu]$ for a partition $\nu\vdash n-|\xi|$.

Equivalently, a removable border strip is a skew diagram $\lambda/\nu$ that is
connected and contains no $2\times2$ block; since the complement of
$[\lambda/\nu]$ in $[\lambda]$ is $[\nu]$, condition (iii) is then automatic,
and (i) and (ii) say exactly that the skew diagram is connected and free of
$2\times2$ blocks. We write $\xi=\lambda/\nu$ in that case. The **size** of
$\xi$ is its number of nodes $|\xi|$; a removable border strip of size $r$ is a
**removable $r$-strip**, and then $\nu\vdash n-r$.

The **height** (also **leg length**) of a nonempty connected border strip
$\xi$ is
$$\operatorname{ht}(\xi):=(\text{number of distinct rows of }[\lambda]\text{ occupied by }\xi)-1.$$

**The counting identity.** If a removable border strip $\xi$ has $r$ nodes and
occupies $c$ distinct columns and $w$ distinct rows of $[\lambda]$, then
$w=r-c+1$, hence $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=r-c\ge0$. Indeed $[\lambda/\nu]$ is a
connected skew diagram with complement a Young diagram, so all its nodes lie
on the rim of $[\lambda]$, the set of nodes $(p,q)$ with
$(p+1,q+1)\notin[\lambda]$, and form a path that moves only downward or
rightward: each node after the first is reached from its predecessor by one
downward step or one rightward step. The $r-1$ steps consist of $w-1$ downward
steps and $c-1$ rightward steps, since the path visits exactly the $w$
occupied rows and exactly the $c$ occupied columns, whence
$r-1=(w-1)+(c-1)$.

In particular $\operatorname{ht}(\xi)=0$ exactly when $\xi$ is a horizontal
strip, that is, occupies at most one node in each column, and in general
$c=r-\operatorname{ht}(\xi)$ is the number of columns occupied. A removable
border strip of size $1$ is exactly a removable node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]): a single node is
edge-connected and contains no $2\times2$ block, and its removal leaves a Young
diagram precisely when the node is removable. No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and $x=(i,j)\in[\lambda]$. Let $H(x)$ be the hook of $x$,
with arm length $a(x)=\lambda_i-j$, leg length $\ell(x)=\lambda'_j-i$ and hook
length $h(x)=a(x)+\ell(x)+1$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); its two endpoints are the last node
$(i,\lambda_i)$ of its arm and the last node $(\lambda'_j,j)$ of its leg. Let
$\xi(x)$ be the unique edge-connected set of nodes of $[\lambda]$ with
endpoints $(i,\lambda_i)$ and $(\lambda'_j,j)$ that lies in the rim of
$[\lambda]$, i.e. consists of nodes $(p,q)$ with $(p+1,q+1)\notin[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]]). Then:

1. $\xi(x)$ is a removable border strip of $\lambda$ of size $h(x)$ and height
   $\ell(x)$ ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]), and
   $[\lambda]\setminus\xi(x)$ is a Young diagram, so $\lambda\setminus\xi(x)$ is
   a partition of $n-h(x)$;
2. every removable border strip of $\lambda$ equals $\xi(x)$ for exactly one
   node $x\in[\lambda]$; hence $x\mapsto\xi(x)$ is a bijection from the nodes
   of $[\lambda]$ onto the removable border strips of $\lambda$.

Consequently the sizes of the removable border strips of $\lambda$ are exactly
the hook lengths of $\lambda$, the height of $\xi(x)$ is the leg length
$\ell(x)$, and $x$ is removable as a node
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]) if and only if $\xi(x)$
has size $1$. No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$ with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let $\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]] for the underlying Murphy elements and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard basis along which this basis is defined). Put $\omega:=(1^n)\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the composition with $n$ parts equal to $1$ (legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial and $m_\omega=1$; hence $$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$ is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard $\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down the column. Set $$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra isomorphism $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$ left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$ sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$ (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above. 2. The **Schur functor** is $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$ with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms: as a **left** $S$-module, $Se$ is the image of the left-$S$-linear projection $s\mapsto se$ on $S$, hence is a direct summand of the regular left module and is projective. Tensoring right $S$-modules with this left module is therefore exact. Equivalently, for a short exact sequence of right modules, an element $ye$ in the target lifts to $xe$ from any lift $x$ of $y$; kernels and injections are likewise preserved by the same idempotent projection. The bimodule corner action makes these maps right $H$-linear. The convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

Set $e_q=e(k,q)$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). Work on a fixed weight space of the lifted free Weyl module. Every hook quantum integer is nonzero because its index is at most $n$ and $[n]!_{\hat q}
e0$ in the domain. The balanced Gram formula [F1] gives its determinant, and the unit power of $\hat q$ has valuation zero. The Jantzen Gram-valuation lemma [F2] thus gives the sum of positive filtration-submodule dimensions as $$\sum_{(a,b),(a,c),\ b<c}  (
u_\pi([h_{ab}]_{\hat q})-
u_\pi([h_{ac}]_{\hat q}))  d_\mu( eta+h_{ac}\mathbf e_b-h_{ac}\mathbf e_c).$$ The signed number is exactly the weight dimension of the corresponding balanced virtual Weyl symbol, including zero and cutoff cases.

Apply step 1.1 to every weight. The Weyl weight-character matrix is unitriangular, so [F3] detects equality of Grothendieck classes and proves part 1. These are classes of the filtration submodules $W_F^\lambda(i)$, not their successive quotients and not simply the radical class.

Establish filtration transport before applying the exact functor. On the lifted Weyl module $W$, the identity $e^*=e$ makes $We\perp W(1-e)$. For $x\in We$ and every $i\ge0$, pairing $x$ with all of $W$ is divisible by $\pi^i$ exactly when its pairing with $We$ is. Thus $W(i)e=(We)(i)$. Reducing modulo $\pi$ commutes with the direct summand projection, giving $W_F(i)e=(We)_F(i)$. The actual corner isomorphism and factor-$1$ form identity [F5] identify the latter with the Murphy Specht filtration. Applying the exact functor to the proved Weyl-class identity therefore transports each submodule and every signed term, proving part 2 even when a reduced cell form is identically zero. For the ordinary convention, apply the same $\theta$ to both modules and conjugate the labels; the independently proved Laurent-unit form factor preserves these divisibility filtrations as well.

Explain the valid multiplicity information. The Weyl form has nonzero simple head, $W_F(1)=\operatorname{rad}W_F$, and $W_F(i)\subseteq\operatorname{rad}W_F$ for $i>0$. Consequently for $\nu\ne\lambda$ its actual multiplicity in $W_F$ is its radical multiplicity, bounded above by its multiplicity in the whole positive sum. This whole-sum multiplicity is positive if and only if that factor occurs in the radical, since the first submodule is the radical and later ones lie inside it. No such conclusion is drawn from an individual positive or negative Weyl coefficient before cancellation. All claims follow from steps 1.1-3.1 and this submodule inclusion.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For $1\le k\le n$ define
$$L_1:=0,\qquad L_k:=q^{-1}T_{(k-1,k)}+q^{-2}T_{(k-2,k)}+\cdots+q^{1-k}T_{(1,k)}\in H\quad(k\ge2),$$
where $T_{(i,k)}$ is the standard basis element indexed by the transposition
$(i\ k)$ ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). The $L_k$
are the **Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements**. They are fixed by the star
anti-automorphism $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$
([[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]): each
transposition $(i\ k)$ is its own inverse, so $T_{(i,k)}^*=T_{(i,k)}$, and the
coefficients $q^{i-k}$ are central, whence
$L_k^*=\sum_{i<k}q^{i-k}T_{(i,k)}=L_k$. They commute pairwise and every
symmetric polynomial in $L_1,\dots,L_n$ with coefficients in $R$ is central in
$H$ ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]).

**q-contents.** The quantum integers $[m]_q$ for $m\ge0$ are those of
[[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]; extend the definition to
negative indices by $[-m]_q:=-q^{-m}[m]_q$ for $m>0$, so that
$[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$ when $q\ne1$ — indeed for $m=-r<0$
one has $-q^{-r}(q^r-1)/(q-1)=(q^{-r}-1)/(q-1)$ — and $[m]_1=m$ for all
$m\in\mathbb Z$, since $[-r]_1=-[r]_1=-r$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$
and $1\le k\le n$ let $\operatorname{content}_t(k)=c-r$ be the content of the
node carrying $k$ ([[def-content-vector-of-a-standard-tableau]]) and define the
**q-content value** $[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$. If $e=e(F,q)<\infty$ for
a field $F$ then $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for every $m\in\mathbb Z$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), so the
q-content value depends only on the residue of the content modulo $e$. At $q=1$
the identification $H_{R,1}(S_n)\cong R[S_n]$ with $T_w\mapsto w$ — the
$R$-linear base change of the specialization isomorphism of
[[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]
— sends $L_k$ to the ordinary Jucys-Murphy element
$X_k=\sum_{j<k}(j\ k)$
([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]), because each
coefficient $q^{j-k}$ specializes to $1$, and
$[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_1=\operatorname{content}_t(k)$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, and let
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ be the Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements
([[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]]). For every $\lambda\vdash n$,
every standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ and every $1\le k\le n$ there exist
$a_v\in R$ with
$$m_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q\,m_t+\sum_{v\rhd t}a_v\,m_v,$$
where $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ is the Murphy basis of the Murphy cell
module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) and the sum is over standard
$\lambda$-tableaux $v$ strictly dominating $t$ in the dominance order on
tableaux ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). In particular $L_k$ acts on
the Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ with Murphy basis $(m_t)$ by a
triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are the q-content values.
Consequently the $L_k$ commute pairwise and every symmetric polynomial in
$L_1,\dots,L_n$ is central in $H$.

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ an invertible element. The **quantum
characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that
$1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists
([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1\ne0$, the least positive
integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so
the two formulations coincide.

Concretely: (i) if $q\ne1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$ — indeed
$(q-1)(1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1})=q^m-1$ and $q-1\ne0$ — so $[e]_q=0$ is equivalent
to $q^e=1$, and a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and
then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{\times}$ (which is $\ge2$
because $q\ne1$); (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$
when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ (the characteristic is a prime, hence at least
$2$, and $m\cdot1_F\ne0$ for $1\le m<p$) and $e=\infty$ when
$\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

If $e<\infty$ then $q\ne1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for
every integer $m$: for $m\ge0$ the sum splits as
$$[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q,$$
so $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ whenever $[e]_q=0$; for the remaining $m<0$ one extends the
closed formula by $[m]_q:=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ when $q\ne1$ and reads $[m]_1:=m\in F$
for the canonical image of the integer $m$ when $q=1$, in which case
$e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ and $[m+e]_1=m+e=m$ in $F$. In particular the
quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter
governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice
principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{\times}$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). For $1\le k\le n$ define
$$L_1:=0,\qquad L_k:=q^{-1}T_{(k-1,k)}+q^{-2}T_{(k-2,k)}+\cdots+q^{1-k}T_{(1,k)}\in H\quad(k\ge2),$$
where $T_{(i,k)}$ is the standard basis element indexed by the transposition
$(i\ k)$ ([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). The $L_k$
are the **Hecke Jucys-Murphy elements**. They are fixed by the star
anti-automorphism $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$
([[lem-the-star-antiautomorphism-of-the-type-a-hecke-algebra]]): each
transposition $(i\ k)$ is its own inverse, so $T_{(i,k)}^*=T_{(i,k)}$, and the
coefficients $q^{i-k}$ are central, whence
$L_k^*=\sum_{i<k}q^{i-k}T_{(i,k)}=L_k$. They commute pairwise and every
symmetric polynomial in $L_1,\dots,L_n$ with coefficients in $R$ is central in
$H$ ([[thm-hecke-jucys-murphy-action-is-dominance-triangular]]).

**q-contents.** The quantum integers $[m]_q$ for $m\ge0$ are those of
[[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]; extend the definition to
negative indices by $[-m]_q:=-q^{-m}[m]_q$ for $m>0$, so that
$[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\in\mathbb Z$ when $q\ne1$ — indeed for $m=-r<0$
one has $-q^{-r}(q^r-1)/(q-1)=(q^{-r}-1)/(q-1)$ — and $[m]_1=m$ for all
$m\in\mathbb Z$, since $[-r]_1=-[r]_1=-r$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$
and $1\le k\le n$ let $\operatorname{content}_t(k)=c-r$ be the content of the
node carrying $k$ ([[def-content-vector-of-a-standard-tableau]]) and define the
**q-content value** $[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$. If $e=e(F,q)<\infty$ for
a field $F$ then $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for every $m\in\mathbb Z$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), so the
q-content value depends only on the residue of the content modulo $e$. At $q=1$
the identification $H_{R,1}(S_n)\cong R[S_n]$ with $T_w\mapsto w$ — the
$R$-linear base change of the specialization isomorphism of
[[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]
— sends $L_k$ to the ordinary Jucys-Murphy element
$X_k=\sum_{j<k}(j\ k)$
([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]), because each
coefficient $q^{j-k}$ specializes to $1$, and
$[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_1=\operatorname{content}_t(k)$.

Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^{\times}$, let $e=e(F,q)$ and assume $e>n$ (with $e=\infty$ allowed); let $\lambda\vdash n$, $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$, and let $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ be the Murphy cell module with Murphy basis $(m_t)_{t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

1. (**Separation**) If $s,t$ are standard $\lambda$-tableaux with $[\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q$ for all $1\le k\le n$ then $s=t$. More precisely, if the q-content values agree for all $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$ for some $i$, then $s=t$ or $t=s(i\ i+1)$. 2. (**Idempotents**) Let $\mathcal R_k$ be the set of distinct q-content values of the entry $k$ over standard tableaux of **all** partitions of $n$. For a standard $\lambda$-tableau $t$ define $$F_t:=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\ \prod_{\substack{c\in\mathcal R_k\\        c\ne[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q}}        \frac{L_k-c}{[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q-c}\in F[L_1,\ldots,L_n].$$ These are orthogonal idempotents of $H$; their actions on $S_{\mathrm M}^\lambda$ project onto the corresponding simultaneous eigenlines. Put $f_t=m_tF_t$. Then $f_tL_k=[\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_qf_t$ and $f_t=m_t+\sum_{s\rhd t}a_sm_s$. The global content sets are essential for the asserted idempotency in $H$, rather than only the induced same-shape endomorphisms. 3. (**Orthogonal seminormal basis**) $\{f_t:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is a basis of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ satisfying $f_tF_s=\delta_{ts}f_t$ and $\langle f_s,f_t\rangle_\lambda=\delta_{st}\langle f_t,f_t\rangle_\lambda$; it is the **seminormal basis** of the Murphy cell module. 4. (**Generator action**) Let $s$ be a standard $\lambda$-tableau, $1\le i<n$ and $t:=s(i\ i+1)$, and put $\rho:=\operatorname{content}_s(i)-\operatorname{content}_s(i+1)\in\mathbb Z$. If $i$ and $i+1$ lie in the same row of $s$ then $f_sT_i=q\,f_s$; if they lie in the same column then $f_sT_i=-f_s$; otherwise $t$ is standard and $$f_sT_i=\alpha_i(s)\,f_t-\frac{1}{[\rho]_q}f_s,\qquad \alpha_i(s):=\begin{cases}1,&s\rhd t,\\[1mm]\dfrac{[1+\rho]_q[1-\rho]_q}{[\rho]_q[-\rho]_q},&t\rhd s,\end{cases}$$ where $[-\rho]_q$ is the extended quantum integer of [[def-hecke-jucys-murphy-elements-and-q-contents]] and for the swapped tableau $\operatorname{content}_t(i)-\operatorname{content}_t(i+1)=-\rho$. No semisimplicity of $H$ is assumed and no choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Contents of the two tableaux: for $s$ with rows $(1,2)$ and $(3)$ the nodes are $(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)$ for $1,2,3$, giving contents $0,1,-1$; for $t$ with rows $(1,3)$ and $(2)$ the nodes are $(1,1),(2,1),(1,2)$ for $1,2,3$, giving contents $0,-1,1$.

Collision: by [F1] and [F2], $[2]_{-1}=0$ and $[1]_{-1}=[-1]_{-1}=1$; hence $[\operatorname{content}_s(1)]_{q}=0=[\operatorname{content}_t(1)]_q$, $[\operatorname{content}_s(2)]_q=1=[\operatorname{content}_t(2)]_q$ and $[\operatorname{content}_s(3)]_q=1=[\operatorname{content}_t(3)]_q$, so the two q-content sequences coincide even though $s\ne t$.

Interpolation and axial distance. The eigenvalue difference that would be needed to distinguish $s$ and $t$ at $k=2$ is $1-1=0$. Equal-value exclusion in a polynomial product does not make its literal denominators zero; it instead loses the factor that could distinguish these tuples. No polynomial in the JM operators can provide the two distinct joint-eigenvalue labels used in the separated-range construction. For the swap of $2$ and $3$, $\rho=1-(-1)=2$ and $[2]_{-1}=0$, so the displayed separated-range generator formula is undefined here.

Verify the failure of a JM-eigenbasis on this cell directly. Put $m_s=1+T_1$ and $m_t=(1+T_1)T_2$ modulo the higher row-shape ideal. The quadratic relation gives $m_sT_1=q m_s$. The higher row symmetrizer is $1+T_1+T_2+T_1T_2+T_2T_1+T_1T_2T_1$, so its vanishing in this cell gives $m_tT_1=-m_s-m_t$. At $q=-1$, since $L_2=q^{-1}T_1=-T_1$, it follows that $m_sL_2=m_s$ and $m_tL_2=m_s+m_t$. Thus $L_2-I$ is nonzero and $(L_2-I)^2=0$ on this two-dimensional cell. It is not diagonalizable over $\mathbb C$, so a simultaneous JM-eigenbasis cannot exist on this cell. Together with step 2.1 this supplies the claimed concrete boundary counterexample, without making a universal claim about all cells outside the separated range.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement refuted carries concrete nonempty data, the two distinct standard tableaux s and t of shape (2,1); the failure is a collision of their two full q-content sequences, and no empty-family case is involved in the witness.
Step 2.1 exhibits [2]_{-1}=0 and step 3.1 uses the vanishing interpolation denominator 1-1=0, the precise mechanism by which the separation hypothesis of the theorem fails at e=2.
Step 2.1 computes the unit values [1]_{-1}=[-1]_{-1}=1, and step 3.1 uses the axial distance rho=2 between the swapped entries, whose quantum integer [2]_{-1}=0 makes the projector F_t undefined.

The degenerate range e<=n is exactly the point of the Statement refuted: at e=2 and n=3 the distinct tableaux are not separated by their q-content sequences and the interpolation denominators of the theorem's spectral projectors vanish.
