u'_i+L-i\qquad(1\le i\le L).$$ Its beta numbers are strictly decreasing nonnegative integers. Conversely, from any strictly decreasing nonnegative sequence $b$ recover the unique partition with conjugate parts $
u'_i=b_i-L+i$, of degree $|
u|=\sum_i b_i-L(L-1)/2$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

For arbitrary $b\in\mathbb Z^L$, first set all its alternating symbols to zero if it has repeated entries or a negative entry. Otherwise there is a unique sorting permutation $w$ taking it to decreasing order; let $
u$ be the recovered partition and let $\epsilon(b)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}$. Uniqueness of the sorting permutation is claimed only in this distinct-entry case. In the fixed degree-$r$ Grothendieck groups define $$[W^b]_{d,r}:= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)[W^
u],&|
u|=r	ext{ and } \ell(
u)\le d,\0,&	ext{otherwise},\end{cases} \qquad [S^b]_r:= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)[S_{\mathrm M}^
u],&|
u|=r,\ 0,&	ext{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$ The notation $[\Delta^b]$ is synonymous with $[W^b]_{d,r}$ when $d,r$ are fixed. The ordinary Dipper-James translation conjugates every partition label and pulls every compared module back by the same $	heta$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

For a composition $\mu$ define the signed semistandard number directly by $$d_\mu(b):= egin{cases}\epsilon(b)|T_0(
u,\mu)|,&b	ext{ has distinct nonnegative entries and }|
u|=|\mu|,\0,&	ext{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$ Here the tableau alphabet is the length of $\mu$; a shape with too many rows automatically has no such tableau ([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]). This function is alternating in the beta entries. It also obeys the branching identity $$d_\mu(b)=\sum_{\substack{C\subseteq\{1,\ldots,L\}\|C|=z}}  d_{ ar\mu}(b-\mathbf1_C),$$ where $z$ is the last nonzero part of $\mu$ and $ ar\mu$ deletes that part. The selected entries are **decreased by one**, not replaced by $-1$. For a decreasing beta sequence this is the deletion of the largest semistandard entries: they occupy a horizontal strip, at most one box in each selected column. Sorting extends the identity to distinct arbitrary sequences; if entries repeat, terms selecting just one of the equal entries cancel in pairs, while terms selecting both or neither vanish. Negative entries remain negative after decrementing. Thus the identity also holds in all zero-symbol cases. At $\mu=0$ its value is the sorting sign for a permutation of $(L-1,\ldots,0)$ and is zero otherwise, so the recursion terminates without another unproved extension rule.

In the formulas of this page take $L=r$ when $r>0$. A nonzero degree-$r$ partition has width at most $r$, so this length suffices; the Weyl cutoff $\ell(
u)\le d$ is retained even when $d<r$. A balanced displacement $+h\mathbf e_b-h\mathbf e_c$ preserves total degree. An unbalanced change is not silently treated as a class in the same fixed-degree group. The empty degree is handled by the empty beta sequence and unit symbol. No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$, let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let
$X=\{h_1>h_2>\cdots>h_m\}$ be a $\beta$-set for $\lambda$, with first-column
hook lengths $b_i(\lambda)$ and $e$-abacus configuration $A_X$ as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]; hooks and their lengths
are those of [[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]], and the hook/bead-gap
dictionary is [[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]].

**$e$-core partition.** The partition $\lambda$ is an **$e$-core** when
$e\notin H(\lambda)$, that is, when no hook of $\lambda$ has length $e$; by
[[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]](iii) this is the case exactly
when no bead of $A_X$ has a gap in the position $e$ labels above it on its own
runner. The empty partition is an $e$-core, and so is every $\lambda$ with
$|\lambda|<e$.

**Runner label sets.** For $i\in\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$ let
$$X^{(e)}_i:=\{a\in\mathbb N_0:ae+i\in X\}$$
be the set of row labels of the beads of $A_X$ on runner $i$. The $X^{(e)}_i$
are finite subsets of $\mathbb N_0$, they are pairwise disjoint, and
$\bigsqcup_{i}X^{(e)}_i$ is the set of all row labels occurring in $A_X$.

**$e$-core.** The **top-packed $\beta$-set** of $X$ is
$$X^{(e)}:=\bigcup_{i=0}^{e-1}\{ae+i:0\le a\le|X^{(e)}_i|-1\},$$
the configuration obtained from $A_X$ by sliding every bead up as far as it
goes on its own runner, i.e. into the topmost $|X^{(e)}_i|$ positions of
runner $i$. The **$e$-core** of $\lambda$ is
$$C_e(\lambda):=P(X^{(e)}).$$

**$e$-quotient and $e$-weight.** Choose the $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$ to be
*normalised*, meaning $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$. Then define the **$e$-quotient** of
$\lambda$ to be the $e$-tuple of partitions
$$Q_e(\lambda):=(\lambda^{(0)},\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)}),\qquad \lambda^{(i)}:=P(X^{(e)}_i),$$
each runner read as a $1$-abacus, and the **$e$-weight** of $\lambda$ to be
$$w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|:=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}|\lambda^{(i)}|.$$
A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of
$\lambda$ are the sets $X_\lambda+l$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$|X_\lambda+l|=|X_\lambda|+l$, so among the $e$ consecutive shifts
$l,\dots,l+e-1$ exactly one has size divisible by $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-abacus configurations as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] and the top-packed set
$X^{(e)}$ of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]. For every $\beta$-set $X$
of $\lambda$ the partition $P(X^{(e)})$ is the same, so the $e$-core
$C_e(\lambda)=P(X^{(e)})$ is a well-defined $e$-core partition, and it is
exactly the terminal partition reached by successively removing removable
border strips of size $e$ from $[\lambda]$ until none is left
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]). In particular every
maximal sequence of such removals gives the same terminal partition
$C_e(\lambda)$, each removed strip has size exactly $e$, and the terminal
partition contains no hook of length $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition with English Young diagram $[\lambda]$, parts
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_m>0$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). For $1\le i\le m$ put
$$b_i(\lambda):=\lambda_i+m-i=h_{i,1}(\lambda),$$
the hook length of the first node of row $i$
([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]); since
$h_{i,1}(\lambda)=\lambda_i+\lambda'_1-i$ and $m=\lambda'_1$, the two expressions
agree. Then
$$X_\lambda:=\{b_1(\lambda)>b_2(\lambda)>\cdots>b_m(\lambda)\}$$
is the set of **first-column hook lengths** of $\lambda$, a finite strictly
decreasing set of positive integers.

A **$\beta$-set** is a finite set $X=\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\}\subseteq\mathbb N_0$ of
nonnegative integers, written in strictly decreasing order. For $l\in\mathbb N_0$
the **$l$-shift** of $X$ is
$$X+l:=\{h+l:h\in X\}\cup\{l-1,l-2,\dots,1,0\}$$
(for $l=0$ this is $X$ itself, the second set being empty), and the **partition
of $X$** is
$$P(X):=(h_1-(m-1),\,h_2-(m-2),\,\dots,\,h_m-0),$$
with trailing zeros deleted; this is a weakly decreasing sequence of
nonnegative integers ending in $h_m$, hence a partition of
$\sum_i h_i-m(m-1)/2$ after deleting its zeros. A $\beta$-set **for** $\lambda$
is a $\beta$-set $X$ with $P(X)=\lambda$.

Let $e\ge2$. **James's $e$-abacus** has $e$ runners $0,1,\dots,e-1$ drawn left to
right, with rows labelled $a=0,1,2,\dots$ downward; the position in row $a$ of
runner $i$ carries the label $ae+i$. An **$e$-abacus configuration** $A$ is a
finite set of **beads** placed in distinct positions of this abacus; a position
without a bead is a **gap**. The configuration $A_X$ of a $\beta$-set $X$ carries
a bead in the positions of $X$, and conversely $X_A$ is the set of position
labels of the beads of $A$; the two constructions are mutually inverse, so they
biject finite $\beta$-sets with finite bead configurations. Finally
$P(A):=P(X_A)$, and $A_\lambda:=A_{X_\lambda}$.

Let $e\in\{2,3,4,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition
with parts $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Then $\lambda$ is
**$e$-regular** when every positive integer occurs as a part of $\lambda$ fewer
than $e$ times, i.e. $z_j(\lambda)<e$ for every $j\ge1$, and **$e$-restricted**
when $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ for every $i\ge1$ (with $\lambda_i:=0$ for
$i>\ell(\lambda)$).

For finite $e$ these are exactly the $p$-regular and $p$-restricted notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $p=e$. For $e=\infty$ both
conditions are vacuous, so every partition is both $e$-regular and
$e$-restricted: the inequalities $z_j(\lambda)<\infty$ and
$\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<\infty$ hold because partitions have finitely many
nonzero parts and each difference is a nonnegative integer. Moreover $\lambda$
is $e$-restricted if and only if its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular: the
multiplicity of the part $i$ in $\lambda'$ is the number of columns of
$[\lambda]$ of height exactly $i$, namely $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$, so the
two conditions $z_i(\lambda')=\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ are the same family
of inequalities, and for $e=\infty$ both sides hold. In particular
$\varnothing$ is simultaneously $e$-regular and $e$-restricted for every $e$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]).

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$ with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let $\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]] for the underlying Murphy elements and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard basis along which this basis is defined). Put $\omega:=(1^n)\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the composition with $n$ parts equal to $1$ (legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial and $m_\omega=1$; hence $$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$ is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard $\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down the column. Set $$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra isomorphism $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$ left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$ sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$ (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above. 2. The **Schur functor** is $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$ with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms: as a **left** $S$-module, $Se$ is the image of the left-$S$-linear projection $s\mapsto se$ on $S$, hence is a direct summand of the regular left module and is projective. Tensoring right $S$-modules with this left module is therefore exact. Equivalently, for a short exact sequence of right modules, an element $ye$ in the target lifts to $xe$ from any lift $x$ of $y$; kernels and injections are likewise preserved by the same idempotent projection. The bimodule corner action makes these maps right $H$-linear. The convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

Let $k$ be a field, $q\in k^	imes$, $d\ge n$, and let $\mathcal F(X)=Xe$ be the right-module Schur functor of [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]. Set $e_q=e(k,q)$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). For each $\lambda\in\Lambda^+(d,n)$ let $W^\lambda$ be the Weyl module with Schur cell form $B_\lambda$ and nonzero simple head $L^\lambda$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Write $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ and $D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ for the independent Murphy cell module and its cell-form quotient ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal F(W^\lambda)\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ as right $H$-modules, and this isomorphism identifies $B_\lambda|_{W^\lambda e}$ exactly with the Murphy cell form. 2. $\mathcal F(L^\lambda)\cong D_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, including the zero quotient; it is nonzero exactly when $\lambda$ is $e_q$-restricted. 3. For every $e_q$-restricted $
u\vdash n$, $$[W^\lambda:L^
u]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):D_{\mathrm M}(
u)].$$

In the page's ordinary Dipper–James normalization ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]), these identities become $$\mathcal F(W^{\lambda'})\cong(S^\lambda)^	heta,\qquad \mathcal F(L^{\lambda'})\cong(D^\lambda)^	heta.$$ The latter module is nonzero exactly for $e_q$-regular $\lambda$ and is zero otherwise. For $e_q$-regular $
u$, $$[W^{\lambda'}:L^{
u'}]=[S^\lambda:D^
u].$$ The accepted ordinary polytabloid comparison identifies $S^\lambda$ with the historical DJ module $P(\lambda)$ and identifies their form radicals through an explicit unit factor. Thus the dictionary concerns the actual ordinary modules, not merely a renamed cell module. A zero Hecke cell-form quotient is not asserted to be its actual module head. No semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed, and $n=0$ is included.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. With the Murphy cellular
basis $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]],
[[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and the canonical tableau
$t^\lambda$ of shape $\lambda\vdash n$
([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell
module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the
Murphy basis: it is the free $R$-module with basis
$\{m_t:=m_{t^\lambda t}:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ - the classes of the
Murphy elements whose *first* index is the canonical tableau - and $H$ acts by
$m_th=\sum_vr_vm_v$ whenever
$m_{t^\lambda t}h\equiv\sum_vr_vm_{t^\lambda v}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$. (The
cellular action rule transforms the second index and fixes the first, so the
diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone do not span a submodule; the module basis is
the fixed-first-index family above.) Its **cell form** is the unique bilinear
form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\times
S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\to R$ with
$$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\langle m_s,m_t\rangle_\lambda\,m_{uv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$; it is symmetric and associative and
$\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a submodule, so
$D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}:=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
is a right $H$-module
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

**Convention (Dipper-James signed cellular normalization).** Let $\theta:H\to H$
be the involutive algebra automorphism defined by
$\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). For a right module $M$,
write $M^\theta$ for the same $R$-module with action $x\cdot h=x\theta(h)$. The
page's ordinary Specht normalization is the signed conjugate Murphy
construction
$$S^{\lambda}:=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta,$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Its form is the form of
$S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ on the same underlying module; because $\theta$
commutes with $*$ this is associative for the twisted action
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Over a field put
$$D^{\lambda}:=S^{\lambda}/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}S^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta.$$
Thus $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(S^{\lambda})^\theta$ and
$D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(D^{\lambda})^\theta$; conjugation alone does not
identify these modules
([[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]],
[[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]). At
$q=1$, $\theta(\sigma)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma$, so these identities
contain tensoring with sign; in characteristic $2$ the sign twist becomes
trivial at $q=1$
([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).
The nonzero quotients in this signed normalization have $e$-regular labels
by [[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]:
that theorem proves the nonzero Murphy quotient criterion in $e$-restricted
labels, and conjugation makes these precisely $e$-regular labels
([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]). No generic root-of-unity
Hecke claim is inferred from the published prime-characteristic group-only sign
dictionary, and no semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$ where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and read in the twist; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. For a class $m\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and any lift $\widetilde m\in M(\lambda')$, the inverse is $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$, independently of the chosen lift.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Enumeration and ordering. Choose a conjugate core beta set long enough that every runner contains a bead, and list its bottom beads $x_1<\cdots<x_e$. Each runner is packed, so replacing $x_k$ by $x_k+e$ gives precisely the $e$ weight-one partitions, denoted $\lambda_k$. For $j>k$, moving $x_j$ instead of $x_k$ gives the more dominant conjugate partition: comparing the sorted bead lists, each partial sum increases when the move starts at the larger bead. Conjugation reverses dominance, hence $\lambda_1\rhd\cdots\rhd\lambda_e$. The largest original partition is $(\gamma_1+e,\gamma_2,\ldots)$, since its added horizontal first-row strip dominates every other placement.

Choose a lift with valuation one. If $q
e1$, its finite quantum characteristic $e$ is its multiplicative order, and is prime to the field characteristic; use $R=F[X]_{(X-q)}$ and $\hat q=X$. The derivative of $X^e-1$ at $q$ is $eq^{e-1}
e0$, so $
u([e]_X)=1$; also $
u([h]_X)=0$ when $e
mid h$. If $q=1$, then $\operatorname{char}F=p=e$. First work over $\mathbb F_p$ with $R=\mathbb Z_{(p)}$, $\hat q=1$, giving $
u([e]_1)=
u(p)=1$ and $
u([h]_1)=0$ for $p
mid h$, and then extend scalars to $F$. This extension preserves the decomposition multiplicities because the q-Schur simple modules are absolutely irreducible and its integral Weyl modules commute with scalar extension. In both cases the generic factorial is nonzero and [F2] applies.

Restriction. If $\lambda$ is not restricted, some $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}\ge e$, so removing the last $e$ boxes of row $i$ leaves a partition. Its size is $|\gamma|$ and its core is $\gamma$, so it equals $\gamma$. Thus $\lambda$ is obtained by adding $e$ boxes to row $i$ of $\gamma$. An $e$-core has $\gamma_r-\gamma_{r+1}<e$ for every $r$, since otherwise it has a removable horizontal $e$-strip. Consequently $i>1$ is impossible: the partition inequality $\gamma_{i-1}\ge\gamma_i+e$ would contradict this core property. Therefore the only nonrestricted member is $\lambda_1=(\gamma_1+e,\gamma_2,\ldots)$; it is indeed nonrestricted because its first-row difference is at least $e$.

Evaluate the balanced formula. A nonzero coefficient involves a hook of length divisible by $e$. A weight-one abacus has exactly one bead-gap pair of equal residue with the gap below the bead: $x_k+e$ and $x_k$; thus its only $e$-divisible hook has length $e$. Any surviving term in [F2] replaces two bead values, and its new runner counts equal the old ones: either $e$ divides the transfer $h_{ac}$, leaving residues fixed, or $e$ divides $h_{ab}=h_{ac}+\beta_b-\beta_c$, exchanging their residues. Hence its sorted symbol is one of the $\lambda_j$. For $j>k$, the distinct bead sets of $\lambda_k$ and $\lambda_j$ differ exactly by replacing $x_k+e,x_j$ with $x_k,x_j+e$. There is exactly one balanced transfer yielding this change: if $x_j<x_k+e$, its two hook lengths are $h_{ab}=e$, $h_{ac}=x_j-x_k$; if $x_j>x_k+e$, they are $h_{ab}=x_j-x_k$, $h_{ac}=e$. The difference $x_j-x_k$ is not divisible by $e$ since bottom beads are on distinct runners. Thus the respective unsigned coefficients are $+1$ and $-1$ by step 1.2. Sorting gives in either case the signed coefficient $(-1)^{j-k+1}$: in the packed core set, exactly one bead from each runner with bottom bead $>x_r$ lies between $x_r$ and $x_r+e$, so moving $x_r$ crosses $e-r$ beads; the relative sorting parity for the two moves, together with their opposite orientation, is $(-1)^{(e-j)-(e-k)+1}$. There are no other terms and no repeated contributions: the two lost and two gained bead values determine the pair and transfer uniquely. Therefore $\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda_k}(i)]=\sum_{j>k}(-1)^{j-k+1}[W^{\lambda_j}]$.

Descending induction and the matrix. For $k=e$, step 2.2 gives zero on the left; all summands are actual submodule classes with nonnegative simple multiplicities, so $W^{\lambda_e}(1)=0$ and $W^{\lambda_e}=L^{\lambda_e}$. Suppose the stated rows are known for $j>k$. Substitution into step 2.2 telescopes to $\sum_{i>0}[W^{\lambda_k}(i)]=[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$. Since $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$ and each later term is a submodule of $W(1)$, positivity shows $W(1)\cong L^{\lambda_{k+1}}$ and $W(i)=0$ for $i\ge2$. The head quotient is $L^{\lambda_k}$, giving $[W^{\lambda_k}]=[L^{\lambda_k}]+[L^{\lambda_{k+1}}]$. Notice that the identity $[W]=[L]+\sum_{i>0}[W(i)]$ is used only after proving all later filtration submodules vanish; it is false for a general Jantzen filtration. Reading simple multiplicities yields the complete $e\times e$ bidiagonal matrix.

Specht rows. Apply the exact functor of [F4] to step 3.1 and use step 2.1: $D^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}=0$, while the other $D^{\lambda_k}_{\mathrm M}$ are the nonzero simples. This gives exactly the three displayed Murphy Specht class identities, hence the full $e\times(e-1)$ Murphy matrix. Conjugation sends the core to $\gamma'$ and the restricted simple labels to regular ones, and the same $\theta$ pullback applied to every module preserves all composition multiplicities. Thus the ordinary Specht matrix has the same entries under the accepted conjugate/sign label dictionary.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$, let $q\in R^{\times}$, let $d,n\ge0$ with $d\ge n$, and let $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $S:=S(d,n)=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for the type-A q-Schur algebra with $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\mu}$ the direct sum of the permutation modules ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]) and let $\{\varphi_{ST}:\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}(d,n),\ S,T\in T_0(\lambda)\}$ be its cellular semistandard basis ([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]] for the underlying Murphy elements and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] for the standard basis along which this basis is defined). Put $\omega:=(1^n)\in\Lambda(d,n)$, the composition with $n$ parts equal to $1$ (legitimate because $d\ge n$), so that the Young subgroup $S_\omega$ is trivial and $m_\omega=1$; hence $$M^{\omega}=m_\omega H=H$$ is the regular right $H$-module. Let $t^{\omega}$ be the unique standard $\omega$-tableau, with entries $1,2,\dots,n$ down its single column; it is in particular the unique row-standard $\omega$-tableau whose entries increase down the column. Set $$e:=\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}\in S.$$

Then:

1. $e$ is the projection of $M$ onto the direct summand $M^{\omega}=H$ along the other summands $M^{\mu}$, $\mu\ne\omega$; in particular $e^2=e$ and $$eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})=\mathrm{End}_H(H),$$ via the algebra isomorphism $$\rho:H\longrightarrow eSe,\qquad h\longmapsto\rho_h,\qquad \rho_h(x):=hx,$$ left multiplication by $h$ on $M^{\omega}=H$ being a right $H$-module endomorphism. Here the isomorphism $eSe\cong\mathrm{End}_H(M^{\omega})$ sends $efe$ to $f|_{M^{\omega}}$ and is inverted by extending an endomorphism of $M^{\omega}$ by zero on the other summands, and the identification $\mathrm{End}_H(H)\cong H$ sends an endomorphism to its value at $1$. By the construction of the semistandard basis elements $\varphi_{ST}$ (Mathas (4.13) with Corollaries 4.9 and 4.12; see the locator above), the diagonal element $\varphi_{t^{\omega}t^{\omega}}$ is exactly the endomorphism of $M$ that is the identity on $M^{\omega}$ and zero on all $M^{\mu}$ with $\mu\ne\omega$, which is the projection asserted above. 2. The **Schur functor** is $$F:\mathrm{mod}\text{-}S\longrightarrow\mathrm{mod}\text{-}H,\qquad F(X):=Xe=X\otimes_SSe,$$ with the right $H$-action transported along $\rho$, so that $(xe)\cdot h:=x\,\rho_h$ for $x\in X$, $h\in H$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). It is exact and $R$-linear on morphisms: as a **left** $S$-module, $Se$ is the image of the left-$S$-linear projection $s\mapsto se$ on $S$, hence is a direct summand of the regular left module and is projective. Tensoring right $S$-modules with this left module is therefore exact. Equivalently, for a short exact sequence of right modules, an element $ye$ in the target lifts to $xe$ from any lift $x$ of $y$; kernels and injections are likewise preserved by the same idempotent projection. The bimodule corner action makes these maps right $H$-linear. The convention is fixed: the functor is $X\mapsto Xe$ on the right, and the left-module formula $X\mapsto eX$ is not used on this page.

In the page's ordinary Dipper–James normalization ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]], [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]), these identities become $$\mathcal F(W^{\lambda'})\cong(S^\lambda)^	heta,\qquad \mathcal F(L^{\lambda'})\cong(D^\lambda)^	heta.$$ The latter module is nonzero exactly for $e_q$-regular $\lambda$ and is zero otherwise. For $e_q$-regular $

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is
an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the
sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents.

Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra, so the identity
$1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$
into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents
([[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and this decomposition is unique up to order
([[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]). A **block** of
$A$ is the two-sided ideal $B=eA=Ae$ cut out by a primitive central idempotent
$e$ (the two descriptions agree because $e$ is central).

The blocks are pairwise orthogonal two-sided ideals:
$B_iB_j\subseteq e_iAe_jA=e_ie_jA=0$ for $i\ne j$, and
$e_i\in B_i$ is the identity of $B_i$ since $e_i(e_ia)=e_ia$ and
$(ae_i)e_i=ae_i$. Moreover $A=B_1\oplus\cdots\oplus B_k$ as $F$-algebras with
units $e_i$: every $a\in A$ is $a=(\sum_ie_i)a=\sum_ie_ia$ with $e_ia\in B_i$,
and if $\sum_ib_i=0$ with $b_i\in B_i$ then multiplying by $e_j$ gives
$b_j=e_jb_j=\sum_ie_jb_i=0$, so the sum is direct. Each $B_i$ is an
indecomposable two-sided ideal: if $B_i=J\oplus J'$ were a direct sum of
nonzero two-sided ideals, the projections of $e_i$ onto $J$ and $J'$ would be
nonzero orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ summing to $e_i$, as is seen by
applying to $e_i$ the $A$-bimodule projections $B_i\to J$ and $B_i\to J'$,
which satisfy $\pi(a x)=a\pi(x)$ and $\pi(xa)=\pi(x)a$; this contradicts
primitivity of $e_i$.

For every (not necessarily finite-dimensional) $A$-module $M$ one has
$M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^ke_iM$ as $A$-modules: $\sum_ie_i=1$ acts as the identity on
$M$, so $M=\sum_ie_iM$, and if $\sum_im_i=0$ with $m_i=e_im_i$ then applying
$e_j$ gives $m_j=0$; each $e_iM$ is $A$-stable because $e_i$ is central. A
simple $A$-module $S$ satisfies $e_iS\ne0$ for exactly one $i$, and then
$S=e_iS$ lies in the corresponding block: $S=(\sum_ie_i)S=\sum_ie_iS$ forces
some $e_iS\ne0$, and if $e_iS\ne0\ne e_jS$ with $i\ne j$ then simplicity gives
$e_iS=S=e_jS$, whence $S=e_iS=e_i(e_jS)=(e_ie_j)S=0$, a contradiction. Nothing
here asserts that a block is semisimple or simple, and the construction is
choice-free.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional
commutative $F$-algebra, and the identity $1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$
into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents of $A$: each $e_i$ is a
nonzero idempotent of $Z(A)$ that is not the sum of two nonzero orthogonal
idempotents of $Z(A)$. No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed and no choice
principle is used.

Let $A$ be a unital ring ([[def-ring]]), with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A: za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$. Suppose that
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k=f_1+\cdots+f_\ell$$
where $\{e_1,\dots,e_k\}$ and $\{f_1,\dots,f_\ell\}$ are finite families of
pairwise orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ that are primitive among central
idempotents: each is nonzero and admits no decomposition as a sum of two nonzero
orthogonal central idempotents (zero parts are omitted). Then $k=\ell$ and there
is a bijection $\sigma$ of the index sets with $e_i=f_{\sigma(i)}$ for all $i$;
in particular the decomposition of $1$ into primitive central idempotents is
unique up to order. No choice principle is used, the families being finite.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^{	imes}$, $d,n\ge0$, and $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Let $\Lambda(d,n)$ be the set of compositions $\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_d)$ of $n$ (so $\mu_i\in\mathbb N$ and $\sum_i\mu_i=n$). Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]], [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]), let $d\ge n$, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl modules of $S_F(d,n)$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Then for partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts, $W^{\lambda}_F$ and $W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same block of $S_F(d,n)$ if and only if $\lambda$ and $\mu$ have the same $e$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). (For $e=\infty$ every partition is its own core and every Weyl module is its own block, the algebra being semisimple.)

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $q\in R^{\times}$. With the Murphy cellular
basis $(\mathcal M,\Lambda)$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$
([[thm-murphy-tableau-elements-form-a-cellular-basis]],
[[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]) and the canonical tableau
$t^\lambda$ of shape $\lambda\vdash n$
([[def-murphy-elements-and-murphy-tableau-elements]]), the **Murphy cell
module** $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the right cell module $C^{\lambda}$ of the
Murphy basis: it is the free $R$-module with basis
$\{m_t:=m_{t^\lambda t}:t\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)\}$ - the classes of the
Murphy elements whose *first* index is the canonical tableau - and $H$ acts by
$m_th=\sum_vr_vm_v$ whenever
$m_{t^\lambda t}h\equiv\sum_vr_vm_{t^\lambda v}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$. (The
cellular action rule transforms the second index and fixes the first, so the
diagonal elements $m_{tt}$ alone do not span a submodule; the module basis is
the fixed-first-index family above.) Its **cell form** is the unique bilinear
form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda:S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\times
S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\to R$ with
$$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv\langle m_s,m_t\rangle_\lambda\,m_{uv}\pmod{H^{\rhd\lambda}}$$
for all $s,t,u,v\in\mathrm{Std}(\lambda)$; it is symmetric and associative and
$\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is a submodule, so
$D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}:=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}/\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$
is a right $H$-module
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]).

**Convention (Dipper-James signed cellular normalization).** Let $\theta:H\to H$
be the involutive algebra automorphism defined by
$\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}=(q-1)-T_i$
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). For a right module $M$,
write $M^\theta$ for the same $R$-module with action $x\cdot h=x\theta(h)$. The
page's ordinary Specht normalization is the signed conjugate Murphy
construction
$$S^{\lambda}:=(S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta,$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Its form is the form of
$S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ on the same underlying module; because $\theta$
commutes with $*$ this is associative for the twisted action
([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Over a field put
$$D^{\lambda}:=S^{\lambda}/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}S^{\lambda}=(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta.$$
Thus $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(S^{\lambda})^\theta$ and
$D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}=(D^{\lambda})^\theta$; conjugation alone does not
identify these modules
([[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]],
[[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]). At
$q=1$, $\theta(\sigma)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma$, so these identities
contain tensoring with sign; in characteristic $2$ the sign twist becomes
trivial at $q=1$
([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).
The nonzero quotients in this signed normalization have $e$-regular labels
by [[thm-simple-type-a-hecke-modules-are-indexed-by-e-regular-partitions]]:
that theorem proves the nonzero Murphy quotient criterion in $e$-restricted
labels, and conjugation makes these precisely $e$-regular labels
([[def-e-regular-and-e-restricted-partitions]]). No generic root-of-unity
Hecke claim is inferred from the published prime-characteristic group-only sign
dictionary, and no semisimplicity or choice principle is assumed.

derivations.claim: Central idempotents of $H$ from blocks of $S$. For a block $C$ of $S$ with primitive central idempotent $\epsilon_C$ put $\tilde\epsilon_C:=\epsilon_Ce=e\epsilon_Ce\in H$. This element is a central idempotent of $H$: it is idempotent because $\epsilon_C$ is, and for $x=ese\in H$ centrality of $\epsilon_C$ gives $x\tilde\epsilon_C=es\epsilon_Ce=e\epsilon_Cse=\tilde\epsilon_Cx$; it is nonzero because it acts as the identity on the nonzero module $W^{\lambda}_Fe=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ for any $\lambda$ with $W^{\lambda}_F\in C$, namely $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\tilde\epsilon_C=W^{\lambda}_Fe\epsilon_Ce=W^{\lambda}_F\epsilon_Ce=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$. Moreover $\tilde\epsilon_C\tilde\epsilon_{C'}=e\epsilon_C\epsilon_{C'}e=0$ for $C\ne C'$ and $\sum_C\tilde\epsilon_C=e\sum_C\epsilon_Ce=e^2=1_H$.

Number of Hecke blocks is at least the number of q-Schur blocks. Decompose each nonzero central idempotent $\tilde\epsilon_C$ of step 1.1 into primitive central idempotents of $H$ using the unique decomposition of $1_H$: every primitive central idempotent $\delta_D$ of $H$ with $\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C=\delta_D$ belongs to exactly one $\tilde\epsilon_C$, because $\delta_D=\delta_D\cdot1_H=\sum_C\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C$ and pairwise orthogonality of the $\delta_D$ forces $\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C\in\{0,\delta_D\}$. Since each $\tilde\epsilon_C\ne0$ has at least one such $\delta_D$, the blocks $D$ of $H$ are partitioned into nonempty supports over the blocks $C$ of $S$, and therefore $\#\{\text{blocks of }H\}\ge\#\{\text{blocks of }S\}$.

A bijection of block sets, and the core criterion. By steps 2.1 and 1.2 the two block counts are equal, so each $\tilde\epsilon_C$ of step 1.1 has exactly one primitive summand and the map $C\mapsto\tilde\epsilon_C$ is a bijection from the blocks of $S$ onto the blocks of $H$. Since $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}=W^{\lambda}_Fe$ and $S^{\mu}_{\mathrm M}=W^{\mu}_Fe$, the modules $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ and $S^{\mu}_{\mathrm M}$ lie in the same Hecke block if and only if $W^{\lambda}_F$ and $W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same q-Schur block: indeed the block of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the image under the bijection of the block of $W^{\lambda}_F$. By the block theorem [F4] the latter holds if and only if $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$, which proves the q-Schur-normalised statement.

Ordinary normalisation and semisimplicity. By [F5], $S^{\lambda}$ and $S^{\mu}$ lie in the same block exactly when $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ and $S^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}$ do. Step 3.1 makes this equivalent to $C_e(\lambda')=C_e(\mu')$, and the identity $C_e(\nu')=C_e(\nu)'$ makes it equivalent to $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$. This identity follows by conjugating every removable border strip in a core-removal sequence; the terminal core also conjugates, by independence of removal order. For $e=\infty$, $S$ is semisimple by [F4]. Its corner $eSe$ is semisimple: in the Wedderburn decomposition of $S$, each idempotent selects a subspace in each matrix factor, and its corner is a product of matrix algebras over the same division rings. Thus $H\cong eSe$ is semisimple; the block bijection separates the partition labels. This proves all assertions.

citations.quote:
Let $F$ be a field, $q=1\in F$, and let $H_{F,1}(S_n)$ be the specialization of
the generic type-A Hecke algebra at $v\mapsto1$, so that
$H_{F,1}(S_n)\cong F[S_n]$ with $T_w\mapsto w$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).
Then the Hecke theory of this page specializes as follows.

1. The Murphy elements $m_\mu=\sum_{w\in S_\mu}T_w$ specialize to the row
   symmetrizers $\sum_{w\in S_\mu}w$, and the Murphy basis $\{m_{st}\}$ of
   $H_{F,1}(S_n)$ specializes to the Murphy basis of the group algebra
   $F[S_n]$ (the base change $\mathbb Z[S_n]\to F[S_n]$ of the integral Murphy
   basis).
2. For every $\lambda\vdash n$ the specialization of the page's Hecke Specht
   module $S^{\lambda}$ ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) is
   the ordinary Specht module in the Dipper-James convention:
   $S^{\lambda}_{q=1}\cong S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ as $F[S_n]$-modules, with
   the standard polytabloid basis ([[thm-standard-polytabloid-basis]]); the
   specialized cell form is the standard bilinear form on $S^{\lambda}$ whose
   radical defines the James quotient $D^{\lambda}$
   ([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]).
3. The quantum characteristic of $q=1$ is $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ when
   $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$, and $e=\infty$ when
   $\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
   ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]); in
   characteristic $p>0$ a partition is $e$-regular exactly when it is
   $p$-regular. Hence $D^{\lambda}_{q=1}\ne0$ exactly for $p$-regular $\lambda$
   ([[thm-specht-radical-quotient-is-nonzero-exactly-for-p-regular-partitions]]),
   and for non-$p$-regular $\lambda$ one has
   $\mathrm{rad}\,S^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}$. This matches the group-side
   classification
   [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]] and the
   conjugate-sign dictionary
   [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]].
   In characteristic $0$ the specialization is split semisimple and all Specht
   modules are irreducible.

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ an invertible element. The **quantum
characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that
$1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists
([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1\ne0$, the least positive
integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so
the two formulations coincide.

Concretely: (i) if $q\ne1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$ — indeed
$(q-1)(1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1})=q^m-1$ and $q-1\ne0$ — so $[e]_q=0$ is equivalent
to $q^e=1$, and a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and
then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{\times}$ (which is $\ge2$
because $q\ne1$); (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$
when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ (the characteristic is a prime, hence at least
$2$, and $m\cdot1_F\ne0$ for $1\le m<p$) and $e=\infty$ when
$\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

If $e<\infty$ then $q\ne1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for
every integer $m$: for $m\ge0$ the sum splits as
$$[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q,$$
so $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ whenever $[e]_q=0$; for the remaining $m<0$ one extends the
closed formula by $[m]_q:=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ when $q\ne1$ and reads $[m]_1:=m\in F$
for the canonical image of the integer $m$ when $q=1$, in which case
$e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ and $[m+e]_1=m+e=m$ in $F$. In particular the
quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter
governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice
principle is used.

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), and let $S^{\lambda}$ be the type-A Hecke Specht module of this page in the Dipper-James convention ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) for $\lambda\vdash n$. Then for all partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ the modules $S^{\lambda}$ and $S^{\mu}$ lie in the same block of $H_{F,q}(S_n)$ if and only if $\lambda$ and $\mu$ have the same $e$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Equivalently the blocks of $H_{F,q}(S_n)$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ of size at most $n$ with $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$, and the block of $S^{\lambda}$ is determined by $C_e(\lambda)$. (For $e=\infty$ the Hecke algebra is semisimple and each partition is its own core, so the statement is the trivial block decomposition.)

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-core $C_e(\lambda)$ and
$e$-weight $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|$
([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Then
$$n=|\lambda|=|C_e(\lambda)|+e\,w_e(\lambda),$$
so $w_e(\lambda)=(n-|C_e(\lambda)|)/e\in\mathbb N_0$. Equivalently every
sequence of removals of removable border strips of size $e$ from $\lambda$ down
to its $e$-core
([[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]) has exactly
$w_e(\lambda)$ steps, and $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|$ equals both the number
of hooks of the multipartition $Q_e(\lambda)$ and, by the bijection of
[[thm-e-quotient-controls-hooks-divisible-by-e]], the number of hooks of
$\lambda$ of length divisible by $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]], [[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]]), let $d\ge n$, and let $W^{\lambda}_F$ be the Weyl modules of $S_F(d,n)$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). Then for partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ with at most $d$ parts, $W^{\lambda}_F$ and $W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same block of $S_F(d,n)$ if and only if $\lambda$ and $\mu$ have the same $e$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently the blocks of $S_F(d,n)$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$, and the block of $W^{\lambda}_F$ is determined by $C_e(\lambda)$. (For $e=\infty$ every partition is its own core and every Weyl module is its own block, the algebra being semisimple.)

No choice principle is used.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-abacus configurations as in
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] and the top-packed set
$X^{(e)}$ of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]. For every $\beta$-set $X$
of $\lambda$ the partition $P(X^{(e)})$ is the same, so the $e$-core
$C_e(\lambda)=P(X^{(e)})$ is a well-defined $e$-core partition, and it is
exactly the terminal partition reached by successively removing removable
border strips of size $e$ from $[\lambda]$ until none is left
([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]],
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]). In particular every
maximal sequence of such removals gives the same terminal partition
$C_e(\lambda)$, each removed strip has size exactly $e$, and the terminal
partition contains no hook of length $e$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebra with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A **central idempotent** of $A$ is
an idempotent $e\in Z(A)$; it is **primitive** when $e\ne0$ and $e$ is not the
sum of two nonzero orthogonal central idempotents.

Then $Z(A)$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $F$-algebra, so the identity
$1\in Z(A)$ admits a decomposition
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k$$
into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents
([[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]]),
and this decomposition is unique up to order
([[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]). A **block** of
$A$ is the two-sided ideal $B=eA=Ae$ cut out by a primitive central idempotent
$e$ (the two descriptions agree because $e$ is central).

The blocks are pairwise orthogonal two-sided ideals:
$B_iB_j\subseteq e_iAe_jA=e_ie_jA=0$ for $i\ne j$, and
$e_i\in B_i$ is the identity of $B_i$ since $e_i(e_ia)=e_ia$ and
$(ae_i)e_i=ae_i$. Moreover $A=B_1\oplus\cdots\oplus B_k$ as $F$-algebras with
units $e_i$: every $a\in A$ is $a=(\sum_ie_i)a=\sum_ie_ia$ with $e_ia\in B_i$,
and if $\sum_ib_i=0$ with $b_i\in B_i$ then multiplying by $e_j$ gives
$b_j=e_jb_j=\sum_ie_jb_i=0$, so the sum is direct. Each $B_i$ is an
indecomposable two-sided ideal: if $B_i=J\oplus J'$ were a direct sum of
nonzero two-sided ideals, the projections of $e_i$ onto $J$ and $J'$ would be
nonzero orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ summing to $e_i$, as is seen by
applying to $e_i$ the $A$-bimodule projections $B_i\to J$ and $B_i\to J'$,
which satisfy $\pi(a x)=a\pi(x)$ and $\pi(xa)=\pi(x)a$; this contradicts
primitivity of $e_i$.

For every (not necessarily finite-dimensional) $A$-module $M$ one has
$M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^ke_iM$ as $A$-modules: $\sum_ie_i=1$ acts as the identity on
$M$, so $M=\sum_ie_iM$, and if $\sum_im_i=0$ with $m_i=e_im_i$ then applying
$e_j$ gives $m_j=0$; each $e_iM$ is $A$-stable because $e_i$ is central. A
simple $A$-module $S$ satisfies $e_iS\ne0$ for exactly one $i$, and then
$S=e_iS$ lies in the corresponding block: $S=(\sum_ie_i)S=\sum_ie_iS$ forces
some $e_iS\ne0$, and if $e_iS\ne0\ne e_jS$ with $i\ne j$ then simplicity gives
$e_iS=S=e_jS$, whence $S=e_iS=e_i(e_jS)=(e_ie_j)S=0$, a contradiction. Nothing
here asserts that a block is semisimple or simple, and the construction is
choice-free.

Let $A$ be a unital ring ([[def-ring]]), with centre
$Z(A):=\{z\in A: za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}$. Suppose that
$$1=e_1+\cdots+e_k=f_1+\cdots+f_\ell$$
where $\{e_1,\dots,e_k\}$ and $\{f_1,\dots,f_\ell\}$ are finite families of
pairwise orthogonal central idempotents of $A$ that are primitive among central
idempotents: each is nonzero and admits no decomposition as a sum of two nonzero
orthogonal central idempotents (zero parts are omitted). Then $k=\ell$ and there
is a bijection $\sigma$ of the index sets with $e_i=f_{\sigma(i)}$ for all $i$;
in particular the decomposition of $1$ into primitive central idempotents is
unique up to order. No choice principle is used, the families being finite.

derivations.claim: Specialisation. Take $q=1\in k^{\times}$ and $e$ the quantum characteristic of $(k,q)$; since $q=1$ and $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$, [F1] gives $e=p$. By [F1] there is an algebra isomorphism $H_{k,1}(S_n)\cong k[S_n]$ carrying the Hecke Specht modules of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$ to the group Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k$, so by [F5] this isomorphism induces a bijection between the blocks of the two algebras that matches $S^{\lambda}$ with $S^{\lambda}_k$; in particular $S^{\lambda}_k$ and $S^{\mu}_k$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if the corresponding Hecke Specht modules lie in the same block of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$.

The core criterion. Applying the Hecke block criterion [F2] with $q=1$ and $e=p$, the Hecke Specht modules of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$ lie in the same block if and only if the labels $\lambda,\mu$ have the same $p$-core. Together with step 1.1 this gives: $S^{\lambda}_k$ and $S^{\mu}_k$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if $C_p(\lambda)=C_p(\mu)$.

The parametrisation by cores and weights. By [F2] the blocks of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$, hence by step 1.1 the blocks of $k[S_n]$, are indexed by the $p$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod p$; the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ corresponds to $C_p(\lambda)$. For $n\ge0$ and such a $\gamma$ put $w:=(n-|\gamma|)/p\in\mathbb N_0$; by [F4] this is exactly the $p$-weight $w_p(\lambda)$ of any Specht label with core $\gamma$, and $n=|\gamma|+pw$. Since $w$ is determined by $n$ and $\gamma$, the map $\gamma\mapsto(\gamma,w)$ is a bijection onto the displayed set of pairs, and the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ is the pair $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$.

Steps 2.1 and 3.1 establish both assertions: the same-block criterion by the $p$-core, and the indexing of the blocks by the pairs $(\gamma,w)$ with $n=|\gamma|+pw$ together with the identification of the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ as $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$. [step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

The classification is stated independently, by a Young-module and Brauer-quotient route, as Theorem 1 of O'Donovan's preprint recorded in the sources; that reference is an independent confirmation of the statement and is not used in the proof above. No choice principle is used anywhere in this item.

**$e$-quotient and $e$-weight.** Choose the $\beta$-set $X$ of $\lambda$ to be
*normalised*, meaning $|X|\equiv0\pmod e$. Then define the **$e$-quotient** of
$\lambda$ to be the $e$-tuple of partitions
$$Q_e(\lambda):=(\lambda^{(0)},\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(e-1)}),\qquad \lambda^{(i)}:=P(X^{(e)}_i),$$
each runner read as a $1$-abacus, and the **$e$-weight** of $\lambda$ to be
$$w_e(\lambda):=|Q_e(\lambda)|:=\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{e-1}|\lambda^{(i)}|.$$
A normalised $\beta$-set exists: by
[[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]] the $\beta$-sets of
$\lambda$ are the sets $X_\lambda+l$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$|X_\lambda+l|=|X_\lambda|+l$, so among the $e$ consecutive shifts
$l,\dots,l+e-1$ exactly one has size divisible by $e$.

Let $e\ge2$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ with $e$-core $C_e(\lambda)$ and
$e$-weight $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|$
([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Then
$$n=|\lambda|=|C_e(\lambda)|+e\,w_e(\lambda),$$
so $w_e(\lambda)=(n-|C_e(\lambda)|)/e\in\mathbb N_0$. Equivalently every
sequence of removals of removable border strips of size $e$ from $\lambda$ down
to its $e$-core
([[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]) has exactly
$w_e(\lambda)$ steps, and $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|$ equals both the number
of hooks of the multipartition $Q_e(\lambda)$ and, by the bijection of
[[thm-e-quotient-controls-hooks-divisible-by-e]], the number of hooks of
$\lambda$ of length divisible by $e$.

1. **Simple heads.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda\ne0$ is
   self-dual and absolutely irreducible, and it is the simple head of
   $S^\lambda_k$, whose unique maximal submodule is
   $R^\lambda=\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)$. If $\lambda$ is not
   $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda=0$.
2. **Pairwise inequivalent.** If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ are both $p$-regular
   and $D^\lambda\cong D^\mu$ as $k[S_n]$-modules, then $\lambda=\mu$.
3. **Complete set.** Every simple $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D^\lambda$
   for exactly one $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$. Equivalently, as
   $\lambda$ ranges over the $p$-regular partitions of $n$, the modules
   $D^\lambda$ form a complete set of representatives of the isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; in particular the number of simple
   $k[S_n]$-modules equals the number of $p$-regular partitions of $n$.

Let $k$ be a splitting field of characteristic $p>0$ (equivalently the residue
field of the fixed splitting $p$-modular system,
[[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]],
[[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]) and let $n\ge0$. Two Specht
modules $S^{\lambda}_k,S^{\mu}_k$ of $k[S_n]$ lie in the same block of
$k[S_n]$ if and only if $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ have the same $p$-core
([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently the blocks of $k[S_n]$
are indexed by the pairs $(\gamma,w)$ with $\gamma$ a $p$-core, $w\in\mathbb
N_0$ and $n=|\gamma|+pw$, and the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ is the pair
$(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$ with $w_p(\lambda)=(n-|C_p(\lambda)|)/p$
([[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]).

1. **Simple heads.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda\ne0$ is

   $S^\lambda_k$, whose unique maximal submodule is

2. **Pairwise inequivalent.** If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ are both $p$-regular

For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$ where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and read in the twist; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. For a class $m\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and any lift $\widetilde m\in M(\lambda')$, the inverse is $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$, independently of the chosen lift.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

Let $k$ be a splitting field of characteristic $p>0$ (equivalently the residue field of the fixed splitting $p$-modular system, [[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]], [[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]) and let $n\ge0$. Two Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k,S^{\mu}_k$ of $k[S_n]$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ have the same $p$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently the blocks of $k[S_n]$ are indexed by the pairs $(\gamma,w)$ with $\gamma$ a $p$-core, $w\in\mathbb N_0$ and $n=|\gamma|+pw$, and the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ is the pair $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$ with $w_p(\lambda)=(n-|C_p(\lambda)|)/p$ ([[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]).

No choice principle is used.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$ and all its subgroups
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For a partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ let
$$S^\lambda_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z},\qquad R^\lambda=S^\lambda_k\cap(S^\lambda_k)^{\perp},\qquad D^\lambda=S^\lambda_k/R^\lambda$$
be the modular Specht quotient of
[[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]], defined using the reduced
integral tabloid form on $M^\lambda_k$.

1. **Simple heads.** If $\lambda$ is $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda\ne0$ is
   self-dual and absolutely irreducible, and it is the simple head of
   $S^\lambda_k$, whose unique maximal submodule is
   $R^\lambda=\operatorname{rad}(S^\lambda_k)$. If $\lambda$ is not
   $p$-regular, then $D^\lambda=0$.
2. **Pairwise inequivalent.** If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ are both $p$-regular
   and $D^\lambda\cong D^\mu$ as $k[S_n]$-modules, then $\lambda=\mu$.
3. **Complete set.** Every simple $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D^\lambda$
   for exactly one $p$-regular partition $\lambda\vdash n$. Equivalently, as
   $\lambda$ ranges over the $p$-regular partitions of $n$, the modules
   $D^\lambda$ form a complete set of representatives of the isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; in particular the number of simple
   $k[S_n]$-modules equals the number of $p$-regular partitions of $n$.

No absolutely irreducible module outside the family $\{D^\lambda\}$ is
constructed, and the statement asserts nothing about fields that are not
splitting fields for $S_n$. The proof uses no averaging and no division by a
group order, and the case $n=0$ and characteristic $2$ are included.

Let $n\ge 0$ and let $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)\vdash n$ be a partition
with Young diagram $[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Throughout, $S_n$
denotes the symmetric group of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, with $S_0=\{1\}$.

**Standard Young subgroups.** For $1\le i\le k$ let
$$B_i:=\{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+2,\ \dots,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i\}$$
be the $i$-th **block** of $\lambda$. The blocks are consecutive intervals of
integers, they are pairwise disjoint, each has $|B_i|=\lambda_i$, and together
they partition $\{1,\dots,n\}$. The **standard Young subgroup** of type
$\lambda$ is
$$S_\lambda:=\{\,\sigma\in S_n:\sigma(B_i)=B_i\text{ for every }1\le i\le k\,\}.$$
This is a subgroup of $S_n$, namely the direct product
$S(B_1)\times\cdots\times S(B_k)$ of the symmetric groups of the individual
blocks, each acting on its block and fixing the remaining entries pointwise;
as in [[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]], the product
decomposition is unique because the blocks are pairwise disjoint and cover
$\{1,\dots,n\}$, so $|S_\lambda|=\lambda_1!\cdots\lambda_k!$. A **Young
subgroup of type $\lambda$** is a subgroup of $S_n$ conjugate to
$S_\lambda$. For $k=0$, that is for $\lambda=\varnothing$ and $n=0$, there are
no blocks and $S_\varnothing=S_0=\{1\}$.

**Row equivalence and tabloids.** Let $t$ and $u$ be $\lambda$-tableaux
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). We say that $t$ and $u$
are **row equivalent**, and write $t\sim u$, when they have the same row sets:
for every row $i$,
$$\{\,t(i,j):1\le j\le\lambda_i\,\}=\{\,u(i,j):1\le j\le\lambda_i\,\}.$$
Equivalently, $t\sim u$ if and only if $u=\rho\cdot t$ for some $\rho\in R_t$:
if $u=\rho\cdot t$ then $\rho$ merely permutes the entries inside each row of
$t$, and conversely, if the row sets agree, then
$\rho(t(i,j)):=u(i,j)$ defines a permutation $\rho$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ that
preserves each row set of $t$, so $\rho\in R_t$ and $\rho\cdot t=u$. Hence
$\sim$ is an equivalence relation on the $\lambda$-tableaux, and the
equivalence class
$$\{t\}:=\{\,u:u\sim t\,\}=\{\,\rho\cdot t:\rho\in R_t\,\}$$
is the **tabloid** of $t$. We draw $\{t\}$ as the diagram $[\lambda]$ filled
with the entries of $t$ and bars between the rows, recording that the order of
the entries inside a row is forgotten. A tabloid is **standard** when it
contains a standard tableau.

**The permutation module.** Let $\Omega_\lambda$ be the finite set of
$\lambda$-tabloids. For $\sigma\in S_n$ and a tabloid $\{t\}$ define
$$\sigma\cdot\{t\}:=\{\sigma\cdot t\}.$$
This is well defined: if $t,u$ are $\lambda$-tableaux with $t\sim u$, then the
row sets of $\sigma\cdot u$ are the $\sigma$-images of the row sets of $u$,
which are the $\sigma$-images of the row sets of $t$, and these are exactly
the row sets of $\sigma\cdot t$
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]); so
$\sigma\cdot u\sim\sigma\cdot t$ and the tabloids $\{\sigma\cdot u\}$ and
$\{\sigma\cdot t\}$ coincide. Because the action on tableaux is a left action,
the induced rule on tabloids satisfies $\mathrm{id}\cdot\{t\}=\{t\}$ and
$\sigma\cdot(\tau\cdot\{t\})=(\sigma\tau)\cdot\{t\}$, so $S_n$ acts on
$\Omega_\lambda$ from the left. The **Young permutation module** attached to
$\lambda$ is the complex vector space
$$M^\lambda:=\mathbb C^{(\Omega_\lambda)}$$
with the tabloids as basis, again written $\{t\}$ for the basis vector of the
tabloid $\{t\}$, equipped with the linear extension of the action above:
$$\sigma\cdot\sum_{\{t\}\in\Omega_\lambda}a_{\{t\}}\,\{t\}:=\sum_{\{t\}\in\Omega_\lambda}a_{\{t\}}\,\{\sigma\cdot t\}.$$
This is the permutation representation of $S_n$ on the finite set
$\Omega_\lambda$ ([[def-trivial-regular-and-permutation-representations]]),
so $M^\lambda$ is a finite-dimensional complex representation of $S_n$.

**The stabilizer of a tabloid.** For every $\lambda$-tableau $t$ one has
$$\sigma\cdot\{t\}=\{t\}\iff \sigma\cdot t\sim t\iff \sigma\in R_t,$$
so the stabilizer in $S_n$ of the tabloid $\{t\}$ is exactly the row
stabilizer $R_t$ ([[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]]). The action
on $\Omega_\lambda$ is transitive: given tabloids $\{t\}$ and $\{s\}$, the
permutation $\sigma$ determined by $\sigma(t(i,j)):=s(i,j)$ satisfies
$\sigma\cdot t=s$, hence $\sigma\cdot\{t\}=\{s\}$. In particular, for the
**standard row-filled $\lambda$-tableau** $t_0$, whose row $i$ carries the
entries of $B_i$ in increasing order, the row sets of $t_0$ are precisely the
blocks $B_1,\dots,B_k$, so $R_{t_0}=S_\lambda$ and the stabilizer of the
tabloid $\{t_0\}$ is the standard Young subgroup $S_\lambda$.

Let $n\ge 0$, let $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $t$ be a $\lambda$-tableau
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). Use the left action of
$S_n$ on tableaux, tabloids, and $M^\lambda$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]). For each
$\gamma\in C_t$, let $\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)$ be its inversion sign in
$S_n$. The order-preserving relabelling
$\iota_n:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, $i\mapsto i-1$, carries each
inversion pair $(i,j)$ bijectively to $(i-1,j-1)$; thus this sign is exactly
the published inversion sign on the finite ordinal
([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). For $n=0$, both groups are
trivial and the sign is $1$.

The **column antisymmetrizer**, **polytabloid**, and **Specht space** are
$$\kappa_t:=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\gamma\quad\in\mathbb C[S_n],\qquad e_t:=\kappa_t\cdot\{t\}\quad\in M^\lambda,\qquad S^\lambda:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{e_s:s\text{ is a }\lambda\text{-tableau}\}.$$
The elements of the sum are in the finite subgroup $C_t$, and each acts by the
declared left action on the tabloid basis, so these are well-defined finite
expressions.

For every tableau, $C_t\cap R_t=\{1\}$: a permutation in both stabilizers
preserves the row and column of each entry, and each row-column intersection
contains at most one node. Thus $\gamma\{t\}$ are distinct as $\gamma$ ranges
over $C_t$, and the coefficient of $\{t\}$ in $e_t$ is $1$. In particular,
$e_t\ne0$. When $n=0$, the empty tableau has $C_t=\{1\}$, so
$\kappa_t=1$, $e_t=\{\varnothing\}$, and $S^\varnothing=\mathbb C$.

derivations.claim: The labels and their cores. The hook-length diagrams of the three partitions of $3$ are $3,2,1$ for $(3)$; $3,1$ in the first row and $1$ in the second for $(2,1)$; and $3,2,1$ vertically for $(1,1,1)$. In each case there is exactly one hook of length $3$ and removing its rim hook leaves the empty partition, so all three partitions have $3$-core $\varnothing$; conversely any partition of $3$ with core $\varnothing$ is one of these, since a partition whose core has size $3$ is its own core, and $\varnothing$ has size $0=3-3$. Dominance orders them as $(3)\rhd(2,1)\rhd(1,1,1)$.

Compute the Weyl matrix directly. First work over $\mathbb F_3$ with lift $R=\mathbb Z_{(3)}$, $\hat q=1$, so the only nonzero hook valuation at rank three is $v([3]_1)=1$. The conjugate beta sequence of $(3)$ is $(3,2,1)$. Its hook pairs $(3,2)$ and $(3,1)$ give the balanced sequences $(5,0,1)$ and $(4,2,0)$, of sorted shapes $(1,1,1)$ with sign $-1$ and $(2,1)$ with sign $+1$, respectively. The other pair has coefficient zero. Thus its positive sum is $[W^{(2,1)}]-[W^{(1,1,1)}]$. For $(2,1)$, beta $(4,2,0)$ and its only nonzero pair $(3,1)$ give $(5,1,0)$, shape $(1,1,1)$ with sign $+1$, so its positive sum is $[W^{(1,1,1)}]$. The column shape has no row pair and zero positive sum, hence $W^{(1,1,1)}=L^{(1,1,1)}$. Positivity and $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$ then show that $W^{(2,1)}(1)=L^{(1,1,1)}$ and every higher submodule is zero, giving $[W^{(2,1)}]=[L^{(2,1)}]+[L^{(1,1,1)}]$. Substitute into the first sum to get $[L^{(2,1)}]$; the same argument gives $[W^{(3)}]=[L^{(3)}]+[L^{(2,1)}]$. This proves exactly the displayed complete Weyl matrix. Scalar extension to any original field $F$ of characteristic three preserves the Weyl modules/forms and the composition series, since all Schur simple heads are absolutely simple by [F2].

Determine the specific corner images directly. The group row symmetrizer $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}w$ satisfies $x_{(3)}^2=6x_{(3)}$, so its rank-one Murphy form is zero in characteristic three. In the rank-one column cell the generator is $1$ and its square coefficient is $1$; the higher ideal contains $1+T_1$ and $1+T_2$ (the latter is a conjugate of the former), so this cell and its nonzero form quotient are the sign module. For the middle cell put $x=1+T_1$, $c_0=x$ and $c_1=xT_2$ modulo the higher row ideal. Its row symmetrizer satisfies $x_{(3)}=x+xT_2+xT_2T_1$, so $c_1T_1=-c_0-c_1$ while $c_0T_1=c_0$; and $T_2^2=1$ gives $c_0T_2=c_1$, $c_1T_2=c_0$. Thus its generator matrices are $M_1=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\-1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $M_2=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The independent cell products $x^2=2x$, $xT_2x=x_{(3)}-x\equiv-x$ and $xT_2^2x=2x$ give $G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ over $F$. Its radical is the line $(1,-1)$; modulo it both generators act by $1$, so $D_{\mathrm M}^{(2,1)}$ is the nonzero trivial module. These two simple images are distinct since $1\ne-1$. The exact corner/form identity [F3] therefore kills precisely $L^{(3)}$ among the three labels. Projecting the Weyl matrix just proved gives all displayed Murphy Specht rows over the original $F$, without any general finite-$e$ nonzero-label criterion.

Dipper-James rows and the direct group computation. Conjugating the partitions $(3)\leftrightarrow(1,1,1)$, $(2,1)\leftrightarrow(2,1)$ and applying the signed $\theta$-pullback to every Hecke module, the rows of step 3.1 become $[S^{(1,1,1)}]=[D^{(2,1)}]$, $[S^{(2,1)}]=[D^{(2,1)}]+[D^{(3)}]$ and $[S^{(3)}]=[D^{(3)}]$ in the $3$-regular labels, that is, the matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with rows $(3),(2,1),(1,1,1)$ and columns $(3),(2,1)$. For the independent direct check, put $w:=e_t+e_u=v_3-v_1+v_2-v_1=v_1+v_2+v_3$ in characteristic $3$: then $w\ne0$ spans a one-dimensional submodule, since $\sigma\cdot v_i=v_{\sigma(i)}$ gives $\sigma\cdot w=w$ for every $\sigma\in S_3$, so it realises the trivial module; and in the quotient, $(12)\cdot e_t+e_t=(v_3-v_2)+(v_3-v_1)=2v_3-v_1-v_2=3v_3-w\equiv0$ shows that $(12)$ acts by $-1$, so the quotient is the sign module. With $S^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$, $S^{(1,1,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$ by [F5], and $D^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$, $D^{(2,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$ by [F4], the direct rows of $S^{(3)},S^{(2,1)},S^{(1,1,1)}$ are $(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$, matching the matrix obtained from the Schur functor entry by entry.

For all $1\le i,j\le n$ one has $X_iX_j=X_jX_i$ in $\mathbb Z[S_n]$, hence in
$R[S_n]$ for every commutative ring $R$; that is, the Jucys-Murphy elements
commute pairwise, and the subalgebra they generate is commutative.

the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $I_1,\ldots,I_r$ be pairwise comaximal ideals, where $r\ge1$. Then the canonical map
$$ R\longrightarrow \prod_{i=1}^r R/I_i,\qquad x\longmapsto(x+I_1,\ldots,x+I_r) $$
is surjective, its kernel is $\bigcap_{i=1}^r I_i$, and
$$ \bigcap_{i=1}^r I_i=\prod_{i=1}^r I_i. $$
Equivalently,
$$ R/\prod_{i=1}^r I_i\cong\prod_{i=1}^r R/I_i. $$

Fix a splitting $p$-modular system $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ for a finite group $G$.
A **$p$-block idempotent** is a primitive central idempotent of $\mathcal O G$
or, after reduction, of $kG$.

If $e$ is such an idempotent, the corresponding **block** is the two-sided
ideal

$$B=\mathcal OGe\qquad\text{or}\qquad B=kGe.$$

The primitive central idempotents are pairwise orthogonal and sum to $1$, so
the algebra splits as a direct product of its block summands.
