$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence, after deleting the zero entries, a terminal word is
$+^a-^b$ for some $a,b\ge0$; cancelled positions remain in their original
places and need not form a contiguous block. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. Uniqueness follows
by induction on the number of nonzero entries. A terminal word admits no
step. Otherwise, two distinct first steps commute and reach a common word
after one further step each. All these successor words have fewer nonzero
entries, so the induction hypothesis identifies their terminal words. Thus
any two reduction sequences have the same terminal word; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.
It has no good node and its cogood $0$-node is $(1,1)$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

Fix a residue $i$ and a partition $\lambda$, and write the **signature** of $\lambda$ at $i$ as the word in the symbols $+$ (addable $i$-node) and $-$ (removable $i$-node) whose letters are the addable and removable $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ read in the fixed increasing-content order of [[def-the-node-order-and-n-i-exponents-for-fock-space]]. Reduce the word by cancelling adjacent pairs $-+$ as long as such a pair remains. The surviving minus letters are called **normal removable** $i$-nodes, and the first surviving minus is the **good node** of $\lambda$ for $e_i$; the surviving plus letters are called **conormal addable** $i$-nodes, and the last surviving plus is the **cogood node** for $f_i$. If no sign of the required type survives, the corresponding operator is $0$ on $|\lambda\rangle$. Equivalently, reading the signature in decreasing content with the reversed symbols, one cancels $+-$ and takes the good node as the last surviving $-$ and the cogood node as the first surviving $+$.

The whole level-one Fock module has the crystal basis $(F_0,B_F)$ with $F_0=\bigoplus_{\lambda}\mathbb Z[q]|\lambda\rangle$ and $B_F=\{|\lambda\rangle+qF_0:\lambda\text{ a partition}\}$. The normalized Kashiwara operators remove the good normal $i$-node and add the cogood conormal $i$-node of the corrected signature of [[def-good-and-cogood-nodes-by-residue-signature-reduction]], and $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ are the surviving minus/plus counts. The graph is a graph on all partitions, not only regular ones; its empty connected component is precisely the set of $e$-regular partitions, while the $e$-restricted labels belong to the transposed model. A pole or a unique Chevalley term does not determine a crystal arrow.

derivations.claim: For every partition $\mu$ and every color $i$, the selection operations of the two readings correspond under transposition.
There is no naming-polarity swap between the two conventions:
The transported normalized operators on $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ are given on all partitions by the modular signature rule.
Weights transform by the reflection.
Restricted case.
Finally, the arrows are not read off from ordinary Chevalley coefficients.

boundaries.evidence: At the vacuum both readings have the single node (1,1) of residue 0, which step 1.1 maps to the unique node on the transposed side, so the arrow tables agree at the empty partition.
Zero values are covered by the count agreement of step 1.1: epsilon_i(mu) = 0 exactly when epsilon_{-i}(mu-prime) = 0, so both sides of the arrow identity vanish together.
Single surviving signs are selected by the first- and last-surviving rules, whose coincidence under conjugation is the position-by-position identification of step 2.1.
At e = 2 the color reflection is the identity on Z/2, so the dictionary reduces to step 1.2's color-fixed comparison without a separate case.
The first surviving - and last surviving + are the endpoint selections compared in step 2.1, and the reversal of step 3.2 exchanges exactly these endpoints.
No choice occurs: step 2.1 reconstructs the transported normalized operators from the explicit conjugation by J, and the selections are deterministic.
One direction of the stated zero equivalence is step 1.1's count identity: epsilon_i(mu) = 0 forces epsilon_{-i}(mu-prime) = 0.
The converse direction is step 1.1 read in the other direction, since the count identity is symmetric between mu and mu-prime.

citations.quote: Fix a finite integer $e \ge 2$ and charge $0$, with the independent-root affine Cartan datum, its lattices and its diagram reflection $\tau$ fixed as in [[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]: $I = \mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}$, simple roots $\alpha_i$, fundamental weights $\Lambda_i$, $\delta$, and $\tau(i) = -i$. A *node* is a pair $(r,c) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, and the *residue* of a node is $\operatorname{res}(r,c) := c - r \bmod e$; this is the level-one, charge-$0$ specialization of the residue used in [[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]. We use the English convention (rows increase downwards) and the node language of [[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] and [[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. A partition $\lambda$ is **$e$-regular** if every positive integer occurs as a part of $\lambda$ fewer than $e$ times, and **$e$-restricted** if $\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1} < e$ for every $a \ge 1$, the sequence being padded by trailing zeros; these are the prime-case notions of [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $e$ in place of the prime $p$. A column of height $e$ is allowed in an $e$-restricted partition. The two classes are exchanged by conjugation: $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular (step 2.1 below). **The modular (restricted) signature.** Let $\lambda$ be a partition and $i \in I$. The $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ are its addable and removable nodes of residue $i$; list them *top to bottom*, that is by increasing row index and then increasing column index, obtaining $A_1,\dots,A_n$, and form the word $\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m = +$ if $A_m$ is addable and $\sigma_m = -$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r < s$ with $\sigma_r = -$, $\sigma_s = +$ and $\sigma_{r+1} = \dots = \sigma_{s-1} = 0$, replace $\sigma_r,\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies above a $+$. The survivors are the *normal* removable and *conormal* addable $i$-nodes; write $\varepsilon_i(\lambda)$ and $\varphi_i(\lambda)$ for their numbers. If $\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *good* $i$-node is the removable node belonging to the first surviving $-$, and $\tilde e_i\lambda := \lambda$ with that node deleted; if $\varphi_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *cogood* $i$-node is the addable node belonging to the last surviving $+$, and $\tilde f_i\lambda$ is $\lambda$ with that node added (otherwise the respective partial operator is undefined). This is Kleshchev's reduced $i$-signature at charge $0$ and level one, with good $=$ top normal and cogood $=$ bottom conormal. **This is the reading used for the restricted (symmetric-group) model**, in which the labels of the level-one basic module are the $e$-restricted shapes; Fayers' equivalent formulation reads the same list with the opposite cancellation and extracts the last surviving $- $ and first surviving $+$, and his increasing-column model of the $e$-restricted labels is the basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$. **The linear (symmetric-group) model and the transport $J$.** Let $$F_{\mathrm{QG}} = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \mathbb{Q}(q)\,|\lambda\rangle$$ be the charge-$0$ level-one partition Fock space with $\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$, where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of nodes of $[\lambda]$ of residue $i$, and with the declared finite node operators $F_i$, $E_i$, $K_h$, $K_d$ and the wedge bar $\psi$ of [[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]] (the operators act on *all* partitions). The **symmetric-group model** $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ is the same $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-vector space with the basis relabelled $M_\lambda := |\lambda'\rangle$; equivalently, $J : F_{\mathrm{sym}} \to F_{\mathrm{QG}}$ is the $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism $$J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle \qquad (\lambda \text{ a partition}),$$ with the field map $q \mapsto q$ (not $q \mapsto q^{-1}$). Transport the structure along $J$: $$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J \quad (h \in P^\vee), \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} \psi J,$$ and give $M_\lambda$ the weight $\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda) := \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The transported operators are defined on the ambient basis of *all* partitions. With $A := \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$ and the local ring $A_0 := \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}(q) : f \text{ is regular at } q = 0 \,\}$, the **standard chart** of the symmetric-group model is $$(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}} := \bigoplus_{\lambda} A_0\, M_\lambda ;$$ the full ambient model is indexed by all partitions, while its basic component in this convention is carried by the $e$-restricted shapes (the comparison with the QG model is made by the results of this page). **Label dictionaries and boundaries.** The conjugation map $C : \lambda \mapsto \lambda'$ exchanges the $e$-restricted and the $e$-regular partitions, preserves the addable/removable *type* of each node and negates residues; it is a comparison map *between* the restricted and the regular models, not an involution of one label set, and it is not the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of Kleshchev's Theorem 11.8, which fixes the restricted label set and negates residues along a good-node path. In the symmetric-group regime (ground field of characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so that $e = p$ is prime) the $e$-restricted partitions are the labels of the simple modules in the dual-Specht convention and the $e$-regular partitions those of James, the two dictionaries being related by $D(\lambda) \cong D^{\lambda'} \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, equivalently $D^\mu \cong D(\mu') \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ for $e$-regular $\mu$ ([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]); for a general Hecke parameter the finite integer $e \ge 2$ is its quantum characteristic (the smallest positive $e$ with $1 + \xi + \dots + \xi^{e-1} = 0$) and need not be prime, so the general finite-$e$ crystal labels are not called symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". At quantum characteristic $e = 0$ (no such positive integer exists, colors $\mathbb{Z}$) no finite affine datum is present: every level-one partition is a crystal label, and no weight formula or finite affine statement is made in this boundary.

Consider the modular reading on the one hand (the top-to-bottom residue signature with good $=$ first surviving $-$ and cogood $=$ last surviving $+$ of [[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]], whose operators delete the good node and add the cogood node on $e$-restricted labels) and the level-one Fock crystal $\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_i$, $\tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_i$ on the other. Conjugation $C(\lambda) = \lambda'$ sends the modular operators on $e$-restricted partitions onto the normalized operators of the **empty connected component** of the QG full partition Fock crystal, with the colors negated: $$C\,\tilde e_i\lambda = \tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}C\lambda, \qquad C\,\tilde f_i\lambda = \tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}C\lambda \qquad (\lambda\ e\text{-restricted}),$$ including the zero values: the left side is zero exactly when the right side is. The survivor counts are the same on both sides, $\varepsilon_i(\lambda) = \varepsilon_{-i}(\lambda')$ and $\varphi_i(\lambda) = \varphi_{-i}(\lambda')$, and the weight transforms by the diagram reflection, $\operatorname{wt}(\lambda') = \tau(\operatorname{wt}(\lambda))$. With the transported full module $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ of [[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]], the modular signatures likewise give its normalized operators on **all** partitions (the transported operators $J^{-1}\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}J$, $J^{-1}\tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}J$), and the restricted subset of that full crystal is its basic component. In both conventions good means removable (deletion, $\tilde e$) and cogood means addable (addition, $\tilde f$): there is no opposite naming-polarity dictionary exchanging deletion with addition. Ordinary Chevalley coefficients, especially negative powers such as $q^{-1}$, do not define these arrows.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function > ([[def-choice-function]]). Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty, there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for all $S \in \mathcal{F}$. An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if $X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$. Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that $f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

With the declared use of the Axiom of Choice in the general integrable-module decomposition, the empty connected component of the full partition crystal of [[thm-the-crystal-of-level-one-fock-space-is-the-good-node-partition-graph]] is the canonical highest weight crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$, with exactly the $e$-regular labels. Its module is $M=U_q(\mathfrak g)|\varnothing\rangle$ and its lower $A_0$-lattice is $M\cap F_0$; it occurs once. More precisely $$F=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}V(\Lambda_0-k\delta)^{\oplus p(k)},$$ a locally weight-finite indexed direct sum in which $p(k)$ is the number of ordinary partitions of $k$; consequently $\mathrm{ch}\,F=\mathrm{ch}\,V(\Lambda_0)\prod_{r\ge1}(1-e^{-r\delta})^{-1}$. A highest **crystal** label need not be a highest **field** standard vector, and the ambient canonical basis need not split these summands.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$. Every $p$-restricted partition $\mu$ of $d$ is obtained from the empty partition by $d$ successive cogood additions: there are residues $i_1,\dots,i_d$ with $$\mu=	ilde f_{i_d}\cdots	ilde f_{i_1}\varnothing;$$ equivalently, every $p$-restricted $\mu
e\varnothing$ has at least one good node, and successive good deletions carry $\mu$ to $\varnothing$ ([[def-good-node-and-cogood-node-crystal-operators]], [[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). Hence, in the graph whose vertices are the $p$-restricted partitions and whose edges join $
u$ to $	ilde f_i
u$ for every $i$ for which the operator is defined, the empty partition is the unique vertex of rank $0$ and every vertex is reached from it; dually every vertex reaches the empty partition by successive good deletions. The argument is choice-free.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $L_1,\dots,L_n\in kS_n$
be the Jucys-Murphy elements $L_r=\sum_{s<r}(s,r)$ of the symmetric group
algebra ([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]). Recall
that they commute pairwise
([[cor-jucys-murphy-elements-commute-pairwise]]), and for $r\le n$ the
element $L_r$ lies in the subalgebra $kS_r\subseteq kS_n$ and therefore
commutes with $S_{r-1}$.

**(i) Primary idempotents.** In the commutative subalgebra
$k[L_1,\dots,L_n]\subseteq kS_n$ the minimal polynomial of each $L_r$ on the
regular module splits into linear factors $X-a$ with $a$ in the prime field
$\mathbb F_p\subseteq k$, and the commuting family admits the following
simultaneous primary decomposition. There are pairwise orthogonal idempotents
$P_{r,a}\in k[L_r]\subseteq k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$, indexed by $r\in\{1,\dots,n\}$
and $a\in\mathbb F_p$, with
$$\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p}P_{r,a}=1,\qquad P_{r,a}P_{r,b}=\delta_{a,b}P_{r,a},$$
such that for every finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module $M$ the action of
$P_{r,a}$ on $M$ is the projection onto the generalized eigenspace
$M_{r,a}=\{m\in M:(L_r-a)^Nm=0\text{ for }N\gg0\}$. The $P_{r,a}$ for
different $r$ commute, and for each sequence $\mathbf i=(i_1,\dots,i_n)$
with entries in $\mathbb F_p$ the products
$$e(\mathbf i):=\prod_{r=1}^nP_{r,i_r}\ \in\ k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$$
are pairwise orthogonal idempotents with $\sum_{\mathbf i}e(\mathbf i)=1$ and
$e(\mathbf i)M=M_{\mathbf i}$, the simultaneous generalized weight space
$M_{\mathbf i}=\{m:(L_r-i_r)^Nm=0\ \forall r,\ N\gg0\}$. Every $P_{r,a}$ and
every $e(\mathbf i)$ is fixed by the antipode $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ of $kS_n$.

**(ii) Content sums and blocks.** The symmetric group $S_n$ permutes the
coordinates of sequences, and two sequences are called *equivalent* when they
differ by a permutation, i.e. when they have the same content (the same
multiset of entries of $\mathbb F_p$). Write $\mathcal C_n=(\mathbb F_p)^n/S_n$ for the set of content classes
(equivalently, multisets of $n$ residues). For $\alpha\in\mathcal C_n$ let
$I_\alpha$ be the set of sequences representing $\alpha$, and put
$$e_\alpha:=\sum_{\mathbf i\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf i)\ \in\ kS_n .$$
Each $e_\alpha$ is a central idempotent of $kS_n$, and distinct $e_\alpha$
are orthogonal; the nonzero $e_\alpha$ are exactly the primitive central
idempotents, that is the block idempotents of $kS_n$
([[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]), and every block
idempotent of $kS_n$ is of the form $e_\alpha$: this last identification of
the content sums with the blocks is the block theorem of Lyle-Mathas and
Brundan recorded as (2.41) in Kleshchev's survey (printed p. 11), with the
content of the block being the content of any of its partitions. The present
item proves the centrality, idempotency and orthogonality of the sums
$e_\alpha$ and then uses only those properties; primitivity and
exhaustiveness are recorded from the cited block theorem, not re-proved here.

**(iii) Residue-summand functors.** For a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module
$M$, a residue $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and a content class
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}$, put
$$e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}:=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i)) \ =\ e_\alpha^{(n-1)}\,P_{n,i},$$
where $(\mathbf j,i)$ denotes concatenation, $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}=\sum_{\mathbf
j\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf j)$ is the content sum computed in $kS_{n-1}$ and
regarded in $kS_n$ through the inclusion $kS_{n-1}\subseteq kS_n$, and
$P_{n,i}\in k[L_n]$. Each $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_n$
commuting with $kS_{n-1}$, the family
$\{e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\}_{i\in\mathbb F_p,\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}$ is a family of pairwise orthogonal
idempotents with $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$, and
$$E_iM:=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M =\bigoplus_{\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$$
is a $kS_{n-1}$-submodule of the restricted module with
$$\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-1}}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iM .$$
Dually, for a finite-dimensional $kS_d$-module $M$ of content
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, i.e. $M=e_\alpha^{(d)}M$, put
$$F_iM:=kS_{d+1}\,e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}M \qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/p),$$
with $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}\in kS_{d+1}$; for a
general finite-dimensional $M$, with the sum indexed by $\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, put
$F_iM:=\bigoplus_\alpha kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$.
Then $\operatorname{Ind}^{S_{d+1}}_{S_d}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}F_iM$,
and all the functors $E_i,F_i$ are additive and exact, preserve
finite-dimensionality, and commute with contragredient duality, because the
projectors are fixed by the antipode. All statements hold at $p=2$; the
construction is choice-free.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, $\mu$ a $p$-restricted partition of $d$ and $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ with $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$; let $A$ be the good $i$-node and $
u=\mu\setminus A$ ([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). For the residue-summand functor $E_i$ of [[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]] the module $E_iD(\mu)$ has simple socle and simple head, both isomorphic to $D(
u)$, and the total (ungraded) multiplicity of $D(
u)$ in $E_iD(\mu)$ is $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$. Thus the Loewy endpoints are simple even though the formal character of $E_iD(\mu)$ may contain the additional normal-node factors of [[thm-normal-node-composition-multiplicities-under-residue-restriction]].

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting $p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of characteristic $p$ for $S_n$ ([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For $\mu\vdash n$ write $S^\mu_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\mu_{\mathbb Z}$ for the field-valued Specht module, $D^\mu=S^\mu_k/R^\mu$ for its modular form quotient ([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]), and let $$S(\mu):=(S^\mu_k)^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(S^\mu_k,k),\qquad (\sigma\cdot f)(x):=f(\sigma^{-1}x)$$ be the **dual Specht module**, with $$D(\mu):=\operatorname{hd}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr) =S(\mu)/\operatorname{rad}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr)$$ its head ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]). Let $\mu'$ be the conjugate partition, and let $S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ be the tensor product of $k[S_n]$-modules with the diagonal action $\sigma\cdot(x\otimes w)=(\sigma\cdot x)\otimes(\sigma\cdot w)$, where $\operatorname{sgn}$ is the one-dimensional sign representation ([[def-sign-representation-and-restriction-of-a-representation]], [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]). 1. **Dual Specht versus sign-twisted conjugate.** If $\mu$ is $p$-restricted (equivalently, by [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]], $\mu'$ is $p$-regular), then $S(\mu)\cong S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$; consequently $S(\mu)$ is nonzero with simple head $$D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn},$$ a nonzero simple $k[S_n]$-module that is self-dual and absolutely irreducible. 2. **Equivalent form for $p$-regular labels.** If $\lambda\vdash n$ is $p$-regular, then $\lambda'$ is $p$-restricted and $$D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')\otimes\operatorname{sgn}.$$ 3. **The two labellings.** The map $\mu\mapsto D(\mu)$ is a bijection from the set of $p$-restricted partitions of $n$ to the set of isomorphism classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; that is, every simple $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D(\mu)$ for exactly one $p$-restricted $\mu\vdash n$. In characteristic $2$ the sign representation is the trivial representation, so the formulas read $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}$ and $D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')$; the transposition is still required, and the two labellings coincide only for self-conjugate partitions. No step divides by a group order or uses averaging, and $n=0$ is included.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $R$ be a commutative ring. In the group ring $R[S_n]$ of the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]], [[def-symmetric-group]], [[def-group-ring]]), where $(j\ k)$ denotes the transposition of the distinct entries $j,k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]), the **Jucys-Murphy elements** are $$X_1:=0,\qquad X_k:=\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}(j\ k)\in R[S_n]\qquad(2\le k\le n).$$ Each $X_k$ is a finite sum of group elements with coefficient $1$, so the formula already defines an element of the integral group ring $\mathbb Z[S_n]$, and its image under the base change $\mathbb Z[S_n]\to R[S_n]$ is the displayed element ([[def-restriction-and-extension-of-scalars]]); for $1\le k\le m\le n$ the element $X_k$ of $R[S_m]$, computed in the subgroup $S_m=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,m\})\subseteq S_n$ of permutations fixing $m+1,\dots,n$, maps to $X_k$ under the inclusion $S_m\hookrightarrow S_n$. Equivalently $X_k=T_k-T_{k-1}$, where $T_k=\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}(i\ j)$ is the sum of all transpositions in $S_k$.

Let $k$ be a field. For the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]), the **sign representation** over $k$ is the one-dimensional representation on $k$ in which $$\sigma \cdot a:=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)a.$$ This is a representation because $\operatorname{sgn}:S_n \to \{\pm 1\}$ is a group homomorphism ([[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]). Now let $\rho:G \to \operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a representation of a group $G$ over $k$, and let $H \le G$ be a subgroup ([[def-subgroup]]). The **restriction** of $\rho$ to $H$ is the representation $$\operatorname{Res}^G_H(V):=\rho|_H:H \longrightarrow \operatorname{GL}(V),\qquad h \longmapsto \rho(h).$$ It has the same underlying vector space $V$ and only forgets the action of the elements outside $H$.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left $A$-module. - Its **radical** is $$ \operatorname{rad}(M)=J(A)M, $$ equivalently the intersection of the maximal submodules, by [[thm-module-radical-is-jacobson-radical-times-the-module]]. - Its **socle** $\operatorname{Soc}(M)$ is the sum of all simple submodules, as in [[def-socle-of-a-module]]. - Its **head** or **top** is the quotient $$ \operatorname{hd}(M):=M/\operatorname{rad}(M), $$ formed using [[def-quotient-module]]. - Its **Loewy series** is the descending radical filtration $$ M\supseteq \operatorname{rad}(M)\supseteq \operatorname{rad}^2(M)\supseteq\cdots $$ together with the corresponding semisimple layers $\operatorname{rad}^i(M)/\operatorname{rad}^{i+1}(M)$. The simple subquotients appearing in the Loewy layers are simple in the sense of [[def-simple-module]].

Fix a finite integer $e \ge 2$ and charge $0$, with the independent-root affine Cartan datum, its lattices and its diagram reflection $\tau$ fixed as in [[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]: $I = \mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}$, simple roots $\alpha_i$, fundamental weights $\Lambda_i$, $\delta$, and $\tau(i) = -i$. A *node* is a pair $(r,c) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, and the *residue* of a node is $\operatorname{res}(r,c) := c - r \bmod e$; this is the level-one, charge-$0$ specialization of the residue used in [[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]. We use the English convention (rows increase downwards) and the node language of [[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] and [[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. A partition $\lambda$ is **$e$-regular** if every positive integer occurs as a part of $\lambda$ fewer than $e$ times, and **$e$-restricted** if $\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1} < e$ for every $a \ge 1$, the sequence being padded by trailing zeros; these are the prime-case notions of [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $e$ in place of the prime $p$. A column of height $e$ is allowed in an $e$-restricted partition. The two classes are exchanged by conjugation: $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular (step 2.1 below). **The modular (restricted) signature.** Let $\lambda$ be a partition and $i \in I$. The $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ are its addable and removable nodes of residue $i$; list them *top to bottom*, that is by increasing row index and then increasing column index, obtaining $A_1,\dots,A_n$, and form the word $\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m = +$ if $A_m$ is addable and $\sigma_m = -$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r < s$ with $\sigma_r = -$, $\sigma_s = +$ and $\sigma_{r+1} = \dots = \sigma_{s-1} = 0$, replace $\sigma_r,\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies above a $+$. The survivors are the *normal* removable and *conormal* addable $i$-nodes; write $\varepsilon_i(\lambda)$ and $\varphi_i(\lambda)$ for their numbers. If $\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *good* $i$-node is the removable node belonging to the first surviving $-$, and $\tilde e_i\lambda := \lambda$ with that node deleted; if $\varphi_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *cogood* $i$-node is the addable node belonging to the last surviving $+$, and $\tilde f_i\lambda$ is $\lambda$ with that node added (otherwise the respective partial operator is undefined). This is Kleshchev's reduced $i$-signature at charge $0$ and level one, with good $=$ top normal and cogood $=$ bottom conormal. **This is the reading used for the restricted (symmetric-group) model**, in which the labels of the level-one basic module are the $e$-restricted shapes; Fayers' equivalent formulation reads the same list with the opposite cancellation and extracts the last surviving $- $ and first surviving $+$, and his increasing-column model of the $e$-restricted labels is the basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$. **The linear (symmetric-group) model and the transport $J$.** Let $$F_{\mathrm{QG}} = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \mathbb{Q}(q)\,|\lambda\rangle$$ be the charge-$0$ level-one partition Fock space with $\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$, where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of nodes of $[\lambda]$ of residue $i$, and with the declared finite node operators $F_i$, $E_i$, $K_h$, $K_d$ and the wedge bar $\psi$ of [[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]] (the operators act on *all* partitions). The **symmetric-group model** $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ is the same $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-vector space with the basis relabelled $M_\lambda := |\lambda'\rangle$; equivalently, $J : F_{\mathrm{sym}} \to F_{\mathrm{QG}}$ is the $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism $$J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle \qquad (\lambda \text{ a partition}),$$ with the field map $q \mapsto q$ (not $q \mapsto q^{-1}$). Transport the structure along $J$: $$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J \quad (h \in P^\vee), \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} \psi J,$$ and give $M_\lambda$ the weight $\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda) := \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The transported operators are defined on the ambient basis of *all* partitions. With $A := \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$ and the local ring $A_0 := \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}(q) : f \text{ is regular at } q = 0 \,\}$, the **standard chart** of the symmetric-group model is $$(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}} := \bigoplus_{\lambda} A_0\, M_\lambda ;$$ the full ambient model is indexed by all partitions, while its basic component in this convention is carried by the $e$-restricted shapes (the comparison with the QG model is made by the results of this page). **Label dictionaries and boundaries.** The conjugation map $C : \lambda \mapsto \lambda'$ exchanges the $e$-restricted and the $e$-regular partitions, preserves the addable/removable *type* of each node and negates residues; it is a comparison map *between* the restricted and the regular models, not an involution of one label set, and it is not the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of Kleshchev's Theorem 11.8, which fixes the restricted label set and negates residues along a good-node path. In the symmetric-group regime (ground field of characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so that $e = p$ is prime) the $e$-restricted partitions are the labels of the simple modules in the dual-Specht convention and the $e$-regular partitions those of James, the two dictionaries being related by $D(\lambda) \cong D^{\lambda'} \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, equivalently $D^\mu \cong D(\mu') \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ for $e$-regular $\mu$ ([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]); for a general Hecke parameter the finite integer $e \ge 2$ is its quantum characteristic (the smallest positive $e$ with $1 + \xi + \dots + \xi^{e-1} = 0$) and need not be prime, so the general finite-$e$ crystal labels are not called symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". At quantum characteristic $e = 0$ (no such positive integer exists, colors $\mathbb{Z}$) no finite affine datum is present: every level-one partition is a crystal label, and no weight formula or finite affine statement is made in this boundary.

This proves part 1 of the Statement:

For part 2, the full $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ has all partitions as vertices and its module is the transport of the modules of [F3], so its field decomposition is $F_{\mathrm{sym}} \cong \bigoplus_{k\ge0} V
Part 3, the James labels and the socle formula.

boundaries.evidence: The empty partition is the highest vertex of the component, reached by zero cogood additions, and step 1.1 identifies it as the J-image of the vacuum.
The quantum-characteristic boundary e = 0 is disposed of separately in step 5.1 and is excluded from the finite affine claims of steps 1.1-4.2.
The level-one constants appear as p(0) = p(1) = 1 in step 4.1's decomposition, and the one-dimensional top weight space is the start of step 2.1.
The prime case includes p = 2, where the sign representation is trivial and -i = i over Z/2, and step 4.2's sign-twist argument covers it without change.
The component's lowest vertex is the vacuum and its full vertex set is identified in step 3.1; every restricted shape is an endpoint of some cogood-addition chain by step 2.1.
The axiom of choice is consumed exactly through the decomposition theorem recorded in step 4.1; steps 1.1-3.1 are choice-free transports.
One direction of the component identification is step 1.1: every vertex of the empty component transposes to an e-restricted shape.
The converse is step 2.1: every e-restricted shape is generated from the empty partition by cogood additions and hence lies in the component.

citations.quote:
There is an explicit semi-infinite wedge bar $\psi$ with the vacuum fixed,
coefficient bar $q\mapsto q^{-1}$ and $U_q$/bar compatibility, whose restriction
to $M=V(\Lambda_0)$ is the normalized highest module bar. On **all** partitions
its integral triangular correction is

$$G(\lambda)=|\lambda\rangle+\sum_{\mu\ \text{strictly dominated by}\ \lambda}d_{\mu,\lambda}(q)|\mu\rangle, \qquad d_{\mu,\lambda}\in q\mathbb Z[q],$$

with diagonal $1$ and same $e$-core support; the family $\{G(\lambda)\}$ is an
$A$-basis of $F_A$ and an $A_0$-basis of $F_0$, with the actual infinity chart
and balanced $\mathbb Z$-intersection. Exactly the $e$-regular $G(\lambda)$ form
the lower global basis of $M$, identified by the two lower-global-basis
suppliers. The ambient basis is not automatically compatible with the other
field irreducible summands. The transpose equality
$d_{\lambda,\mu}=d_{\mu',\lambda'}$ is **false** in general; the source symmetry
concerns the bar matrix, not $D$. Ambient natural-form dual coefficients use
$(D^{-1})^{\mathsf T}$, and basic upper coefficients require the restricted Gram
inverse and need not be Laurent polynomials.

Fix a finite integer $e \ge 2$. In the symmetric-group convention of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]]:

1. The empty component of the transported full Fock crystal $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$
   is **exactly the set of $e$-restricted partitions**, its operators are the
   modular good-node deletions and cogood-node additions, its weight function is
   $\operatorname{wt}(\lambda) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$, the
   counts $\varepsilon_i$, $\varphi_i$ are the numbers of normal and of
   conormal $i$-nodes, and the component is $B(\Lambda_0)$: every $e$-restricted
   shape is reached from the empty partition by successive cogood additions.
2. The full $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ has all partitions as vertices and is reducible;
   its transported field decomposition is
   $F_{\mathrm{sym}} \cong \bigoplus_{k \ge 0} V(\Lambda_0 - k\delta)^{\oplus p(k)}$
   with $p(k)$ the number of partitions of $k$, so its other vertices are
   exactly the non-restricted shapes.
3. In the symmetric-group regime (algebraically closed field $k$ of
   characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so $e = p$ is prime) the
   $e$-restricted labels $\lambda$ are the simple $kS_d$-modules in the
   dual-Specht convention, and for every $i$ with $\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$
   $$\operatorname{soc}\bigl(E_{-i}D^{\lambda'}\bigr) = D^{(\tilde e_i\lambda)'},$$
   where $D^{\lambda'}$ is the James-labelled simple, $E_{-i}$ the
   residue-summand functor after the sign twist, and $D^{(\tilde e_i\lambda)'}$
   the James label of the deleted shape. That is, the standard $E_{-i}$ is the
   residue functor twisted by the sign representation.
4. At quantum characteristic $e = 0$ (colors $\mathbb{Z}$) every level-one
   partition is a label of the empty $\mathfrak{sl}_\infty$ crystal, there are
   no same-content corner cancellations, and no finite affine datum, weight
   formula or Hecke module statement is made.

General finite-$e$ Hecke crystal labels remain valid, but they are not called
symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". The axiom of choice is used
exactly as declared in the contract, through the highest-weight decomposition of
the full Fock module; the component identification of part 1 is choice-free.

Fix a finite integer $e \ge 2$ and charge $0$, with the independent-root affine
Cartan datum, its lattices and its diagram reflection $\tau$ fixed as in
[[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]: $I = \mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}$, simple
roots $\alpha_i$, fundamental weights $\Lambda_i$, $\delta$, and
$\tau(i) = -i$. A *node* is a pair $(r,c) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, and
the *residue* of a node is $\operatorname{res}(r,c) := c - r \bmod e$; this is
the level-one, charge-$0$ specialization of the residue used in
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]. We use the
English convention (rows increase downwards) and the node language of
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] and
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

A partition $\lambda$ is **$e$-regular** if every positive integer occurs as a
part of $\lambda$ fewer than $e$ times, and **$e$-restricted** if
$\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1} < e$ for every $a \ge 1$, the sequence being padded
by trailing zeros; these are the prime-case notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $e$ in place of the prime
$p$. A column of height $e$ is allowed in an $e$-restricted partition. The two
classes are exchanged by conjugation: $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if
its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular (step 2.1 below).

**The modular (restricted) signature.** Let $\lambda$ be a partition and
$i \in I$. The $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ are its addable and removable nodes of
residue $i$; list them *top to bottom*, that is by increasing row index and then
increasing column index, obtaining $A_1,\dots,A_n$, and form the word
$\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m = +$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m = -$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r < s$ with $\sigma_r = -$,
$\sigma_s = +$ and $\sigma_{r+1} = \dots = \sigma_{s-1} = 0$, replace
$\sigma_r,\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies above a $+$. The survivors
are the *normal* removable and *conormal* addable $i$-nodes; write
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda)$ and $\varphi_i(\lambda)$ for their numbers. If
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *good* $i$-node is the removable node
belonging to the first surviving $-$, and $\tilde e_i\lambda := \lambda$ with
that node deleted; if $\varphi_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *cogood* $i$-node is the
addable node belonging to the last surviving $+$, and $\tilde f_i\lambda$ is
$\lambda$ with that node added (otherwise the respective partial operator is
undefined). This is Kleshchev's reduced $i$-signature at charge $0$ and level
one, with good $=$ top normal and cogood $=$ bottom conormal. **This is the
reading used for the restricted (symmetric-group) model**, in which the labels
of the level-one basic module are the $e$-restricted shapes; Fayers' equivalent
formulation reads the same list with the opposite cancellation and extracts the
last surviving $- $ and first surviving $+$, and his increasing-column model of
the $e$-restricted labels is the basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$.

**The linear (symmetric-group) model and the transport $J$.** Let
$$F_{\mathrm{QG}} = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \mathbb{Q}(q)\,|\lambda\rangle$$
be the charge-$0$ level-one partition Fock space with
$\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$,
where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of nodes of $[\lambda]$ of residue $i$, and
with the declared finite node operators $F_i$, $E_i$, $K_h$, $K_d$ and the wedge
bar $\psi$ of [[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]] (the
operators act on *all* partitions). The **symmetric-group model** $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$
is the same $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-vector space with the basis relabelled
$M_\lambda := |\lambda'\rangle$; equivalently, $J : F_{\mathrm{sym}} \to F_{\mathrm{QG}}$
is the $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism
$$J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle \qquad (\lambda \text{ a partition}),$$
with the field map $q \mapsto q$ (not $q \mapsto q^{-1}$). Transport the
structure along $J$:
$$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J \quad (h \in P^\vee), \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} \psi J,$$
and give $M_\lambda$ the weight
$\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda) := \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The
transported operators are defined on the ambient basis of *all* partitions.
With $A := \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$ and the local ring
$A_0 := \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}(q) : f \text{ is regular at } q = 0 \,\}$, the
**standard chart** of the symmetric-group model is
$$(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}} := \bigoplus_{\lambda} A_0\, M_\lambda ;$$
the full ambient model is indexed by all partitions, while its basic component
in this convention is carried by the $e$-restricted shapes (the comparison with
the QG model is made by the results of this page).

**Label dictionaries and boundaries.** The conjugation map $C : \lambda \mapsto \lambda'$
exchanges the $e$-restricted and the $e$-regular partitions, preserves the
addable/removable *type* of each node and negates residues; it is a comparison
map *between* the restricted and the regular models, not an involution of one
label set, and it is not the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of
Kleshchev's Theorem 11.8, which fixes the restricted label set and negates
residues along a good-node path. In the symmetric-group regime (ground field of
characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so that $e = p$ is prime) the
$e$-restricted partitions are the labels of the simple modules in the
dual-Specht convention and the $e$-regular partitions those of James, the two
dictionaries being related by
$D(\lambda) \cong D^{\lambda'} \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, equivalently
$D^\mu \cong D(\mu') \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ for $e$-regular $\mu$
([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]);
for a general Hecke parameter the finite integer $e \ge 2$ is its quantum
characteristic (the smallest positive $e$ with $1 + \xi + \dots + \xi^{e-1} = 0$)
and need not be prime, so the general finite-$e$ crystal labels are not called
symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". At quantum characteristic
$e = 0$ (no such positive integer exists, colors $\mathbb{Z}$) no finite affine
datum is present: every level-one partition is a crystal label, and no weight
formula or finite affine statement is made in this boundary.

derivations.claim: Finite weight spaces and the ambient form. By [F5] each $V_w$ is finite-dimensional, and $B$ restricts to a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on it with the standard basis orthonormal. The restricted labels $\lambda$ of weight $w$ are finitely many by [F5], so $D_{\mathrm{rect}}$ has finitely many columns, and the corresponding $G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda)$ are linearly independent because they are distinct elements of the lower global basis of $M_{\mathrm{sym}}$ from [F2] (respectively the defining family of [F1] transported).

Support of the transition polynomials. By [F1] the QG coefficients are $1$ on the diagonal, lie in $q\mathbb{Z}[q]$ off it, and vanish unless $
u$ is strictly dominated by $\lambda'$ and has the same $e$-core; transporting, $d_{(\lambda,\lambda)} = 1$, the off-diagonal $d_{(\lambda,\mu)}$ lie in $q\mathbb{Z}[q]$, and they vanish unless $\mu'$ is strictly dominated by $\lambda'$, equivalently $\mu$ strictly dominates $\lambda$, and $\mu$ shares the $e$-core of $\lambda$. For the remaining weight condition: the bar of [F1] reverses the wedge word and multiplies by a scalar read off the residue multiset, hence maps each Fock weight space to itself up to the $q$-semilinear coefficient; the triangular correction recursion producing $G_{\mathrm{QG}}(\lambda')$ from $\psi(|\lambda'angle)$ therefore runs inside the weight space of $|\lambda'angle$, so every standard vector $|
uangle$ occurring in $G_{\mathrm{QG}}(\lambda')$ has the same residue multiset as $\lambda'$; transported, $d_{(\lambda,\mu)} 
e 0$ forces $m_j(\mu') = m_j(\lambda')$ for all $j$, that is, the full reflected residue weight of $\mu$ equals that of $\lambda$.

The ambient upper coordinates. Let $D:=D_{\mathrm{rect}}$, with $D_{\mu\lambda}=d_{(\lambda,\mu)}$. The matrix $H=D^{\mathsf t}D$ is the Gram matrix of the basic lower vectors under the ambient orthonormal form. Since $D(0)$ has distinct coordinate columns, $H(0)=I$ by [F5], proving $\det H\ne0$. The columns of $DH^{-1}$ lie in the column space of $D$, namely $(M_{\mathrm{sym}})_w$, and $(DH^{-1})^{\mathsf t}D=H^{-1}H=I$, so they pair as the dual family. Nondegeneracy of $H$ makes this family unique inside the basic subspace. In the whole ambient space the pairing equations determine a coset modulo the orthogonal complement of the basic subspace. The coefficients $e_{(\lambda,\mu)}=(DH^{-1})_{\mu\lambda}$ are in $\mathbb Q(q)$.

The worked instance at $e = 2$. The weight space of $M_{1,1}$ consists of the standard shapes $(2)$ and $(1,1)$ and of the restricted labels $(1,1)$ only, since $(2)$ is not $2$-restricted. By [F4] the QG lower basis has $G(2) = |2\rangle + q|11\rangle$; transposition gives $2' = (1,1)$ and $(1,1)' = 2$, so $G_{\mathrm{sym}}(1,1) = J^{-1}G(2) = M_{1,1} + qM_2$, whence $D_{\mathrm{rect}} = \binom{q}{1}$ with rows $(2),(1,1)$, $H = D^{\mathsf{t}}D = 1 + q^2$, and $G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(1,1) = \frac{qM_2^* + M_{1,1}^*}{1+q^2}$; the coefficient $\frac{1}{1+q^2}$ is not in $A = \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$, since a Laurent polynomial has no pole at a root of $1+q^2$, so the ambient coordinates are genuinely rational, while the leading term and the integrality of $d$ are as in steps 1.1 and 2.1.

The full ambient dual matrix. On the whole Fock space, $D_{\mathrm{full}}$ is unitriangular by [F1] with off-diagonal entries in $q\mathbb{Z}[q]$; its dual basis with respect to the ambient form $B$ has coefficient matrix the transpose inverse $D_{\mathrm{full}}^{-\mathsf{t}}$, by the same computation as step 2.2 applied to the square unitriangular matrix (here the standard basis of the whole space is orthonormal and the family $\{G(\mu)\}$ is a basis). We claim $D_{\mathrm{full}}^{-1}$ has entries in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$: in every finite truncation the strictly triangular part $N$ of $D_{\mathrm{full}} = 1 + N$ satisfies $N^{m} = 0$ for large $m$, so $(1+N)^{-1} = 1 - N + N^2 - \dots$ is a finite sum with entries in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$; hence $D_{\mathrm{full}}^{-\mathsf{t}}$ is Laurent integral, in contrast with the non-integral ambient coordinates of step 3.1.

The exact integral upper basis and the form identification. On the QG standard frame the ambient form is orthonormal. For an addition $\mu=
u+\gamma$ of residue $i$, the node coefficient of $F_i$ is $q^{N_i^r}$, while that of $q^{-1}K_iE_i$ on the reverse edge is $q^{N_i(
u)-1-N_i^l}$. The splitting identity $N_i^r+N_i^l=N_i(
u)-1$ makes them equal ([[def-the-node-order-and-n-i-exponents-for-fock-space]], [[thm-the-fock-space-node-formulas-satisfy-the-quantum-affine-relations]]). The diagonal toral operators are self-adjoint, and symmetry supplies the reverse $E_i$ identity; thus the ambient form is contravariant for $\sigma(F_i)=q^{-1}K_iE_i$ and $\sigma(E_i)=qF_iK_i^{-1}$. Its restriction to the vacuum basic module is normalized by $B(\varnothing,\varnothing)=1$, and uniqueness of the normalized highest-weight contravariant form identifies it with the QG form ([[def-contravariant-form-on-an-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module]]). The linear relabelling $J$ permutes the orthonormal standard frame and transports the action, so the same identification holds on $M_{\mathrm{sym}}$. Consequently [F3] makes the vectors of step 2.2 the transported upper global basis, free over $A$ in the restricted integral dual lattice and perfectly paired with the lower $A$-span. Their standard-frame coefficients can be rational as in step 3.1; this does not contradict integrality in the upper basis and implies no lower-$A$ selfduality or $A$-unit Gram matrix.

Upper bar and charts. By [F3] the upper bar $\psi^\vee$ fixes each upper basis element, the upper basis comes with its own dual zero and infinity charts whose balanced $\mathbb{Z}$-intersection is the upper lattice, and the upper operators satisfy the exact mixed adjunction with the lower operators, with reductions at $0$ equal to the lower crystal operators; transporting these statements along $J^{-1}$ gives the corresponding upper bar, charts and operators in the symmetric-group convention, distinct from the ordinary lower bar of [F1].

Distinctions and boundary. The construction of steps 1.1 and 2.1 is a **linear** relabelling: $J$ fixes $q$ and only transposes labels, whereas the semilinear involution $|\mu\rangle \mapsto |\mu'\rangle$ of [F4] is the one appearing in adjoint-bar statements, of which LT's symmetry $G^\dagger(\lambda)' = G^-(\lambda')$ is the instance; in particular it does not identify the lower coefficient matrix with its transpose, and by [F1] the equality $d_{\lambda\mu} = d_{\mu'\lambda'}$ for all lower coefficients is false. citations.quote: Fix a finite integer $e \ge 2$ and charge $0$, with the independent-root affine Cartan datum, its lattices and its diagram reflection $\tau$ fixed as in [[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]: $I = \mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}$, simple roots $\alpha_i$, fundamental weights $\Lambda_i$, $\delta$, and $\tau(i) = -i$. A column of height $e$ is allowed in an $e$-restricted partition. The two classes are exchanged by conjugation: $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular (step 2.1 below). **The modular (restricted) signature.** Let $\lambda$ be a partition and $i \in I$. The $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ are its addable and removable nodes of residue $i$; list them *top to bottom*, that is by increasing row index and then increasing column index, obtaining $A_1,\dots,A_n$, and form the word $\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m = +$ if $A_m$ is addable and $\sigma_m = -$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r < s$ with $\sigma_r = -$, $\sigma_s = +$ and $\sigma_{r+1} = \dots = \sigma_{s-1} = 0$, replace $\sigma_r,\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies above a $+$. The survivors are the *normal* removable and *conormal* addable $i$-nodes; write $\varepsilon_i(\lambda)$ and $\varphi_i(\lambda)$ for their numbers. If $\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *good* $i$-node is the removable node belonging to the first surviving $-$, and $\tilde e_i\lambda := \lambda$ with that node deleted; if $\varphi_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *cogood* $i$-node is the addable node belonging to the last surviving $+$, and $\tilde f_i\lambda$ is $\lambda$ with that node added (otherwise the respective partial operator is undefined). This is Kleshchev's reduced $i$-signature at charge $0$ and level one, with good $=$ top normal and cogood $=$ bottom conormal. **This is the reading used for the restricted (symmetric-group) model**, in which the labels of the level-one basic module are the $e$-restricted shapes; Fayers' equivalent formulation reads the same list with the opposite cancellation and extracts the last surviving $- $ and first surviving $+$, and his increasing-column model of the $e$-restricted labels is the basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$. **The linear (symmetric-group) model and the transport $J$.** Let $$F_{\mathrm{QG}} = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \mathbb{Q}(q)\,|\lambda\rangle$$ be the charge-$0$ level-one partition Fock space with $\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$, where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of nodes of $[\lambda]$ of residue $i$, and with the declared finite node operators $F_i$, $E_i$, $K_h$, $K_d$ and the wedge bar $\psi$ of [[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]] (the operators act on *all* partitions). The **symmetric-group model** $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ is the same $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-vector space with the basis relabelled $M_\lambda := |\lambda'\rangle$; equivalently, $J : F_{\mathrm{sym}} \to F_{\mathrm{QG}}$ is the $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism $$J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle \qquad (\lambda \text{ a partition}),$$ with the field map $q \mapsto q$ (not $q \mapsto q^{-1}$). Transport the structure along $J$: $$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J \quad (h \in P^\vee), \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} \psi J,$$ and give $M_\lambda$ the weight $\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda) := \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The transported operators are defined on the ambient basis of *all* partitions. In the symmetric-group regime (ground field of characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so that $e = p$ is prime) the $e$-restricted partitions are the labels of the simple modules in the dual-Specht convention and the $e$-regular partitions those of James, the two dictionaries being related by $D(\lambda) \cong D^{\lambda'} \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, equivalently $D^\mu \cong D(\mu') \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ for $e$-regular $\mu$ ([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]); for a general Hecke parameter the finite integer $e \ge 2$ is its quantum characteristic (the smallest positive $e$ with $1 + \xi + \dots + \xi^{e-1} = 0$) and need not be prime, so the general finite-$e$ crystal labels are not called symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". At quantum characteristic $e = 0$ (no such positive integer exists, colors $\mathbb{Z}$) no finite affine datum is present: every level-one partition is a crystal label, and no weight formula or finite affine statement is made in this boundary.

For a fixed residue $i$ list the addable and removable $i$-nodes of a partition **by increasing content** $c-r$; larger content is read as further right or higher. For an addable $i$-node $\gamma$ of $\lambda$ (so that $\mu=\lambda+\gamma$) define $$N_i^r(\lambda,\gamma):=\#\{\text{addable }i\text{-nodes of }\lambda\text{ with content}>\text{content}(\gamma)\}-\#\{\text{removable }i\text{-nodes of }\lambda\text{ with content}>\text{content}(\gamma)\},$$ and for a removable $i$-node $\gamma$ of $\mu$ (so that $\lambda=\mu-\gamma$) define $N_i^l(\lambda,\mu)$ by the same formula inside the smaller diagram $\lambda=\mu-\gamma$ with $>$ replaced by $<$, always excluding $\gamma$ itself. The constructed node operators on **all** partition vectors make the charge-$0$ partition Fock space $F$ into a $P$-graded integrable module for $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_e)$ with the fixed coproduct and the cyclic Cartan datum: all toral commutation rules and mixed commutators $[E_i,F_j]=\delta_{ij}(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$ hold, and both quantum Serre sums vanish, including the cubic $e=2$ case with $a_{01}=a_{10}=-2$ and $[3]=q^2+1+q^{-2}$. Ordinary standard coefficients may have $q^{-1}$ poles; normalized Kashiwara lattice stability is a separate statement.

Ordinary Chevalley coefficients, especially negative powers such as $q^{-1}$, do not define these arrows.

This is Kleshchev's reduced $i$-signature at charge $0$ and level one, with good $=$ top normal and cogood $=$ bottom conormal. **This is the reading used for the restricted (symmetric-group) model**, in which the labels of the level-one basic module are the $e$-restricted shapes; Fayers' equivalent formulation reads the same list with the opposite cancellation and extracts the last surviving $- $ and first surviving $+$, and his increasing-column model of the $e$-restricted labels is the basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$. **The linear (symmetric-group) model and the transport $J$.** Let $$F_{\mathrm{QG}} = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \mathbb{Q}(q)\,|\lambda\rangle$$ be the charge-$0$ level-one partition Fock space with $\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$, where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of nodes of $[\lambda]$ of residue $i$, and with the declared finite node operators $F_i$, $E_i$, $K_h$, $K_d$ and the wedge bar $\psi$ of [[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]] (the operators act on *all* partitions). The **symmetric-group model** $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ is the same $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-vector space with the basis relabelled $M_\lambda := |\lambda'\rangle$; equivalently, $J : F_{\mathrm{sym}} \to F_{\mathrm{QG}}$ is the $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism $$J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle \qquad (\lambda \text{ a partition}),$$ with the field map $q \mapsto q$ (not $q \mapsto q^{-1}$). Transport the structure along $J$: $$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J \quad (h \in P^\vee), \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} \psi J,$$ and give $M_\lambda$ the weight $\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda) := \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The transported operators are defined on the ambient basis of *all* partitions. With $A := \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$ and the local ring $A_0 := \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}(q) : f \text{ is regular at } q = 0 \,\}$, the **standard chart** of the symmetric-group model is $$(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}} := \bigoplus_{\lambda} A_0\, M_\lambda ;$$ the full ambient model is indexed by all partitions, while its basic component in this convention is carried by the $e$-restricted shapes (the comparison with the QG model is made by the results of this page). **Label dictionaries and boundaries.** The conjugation map $C : \lambda \mapsto \lambda'$ exchanges the $e$-restricted and the $e$-regular partitions, preserves the addable/removable *type* of each node and negates residues; it is a comparison map *between* the restricted and the regular models, not an involution of one label set, and it is not the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of Kleshchev's Theorem 11.8, which fixes the restricted label set and negates residues along a good-node path. In the symmetric-group regime (ground field of characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so that $e = p$ is prime) the $e$-restricted partitions are the labels of the simple modules in the dual-Specht convention and the $e$-regular partitions those of James, the two dictionaries being related by $D(\lambda) \cong D^{\lambda'} \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, equivalently $D^\mu \cong D(\mu') \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ for $e$-regular $\mu$ ([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]); for a general Hecke parameter the finite integer $e \ge 2$ is its quantum characteristic (the smallest positive $e$ with $1 + \xi + \dots + \xi^{e-1} = 0$) and need not be prime, so the general finite-$e$ crystal labels are not called symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". At quantum characteristic $e = 0$ (no such positive integer exists, colors $\mathbb{Z}$) no finite affine datum is present: every level-one partition is a crystal label, and no weight formula or finite affine statement is made in this boundary.

With the declared use of the Axiom of Choice in the general integrable-module decomposition, the empty connected component of the full partition crystal of [[thm-the-crystal-of-level-one-fock-space-is-the-good-node-partition-graph]] is the canonical highest weight crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$, with exactly the $e$-regular labels. Its module is $M=U_q(\mathfrak g)|\varnothing\rangle$ and its lower $A_0$-lattice is $M\cap F_0$; it occurs once. More precisely $$F=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}V(\Lambda_0-k\delta)^{\oplus p(k)},$$ a locally weight-finite indexed direct sum in which $p(k)$ is the number of ordinary partitions of $k$; consequently $\mathrm{ch}\,F=\mathrm{ch}\,V(\Lambda_0)\prod_{r\ge1}(1-e^{-r\delta})^{-1}$. A highest **crystal** label need not be a highest **field** standard vector, and the ambient canonical basis need not split these summands.

**Assume the axiom of choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M$ be a chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight module that is integrable, has finite-dimensional label-weight spaces and weight set contained in a finite union of cones $\lambda-Q_+$ ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]), and let $(L,B)$ be a crystal basis of $M$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]).

(i) **Splitting along the top isotypic part.** Let $\lambda$ be a maximal weight of $M$, put $N_0:=U_q(\mathfrak g)M_\lambda$ and let $N_1$ be the sum of the remaining simple constituents, so that $M=N_0\oplus N_1$ and $N_0\cong V(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$ with $m=\dim M_\lambda$. Then $L=(L\cap N_0)\oplus(L\cap N_1)$, $B=\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_0)/q(L\cap N_0)\bigr)\sqcup\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_1)/q(L\cap N_1)\bigr)$, and both pairs are crystal bases of $N_0$ and $N_1$.

(ii) **Uniqueness.** There is a locally weight-finite indexed family $(\lambda_j)_{j\in J}$ in $P^+$ and an isomorphism of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-modules $\Phi:M\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\bigoplus_{j\in J}V(\lambda_j)$ with $\Phi(L)=\bigoplus_j\mathcal L(\lambda_j)$ and $\Phi$ inducing a bijection $B\to\bigsqcup_j\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$ of crystals. The multiset $\{\lambda_j:j\in J\}$ is the multiset of highest weights of the simple integrable constituents of $M$: the number of $j$ with $\lambda_j=\lambda$ equals the multiplicity $[M:V(\lambda)]$.

(iii) **Components.** Through $\Phi$ the connected components of the crystal $B$ are exactly the canonical highest weight crystals $\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$; each component has a unique highest weight element $b$, of dominant weight $\lambda$, and equals the lowering-generated subcrystal $F(b)$ of [[def-highest-weight-element-and-connected-highest-weight-crystal]]. In particular the crystal graph of any crystal basis of $M$ is determined up to isomorphism by $M$, and no other highest weight elements occur.

**Choice.** The axiom of choice is declared in [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and used to obtain the decomposition of $M$ into simple integrable highest weight modules from [[prop-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-modules-are-semisimple]], which selects a maximal independent family of simple submodules simultaneously. It also permits simultaneous choices of lifts of the finite residue bases in the possibly infinite family of top spaces. After those choices, each lattice and crystal argument is finite and choice-free. No incompatible-axiom branch is used, and no global $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness is assumed. The index set $J$ need not be finite in affine or indefinite type; local weight finiteness means only finitely many summands contribute to any fixed label-weight space.

There is an explicit semi-infinite wedge bar $\psi$ with the vacuum fixed, coefficient bar $q\mapsto q^{-1}$ and $U_q$/bar compatibility, whose restriction to $M=V(\Lambda_0)$ is the normalized highest module bar. On **all** partitions its integral triangular correction is $$G(\lambda)=|\lambda\rangle+\sum_{\mu\ \text{strictly dominated by}\ \lambda}d_{\mu,\lambda}(q)|\mu\rangle, \qquad d_{\mu,\lambda}\in q\mathbb Z[q],$$ with diagonal $1$ and same $e$-core support; the family $\{G(\lambda)\}$ is an $A$-basis of $F_A$ and an $A_0$-basis of $F_0$, with the actual infinity chart and balanced $\mathbb Z$-intersection. Exactly the $e$-regular $G(\lambda)$ form the lower global basis of $M$, identified by the two lower-global-basis suppliers. The ambient basis is not automatically compatible with the other field irreducible summands. The transpose equality $d_{\lambda,\mu}=d_{\mu',\lambda'}$ is **false** in general; the source symmetry concerns the bar matrix, not $D$. Ambient natural-form dual coefficients use $(D^{-1})^{\mathsf T}$, and basic upper coefficients require the restricted Gram inverse and need not be Laurent polynomials.

citations.quote: Let $\mathbb Z[t]$ be the polynomial ring over the integers ([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]]) and let $$S=\{t^k:k\ge0\}.$$ The set $S$ is multiplicative, and the **Laurent polynomial ring** is the principal localisation $$\Lambda_1:=\mathbb Z[t]_S=S^{-1}\mathbb Z[t]$$ ([[def-principal-localisation]], [[def-multiplicative-subset-and-loc

Let $K$ be a field and let $v$ be a discrete valuation on $K$ ([[def-discrete-valuation]]). Its **valuation ring** is $$ V_v:=\{x\in K:v(x)\ge 0\}. $$ This is a valuation ring in the sense of [[def-valuation-ring]]. A **discrete valuation ring** (DVR) is a subring $V\subseteq K$ of the form $V=V_v$ for some discrete valuation $v$ on $K$.

Let $R$ be a ring ([[def-ring]]) with identity $1_R$ and zero $0_R$. For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ let $n \cdot 1_R$ be the additive natural power of $1_R$ in the abelian group $(R,+,0_R)$ ([[def-group-power]], [[def-group]]): thus $0 \cdot 1_R = 0_R$ and $\sigma(n)\cdot 1_R = n \cdot 1_R + 1_R$.

derivations.claim: Reduction to $N$ and to $A/B$. Since $Bt^v$ is a unit of $F[t,t^{-1}]$ with inverse $B^{-1}t^{-v}$ by [F1], the identity $At^u-Bt^v=Bt^v\bigl((A/B)t^N-1\bigr)$ and [F2] give $v_1(At^u-Bt^v)=v_1\bigl((A/B)t^N-1\bigr)$; moreover if $N<0$ then $t^{N}-1=-t^{N}(t^{-N}-1)$ with $-t^{N}$ a unit, so $v_1(t^{N}-1)=v_1(t^{|N|}-1)$ by [F1] and [F2]. [F1, F2]

The case $A=B$, $N=0$. Then $f=At^u-Bt^v=At^u-At^u=0$ by [F1], the zero element of $F[t,t^{-1}]$; since $(t-1)^n\mid0$ for every $n$, the set in the definition of $v_1$ is unbounded and no finite value is assigned. [F1]

The case $A\ne B$. Evaluating the Laurent polynomial $(A/B)t^N-1$ at $t=1$ gives $A/B-1\ne0$, so the factor $t-1$ cannot divide $(A/B)t^N-1$: a product containing $t-1$ would evaluate to $0$ under the ring homomorphism $f\mapsto f(1)$ with $1\mapsto1$. Hence $v_1((A/B)t^N-1)=0$ by [F2], and the reduction of step 1.1 gives $v_1(f)=0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

The case $A=B$, $\operatorname{char}F=0$, $N\ne0$. Here $f=A(t^u-t^v)=At^v(t^N-1)$ with $At^v$ a unit, so by step 1.1 the valuation equals $v_1(t^{|N|}-1)$, while $t^{|N|}-1=(t-1)(1+t+\cdots+t^{|N|-1})$ with second factor evaluating at $t=1$ to $|N|\cdot1_F\ne0$ by [F3] and therefore of valuation $0$ by [F2]; the valuation is additive on this factorisation of the nonzero polynomial $t^{|N|}-1$, so $v_1(f)=1$.
