Let $A$ be a commutative ring and let $z\in A$ be a unit. Fix an integer
$n\ge0$.

**The nondegenerate affine presentation.** The algebra
$H_n^{\mathrm{aff}}(A;z)$ is the $A$-algebra presented by commuting units
$X_1,\dots,X_n$ and generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]) subject to
$$T_r^2=(z-1)T_r+z,\qquad T_rT_{r+1}T_r=T_{r+1}T_rT_{r+1},\qquad T_rT_s=T_sT_r\quad(|r-s|>1),$$
$$T_rX_rT_r=zX_{r+1},\qquad T_rX_s=X_sT_r\quad(s\notin\{r,r+1\}),$$
the last two relations being the Bernstein relation and the distant mixed
commutation, and with $T_r$ invertible as a consequence of its quadratic
relation. For $n=0$ the algebra is $A$.

**The degenerate affine presentation.** The algebra
$H_n^{\deg}(A)$ is the $A$-algebra presented by commuting generators
$x_1,\dots,x_n$ and symmetric-group generators $s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}$ subject to
the Coxeter relations $s_r^2=1$, $s_rs_{r+1}s_r=s_{r+1}s_rs_{r+1}$,
$s_rs_t=s_ts_r$ for $|r-t|>1$ together with the mixed relations
$$s_rx_r=x_{r+1}s_r-1,\qquad s_rx_{r+1}=x_rs_r+1,\qquad s_rx_t=x_ts_r\quad(t\notin\{r,r+1\}).$$

**Auxiliary cyclotomic quotients.** For a monic polynomial
$f(u)=u^{\ell}+a_{\ell-1}u^{\ell-1}+\dots+a_0$ in $A[u]$ of degree $\ell$
impose the single relation $f(X_1)=0$ (respectively $f(x_1)=0$) on the FIRST
polynomial generator and call the resulting quotient the **monic cyclotomic
quotient**; when $\ell=0$, so that $f=1$, the quotient at positive rank is the
zero algebra, while rank zero remains $A$. In the nondegenerate case the
constant term $a_0$ is required to be a unit. The first-strand convention
imposed here (cyclotomic relation on $X_1$, and later induction appending on
the right) is the one used on this page.

**The charged cyclic specialization.** Let $A=F$ be a field, let
$z=q_H\in F^{\times}$ have finite quantum characteristic $e\ge2$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), and let
$I=\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z$ be the cyclic **label set** of residues, with a
dominant cyclic type-A weight $(\lambda_i)_{i\in I}$, $\lambda_i\ge0$, and
$\ell=\sum_i\lambda_i$
([[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]). If $q_H\ne1$ use the
nondegenerate presentation and put $c_i:=q_H^{\,i}$; if $q_H=1$ (which forces
$\operatorname{char}F=e$) use the degenerate presentation and put
$c_i:=i\cdot1_F$. Impose
$$f(z_1)=\prod_{i\in I}(z_1-c_i)^{\lambda_i}$$
on the first generator ($z_1=X_1$ in the nondegenerate branch and $z_1=x_1$ in
the degenerate branch) and write $H_d^\Lambda$ for the resulting **charged
cyclotomic quotient** of rank $d$. This charged finite-$e$ branch is the scope
of the present page; the arbitrary-base affine and monic definitions above
supply its universal PBW and trace proof inputs. The definition itself asserts
no basis, no spectrum, no primitive block decomposition and no
Brundan–Kleshchev isomorphism. The grading variable $v$ of the KLR side is
independent of $q_H$.

**Well-definedness notes.** The nondegenerate parameters $c_i=q_H^i$ are
distinct because $q_H$ has multiplicative order exactly $e$; the degenerate
parameters $c_i=i\cdot1_F$ are distinct because $\operatorname{char}F=e$ makes
$i\cdot1_F\ne j\cdot1_F$ for $0\le i<j<e$. In the nondegenerate branch no
embedding of the label set $\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z$ into $F$ is claimed or used:
$i$ is only a label for the value $q_H^i$. All these definitions are given by
generators, relations and a two-sided quotient ideal and use no choice
principle.

Work over the field $\mathbb C$ and fix an integer $d\ge 0$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[def-commutative-ring]]). Let
$\mathcal F_d$ be the free associative unital $\mathbb C$-algebra on the
$d+(d-1)$ symbols $x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ (for $d=0$ there is only
the unit; for $d=1$ only $x_1$), with its word basis and universal property
([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]), and let
$I_d\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}\mathcal F_d$ be the two-sided ideal
([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]], [[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]])
generated by the following elements:

- $x_ix_j-x_jx_i$ for all $1\le i,j\le d$;
- $s_i^2-1$, $s_is_{i+1}s_i-s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1}$, and $s_is_j-s_js_i$ for
  $|i-j|>1$, for $1\le i,j\le d-1$;
- $s_ix_j-x_js_i$ for $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$, $s_ix_{i+1}-x_is_i-1$, and
  $x_{i+1}s_i-s_ix_i-1$, for $1\le i\le d-1$ and $1\le j\le d$.

The **degenerate affine Hecke algebra** is the quotient $\mathbb C$-algebra
$$H_d:=\mathcal F_d/I_d$$
with unit element written $1$ ([[thm-quotient-ring-laws]]). We keep the symbols
$x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ for their images, and for $w\in S_d$ we write
$w$ for the image in $H_d$ of any word in the $s_i$ representing $w$; this is
independent of the chosen word once the basis theorem below is proved. For
$a\in\mathbb C$, the notation $H_d/(x_1-a)$ means the quotient by the two-sided
ideal generated by $x_1-a$.

The verification below establishes exactly the structure of $H_d$ used
throughout this page: the ordered monomials
$$x_1^{r_1}\cdots x_d^{r_d}w,\qquad r_1,\dots,r_d\ge0,\ w\in S_d,$$
form a $\mathbb C$-basis, so that
$H_d\cong\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C[S_d]$ as a vector
space with polynomial and group-algebra subalgebras
([[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]], [[def-group-ring]]);
$H_0=\mathbb C$ and $H_1=\mathbb C[x_1]$; for every $a$ there is a unique
algebra isomorphism
$$H_d/(x_1-a)\cong\mathbb C[S_d],\qquad x_j\longmapsto a+\sum_{k<j}(k\ j);$$
and total polynomial degree is an algebra filtration whose associated graded is
the semidirect product $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\rtimes\mathbb C[S_d]$ in which
$s_i$ acts by swapping $x_i$ and $x_{i+1}$. The cross relation is
inhomogeneous, so it does not turn $H_d$ into a graded algebra with
$\deg x_i=1$ and $\deg s_i=0$.

derivations.claim: The coefficient completions. A symmetric polynomial in the commuting $x$ is central: the mixed relation gives $s_rf=(\sigma_rf)s_r-(f-\sigma_rf)/(x_r-x_{r+1})$, first on monomials by induction, then on polynomials. A symmetric $f$ has zero correction. The fiber of the elementary symmetric polynomials over their values on $\beta$ consists exactly of the ordered permutations of $\beta$: the coordinates are roots with multiplicities of $\prod_{a\in\beta}(t-a)$. Its radical is the intersection of the finitely many corresponding maximal ideals, by the polynomial factorization and the fact that every coordinate satisfies this monic polynomial. The elementary-symmetric ideal and this radical have cofinal powers, since the fiber is finite dimensional and its radical nilpotent. Chinese remainders and completion therefore give $\mathcal B_\beta$ with local coordinates $x_r-\nu_r$. On the KLR side symmetric dot polynomials are central by [F1], and the same argument at the all-zero fiber shows that its coefficient completion is $\mathcal B_\beta$.

Invertible tables. If $a\ne b$ the integer $a-b$ is a nonzero unit in $k$, so $z^{-1}$ exists as a formal geometric series. In the backward case $a=b+1$, $q=z^{-1}$ has constant $1$. In the other unequal cases $q=1-z^{-1}$ has constant $1-(a-b)^{-1}$, which could vanish only when $a-b=1$, already excluded. Equal colors give constant $1$. For unequal colors $p_{ba}(v,u)=-p_{ab}(u,v)$. Direct multiplication gives $q_{ab}(u,v)q_{ba}(v,u)=1-z^{-2}$ on nonadjacent colors; on a forward arrow it gives $-(z-1)/z^2=(1-z^{-2})/(v-u)$ since $z=-1+u-v$; on a backward arrow it gives $(z+1)/z^2=(1-z^{-2})/(u-v)$ since $z=1+u-v$. Thus $Q_{ab}q_{ab}\sigma(q_{ba})=1-p_{ab}^2$ in all unequal cases, with no division by a nonunit left unresolved.

A concrete KLR action. On $\mathcal B_\beta$, dots multiply and idempotents project. Define $E_r=(\sigma_r-1)/(y_r-y_{r+1})$ on equal adjacent colors. The numerator is divisible by the denominator for polynomials and formal series, so $E_r$ preserves the coefficient algebra. For unequal source colors $(a,b)$ define $\psi_r(fe(\nu))=c_{ab}(y_r,y_{r+1})\sigma_r(f)e(s_r\nu)$, where $c_{ab}(u,v)=v-u$ if $a=b+1$ and $c_{ab}(u,v)=1$ otherwise. These explicit operators prove the local relations in the following five cases.

Quadratic and dot moves. Write $\delta=u-v$. On equal colors $E^2=0$, since $E(f)$ is invariant under $\sigma$, and $Eu-vE=-1$, $Ev-uE=1$ follow by expanding the numerator. On unequal colors the dot moves are permutation identities and $\psi^2=c_{ba}(u,v)c_{ab}(v,u)=Q_{ab}(u,v)$. Indeed these products are $v-u$ on a forward arrow, $u-v$ on a backward arrow, and $1$ off edges. Disjoint crossings commute because their variables and their two-color factors are disjoint. Idempotent moves and commutative dot relations hold by construction.

Three distinct colors. Put $u=y_1,v=y_2,w=y_3$, $s=\sigma_1,t=\sigma_2$, $\rho=sts=tst$, $L=\psi_1\psi_2\psi_1$, $M=\psi_2\psi_1\psi_2$. On a source $(a,b,c)$ with all colors distinct, direct consecutive application of step 3.1 gives both $L(f)$ and $M(f)$ equal to $c_{bc}(u,v)c_{ac}(u,w)c_{ab}(v,w)\rho(f)$ in the $(c,b,a)$ summand. The three pair factors commute. Hence $L=M$ for every edge pattern among three distinct integer colors.

Exactly the first two equal. On $(a,a,b)$, $a\ne b$, put $h=c_{ab}(u,v)c_{ab}(u,w)$. Consecutive application gives $L(f)=h\,stE_1(f)$ and $M(f)=E_2(h\,stf)$. The polynomial $h$ is symmetric in $v,w$, including the backward case $h=(v-u)(w-u)$, so the product rule $E_2(hg)=E_2(h)g+t(h)E_2(g)$ gives $M(f)=hE_2stf$. Finally $E_2st=stE_1$: both sides equal $(\rho-st)/(v-w)$, with the denominator transformed when the permutation lies to its left. Thus $L=M$.

Exactly the last two equal. On $(a,b,b)$, $a\ne b$, put $h=c_{ab}(u,w)c_{ab}(v,w)$. The two words give $L(f)=E_1(h\,tsf)$ and $M(f)=h\,tsE_2(f)$. Here $h$ is symmetric in $u,v$, including $h=(w-u)(w-v)$ when $a=b+1$. The product rule gives $L(f)=hE_1tsf$. The identity $E_1ts=tsE_2=(\rho-ts)/(u-v)$ now yields $L=M$. This explicitly checks the second repeated-neighbor pattern.

Equal outer colors. On $(a,b,a)$, $a\ne b$, full expansion of the single middle divided difference gives $L(f)=c_{ba}(u,v)[c_{ab}(v,w)\rho(f)-c_{ab}(v,u)f]/(u-w)$ and $M(f)=c_{ab}(v,w)[c_{ba}(u,v)\rho(f)-c_{ba}(w,v)f]/(u-w)$. The $\rho(f)$ terms cancel, and step 4.1 gives $(L-M)(f)=[Q_{ab}(w,v)-Q_{ab}(u,v)]f/(u-w)$. Thus the correction is $+1$ for $a\to b$, $-1$ for $a\leftarrow b$, and zero off edges. The displayed expressions have removable denominators because their original numerators come from divided differences; the final quotient is a polynomial.

All three equal. For $\Delta=(u-v)(u-w)(v-w)$, expand the three factors $E=(\sigma-1)/(\text{dot difference})$ in either order. Moving permutations to the right gives the complete identity $E_1E_2E_1=E_2E_1E_2=(\rho-st-ts+s+t-1)/\Delta$. For example the $\rho$ coefficient is $1/\Delta$, the $st$ and $ts$ coefficients are $-1/\Delta$, the $s,t$ coefficients are $1/\Delta$, and the identity coefficient is $-1/\Delta$. Both sides preserve formal series by their original divided-difference formulas, so this rational equality proves their equality without inverting dots in the algebra. This supplies the all-equal case omitted in the cited source.

Faithfulness for the KLR action. Moving dots to the right using step 4.1, and replacing repeated crossings and braid differences using steps 5.1–9.1, spans the presented KLR algebra by $\psi_w f(y)e(\nu)$ for fixed reduced words $w$. Termination uses crossing length: every quadratic reduction or braid correction has smaller length; reduced words for a permutation are connected by the elementary symmetric-group braid moves. In the rational-function action each $\psi_w$ has leading term a nonzero coefficient times $w$, and all other terms have smaller permutation length. Distinct permutations of variables are linearly independent over the rational-function field: a shortest putative relation, evaluated on $fg$ minus one selected automorphism's value on $g$ times its evaluation on $f$, gives a shorter nonzero relation. Hence these spanning monomials are independent. The same triangular argument over fractions of formal series proves faithfulness of the completed action, whose elements are the finite sum over $w,\nu$ with formal coefficient $f$.

Why formal extension is legitimate. There are finitely many $w,\nu$, and each basis vector $\psi_we(\nu)$ has a finite crossing degree. Symmetric positive-degree dots form a central ideal with powers cofinal with dot-degree powers in each coefficient algebra by step 1.1. The PBW module just proved is consequently finite free over its right coefficient algebra and completes coefficientwise. Multiplication extends continuously: moving a formal coefficient through a crossing uses a variable permutation or one divided difference, decreasing its order by at most one, so any finite product has a uniform finite order loss. The displayed completed PBW expansion is therefore the actual central completion, rather than an additional relation imposed on $R_\beta$.

The common degenerate Hecke operator. In the fraction algebra set $Z_r=x_r-x_{r+1}$ and $S_r=(1+Z_r^{-1})\sigma_r-Z_r^{-1}$. On an unequal source component the diagonal term is $-z^{-1}f$, while its crossing coefficient on the target component is $1+(b-a+u-v)^{-1}$. On equal colors this operator is $\sigma_r-(1-\sigma_r)/(u-v)$ and preserves formal series. Thus $S_r$ acts on $\mathcal B_\beta$ in every case. All identities in the next two steps are computed in the fraction algebra and then hold for these regular operators. This use of auxiliary fractions does not assert that a dot difference is invertible in the completion or its quotients.

Hecke quadratic and mixed identities. Let $A=Z_r^{-1}$; then $\sigma_r(A)=-A$. Expanding $S_r^2$ gives identity coefficient $(1+A)(1-A)+A^2=1$ and crossing coefficient $(1+A)A-A(1+A)=0$. Thus $S_r^2=1$, including equal colors. In $S_rx_{r+1}-x_rS_r$ the crossing terms cancel and the diagonal term is $A(x_r-x_{r+1})=1$. Disjoint $S_r$ commute, and dots outside the pair commute with $S_r$. These are precisely the quadratic, mixed and far-commuting relations of [F2].

Complete Hecke braid coefficients. In spectral variables put $Z=x_1-x_2$, $U=x_2-x_3$, $V=Z+U$, $A=Z^{-1}$, $B=U^{-1}$, $C=V^{-1}$. Both products $S_1S_2S_1$ and $S_2S_1S_2$ have coefficients, in permutation order $(1,s,t,st,ts,\rho)$, equal to $(-C-ABC,\ (1+A)BC,\ (1+B)AC,\ -B(1+A)(1+C),\ -A(1+B)(1+C),\ (1+A)(1+B)(1+C))$. To verify the reductions, multiply using $(f\sigma)(g\eta)=f\sigma(g)\sigma\eta$, $s(A)=-A$, $s(B)=C$, $t(B)=-B$, $t(A)=C$, and $AB=C(A+B)$. For example the raw $s$ coefficient in the first word is $A(1+A)(B-C)=(1+A)BC$; its raw identity coefficient is $-(1-A^2)C-A^2B=-C-ABC$. Interchanging $A,B$ and $s,t$ gives the second word's identical six coefficients.

All five reverse braid cases. Step 14.1 is a rational identity in independent spectral variables, before assigning colors. Substitute $(x_1,x_2,x_3)=(a+u,b+v,c+w)$ on each source component and apply the color-permuting operators. It proves the full Hecke braid separately on $(a,b,c)$ with all distinct, $(a,a,b)$, $(a,b,b)$, $(a,b,a)$ and $(a,a,a)$, because each is the restriction of the same six-coefficient identity and every $S_r$ preserves $\mathcal B_\beta$ by step 12.1. Even when a displayed spectral denominator has zero constant, cancellation occurs in the original regular operators, and injectivity into fractions preserves the equality. Thus the all-equal reverse case also has a complete coefficient computation.

Faithfulness for the Hecke action. The mixed relation moves polynomials to the right of $s$-words and the exact symmetric-group relations reduce each word to $s_w$, so $H_n^{\mathrm{dg}}$ is spanned by $s_wf(x)$. In the action of steps 12.1–15.1 its leading permutation coefficient is the product of nonzero rational factors $1+Z^{-1}$ along a reduced word. All lower terms have shorter permutation length. The shortest-relation argument of step 10.1 proves independence and therefore the affine Hecke PBW basis. Completing at the central ideal of step 1.1 gives the finite coefficientwise PBW module $\sum_{w,\nu}s_w k[\![y]\!]e(\nu)$; its operator action remains faithful by the same argument over formal fractions. The coefficients $1+Z^{-1}$ need only be nonzero in that field, not units in the coefficient ring.

Comparing the explicit tables. On an unequal source $(a,b)$, $S_r+p_{ab}$ has only the crossing term. Its target coefficient is $1+\zeta^{-1}$, where $\zeta=b-a+u-v$. Right multiplication by $q_{ab}^{-1}$ substitutes $(v,u)$ on that target. If $a\to b$, $q_{ab}(v,u)=1+\zeta^{-1}$, giving coefficient $1$; if $a\leftarrow b$, $q_{ab}(v,u)=-\zeta^{-1}$ and $\zeta=-1+u-v$, giving coefficient $-(\zeta+1)=v-u$; off edges the quotient is again $1$. On equal colors $S_r=\sigma_r-(1-\sigma_r)/(u-v)$, and $(S_r+1)(1+v-u)^{-1}=(\sigma_r-1)/(u-v)=E_r$ by moving the inverse through $\sigma_r$. Thus $(S_r+p)q^{-1}=\psi_r$ in the faithful action. Equivalently $\psi_rq-p=S_r$.

Homomorphisms in both directions. Faithfulness in steps 10.1–11.1 and 16.1 transfers the concrete equalities to the completed presented algebras. Step 17.1 identifies the forward images with the operators checked in steps 4.1–9.1, so all KLR relations hold in $\widehat H_\beta^{\mathrm{dg}}$. It identifies the reverse images with the operators checked in steps 13.1–15.1, so all Hecke relations hold in $\widehat R_\beta$. The coefficient-algebra maps identify the central completion topologies: the symmetric ideal vanishing at the spectral multiset and the all-zero dot ideal have cofinal powers on $\mathcal B_\beta$ by step 1.1. Therefore the maps extend continuously to the stated completions. This proves both directions locally rather than importing a cyclic finite-$e$ theorem.

Inverse composites and uniformity. The coefficient maps fix every $e(\nu)$ and invert $y_r=x_r-\nu_r$ componentwise. The crossing composites are $(\psi_rq-p+p)q^{-1}=\psi_r$ and $((s_r+p)q^{-1})q-p=s_r$, with the same right multiplication order. Hence each composite is the identity on its generators, coefficient series and completion. None of $p,q,c$ depends on the rank, multiset, interval endpoints, level or cyclotomic charge, so enlarging an interval preserves every formula on the old tuples. Nilpotent dots permit finite evaluation of series, and every proved identity survives a quotient. Rank zero has coefficient algebra $k$ and both maps are the identity; empty positive-rank sectors have zero algebra. No assertion about cyclotomic support, based Grothendieck classes or Specht modules is needed for this local comparison.

derivations.claim: **Bind the actual proved suppliers.** The arbitrary-base affine presentations in the Statement specialize the common defining generators and relations over k, with first-strand monic polynomials $\prod_j(t-m_j)$ and $\prod_j(t-\xi^{m_j})$; the latter has unit constant term. Thus the finite-dimensional spanning and spectral-support proof [F1] applies at every level and rank. Its line datum satisfies the native quadratic symmetry and homogeneous extremal conditions with $d_i=1$, and its standard exponents are exactly $\lambda_i=\#\{j:m_j=i\}$. On every finite interval its support proof gives actual whole-algebra equality, global nilpotent dots and polynomial projectors over k, not just a supported corner. The two local suppliers in [F2] use the SAME native $\tau$ and set $\psi=-\tau$: both have $\psi u-v\psi=-1$, $\psi v-u\psi=1$, quadratic $Q_{a,a+1}=v-u$, $Q_{a+1,a}=u-v$, and braid difference $\psi_1\psi_2\psi_1-\psi_2\psi_1\psi_2=[Q(u,v)-Q(w,v)]/(w-u)$ on $(a,b,a)$. Their pair series are fixed for all integer pairs and all ranks; the nondegenerate symbol q is our $\xi$. Their proofs give faithful ACTUAL affine polynomial presentations before completion and before any quotient, then identify the true central completions with one formal dot ring per word. They prove both map directions on all five equality patterns of three colors, including all equal, and inverse composites with the displayed right multiplication order. Therefore they apply to exactly the affine blocks under consideration; no finite cyclic quantum characteristic, generic-rank faithfulness or cyclotomic polynomial faithfulness is assumed.

Evaluate a formal series in commuting nilpotent dots by its finite Taylor sum. This evaluation is independent of the nilpotence exponent chosen: every larger truncation differs only by zero monomials. A series with nonzero constant term is a unit by a terminating geometric expansion. Thus all replacements in the Statement are defined. By [F1] only finitely many words survive in any rank. The local relation verifications in [F2], applied on those words, give homomorphisms between the affine presentations before checking the first-strand quotient. No cyclic wraparound or reduction of integer colors is used.

On a first color $i$, write the degenerate cyclotomic polynomial as $f(i+y)=y^{\lambda_i}U_i(y)$, where $U_i(y)=\prod_{m_j\ne i}(i-m_j+y)$. Its constant term is nonzero in characteristic zero. In the other branch $g(\xi^i(1-y))=(-\xi^i)^{\lambda_i}y^{\lambda_i}V_i(y)$, where $V_i(y)=\prod_{m_j\ne i}(\xi^i-\xi^{m_j}-\xi^iy)$. Infinite multiplicative order makes its constant term nonzero. Both auxiliary factors are units after nilpotent evaluation. Thus the Hecke cyclotomic relation on each projector is equivalent to $y_1^{\lambda_i}e(i,\ldots)=0$. If $\lambda_i=0$, the unit polynomial kills the entire projector. This proves both directions of cyclotomic IDEAL transport: in each completed word corner the transformed Hecke generator is an invertible scalar and unit power series times $y_1^{\lambda_i}e(i,\ldots)$. Multiplication by that factor gives containment in the KLR-generated two-sided ideal; multiplication by its inverse gives the reverse containment. Summing the finitely many orthogonal first-color corners proves equality of the full two-sided ideals. On either nilpotent quotient these units evaluate by finite Taylor sums, so the actual affine maps descend to homomorphisms of the entire cyclotomic algebras in both directions. This does not assume that a restricted supported subalgebra is the full quotient.

u)R_d^\lambda$, each $\sigma_d(x_r)$ has sole generalized eigenvalue $
u_r$, or $\sigma_d(X_r)$ has sole generalized eigenvalue $\xi^{
u_r}$. Distinct colors have distinct values, and the orthogonal word idempotents sum to one. The simultaneous primary projector is therefore precisely left multiplication by $e_R(
u)$. The Hecke polynomial projector maps to this idempotent: its Chinese-remainder polynomial is one modulo the corresponding primary factors and zero modulo all other factors. Hence $\sigma_d(e_H(
u))=e_R(
u)$. The forward map already sends $e_R(

Both composites fix the word projectors by step 4.1 and the dots by direct substitution $x_r-
u_r=y_r$, or $1-\xi^{-

u)$ to $((s_r+p_{ab})q_{ab}^{-1}q_{ab}-p_{ab})e_H(
u)=s_re_H(
u)$; the formula with $T,P,Q$ is identical. The polynomial generators are fixed, and the units $X_r^{-1}$ are fixed because inverses are unique. Thus the homomorphisms are inverse on every generator, without commuting a crossing through its series.

For ranks through $D>0$ at positive level use the common interval $W_D=[\min S-D,\max S+D]\cap\mathbb Z$. It contains the support through rank $D$ and one unused ghost color beyond each endpoint of $B_D$. A crossing permutes existing colors and never creates one; nevertheless these endpoint colors keep every boundary edge of a surviving color represented by the integer-line convention. For operations reaching rank $D+t$, use $W_{D+t}$, and enlarge further to contain any specified color and its neighbors. All extra word idempotents vanish by [F1]. Since [F2] fixes the same series for each ordered pair in every interval, evaluation on surviving words is unchanged by enlargement. The resulting maps are independent of windows and glue across all finite rank bounds.

Let $\iota_H:H_d\to H_{d+1}$ send each existing Hecke generator to the generator with the same index. It is a homomorphism because all rank-$d$ relations, including the first-strand relation, hold in rank $d+1$. Its spectral projector satisfies $\iota_H(e_H(\nu))=\sum_a e_H(\nu,a)$: the first $d$ polynomial generators give a representation of $H_d$ on the rank-$d+1$ regular module, so their primary projector is the sum of exactly these joint projectors. The minimal polynomial of each rank-d algebra generator on its regular module annihilates that algebra element itself, hence every representation of $H_d$; the same is true of the polynomial primary projectors. Thus the first-d primary decomposition on the rank-d+1 regular module contains exactly the rank-d allowed eigenvalues, and every prefix violating rank-d support is zero. This is the algebra-identity consequence of [F1], rather than an unsupported extension of a regular-module assertion. This argument also holds for $d=0$, where the empty projector is one.

Define $\iota_R=\sigma_{d+1}\iota_H\phi_d$. The established inverse maps make this a homomorphism. Steps 4.1 and 7.1 give $\iota_R(e_R(
u))=\sum_a e_R(
u,a)$. The unchanged polynomial generators give the usual prefix dots. For $r<d$, the rank-independent pair series in [F2] and cancellation in step 5.1 give $\iota_R(\psi_re_R(
u))=\sum_a\psi_re_R(
u,a)$. These are exactly the standard right-appending KLR maps, so the individually constructed isomorphisms commute with the actual tower maps. Injectivity of the tower maps is neither needed nor inferred.

Put $\epsilon_i^R=\sum_\nu e_R(\nu,i)$ in rank $d+1$, and define $\epsilon_i^H$ by the analogous spectral sum. Step 4.1 gives $\phi_{d+1}(\epsilon_i^R)=\epsilon_i^H$. Each last-color projector commutes with every prefix generator, since prefix crossings permute only the first $d$ colors and prefix dots preserve all colors. On left modules color restriction is $N\mapsto\epsilon_iN$, with the rank-$d$ action through its prefix map. Color induction is $M\mapsto A_{d+1}\epsilon_i\otimes_{A_d}M$. Step 8.1 identifies both prefix actions, and the algebra isomorphism identifies these induction bimodules on both sides. Explicitly $a\epsilon_i\otimes m\mapsto\phi_{d+1}(a)\epsilon_i\otimes m$ is a balanced bijection, with inverse obtained from $\sigma_{d+1}$. Restriction agrees by the same projector equality. These formulas are natural in module maps.

Composing the two comparisons through the same $R_d^\lambda$ proves the claimed degenerate/nondegenerate tower equivalence. Naturality from step 9.1 intertwines repeated induction and restriction, while step 6.1 covers every specified finite rank cut. At level zero use the identity on rank zero and the unique maps between zero algebras in positive rank; the sole map from rank zero to rank one is the map to zero, and all positive-rank functors vanish. Thus all ranks and levels are included. The actual presentation and convention binding in step 1.1 discharges [F1]–[F2], so this proves the entire all-rank, all-level tower comparison. No based or standard-class theorem is inferred merely from these algebra isomorphisms.

The expression is a finite sum of products of two complex numbers, so $b$ is a symmetric bilinear form; writing $\overline{x}=\sum_T\overline{x_T}T$ for the coefficientwise conjugate, $b(x,y)=\sum_Tx_Ty_T=\sum_T\overline{\overline{x_T}}y_T=\langle\overline{x},y\rangle$ by [F2]. If $\sigma\in S_n$ permutes the tabloid basis, then the coefficient of $T$ in $\sigma x$ is $x_{\sigma^{-1}T}$, so $b(\sigma x,\sigma y)=\sum_Tx_{\sigma^{-1}T}y_{\sigma^{-1}T}=\sum_Tx_Ty_T=b(x,y)$ after reindexing the finite basis. Hence $b$ is $S_n$-invariant.

The Specht module is stable under coefficientwise conjugation: $\overline{S^\lambda}=S^\lambda$. Each polytabloid is a finite integer combination of tabloid basis vectors, since $\kappa_s$ permutes the tabloid basis with signs $\pm1$, so $\overline{e_s}=e_s$ by [F1]. Let $\operatorname{ch}:R_S\to\Lambda$ be the Frobenius characteristic restricted
to the graded ordinary representation ring of the symmetric groups
([[def-frobenius-characteristic-map]],
[[def-graded-ordinary-representation-ring-of-symmetric-groups]]). By
[[thm-frobenius-characteristic-is-an-isometric-graded-ring-isomorphism]] it is a
degree-preserving $\mathbb Z$-module isomorphism onto the stable symmetric
function ring $\Lambda=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}\Lambda^m$, so its restriction
$\operatorname{ch}:R(S_m)\to\Lambda^m$ is an isomorphism for every $m\ge0$.

For $f\in\Lambda^m$ and $g\in\Lambda^n$ define
$$f*g:=\begin{cases}\operatorname{ch}\bigl(\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(f)\cdot\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(g)\bigr),&m=n,\\[2pt]0,&m\ne n,\end{cases}$$
where $\cdot$ is the pointwise (internal tensor) product of class functions on
$S_m$; extend $*$ bilinearly to all of $\Lambda$. Call $*$ the
**internal (Kronecker) product** of symmetric functions.

**Well-definedness.** For $m=n$ the class functions $\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(f)$
and $\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(g)$ lie in $R(S_m)$, the integral span of the
irreducible characters of $S_m$
([[def-graded-ordinary-representation-ring-of-symmetric-groups]]). The
pointwise product of two honest characters of $S_m$ is again an honest
character, namely the character of the tensor product of the underlying
representations ([[thm-characters-of-direct-sums-tensor-products-and-duals]]),
and products of $\mathbb Z$-combinations of characters are computed
bilinearly; hence the pointwise product of two elements of $R(S_m)$ lies in
$R(S_m)$, and applying the isomorphism $\operatorname{ch}$ lands in $\Lambda^m$.
The product is therefore well defined and takes $\Lambda^m\times\Lambda^m$ to
$\Lambda^m$.

**Basic properties.** The product is bilinear by construction and inherits
commutativity and associativity from the pointwise product of class functions.
It preserves degrees, in the sense that $\Lambda^m*\Lambda^n\subseteq\Lambda^m$
for $m=n$ and is $0$ for $m\ne n$. On $\Lambda^n$ the unit is
$h_n=s_{(n)}=\operatorname{ch}(\text{trivial character of }S_n)$, because the
trivial character is the unit for pointwise multiplication on $R(S_n)$
([[thm-frobenius-characteristic-sends-specht-characters-to-schur-functions]]
identifies $\operatorname{ch}(\chi^{(n)})=s_{(n)}=h_n$). The graded direct sum
$\Lambda$ has **no global unit** for $*$: if $e\in\Lambda$ had finite degree
support and $n$ were a degree with $e_n=0$ while $\Lambda^n\ne0$, then
$(e*h_n)_n=e_n*h_n=0\ne h_n$, so $e*h_n\ne h_n$; a global unit would require
$e_n$ to be a unit of $(\Lambda^n,*)$ for every $n$. In particular the ordinary
product unit $1\in\Lambda^0$ is not a unit for $*$ on the positive degrees.

**Schur expansion.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$, the definition and
the Specht character dictionary $\operatorname{ch}(\chi^\lambda)=s_\lambda$
([[thm-frobenius-characteristic-sends-specht-characters-to-schur-functions]])
give
$$s_\lambda*s_\mu=\operatorname{ch}\bigl(\chi^\lambda\cdot\chi^\mu\bigr)=\operatorname{ch}\Bigl(\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\chi^\nu\Bigr)=\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\,s_\nu,$$
because $\chi^\lambda\chi^\mu$ is the character of
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ and its decomposition has multiplicities
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the transport goes through the
choice-free Frobenius characteristic isomorphism and finite-dimensional
representation theory of finite groups.

For partitions $\rho,\sigma\vdash n$ one has
$$p_\rho*p_\sigma=\delta_{\rho,\sigma}\,z_\rho\,p_\rho,\qquad z_\rho=\prod_{i\ge1}i^{m_i(\rho)}m_i(\rho)!,$$
where $m_i(\rho)$ is the number of parts of $\rho$ equal to $i$. Consequently
$$s_\lambda*s_\mu=\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\,s_\nu$$
for all $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$. The internal product on $\Lambda^n$ is therefore
diagonal in the power-sum basis, with $z_\rho$ the diagonal scalars, and it has
the integer structure constants $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ in the Schur basis.

Fix an integer $n\ge0$ and work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be
partitions of $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ be the tensor product of their complex
Specht modules, a finite-dimensional complex $S_n$-module
([[def-tensor-product-of-complex-representations]],
[[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). The
**Kronecker coefficient** $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ of a third partition
$\nu\vdash n$ is the multiplicity of $S^\nu$ in this tensor product:

$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu):=\frac{\dim_{\mathbb C}\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}}{\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu},$$

where $\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}$ is the isotypic
component of type $S^\nu$
([[def-isotypic-component-of-a-completely-reducible-representation]]).

**Well-definedness.** The module $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ is
finite-dimensional, and $\operatorname{char}\mathbb C=0$ does not divide the
order of the finite group $S_n$, so complex Maschke's theorem gives complete
reducibility
([[thm-maschkes-theorem-for-finite-groups-over-fields-whose-characteristic-does-not-divide-the-group-order]],
[[cor-finite-dimensional-representations-are-completely-reducible-when-char-k-does-not-divide-group-order]],
[[def-completely-reducible-representation]]). The complex Specht modules
$S^\nu$, $\nu\vdash n$, are a complete list of pairwise inequivalent
irreducible $S_n$-modules
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]],
[[cor-distinct-specht-modules-are-inequivalent]]). Consequently a decomposition
into irreducibles has the form
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\cong\bigoplus_{\nu\vdash n}m_\nu S^\nu$
with nonnegative integer multiplicities $m_\nu$, and the isotypic component of
type $S^\nu$ is the direct sum of exactly the $m_\nu$ copies of $S^\nu$
appearing in any such decomposition; in particular
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu)_{(S^\nu)}=m_\nu\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu$
and $\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu>0$ because $S^\nu$ is irreducible. Hence
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=m_\nu$ is a nonnegative integer, independent of the chosen
decomposition, and $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ is by definition the multiplicity of
$S^\nu$ in $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$.

**The internal product.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ call
$$(\lambda,\mu)\longmapsto S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$$
the **internal (Kronecker) product** of the $S_n$-representations $S^\lambda$
and $S^\mu$. Unlike the outer induction product
$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_b}^{S_{a+b}}(S^\alpha\boxtimes S^\beta)$ of
[[thm-outer-littlewood-richardson-rule]], which takes a pair of modules of
degrees $a$ and $b$ to a module of degree $a+b$, the internal product keeps the
rank: both inputs and the output are $S_n$-modules of the same degree $n$. The
two operations are different constructions on different data; the outer product
is mentioned here only for contrast and is not used in this definition.

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the tensor product, Maschke's theorem,
the Specht classification and the isotypic decomposition are finite-dimensional
complex representation theory of a finite group.

For all partitions $\lambda,\mu,\nu\vdash n$:

(a) $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ is a nonnegative integer;

(b) $g$ is invariant under every permutation of the three arguments, that is
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=g(\mu,\lambda,\nu)=g(\lambda,\nu,\mu)=\cdots$ for all six
orderings;

(c) conjugating exactly two of the three partitions preserves the coefficient:
$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=g(\lambda',\mu',\nu)=g(\lambda',\mu,\nu')=g(\lambda,\mu',\nu'),$$
where $\lambda'$ denotes the conjugate partition.

No positive combinatorial rule for the coefficients is asserted.

Let $\lambda\vdash n$, $\tau\vdash r$ and $\theta\vdash n-r$. Then, in
$\Lambda^n$,
$$s_\lambda*(s_\tau s_\theta)=\sum_{\alpha\vdash r,\ \beta\vdash n-r}c^\lambda_{\alpha\beta}\,(s_\alpha*s_\tau)(s_\beta*s_\theta),$$
where $c^\lambda_{\alpha\beta}$ is the Littlewood–Richardson coefficient. Both
sides have degree $n$ and the sum is finite.

Let $c^\lambda_{\mu
u}$ be the Littlewood–Richardson coefficient of the inherited definition, the number of Littlewood–Richardson tableaux of shape $\lambda/\mu$ and content $
u$ ([[def-littlewood-richardson-tableau-and-coefficient]], [[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]], [[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]], [[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Then for all partitions $\mu,
u$,

u=\sum_{\lambda\,\supseteq\,\mu,\ |\lambda|=|\mu|+|
u|}c^\lambda_{\mu
u}s_\lambda\qquad	ext{in }\Lambda,$$
where the sum is finite and zero terms may be omitted; equivalently, for every $\lambda\supseteq\mu$,

No choice principle is used.

Let $\lambda,
u$ be partitions with $[\lambda]\subseteq[
u]$, and let $\mu$ be a partition with $|
u|=|\lambda|+|\mu|$. Use the conventions of [[def-skew-diagram-and-semistandard-skew-tableau]] for the skew diagram $
u/\lambda$ and for semistandard skew tableaux of shape $
u/\lambda$, and those of [[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]] for the content of a tableau; recall that entries of a semistandard skew tableau weakly increase along rows and strictly increase down columns ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]] fixes the English row and column coordinates).

The **reading word** $w(T)$ of a semistandard skew tableau $T$ of shape $
u/\lambda$ is the word obtained by reading the rows of $T$ from right to left, beginning with the top row and proceeding to the bottom row. The word $w(T)=a_1a_2\cdots a_N$ is a **lattice word** (a lattice permutation) if in every prefix $a_1\cdots a_p$ and for every $i\ge1$ the number of letters $i$ in the prefix is at least the number of letters $i+1$; the empty word is a lattice word vacuously.

A **Littlewood--Richardson tableau** (LR tableau) of shape $
u/\lambda$ and content $\mu$ is a semistandard skew tableau of shape $
u/\lambda$ and content $\mu$ whose reading word is a lattice word. The **Littlewood--Richardson coefficient** $c^
u_{\lambda\mu}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ is the number of LR tableaux of shape $
u/\lambda$ and content $\mu$; it is $0$ when $[\lambda]
ot\subseteq[
u]$, when $|
u|
e|\lambda|+|\mu|$, or when no such tableau exists. For $\mu=\varnothing$ and $
u=\lambda$ the empty skew tableau is the unique tableau of content $\varnothing$, its reading word is empty, and hence $c^\lambda_{\lambda\varnothing}=1$; more generally $c^\lambda_{\lambda\mu}=0$ unless $\mu=\varnothing$, and $c^
u_{\lambda\mu}=0$ unless $\lambda\subseteq
u$ and $|
u|=|\lambda|+|\mu|$.

For every partition $\lambda$, let $s_\lambda\in\Lambda$ be the stable Schur
function defined by bialternants
([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]). For any integers
$r\ge\ell(\lambda)$ and $c\ge\ell(\lambda')$, pad $\lambda$ and $\lambda'$
with zero parts to lengths $r$ and $c$, respectively. Then
$$s_\lambda=\det\bigl(h_{\lambda_i-i+j}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le r}=\det\bigl(e_{\lambda'_i-i+j}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le c},$$
where $h_k,e_k\in\Lambda$ are the stable complete and elementary functions
([[thm-elementary-and-complete-families-freely-generate-the-stable-ring]],
[[def-elementary-symmetric-polynomials]],
[[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]). In these
determinants use $h_0=e_0=1$, set $h_k=e_k=0$ for $k<0$, and take the empty
determinant to be $1$.

For every $d\ge0$, the stable Schur functions $\{s_\lambda:\lambda\vdash d\}$
form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of $\Lambda^d$ and are orthonormal for the Hall form:
$$\langle s_\lambda,s_\mu\rangle_H=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$$
for all partitions $\lambda,\mu$.

For integers $N,d\ge0$, let $A_N^d$ be the degree-$d$ homogeneous part of
$\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_N]^{S_N}$, using
[[def-symmetric-polynomial]] and the convention $A_0^0=\mathbb Z$ and
$A_0^d=0$ for $d>0$. For $M\ge N$, the transition
$\pi_{M,N}:A_M^d\to A_N^d$ sets $x_{N+1},\ldots,x_M$ equal to zero.
These maps compose, so define
$$\Lambda^d:=\varprojlim_{N\ge0}A_N^d,\qquad \Lambda:=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}\Lambda^d.$$

An element of $\Lambda^d$ is a compatible sequence of homogeneous
degree-$d$ symmetric polynomials, one in each rank. Multiplication of a
degree-$a$ sequence and a degree-$b$ sequence is coordinatewise polynomial
multiplication and lies in $\Lambda^{a+b}$; compatibility follows because
each $\pi_{M,N}$ is a ring homomorphism. Extend this product distributively
to $\Lambda$. The unit is the compatible constant sequence $1$, and each
element of $\Lambda$ has only finitely many nonzero homogeneous components.

This direct sum is not the ungraded inverse limit of the rings
$\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_N]^{S_N}$. For example, the compatible sequence
$\prod_{i=1}^N(1+x_i)$ belongs to that ungraded inverse limit and has nonzero
homogeneous components in every degree, so it is not an element of the direct
sum $\Lambda$. The partition notation and empty partition follow
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

**Partitions.** Let $n\ge 0$ be an integer. A **partition of $n$** is a finite
weakly decreasing sequence $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ of positive
integers with $\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k=n$. Its entries are the **parts** of
$\lambda$ and $k$ is the **number of parts**. For $n=0$ the only partition is
the **empty partition** $\varnothing$, the empty sequence with $k=0$; for
$n\ge 1$ one has $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge 1$ and
$k\le n$. We write $\lambda\vdash n$. Trailing zeros are not parts: a finite
sequence of nonnegative integers ending in $0$ is not a partition, so the
number of parts of $\lambda$ is determined by $\lambda$ and
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ is a different data type from
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k,0)$.

**English Young diagrams.** The **(English) Young diagram** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$[\lambda]:=\{\,(i,j)\;:\;1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le \lambda_i\,\}\subseteq\mathbb N\times\mathbb N,$$
where $i$ numbers the **rows** downward and $j$ numbers the **columns**
rightward. An element of $[\lambda]$ is a **node**, or box, of the diagram. Row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ carries $\lambda_i$ nodes, and column $j$ carries
$$\lambda'_j:=\#\{\,i: \lambda_i\ge j\,\}$$
nodes, a quantity that is $0$ beyond the last column (and for every $j\ge1$ when $\lambda=\varnothing$). Since a partition is weakly
decreasing, $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$: if $[\mu]=[\lambda]$, then row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ is row $i$ of $[\mu]$, so $\mu_i=\lambda_i$ for every $i$
and $\mu=\lambda$. In particular $[\varnothing]=\emptyset$, the empty diagram.

**Conjugation.** The **conjugate partition** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$\lambda':=(\lambda'_1,\lambda'_2,\dots,\lambda'_{\lambda_1}),$$
the sequence of column heights of $[\lambda]$, with $\varnothing':=\varnothing$
for the empty partition. This is again a partition of $n$, and
$[\lambda']$ is the transpose of $[\lambda]$:
for $1\le i\le\lambda_1$ and $1\le j\le k$,
$$(i,j)\in[\lambda']\iff j\le\lambda'_i\iff \lambda_j\ge i\iff (j,i)\in[\lambda].$$
Outside these bounds neither diagram contains the corresponding node; for the empty partition both diagrams are empty.
Conjugation is an involution, $\lambda''=\lambda$, because
$\lambda''_i=\#\{j:\lambda'_j\ge i\}$ counts the columns of $[\lambda]$ of
height at least $i$, that is, the columns $j$ with at least $i$ rows of length
$\ge j$, which by weak decrease is exactly the set of $j\le\lambda_i$. Thus
$\lambda\mapsto\lambda'$ is a bijection on the partitions of $n$, exchanging
the number of parts with the largest part for nonempty partitions.

**Size zero.** The symmetric group of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is
$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]) for every
$n\ge 0$, and we fix
$$S_0:=\operatorname{Sym}(\emptyset)=\{1\},$$
the trivial group; for $n=0$ the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is empty and the group
acts trivially on every size-zero object below. This is the convention used
whenever the constructions of this page are read at $n=0$.

derivations.claim: For $0\le q\le n$ and $\eta\vdash q$, apply [F2] to $h_{n-q}s_\eta$ and use the unit in [F1], then extract $[s_\mu]$ using [F3]. This gives the finite coefficient identity $K_n(q,\eta):=[s_\mu](s_\lambda*(h_{n-q}s_\eta))=\sum_{\alpha\vdash n-q,\ \beta,\gamma\vdash q}c^\lambda_{\alpha\beta}c^\mu_{\alpha\gamma}g(\beta,\eta,\gamma)$. Every nonzero summand has $\alpha\subseteq\rho$; writing $e_i:=\rho_i-\alpha_i$ gives $\sum_i e_i=q-g_0$, so $0\le e_i\le q-g_0\le q$. If $\ell=0$, then $n=s=r=0$, all three partitions are empty, and the degree-zero unit gives $g(\varnothing,\varnothing,\varnothing)=1$, proving the claim; hence assume $\ell\ge1$ for the rest of the proof.

For part (ii) only, and put $D_{\ell+1}=0$, $\rho_{\ell+1}=0$. One has $\delta_i\le\rho_i-\rho_{i+1}$. If $D_j>0$, let $b\ge j$ be the last index with $\delta_b>0$; telescoping gives $D_j\le\rho_j-\rho_b+\delta_b\le\rho_j-2s$. Hence $\varphi(\theta)_j\ge s$ when $D_j>0$, and when $D_j=0$ its value is $\theta_j\ge0$. If $\delta_j=0$, consecutive parts of $\varphi(\theta)$ have the same difference as those of $\theta$. If $\delta_j>0$ and $j<\ell$, then $\varphi(\theta)_j-\varphi(\omega)_{j+1}=\theta_j-\omega_{j+1}-\delta_j=\theta_j-\rho_j+2s\ge s\ge0$. Since $\theta\subseteq\omega$, this proves weak decrease at every remaining boundary. Thus $\varphi$ maps the stated domain to partitions, is injective, and satisfies $|\varphi(\theta)|=|\theta|-\sum_jD_j$.

Independently of case (ii), expand the Jacobi–Trudi determinant for $
u=(n-s,
u_2,\ldots)$ along the first row. Its $j$th cofactor $B_j$, indexed by $0\le j\le\ell-1$, depends only on $(
u_2,\ldots,
u_\ell)$ and is homogeneous of degree $s-j$, since every product in that minor has that degree. Thus $s_
u=\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}(-1)^j h_{n-s+j}B_j$, with $B_j=0$ when $j>s$; for $j\le s$, expand $B_j$ in the Schur basis of degree $q=s-j$. By symmetry [F1], $g(\lambda,\mu,
u)=[s_\mu](s_\lambda*s_
u)$ is therefore a signed sum of $K_n(q,\eta)$ with $0\le q\le s$. If $|\lambda_i-\mu_i|>s$ for some $i$, then $g_0\ge|\lambda_i-\mu_i|>s$: the sums of the positive row differences in either direction agree because $|\lambda|=|\mu|$. Step 1.1 then has no contributing $\alpha$ for any $q\le s$. Every term vanishes, proving part (i).

Return to case (ii) and put $r:=|\varphi(\lambda)|=|\varphi(\mu)|$. If any $\delta_i>0$, step 1.2 gives $ho_1-D_1\ge2s$ and therefore $r\ge2s$, so $r-s\ge s\ge
u_2$. If every $\delta_i=0$, then $r=n$ and $r-s=
u_1\ge
u_2$. Thus $\varphi(
u)$ is a partition. To bound $r$, use $\delta_i\geho_i-\omega_{i+1}-2s$ and telescope to obtain $\lambda_j-D_j\le2s(\ell-j+1)+\sum_{i=j}^{\ell}(\lambda_i-ho_i)+\sum_{i=j+1}^{\ell}(\omega_i-\lambda_i)\le3s(\ell-j+1)$; the last two sums together equal $(\lambda_j-ho_j)+\sum_{i=j+1}^{\ell}(\omega_i-ho_i)\le s(\ell-j+1)$. Therefore $r\le3s\ell(\ell+1)/2\le2s\ell^2$ for $\ell\ge3$. If $\ell=2$, equal total sizes imply $\omega_2=ho_2+a$ and $n=ho_1+ho_2+a$, where $a=|\lambda_1-\mu_1|=|\lambda_2-\mu_2|\le s$; then $r=n-\delta_1-2\delta_2\le(ho_1+ho_2+a)-(ho_1-ho_2-a-2s)-2(ho_2-2s)=6s+2a\le8s$. If $\ell=1$, then $s=0$, $\lambda=\mu=
u=(n)$ and $\delta_1=n$, giving $r=0$.

Fix $q\le s$. The map $\alpha\mapsto\varphi(\alpha)$ is a bijection from partitions $\alpha\subseteq\rho$ of size $n-q$ to partitions $\theta\subseteq\varphi(\rho)$ of size $r-q$. If either set is nonempty, its total deficit from $\rho$ or $\varphi(\rho)$ is $q-g_0\le s$. For the forward direction this proves $\alpha_j\ge\rho_j-s$, so step 1.2 applies. Conversely, given $\theta$ in the second set, set $\alpha_j:=\theta_j+D_j$. These parts are nonnegative and have consecutive differences $(\theta_j-\theta_{j+1})+\delta_j\ge0$. They satisfy $\alpha\subseteq\rho$, $|\alpha|=n-q$, and $\rho_j-\alpha_j=\varphi(\rho)_j-\theta_j\le q-g_0\le s$. This is the inverse. Empty index sets, including $q<g_0$, correspond as well.

For such an $\alpha$, shift every cell $(j,c)$ of $\lambda/\alpha$ to $(j,c-D_j)$. Its image is $\varphi(\lambda)/\varphi(\alpha)$, with each row order and the whole reading word preserved. Within runs of rows with $\delta_j=0$, consecutive rows share columns in exactly the same way. At a cut $\delta_j>0$, the original rows have no common skew column across the cut, since $\alpha_j\ge\rho_j-s>\omega_{j+1}\ge\lambda_{j+1}$. The shifted rows likewise have no common skew column across it, because $\varphi(\alpha)_j-\varphi(\omega)_{j+1}=\alpha_j-\rho_j+2s\ge s\ge0$. The partition inequalities imply the same separation for every row above and below the cut. Thus all column comparisons, weak row inequalities, content and lattice-word conditions are preserved in both directions. Consequently $c^\lambda_{\alpha\beta}=c^{\varphi(\lambda)}_{\varphi(\alpha),\beta}$ for every $\beta\vdash q$, and the identical argument gives $c^\mu_{\alpha\gamma}=c^{\varphi(\mu)}_{\varphi(\alpha),\gamma}$.

Apply step 1.1 to the reduced outer partitions of size $r$. Because intersection commutes with subtracting the same row vector, their intersection is $\varphi(\rho)$. Steps 2.3 and 3.1 identify the two finite sums term by term, with the same $\beta,\gamma,\eta$ and unchanged $g(\beta,\eta,\gamma)$, so $K_n(q,\eta)=[s_{\varphi(\mu)}](s_{\varphi(\lambda)}*(h_{r-q}s_\eta))$ for every $q\le s$. All degrees are nonnegative: if a reduction occurs then $r\ge2s$ by step 2.2, and otherwise $r=n\ge s$.

The first-row Jacobi–Trudi expansion for $\varphi(
u)=(r-s,
u_2,\ldots)$ has exactly the cofactors $B_j$ of step 2.1, since its tail is unchanged. Replacing each $K_n(q,\eta)$ by its equal reduced coefficient from step 4.1 in that finite signed expansion gives $g(\lambda,\mu,
u)=g(\varphi(\lambda),\varphi(\mu),\varphi(
u))$. Step 2.2 gives the asserted size bound, completing part (ii).

Steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove part(i): a row difference greater than s implies g0>s, so every common-index sum for q<=s is empty and the coefficient vanishes; no Pieri or nonnegative-sum argument is invoked.
Step 1.1 uses the degreewise unit h_(n-q) explicitly, including q=0 and empty eta; the one-row length case ell=1 has s=0 and r=0 by step 2.2.

Step 1.2 separately handles D_j=0 and D_j>0, and unchanged boundaries delta_j=0; steps 2.3 and 3.1 prove the inverse-index and tableau correspondence also at a shortened last cut and at separation equality, without a granted boundary.

Step 2.1 treats all cofactors j=0,...,ell-1 and the vanishing j>s terms; step 2.2 proves the size bound separately for ell=1, ell=2 and ell>=3; steps 2.3 and 4.1 cover all q<=s, including q=0 and q=s.

Steps 1.1, 2.1, 2.3 and 3.1 use finite sums, finite determinants, the explicit inverse theta+D and deterministic cell translations; no arbitrary choice or choice-dependent hypothesis enters the proof.

Step 2.1 proves the row-difference vanishing implication and step 5.1 proves unconditional bounded reduction in the complementary row-difference case, with the corrected map and the bound from step 2.2; no weak-decrease or open-obligation premise remains.

**(i)** If $|\lambda_i-\mu_i|>s$ for some $i\le\ell$, then $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=0$.

**(ii)** Otherwise put $\rho:=\lambda\cap\mu$, $\omega:=\lambda\cup\mu$, $\omega_{\ell+1}:=0$, and define

$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=g(\varphi(\lambda),\varphi(\mu),\varphi(\nu)),\qquad r\le2s\ell^2.$$

**Partitions.** Let $n\ge 0$ be an integer. A **partition of $n$** is a finite
weakly decreasing sequence $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ of positive
integers with $\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k=n$. Its entries are the **parts** of
$\lambda$ and $k$ is the **number of parts**. For $n=0$ the only partition is
the **empty partition** $\varnothing$, the empty sequence with $k=0$; for
$n\ge 1$ one has $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge 1$ and
$k\le n$. We write $\lambda\vdash n$. Trailing zeros are not parts: a finite
sequence of nonnegative integers ending in $0$ is not a partition, so the
number of parts of $\lambda$ is determined by $\lambda$ and
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ is a different data type from
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k,0)$.

**English Young diagrams.** The **(English) Young diagram** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$[\lambda]:=\{\,(i,j)\;:\;1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le \lambda_i\,\}\subseteq\mathbb N\times\mathbb N,$$
where $i$ numbers the **rows** downward and $j$ numbers the **columns**
rightward. An element of $[\lambda]$ is a **node**, or box, of the diagram. Row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ carries $\lambda_i$ nodes, and column $j$ carries
$$\lambda'_j:=\#\{\,i: \lambda_i\ge j\,\}$$
nodes, a quantity that is $0$ beyond the last column (and for every $j\ge1$ when $\lambda=\varnothing$). Since a partition is weakly
decreasing, $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$: if $[\mu]=[\lambda]$, then row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ is row $i$ of $[\mu]$, so $\mu_i=\lambda_i$ for every $i$
and $\mu=\lambda$. In particular $[\varnothing]=\emptyset$, the empty diagram.

**Conjugation.** The **conjugate partition** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$\lambda':=(\lambda'_1,\lambda'_2,\dots,\lambda'_{\lambda_1}),$$
the sequence of column heights of $[\lambda]$, with $\varnothing':=\varnothing$
for the empty partition. This is again a partition of $n$, and
$[\lambda']$ is the transpose of $[\lambda]$:
for $1\le i\le\lambda_1$ and $1\le j\le k$,
$$(i,j)\in[\lambda']\iff j\le\lambda'_i\iff \lambda_j\ge i\iff (j,i)\in[\lambda].$$
Outside these bounds neither diagram contains the corresponding node; for the empty partition both diagrams are empty.
Conjugation is an involution, $\lambda''=\lambda$, because
$\lambda''_i=\#\{j:\lambda'_j\ge i\}$ counts the columns of $[\lambda]$ of
height at least $i$, that is, the columns $j$ with at least $i$ rows of length
$\ge j$, which by weak decrease is exactly the set of $j\le\lambda_i$. Thus
$\lambda\mapsto\lambda'$ is a bijection on the partitions of $n$, exchanging
the number of parts with the largest part for nonempty partitions.

**Size zero.** The symmetric group of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is
$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]) for every
$n\ge 0$, and we fix
$$S_0:=\operatorname{Sym}(\emptyset)=\{1\},$$
the trivial group; for $n=0$ the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is empty and the group
acts trivially on every size-zero object below. This is the convention used
whenever the constructions of this page are read at $n=0$.

For all partitions $\lambda,\mu,\nu\vdash n$,
$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=\bigl\langle\chi^\lambda\chi^\mu,\chi^\nu\bigr\rangle=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\chi^\lambda(\sigma)\chi^\mu(\sigma)\chi^\nu(\sigma),$$
where $\chi^\lambda\chi^\mu$ is the pointwise product of class functions and the
sum uses the real-valuedness of the irreducible characters, so that no
conjugation appears on the third factor.

The conjugacy classes of $S_n$ are in bijection with the tuples of
nonnegative integers $(c_1,\ldots,c_n)$ satisfying
$$\sum_{k=1}^n kc_k=n.$$
For $n=0$, the unique empty tuple indexes the identity class of $S_0$.

If $\sigma\in S_n$ has $c_k$ cycles of length $k$, including fixed points when
$k=1$, then
$$|C_{S_n}(\sigma)|=\prod_{k=1}^n k^{c_k}c_k!.$$
The formula uses the empty product $1$ when $n=0$.

Let $n\ge 0$ and let $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)\vdash n$ be a partition
with Young diagram $[\lambda]$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Throughout, $S_n$
denotes the symmetric group of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, with $S_0=\{1\}$.

**Standard Young subgroups.** For $1\le i\le k$ let
$$B_i:=\{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+2,\ \dots,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i\}$$
be the $i$-th **block** of $\lambda$. The blocks are consecutive intervals of
integers, they are pairwise disjoint, each has $|B_i|=\lambda_i$, and together
they partition $\{1,\dots,n\}$. The **standard Young subgroup** of type
$\lambda$ is
$$S_\lambda:=\{\,\sigma\in S_n:\sigma(B_i)=B_i\text{ for every }1\le i\le k\,\}.$$
This is a subgroup of $S_n$, namely the direct product
$S(B_1)\times\cdots\times S(B_k)$ of the symmetric groups of the individual
blocks, each acting on its block and fixing the remaining entries pointwise;
as in [[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]], the product
decomposition is unique because the blocks are pairwise disjoint and cover
$\{1,\dots,n\}$, so $|S_\lambda|=\lambda_1!\cdots\lambda_k!$. A **Young
subgroup of type $\lambda$** is a subgroup of $S_n$ conjugate to
$S_\lambda$. For $k=0$, that is for $\lambda=\varnothing$ and $n=0$, there are
no blocks and $S_\varnothing=S_0=\{1\}$.

**Row equivalence and tabloids.** Let $t$ and $u$ be $\lambda$-tableaux
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). We say that $t$ and $u$
are **row equivalent**, and write $t\sim u$, when they have the same row sets:
for every row $i$,
$$\{\,t(i,j):1\le j\le\lambda_i\,\}=\{\,u(i,j):1\le j\le\lambda_i\,\}.$$
Equivalently, $t\sim u$ if and only if $u=\rho\cdot t$ for some $\rho\in R_t$:
if $u=\rho\cdot t$ then $\rho$ merely permutes the entries inside each row of
$t$, and conversely, if the row sets agree, then
$\rho(t(i,j)):=u(i,j)$ defines a permutation $\rho$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ that
preserves each row set of $t$, so $\rho\in R_t$ and $\rho\cdot t=u$. Hence
$\sim$ is an equivalence relation on the $\lambda$-tableaux, and the
equivalence class
$$\{t\}:=\{\,u:u\sim t\,\}=\{\,\rho\cdot t:\rho\in R_t\,\}$$
is the **tabloid** of $t$. We draw $\{t\}$ as the diagram $[\lambda]$ filled
with the entries of $t$ and bars between the rows, recording that the order of
the entries inside a row is forgotten. A tabloid is **standard** when it
contains a standard tableau.

**The permutation module.** Let $\Omega_\lambda$ be the finite set of
$\lambda$-tabloids. For $\sigma\in S_n$ and a tabloid $\{t\}$ define
$$\sigma\cdot\{t\}:=\{\sigma\cdot t\}.$$
This is well defined: if $t,u$ are $\lambda$-tableaux with $t\sim u$, then the
row sets of $\sigma\cdot u$ are the $\sigma$-images of the row sets of $u$,
which are the $\sigma$-images of the row sets of $t$, and these are exactly
the row sets of $\sigma\cdot t$
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]); so
$\sigma\cdot u\sim\sigma\cdot t$ and the tabloids $\{\sigma\cdot u\}$ and
$\{\sigma\cdot t\}$ coincide. Because the action on tableaux is a left action,
the induced rule on tabloids satisfies $\mathrm{id}\cdot\{t\}=\{t\}$ and
$\sigma\cdot(\tau\cdot\{t\})=(\sigma\tau)\cdot\{t\}$, so $S_n$ acts on
$\Omega_\lambda$ from the left. The **Young permutation module** attached to
$\lambda$ is the complex vector space
$$M^\lambda:=\mathbb C^{(\Omega_\lambda)}$$
with the tabloids as basis, again written $\{t\}$ for the basis vector of the
tabloid $\{t\}$, equipped with the linear extension of the action above:
$$\sigma\cdot\sum_{\{t\}\in\Omega_\lambda}a_{\{t\}}\,\{t\}:=\sum_{\{t\}\in\Omega_\lambda}a_{\{t\}}\,\{\sigma\cdot t\}.$$
This is the permutation representation of $S_n$ on the finite set
$\Omega_\lambda$ ([[def-trivial-regular-and-permutation-representations]]),
so $M^\lambda$ is a finite-dimensional complex representation of $S_n$.

**The stabilizer of a tabloid.** For every $\lambda$-tableau $t$ one has
$$\sigma\cdot\{t\}=\{t\}\iff \sigma\cdot t\sim t\iff \sigma\in R_t,$$
so the stabilizer in $S_n$ of the tabloid $\{t\}$ is exactly the row
stabilizer $R_t$ ([[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]]). The action
on $\Omega_\lambda$ is transitive: given tabloids $\{t\}$ and $\{s\}$, the
permutation $\sigma$ determined by $\sigma(t(i,j)):=s(i,j)$ satisfies
$\sigma\cdot t=s$, hence $\sigma\cdot\{t\}=\{s\}$. In particular, for the
**standard row-filled $\lambda$-tableau** $t_0$, whose row $i$ carries the
entries of $B_i$ in increasing order, the row sets of $t_0$ are precisely the
blocks $B_1,\dots,B_k$, so $R_{t_0}=S_\lambda$ and the stabilizer of the
tabloid $\{t_0\}$ is the standard Young subgroup $S_\lambda$.

Let $n\ge0$, let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$, let $M^\mu$ be the complex Young
permutation module of shape $\mu$ with its tabloid basis
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]), and let
$S^\lambda\subseteq M^\lambda$ be the complex Specht module
([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). Write
$K_{\lambda,\mu}$ for the Kostka number
([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]) and, for an integer $r\ge0$,
let $(S^\lambda)^{\oplus r}$ denote a direct sum of $r$ copies of
$S^\lambda$, the zero module when $r=0$. Then:

1. **(Isomorphism type.)** $M^\mu$ is completely reducible and there is an
   isomorphism of $\mathbb C S_n$-modules
   $$M^\mu\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash n}(S^\lambda)^{\oplus K_{\lambda,\mu}},$$
   the sum being over the finitely many partitions of $n$.
2. **(Multiplicity.)** In every decomposition of $M^\mu$ as a direct sum of
   irreducible subrepresentations the number of summands isomorphic to
   $S^\lambda$ equals $K_{\lambda,\mu}$; that is, the multiplicity
   $[M^\mu:S^\lambda]$ is well defined and equal to the Kostka number
   $K_{\lambda,\mu}$, independently of the decomposition.

Fix $\lambda,\mu,\nu\vdash n$ and an integer $k\ge1$. Write $(t^k)$ for $k$ parts equal to $t$ and $(tk)$ for the one-part partition of size $tk$, and read missing parts as zero. Put $s:=n-\nu_1$, with $\nu_1=0$ if $n=0$.

Work in $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$, the
$\mathbb Q$-scalar extension of the stable graded ring
([[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]]). Its power sums
$p_1,p_2,\dots$ ([[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]])
are algebraically independent generators:
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[p_1,p_2,\dots]$, and for every $d$ the products
$p_\lambda$, $\lambda\vdash d$, form a $\mathbb Q$-basis of
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d$
([[prop-power-sums-form-a-rational-not-integral-stable-basis]]).

A **specialization** is a $\mathbb Q$-algebra homomorphism
$f\mapsto f[A]$ from $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ to a commutative
$\mathbb Q$-algebra. By the algebraic independence of the power sums, a
specialization is determined by the sequence of values $\bigl(p_k[A]\bigr)_{k\ge1}$,
and conversely every sequence of elements of a commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebra
extends uniquely to a specialization. For specializations $A,B$, a scalar
$c\in\mathbb Q$ and a one-letter alphabet $t$ one defines the specializations
$A+B$, $-A$, $AB$, $c\cdot A$ and $tA$ by their power-sum values

$$p_k[A+B]:=p_k[A]+p_k[B],\qquad p_k[-A]:=-p_k[A],\qquad p_k[AB]:=p_k[A]\,p_k[B],$$

$$p_k[c\cdot A]:=c\,p_k[A],\qquad p_k[t]:=t^k\ \ \text{and hence}\ \ p_k[tA]=t^k p_k[A].$$

Here $c\cdot A$ is a coefficient multiplicity, to be distinguished from the
one-letter alphabet $t$, for which $p_k[t]=t^k$ is a power and
$p_k[tA]=t^k p_k[A]$; all occurrences of $tX$, $t^{-1}$, $tA$ and
$\sigma[t]$ on this page use this one-letter convention. The symbol $1$
denotes the one-letter alphabet with $p_k[1]=1$ for all $k$, and $-1$ denotes
its plethystic negative with $p_k[-1]=-1$ for all $k$
([[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]); it is
**not** the ordinary one-letter alphabet whose letter is minus one, for which
$p_k$ would equal $(-1)^k$. One writes $f[A+B]$, $f[-A]$, $f[AB]$ and
$f[c\cdot A]$ for the images of $f$ under these specializations.

Define $X^{\perp}$ to be the specialization with $f[X^{\perp}]:=f^{\perp}$ for
all $f$, where $f^{\perp}$ is the adjoint of multiplication by $f$ with respect
to the Hall inner product $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_H$
([[def-hall-inner-product-on-symmetric-functions]]), characterized by
$\langle f^{\perp}g,h\rangle_H=\langle g,fh\rangle_H$. It exists and is unique
because the Hall form is nondegenerate on each finite-dimensional graded piece
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d$; the adjoints of commuting multiplication operators
commute, so the operators $f^{\perp}$ span a commutative
$\mathbb Q$-algebra and $X^{\perp}$ is a specialization in the sense above.

Define the series
$$\sigma[X]:=\sum_{n\ge0}h_n[X],$$
$h_n$ the complete homogeneous symmetric function
([[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]).
Here $\sigma$ is interpreted in the graded completion of $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$
(or with a formal degree variable): it is a formal series, not an element of
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$, and every occurrence of $\sigma$ below is to be read
degree by degree. Every Hall pairing of a series with a polynomial is the
finite sum obtained by truncating to the degrees of the polynomial. No
convergence of a scalar infinite sum is asserted, and no value of $\sigma$ at

([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Write

$$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[p_1,p_2,\ldots],$$

$\mathbb Q$-basis of $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d$. These families are not in
general $\mathbb Z$-bases of $\Lambda^d$: in degree two,

basis.

For partitions $\lambda$ and $\rho$ of the same integer, let $N(\lambda,\rho)$
be the number of ways to distribute the cycles of a permutation $w$ of cycle
type $\rho$ among the $\ell(\lambda)$ rows, labelled $1,\dots,\ell(\lambda)$,
so that row $j$ receives cycles whose lengths sum to $\lambda_j$. Cycles of
equal length count as **distinct** here, because they are distinct cycles of
$w$; equivalently,

$$N(\lambda,\rho)=\sum_{(m_i^{(j)})}\ \prod_{i\ge1}\frac{m_i(\rho)!}{\prod_j m_i^{(j)}!},$$

the sum over all matrices $(m_i^{(j)})$ of nonnegative integers with
$\sum_j m_i^{(j)}=m_i(\rho)$ for every $i$ and

$$h_\lambda=\sum_{\rho\vdash|\lambda|}N(\lambda,\rho)\,\frac{p_\rho}{z_\rho}\qquad\text{in }\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}.$$

In particular $h_d=\sum_{\rho\vdash d}p_\rho/z_\rho$ for every $d\ge0$.

$$p_k:=x_1^k+\cdots+x_n^k.$$

For $k\ge0$, the **$k$-th complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial** is

$$h_k:=\sum_{a_1+\cdots+a_n=k}x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}.$$

Thus $h_0=1$, while for $n=0$ one has $h_k=0$ when $k>0$. Both families are fixed by every permutation of the variables.

Put $e_0=1$ and $e_k=0$ for $k>n$. For every $k\ge1$,

$$k e_k=\sum_{i=1}^k(-1)^{i-1}e_{k-i}p_i.$$

In particular, for $k\le n$ this recursively relates $e_k$ to $p_1,\ldots,p_k$, while for $k>n$ it gives

$$p_k-e_1p_{k-1}+\cdots+(-1)^ne_np_{k-n}=0.$$

No division is used, so the identities hold over every commutative ring.

$$ (uv)_{a,b}:=\sum_{i=0}^{a}\sum_{j=0}^{b}u_{i,j}v_{a-i,b-j},$$
where multiplication in each tensor factor is the graded multiplication of
$\Lambda$. This is a finite sum for each fixed $(a,b)$, so it defines a
commutative ring; the unit has component $1\otimes1$ at $(0,0)$ and zero
elsewhere.

The **Cauchy kernel** is the element
$$\Omega(x,y):=\prod_{r,s\ge1}(1-x_r y_s)^{-1}$$
interpreted bidegree by bidegree: its degree-$(d,d)$ component is the stable
degree-$d$ coefficient of the finite products, and all components $(a,b)$ with
$a\ne b$ are zero. Thus $\Omega$ belongs to the diagonal bidegrees of this
completion, not to the finite-support graded ring $\Lambda$ itself.

Let $\Omega(x,y)$ be the Cauchy kernel in the bidegree completion
[[def-bidegree-completed-symmetric-function-tensor-product]]. In
$\Lambda(x)\widehat\otimes\Lambda(y)$,
$$\Omega(x,y)=\sum_\lambda h_\lambda(x)m_\lambda(y)=\sum_\lambda s_\lambda(x)s_\lambda(y).$$
In the componentwise rational completion
$$\prod_{a,b\ge0}\bigl(\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^a(x)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^b(y)\bigr),$$
it also has the expansion
$$\Omega(x,y)=\sum_\lambda z_\lambda^{-1}p_\lambda(x)p_\lambda(y),\qquad z_\lambda:=\prod_{r\ge1}r^{m_r(\lambda)}m_r(\lambda)!,\qquad m_r(\lambda):=\#\{i:\lambda_i=r\}.$$
All three sums are by bidegree $(d,d)$; the empty products indexed by
$\varnothing$ equal $1$.

Let $\lambda,

The **reading word** $w(T)$ of a semistandard skew tableau $T$ of shape $
u/\lambda$ is the word obtained by reading the rows of $T$ from right to left, beginning with the top row and proceeding to the bottom row. The word $w(T)=a_1a_2\cdots a_N$ is a **lattice word** (a lattice permutation) if in every prefix $a_1\cdots a_p$ and for every $i\ge1$ the number of letters $i$ in the prefix is at least the number of letters $i+1$; the empty word is a lattice word vacuously.

u/\lambda$ and content $\mu$ is a semistandard skew tableau of shape $
u/\lambda$ and content $\mu$ whose reading word is a lattice word. The **Littlewood--Richardson coefficient** $c^
u_{\lambda\mu}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ is the number of LR tableaux of shape $
