u_{\lambda\mu}=0$ unless $\lambda\subseteq
u$ and $|
u|=|\lambda|+|\mu|$.

For all partitions $\alpha,\beta$ and every integer
$n\ge\max\{|\alpha|+\alpha_1,\,|\beta|+\beta_1\}$:
$$s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]}=\sum_\gamma
\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\,s_{\gamma[n]},$$
an identity in the symmetric function ring, where $s_{\gamma[n]}$ is the
Jacobi–Trudi determinant attached to the integer sequence
$\gamma[n]=(n-|\gamma|,\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\dots)$, equal to $0$ or $\pm1$ times
a Schur function
([[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]],
[[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]), and $*$ is the internal product
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

For an ordinary partition $\delta\vdash n$ the coefficient of $s_\delta$ is
$$g^\delta_{\alpha[n],\beta[n]}
=\sum_\gamma \bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\,
\langle s_{\gamma[n]},s_\delta\rangle_H,$$
where each Hall factor is $0$ or a sign coming from Jacobi–Trudi
straightening ([[thm-schur-functions-form-an-orthonormal-integral-basis]]).
At small admissible ranks the signed terms can cancel or coalesce;
individual coefficients need not yet equal their reduced values. The range
displayed is precisely the set of $n$ for which $\alpha[n]$ and $\beta[n]$
are partitions.

**Padded sequences.** For a partition $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ and an
integer $n$ the first-row padding is the sequence
$\alpha[n]:=(n-|\alpha|,\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$, a partition of $n$ exactly
when $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$
([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]],
[[def-padded-kronecker-coefficient-sequence]]).

**The Jacobi–Trudi completion.** For an arbitrary finite sequence of integers
$\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m)$, define
$$s_\mu:=\det\bigl(h_{\mu_j-j+i}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m},$$
where $h_0=1$ and $h_k=0$ for $k<0$
([[thm-jacobi-trudi-and-dual-jacobi-trudi-identities]]); for the empty sequence
the empty determinant is $1$. Every such determinant is $0$ or $\pm1$ times a
Schur function. Indeed, put $q_j:=\mu_j+m-j$. If $q_j=q_k$ for $j\ne k$, the
$j$-th and $k$-th columns of the matrix agree, so the determinant vanishes.
Otherwise let $\sigma$ be the permutation sorting $q$ into decreasing order
$q_{\sigma(1)}>\cdots>q_{\sigma(m)}$ and set $\nu_j:=q_{\sigma(j)}+j-m$; then
$\nu$ is weakly decreasing and, permuting columns with sign
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ and using
$h_{\nu_j-j+i}=h_{q_{\sigma(j)}+i-m}$, the determinant equals
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\det(h_{\nu_j-j+i})$. If $\min_jq_j<0$ then
$\nu_m<0$ and the last column of this determinant is zero, so the value is
$0$; if $\min_jq_j\ge0$ then $\nu$ is a partition of $|\mu|$ with at most $m$
parts and the Jacobi–Trudi identity gives the value
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)s_\nu$. In particular $s_{\alpha[n]}\in\Lambda^n$
for every $n\ge0$, and $s_{\alpha[n]}=0$ for $n<0$: every term of the
determinant expansion has total degree $n$, so for $n<0$ some factor has
negative index and vanishes.

**The operators $U_n$ and $V$.** The Schur functions form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of
$\Lambda$ ([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]), so there are unique
$\mathbb Z$-linear endomorphisms $U_n$ ($n\in\mathbb Z$) and $V$ of $\Lambda$
determined on the Schur basis by
$$U_n(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda[n]},\qquad V(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda+(1)},$$
where $\lambda+(1)=(\lambda_1+1,\lambda_2,\dots)$. Thus $U_n$ carries
$\Lambda^{|\lambda|}$ into the line spanned by $s_{\lambda[n]}\in\Lambda^n$
(and is the zero map for $n<0$), while $V$ raises degree by one. The operators
are extended linearly, and $V^k$ denotes the $k$-fold iterate of $V$.

**The stabilization index.** The internal product $*$ on $\Lambda$ is the
degree-preserving product of
[[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]] and
[[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]. For partitions
$\alpha,\beta$, define $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ to be the least
integer $n_0\ge0$ such that
$$s_{\alpha[n_0+k]}*s_{\beta[n_0+k]}=V^k\bigl(s_{\alpha[n_0]}*s_{\beta[n_0]}\bigr)
\qquad\text{for all }k>0,$$
following the source. This definition records the source's convention only: it
does not assert that such an $n_0$ exists, nor that a value of $n_0$ satisfying
the display is least for any other property. Existence, least-ness and the
exact value of $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ are proved in
[[thm-exact-global-stabilization-threshold-for-a-fixed-kronecker-product]].

Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be partitions with $|\gamma|=|\alpha|+|\beta|$. Then
$$\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}=c^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta},$$
the Littlewood–Richardson coefficient
([[def-littlewood-richardson-tableau-and-coefficient]]). In particular
$$\bar g^{\alpha+\beta}_{\alpha,\beta}
=c^{\alpha+\beta}_{\alpha,\beta}=1,$$
where $\alpha+\beta=(\alpha_1+\beta_1,\alpha_2+\beta_2,\dots)$.

For partitions $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ define the **reduced (stable) Kronecker
coefficient** $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}$ to be the eventual value of the
padded sequence $n\mapsto g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ furnished by
[[thm-murnaghan-stability-for-kronecker-coefficients]]; equivalently
$$\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}:=\lim_{n\to\infty}g^{\gamma[n]}_{\alpha[n],\beta[n]},$$
where the sequence is defined for
$n\ge\max\{|\alpha|+\alpha_1,|\beta|+\beta_1,|\gamma|+\gamma_1\}$ and set to
$0$ below ([[def-padded-kronecker-coefficient-sequence]],
[[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

**Well-definedness.** The sequence is eventually constant by the Murnaghan
stability theorem, and the eventual value of an eventually constant sequence
of nonnegative integers is a unique nonnegative integer; no choice is
involved. Two immediate conventions: (i) $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}=
\bar g^\gamma_{\beta,\alpha}$ for all $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$, because
$V_\mu\otimes V_\nu\cong V_\nu\otimes V_\mu$ and the Kronecker coefficients
are symmetric in their two lower indices; (ii) for fixed $\alpha,\beta$ only
finitely many $\gamma$ have $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\ne0$, because the
finite set $S(\alpha,\beta)$ of the stability theorem carries the whole
support. The values used later and verified in the source's introduction for
$\alpha=\beta=(2)$ are $\bar g^{(2)}_{(2),(2)}=2$ and
$\bar g^{(4)}_{(2),(2)}=1$; they are read off from the displayed stable row
and are not used as logical inputs anywhere on this page.

If $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}>0$ then
$$|\alpha|\le|\beta|+|\gamma|,\qquad |\beta|\le|\alpha|+|\gamma|,
\qquad |\gamma|\le|\alpha|+|\beta|$$
(Murnaghan's inequalities). Hence the support $\operatorname{Supp}(\alpha,\beta)$
of the nonzero reduced coefficients with fixed $\alpha,\beta$ lies in the
triangle region of the weight lattice.

**Padded sequences.** For a partition $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ and an
integer $n$ the first-row padding is the sequence
$\alpha[n]:=(n-|\alpha|,\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$, a partition of $n$ exactly
when $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$
([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]],
[[def-padded-kronecker-coefficient-sequence]]).

**The Jacobi–Trudi completion.** For an arbitrary finite sequence of integers
$\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m)$, define
$$s_\mu:=\det\bigl(h_{\mu_j-j+i}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m},$$
where $h_0=1$ and $h_k=0$ for $k<0$
([[thm-jacobi-trudi-and-dual-jacobi-trudi-identities]]); for the empty sequence
the empty determinant is $1$. Every such determinant is $0$ or $\pm1$ times a
Schur function. Indeed, put $q_j:=\mu_j+m-j$. If $q_j=q_k$ for $j\ne k$, the
$j$-th and $k$-th columns of the matrix agree, so the determinant vanishes.
Otherwise let $\sigma$ be the permutation sorting $q$ into decreasing order
$q_{\sigma(1)}>\cdots>q_{\sigma(m)}$ and set $\nu_j:=q_{\sigma(j)}+j-m$; then
$\nu$ is weakly decreasing and, permuting columns with sign
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ and using
$h_{\nu_j-j+i}=h_{q_{\sigma(j)}+i-m}$, the determinant equals
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\det(h_{\nu_j-j+i})$. If $\min_jq_j<0$ then
$\nu_m<0$ and the last column of this determinant is zero, so the value is
$0$; if $\min_jq_j\ge0$ then $\nu$ is a partition of $|\mu|$ with at most $m$
parts and the Jacobi–Trudi identity gives the value
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)s_\nu$. In particular $s_{\alpha[n]}\in\Lambda^n$
for every $n\ge0$, and $s_{\alpha[n]}=0$ for $n<0$: every term of the
determinant expansion has total degree $n$, so for $n<0$ some factor has
negative index and vanishes.

**The operators $U_n$ and $V$.** The Schur functions form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of
$\Lambda$ ([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]), so there are unique
$\mathbb Z$-linear endomorphisms $U_n$ ($n\in\mathbb Z$) and $V$ of $\Lambda$
determined on the Schur basis by
$$U_n(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda[n]},\qquad V(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda+(1)},$$
where $\lambda+(1)=(\lambda_1+1,\lambda_2,\dots)$. Thus $U_n$ carries
$\Lambda^{|\lambda|}$ into the line spanned by $s_{\lambda[n]}\in\Lambda^n$
(and is the zero map for $n<0$), while $V$ raises degree by one. The operators
are extended linearly, and $V^k$ denotes the $k$-fold iterate of $V$.

**The stabilization index.** The internal product $*$ on $\Lambda$ is the
degree-preserving product of
[[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]] and
[[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]. For partitions
$\alpha,\beta$, define $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ to be the least
integer $n_0\ge0$ such that
$$s_{\alpha[n_0+k]}*s_{\beta[n_0+k]}=V^k\bigl(s_{\alpha[n_0]}*s_{\beta[n_0]}\bigr)
\qquad\text{for all }k>0,$$
following the source. This definition records the source's convention only: it
does not assert that such an $n_0$ exists, nor that a value of $n_0$ satisfying
the display is least for any other property. Existence, least-ness and the
exact value of $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ are proved in
[[thm-exact-global-stabilization-threshold-for-a-fixed-kronecker-product]].

For every $d\ge0$, the stable Schur functions $\{s_\lambda:\lambda\vdash d\}$
form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of $\Lambda^d$ and are orthonormal for the Hall form:
$$\langle s_\lambda,s_\mu\rangle_H=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$$
for all partitions $\lambda,\mu$.

Let $\operatorname{ch}:R_S\to\Lambda$ be the Frobenius characteristic restricted
to the graded ordinary representation ring of the symmetric groups
([[def-frobenius-characteristic-map]],
[[def-graded-ordinary-representation-ring-of-symmetric-groups]]). By
[[thm-frobenius-characteristic-is-an-isometric-graded-ring-isomorphism]] it is a
degree-preserving $\mathbb Z$-module isomorphism onto the stable symmetric
function ring $\Lambda=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}\Lambda^m$, so its restriction
$\operatorname{ch}:R(S_m)\to\Lambda^m$ is an isomorphism for every $m\ge0$.

For $f\in\Lambda^m$ and $g\in\Lambda^n$ define
$$f*g:=\begin{cases}\operatorname{ch}\bigl(\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(f)\cdot\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(g)\bigr),&m=n,\\[2pt]0,&m\ne n,\end{cases}$$
where $\cdot$ is the pointwise (internal tensor) product of class functions on
$S_m$; extend $*$ bilinearly to all of $\Lambda$. Call $*$ the
**internal (Kronecker) product** of symmetric functions.

**Well-definedness.** For $m=n$ the class functions $\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(f)$
and $\operatorname{ch}^{-1}(g)$ lie in $R(S_m)$, the integral span of the
irreducible characters of $S_m$
([[def-graded-ordinary-representation-ring-of-symmetric-groups]]). The
pointwise product of two honest characters of $S_m$ is again an honest
character, namely the character of the tensor product of the underlying
representations ([[thm-characters-of-direct-sums-tensor-products-and-duals]]),
and products of $\mathbb Z$-combinations of characters are computed
bilinearly; hence the pointwise product of two elements of $R(S_m)$ lies in
$R(S_m)$, and applying the isomorphism $\operatorname{ch}$ lands in $\Lambda^m$.
The product is therefore well defined and takes $\Lambda^m\times\Lambda^m$ to
$\Lambda^m$.

**Basic properties.** The product is bilinear by construction and inherits
commutativity and associativity from the pointwise product of class functions.
It preserves degrees, in the sense that $\Lambda^m*\Lambda^n\subseteq\Lambda^m$
for $m=n$ and is $0$ for $m\ne n$. On $\Lambda^n$ the unit is
$h_n=s_{(n)}=\operatorname{ch}(\text{trivial character of }S_n)$, because the
trivial character is the unit for pointwise multiplication on $R(S_n)$
([[thm-frobenius-characteristic-sends-specht-characters-to-schur-functions]]
identifies $\operatorname{ch}(\chi^{(n)})=s_{(n)}=h_n$). The graded direct sum
$\Lambda$ has **no global unit** for $*$: if $e\in\Lambda$ had finite degree
support and $n$ were a degree with $e_n=0$ while $\Lambda^n\ne0$, then
$(e*h_n)_n=e_n*h_n=0\ne h_n$, so $e*h_n\ne h_n$; a global unit would require
$e_n$ to be a unit of $(\Lambda^n,*)$ for every $n$. In particular the ordinary
product unit $1\in\Lambda^0$ is not a unit for $*$ on the positive degrees.

**Schur expansion.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$, the definition and
the Specht character dictionary $\operatorname{ch}(\chi^\lambda)=s_\lambda$
([[thm-frobenius-characteristic-sends-specht-characters-to-schur-functions]])
give
$$s_\lambda*s_\mu=\operatorname{ch}\bigl(\chi^\lambda\cdot\chi^\mu\bigr)=\operatorname{ch}\Bigl(\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\chi^\nu\Bigr)=\sum_{\nu\vdash n}g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\,s_\nu,$$
because $\chi^\lambda\chi^\mu$ is the character of
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ and its decomposition has multiplicities
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the transport goes through the
choice-free Frobenius characteristic isomorphism and finite-dimensional
representation theory of finite groups.

Fix an integer $n\ge0$ and work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be
partitions of $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ be the tensor product of their complex
Specht modules, a finite-dimensional complex $S_n$-module
([[def-tensor-product-of-complex-representations]],
[[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). The
**Kronecker coefficient** $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ of a third partition
$\nu\vdash n$ is the multiplicity of $S^\nu$ in this tensor product:

$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu):=\frac{\dim_{\mathbb C}\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}}{\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu},$$

where $\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}$ is the isotypic
component of type $S^\nu$
([[def-isotypic-component-of-a-completely-reducible-representation]]).

**Well-definedness.** The module $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ is
finite-dimensional, and $\operatorname{char}\mathbb C=0$ does not divide the
order of the finite group $S_n$, so complex Maschke's theorem gives complete
reducibility
([[thm-maschkes-theorem-for-finite-groups-over-fields-whose-characteristic-does-not-divide-the-group-order]],
[[cor-finite-dimensional-representations-are-completely-reducible-when-char-k-does-not-divide-group-order]],
[[def-completely-reducible-representation]]). The complex Specht modules
$S^\nu$, $\nu\vdash n$, are a complete list of pairwise inequivalent
irreducible $S_n$-modules
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]],
[[cor-distinct-specht-modules-are-inequivalent]]). Consequently a decomposition
into irreducibles has the form
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\cong\bigoplus_{\nu\vdash n}m_\nu S^\nu$
with nonnegative integer multiplicities $m_\nu$, and the isotypic component of
type $S^\nu$ is the direct sum of exactly the $m_\nu$ copies of $S^\nu$
appearing in any such decomposition; in particular
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu)_{(S^\nu)}=m_\nu\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu$
and $\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu>0$ because $S^\nu$ is irreducible. Hence
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=m_\nu$ is a nonnegative integer, independent of the chosen
decomposition, and $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ is by definition the multiplicity of
$S^\nu$ in $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$.

**The internal product.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ call
$$(\lambda,\mu)\longmapsto S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$$
the **internal (Kronecker) product** of the $S_n$-representations $S^\lambda$
and $S^\mu$. Unlike the outer induction product
$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_b}^{S_{a+b}}(S^\alpha\boxtimes S^\beta)$ of
[[thm-outer-littlewood-richardson-rule]], which takes a pair of modules of
degrees $a$ and $b$ to a module of degree $a+b$, the internal product keeps the
rank: both inputs and the output are $S_n$-modules of the same degree $n$. The
two operations are different constructions on different data; the outer product
is mentioned here only for contrast and is not used in this definition.

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the tensor product, Maschke's theorem,
the Specht classification and the isotypic decomposition are finite-dimensional
complex representation theory of a finite group.

derivations.claim: *Upper bound on the support.* Let $\gamma$ have $\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\ne0$ and choose a nonzero summand of [F1]. By [F2], $\gamma_1\le\mu_1+\theta_1+\pi_1\le|\mu|+\theta_1+\pi_1$, so $|\gamma|+\gamma_1\le(|\mu|+|\theta|+|\pi|)+(|\mu|+\theta_1+\pi_1)=2|\mu|+|\theta|+\theta_1+|\pi|+\pi_1$; using $|\mu|=|\lambda|=|\eta|$ this is $(|\lambda|+|\theta|+\theta_1)+(|\eta|+|\pi|+\pi_1)\le(|\alpha|+\alpha_1)+(|\beta|+\beta_1)$ by [F2]. Hence every nonzero reduced coefficient has $|\gamma|+\gamma_1\le N$.

*Both inputs empty.* Here $N=0$, $\alpha[n]=\beta[n]=(n)$ for every $n\ge0$, and $s_{(n)}*s_{(n)}=s_{(n)}$ by [F7]; also $V^n(1)=V^n(s_\varnothing)=s_{(n)}$ by [F6], since $V$ adds a box to the first row and $s_{\varnothing}=1$. Hence $s_{\alpha[n+k]}*s_{\beta[n+k]}=s_{(n+k)}=V^k(s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]})$ for all $n\ge0,k>0$, with no negative-rank product invoked, so $\operatorname{stab}(\varnothing,\varnothing)=0$, the least possible value of the defining index.

*Attainment and identification of the maximum.* The partition $\gamma^\ast:=\alpha+\beta$ satisfies $|\gamma^\ast|+\gamma^\ast_1=|\alpha|+|\beta|+(\alpha_1+\beta_1)=N$ and $\bar g^{\gamma^\ast}_{\alpha,\beta}=c^{\gamma^\ast}_{\alpha,\beta}=1$ by [F4]; hence $\max\{|\gamma|+\gamma_1:\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\ne0\}=N$. In particular $|\gamma|+\gamma_1\le n$ for every support label and every $n\ge N$, so all support labels $\gamma[n]$ are ordinary partitions at such $n$; this is the assertion of the source's Lemma 3.1 combined with the evaluation of the maximum.

*$V$-stability from $N$.* For $n\ge N$ the identity of [F3] is available (the thresholds $|\alpha|+\alpha_1,|\beta|+\beta_1$ are $\le N$) and every $\gamma[n]$ in the finite support is a partition by step 2.1; applying [F3] at $n+k$ and using [F4] term by term gives $s_{\alpha[n+k]}*s_{\beta[n+k]}=\sum_\gamma\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}s_{\gamma[n+k]}=\sum_\gamma\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}V^k(s_{\gamma[n]})=V^k(s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]})$ for all $k>0$, together with the fixed nonnegative Schur expansion at every rank $n\ge N$. Hence $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)\le N$ in the sense of the Definition.

*$N$ is not in the image of $V$, when $N>0$.* If $N>0$ then $\alpha$ or $\beta$ is nonempty and the partition $(\alpha+\beta)[N]=(N-|\alpha|-|\beta|,(\alpha+\beta)_1,\dots)=(\alpha_1+\beta_1,\alpha_1+\beta_1,\dots)$ has equal first two parts, which are positive because at least one of $\alpha,\beta$ is nonempty. At rank $N$ the coefficient of $s_{(\alpha+\beta)[N]}$ in the product is $\bar g^{\alpha+\beta}_{\alpha,\beta}=1$ by [F4] and step 3.1. If $N>0$ and the product at $N$ lay in the image of $V$, then by [F6] its coefficient of $s_{(\alpha+\beta)[N]}$ would be $0$, a contradiction.

*Least-ness, both inputs nonempty.* Suppose $\alpha\ne\varnothing\ne\beta$. Then $N-1=|\alpha|+|\beta|+\alpha_1+\beta_1-1\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ and $\ge|\beta|+\beta_1$, since $|\beta|+\beta_1\ge1$ and $|\alpha|+\alpha_1\ge1$; so $N-1$ is an admissible rank and the product at $N-1$ is defined. If some $n_0<N$ satisfied the stabilization condition of the Definition, then the product at $N$ would equal $V^{N-n_0}$ of the product at $n_0$, which lies in the image of $V$, contradicting step 4.1; taking $n_0=N-1$ shows in particular that the product at $N$ is not $V$ of the product at $N-1$. Hence $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)=N$ in this case.

*Least-ness, exactly one input empty.* Say $ eta=\varnothing
e\alpha$, so $N=|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ is the least rank at which $\alpha[n]$ (and $ eta[n]=(n)$) is an ordinary partition. By [F5], every $\gamma$ with $ ar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\varnothing}
e0$ satisfies $|\gamma|\le|\alpha|\le|\emptyset|+|\gamma|=|\gamma|$, hence $|\gamma|=|\alpha|$, and then [F4] gives $ ar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\varnothing}=c^\gamma_{\alpha,\varnothing}=\delta_{\gamma,\alpha}$; so the product at rank $N$ is exactly $s_{\alpha[N]}$, whose first two parts are $\alpha_1,\alpha_1$ with $\alpha_1\ge1$. The obstruction of step 4.1 therefore applies at $N$: the product at $N$ does not lie in the image of $V$, so no $n_0<N$ can satisfy the stabilization condition, while $n_0=N$ does by step 3.1. The case $\alpha=\varnothing
e eta$ is symmetric.

*Conclusion.* Combining steps 3.1, 5.1, 5.2 and 1.2 gives $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)=N=|\alpha|+|\beta|+\alpha_1+\beta_1$ in all cases, with the fixed nonnegative expansion and $V$-stability from $N$ onward; the statement claims nothing about sharpness for an individual coefficient, and the proof used only finite sums, the proved all-rank expansion and the unit of the internal product. No choice principle is used.

citations.quote:
For all partitions $\lambda,\mu,\nu\vdash n$,
$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=\bigl\langle\chi^\lambda\chi^\mu,\chi^\nu\bigr\rangle=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\chi^\lambda(\sigma)\chi^\mu(\sigma)\chi^\nu(\sigma),$$
where $\chi^\lambda\chi^\mu$ is the pointwise product of class functions and the
sum uses the real-valuedness of the irreducible characters, so that no
conjugation appears on the third factor.

For every $n\ge0$, the modules $\{S^\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ form a
complete irredundant list, up to isomorphism, of finite-dimensional irreducible
complex $S_n$-representations.

Let $n\ge 0$, let $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $t$ be a $\lambda$-tableau
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). Use the left action of
$S_n$ on tableaux, tabloids, and $M^\lambda$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]). For each
$\gamma\in C_t$, let $\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)$ be its inversion sign in
$S_n$. The order-preserving relabelling
$\iota_n:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, $i\mapsto i-1$, carries each
inversion pair $(i,j)$ bijectively to $(i-1,j-1)$; thus this sign is exactly
the published inversion sign on the finite ordinal
([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). For $n=0$, both groups are
trivial and the sign is $1$.

The **column antisymmetrizer**, **polytabloid**, and **Specht space** are
$$\kappa_t:=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\gamma\quad\in\mathbb C[S_n],\qquad e_t:=\kappa_t\cdot\{t\}\quad\in M^\lambda,\qquad S^\lambda:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{e_s:s\text{ is a }\lambda\text{-tableau}\}.$$
The elements of the sum are in the finite subgroup $C_t$, and each acts by the
declared left action on the tabloid basis, so these are well-defined finite
expressions.

For every tableau, $C_t\cap R_t=\{1\}$: a permutation in both stabilizers
preserves the row and column of each entry, and each row-column intersection
contains at most one node. Thus $\gamma\{t\}$ are distinct as $\gamma$ ranges
over $C_t$, and the coefficient of $\{t\}$ in $e_t$ is $1$. In particular,
$e_t\ne0$. When $n=0$, the empty tableau has $C_t=\{1\}$, so
$\kappa_t=1$, $e_t=\{\varnothing\}$, and $S^\varnothing=\mathbb C$.

For every $n\ge0$ and every $\lambda\vdash n$, let $S^\lambda$ be the complex
Specht module of shape $\lambda$
([[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]) and $\chi^\lambda$
its character, an irreducible character of $S_n$
([[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]]). Then

$$\operatorname{ch}(\chi^\lambda)=s_\lambda\in\Lambda^n,$$

the stable Schur function of shape $\lambda$
([[def-stable-schur-function-by-bialternants]]). In particular $\operatorname{ch}$
maps the $\mathbb Z$-basis $\{\chi^\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ of $R(S_n)$ to the
$\mathbb Z$-basis $\{s_\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ of $\Lambda^n$, and all values
$\chi^\lambda(\rho)$ are integers.

Fix an integer $n\ge0$ and work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be
partitions of $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ be the tensor product of their complex
Specht modules, a finite-dimensional complex $S_n$-module
([[def-tensor-product-of-complex-representations]],
[[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). The
**Kronecker coefficient** $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ of a third partition
$\nu\vdash n$ is the multiplicity of $S^\nu$ in this tensor product:

$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu):=\frac{\dim_{\mathbb C}\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}}{\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu},$$

where $\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}$ is the isotypic
component of type $S^\nu$
([[def-isotypic-component-of-a-completely-reducible-representation]]).

**Well-definedness.** The module $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ is
finite-dimensional, and $\operatorname{char}\mathbb C=0$ does not divide the
order of the finite group $S_n$, so complex Maschke's theorem gives complete
reducibility
([[thm-maschkes-theorem-for-finite-groups-over-fields-whose-characteristic-does-not-divide-the-group-order]],
[[cor-finite-dimensional-representations-are-completely-reducible-when-char-k-does-not-divide-group-order]],
[[def-completely-reducible-representation]]). The complex Specht modules
$S^\nu$, $\nu\vdash n$, are a complete list of pairwise inequivalent
irreducible $S_n$-modules
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]],
[[cor-distinct-specht-modules-are-inequivalent]]). Consequently a decomposition
into irreducibles has the form
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\cong\bigoplus_{\nu\vdash n}m_\nu S^\nu$
with nonnegative integer multiplicities $m_\nu$, and the isotypic component of
type $S^\nu$ is the direct sum of exactly the $m_\nu$ copies of $S^\nu$
appearing in any such decomposition; in particular
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu)_{(S^\nu)}=m_\nu\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu$
and $\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu>0$ because $S^\nu$ is irreducible. Hence
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=m_\nu$ is a nonnegative integer, independent of the chosen
decomposition, and $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ is by definition the multiplicity of
$S^\nu$ in $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$.

**The internal product.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ call
$$(\lambda,\mu)\longmapsto S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$$
the **internal (Kronecker) product** of the $S_n$-representations $S^\lambda$
and $S^\mu$. Unlike the outer induction product
$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_b}^{S_{a+b}}(S^\alpha\boxtimes S^\beta)$ of
[[thm-outer-littlewood-richardson-rule]], which takes a pair of modules of
degrees $a$ and $b$ to a module of degree $a+b$, the internal product keeps the
rank: both inputs and the output are $S_n$-modules of the same degree $n$. The
two operations are different constructions on different data; the outer product
is mentioned here only for contrast and is not used in this definition.

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the tensor product, Maschke's theorem,
the Specht classification and the isotypic decomposition are finite-dimensional
complex representation theory of a finite group.

For all partitions $\alpha,\beta$ with missing parts read as zero,
$$\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)=N:=|\alpha|+|\beta|+\alpha_1+\beta_1,$$
with $\operatorname{stab}$ as in
[[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]].

More precisely. At every $n\ge N$ all support labels $\gamma[n]$ of the
finite support of $\bar g^\bullet_{\alpha,\beta}$ are ordinary partitions, the
full product has the fixed nonnegative Schur expansion
$s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]}=\sum_\gamma\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}s_{\gamma[n]}$,
and the family is $V$-stable from $N$ onward. If both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are
nonempty, $N-1$ is admissible and the product at $N$ is not $V$ of the product
at $N-1$: the coefficient of $s_{(\alpha+\beta)[N]}$ is $1$, its first two
parts are equal, and no such Schur basis vector lies in the image of $V$. If
exactly one input is empty, $N$ is already the least ordinary input rank, and
the same image obstruction at $N$ excludes any earlier stabilization index in
the Jacobi–Trudi convention of the Definition. If both inputs are empty,
$N=0$, $s_{(n)}*s_{(n)}=s_{(n)}$ (including $s_{(0)}=1$) and $V^n(1)=s_{(n)}$,
so stabilization begins at zero and no negative-rank product is invoked. No
sharpness for an individual coefficient is claimed.

For all partitions $\alpha,\beta$ and every integer
$n\ge\max\{|\alpha|+\alpha_1,\,|\beta|+\beta_1\}$:
$$s_{\alpha[n]}*s_{\beta[n]}=\sum_\gamma
\bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\,s_{\gamma[n]},$$
an identity in the symmetric function ring, where $s_{\gamma[n]}$ is the
Jacobi–Trudi determinant attached to the integer sequence
$\gamma[n]=(n-|\gamma|,\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\dots)$, equal to $0$ or $\pm1$ times
a Schur function
([[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]],
[[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]), and $*$ is the internal product
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

For an ordinary partition $\delta\vdash n$ the coefficient of $s_\delta$ is
$$g^\delta_{\alpha[n],\beta[n]}
=\sum_\gamma \bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\,
\langle s_{\gamma[n]},s_\delta\rangle_H,$$
where each Hall factor is $0$ or a sign coming from Jacobi–Trudi
straightening ([[thm-schur-functions-form-an-orthonormal-integral-basis]]).
At small admissible ranks the signed terms can cancel or coalesce;
individual coefficients need not yet equal their reduced values. The range
displayed is precisely the set of $n$ for which $\alpha[n]$ and $\beta[n]$
are partitions.

Let $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ be a partition with $|\alpha|=\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_k$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let $n\ge0$ be
an integer. Whenever

$$n\;\ge\;|\alpha|+\alpha_1,$$

define the **first-row padding** of $\alpha$ to size $n$ to be
$$\alpha[n]:=\bigl(n-|\alpha|,\ \alpha_1,\ \alpha_2,\ \dots,\ \alpha_k\bigr).$$

The threshold is exact.

**Above the threshold.** Suppose $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$. Then
$n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1\ge0$, so every entry of the displayed sequence is a
nonnegative integer, the entries sum to $(n-|\alpha|)+|\alpha|=n$, and the
sequence is weakly decreasing because $n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1$ and $\alpha$ is
weakly decreasing ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).
If $\alpha$ is nonempty then $\alpha_1\ge1$, hence $n-|\alpha|\ge1$ and the
displayed sequence is a partition of $n$ with positive parts. If
$\alpha=\varnothing$ then the displayed sequence is $(n)$; this is a partition
of $n$ for every $n\ge1$, while for $n=0$ one takes $\varnothing[0]:=\varnothing$,
the unique partition of $0$. Thus the padding is defined and is a partition of
$n$ on the whole displayed range.

**Below the threshold.** If $\alpha$ is nonempty and $n<|\alpha|+\alpha_1$,
then $n-|\alpha|<\alpha_1$; if also $n\ge|\alpha|$ the leading entry is
nonnegative but smaller than the second entry $\alpha_1$, and if $n<|\alpha|$
it is negative. In both cases the displayed sequence is not a partition, so
$\alpha[n]$ is left undefined. The threshold $|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ is therefore
the exact size at which the padded family begins: at
$n=|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ the padding equals $(\alpha_1,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots)$,
which is a partition with a repeated first part when $\alpha$ is nonempty.

**Neutrality of the notation.** This definition records a family of partitions;
it asserts no constancy of any quantity along the family and no stability
property. The same notation is used by the FI-module and
representation-stability developments, where the padding threshold reappears as
the generation degree of the family under consideration.

Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be partitions
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]) and put
$$n_0:=\max\bigl\{|\alpha|+\alpha_1,\ |\beta|+\beta_1,\ |\gamma|+\gamma_1\bigr\},$$
where the first part of the empty partition is read as $0$. For every integer
$n\ge n_0$ the three first-row paddings $\alpha[n]$, $\beta[n]$, $\gamma[n]$ are
partitions of $n$, by
[[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]] and the choice of $n_0$ as the maximum
of the three thresholds. On that range define the **padded Kronecker
coefficient sequence** by
$$g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma):=g\bigl(\alpha[n],\ \beta[n],\ \gamma[n]\bigr),$$
the Kronecker coefficient of three partitions of $n$
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]).

**Domain.** The threshold $n_0$ is exactly where the common domain of the three
padded families starts: for $n\ge n_0$ all three padded sequences are
partitions of $n$, while for $n<n_0$ at least one of the three padded
sequences is not a partition of $n$ and the expression is left undefined. In
particular the sequence is indexed by the integers $n\ge n_0$ and not by all

asserts neither that $g_n(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ is eventually constant, nor any
bound on it, nor any comparison between different values of $n$; Murnaghan
stability is a theorem about this sequence proved elsewhere, and this
definition is available as its noncircular input.

derivations.claim: *Rank four, computed independently.* At $n=4$ the product is $s_{2,2}*s_{2,2}$; by [F1] and [F2], $g^\delta_{(2,2),(2,2)}=\sum_{\rho\vdash4}\chi^\delta(\rho)\chi^{(2,2)}(\rho)^2/z_\rho$ with the character values of [F1], so $\chi^{(2,2)}(\rho)^2=(4,0,4,1,0)$ and $z_\rho=(24,4,8,3,4)$ on the five classes. Class by class this gives $g^{(4)}=\tfrac4{24}+\tfrac48+\tfrac13=1$, $g^{(1,1,1,1)}=\tfrac4{24}+\tfrac48+\tfrac13=1$, $g^{(2,2)}=\tfrac{2\cdot4}{24}+\tfrac{2\cdot4}{8}-\tfrac13=1$, $g^{(3,1)}=\tfrac{3\cdot4}{24}-\tfrac48=0$ and $g^{(2,1,1)}=\tfrac{3\cdot4}{24}-\tfrac48=0$; the dimensions $1\cdot1+1\cdot1+1\cdot2=4=(\dim V_{(2,2)})^2$ confirm the total. Hence $s_{2,2}*s_{2,2}=s_4+s_{1,1,1,1}+s_{2,2}$, matching the displayed rank-four product.

*Stability at ranks eight and nine.* By [F4], $V(s_{6,2})=s_{7,2}$, $V(s_{5,1,1,1})=s_{6,1,1,1}$, $V(s_{6,2})=s_{7,2}$, $V(s_{7,1})=s_{8,1}$, $V(s_{6,1,1})=s_{7,1,1}$, $V(s_{5,2,1})=s_{6,2,1}$, $V(s_{4,2,2})=s_{5,2,2}$, $V(s_{5,3})=s_{6,3}$, $V(s_{4,3,1})=s_{5,3,1}$ and $V(s_{4,4})=s_{5,4}$; applying these term by term to the rank-eight displayed expansion reproduces the rank-nine displayed expansion exactly, including the multiplicities $2$.

*The reduced coefficients.* The stable row displays multiplicities $1,1,2,1,1,2,1,1,1,1$ for the labels $\varnothing,(1,1,1),(2),(1),(1,1),(2,1),(2,2),(3),(3,1),(4)$ read off in the order $\bullet,\bullet,1,1,1$, etc.; by [F3] the coefficient of $s_{\gamma[n]}$ in the rank-$n$ product equals $\bar g^\gamma_{(2),(2)}$ for every $n\ge8$, so these are exactly the reduced coefficients, and all other $\gamma$ have $\bar g^\gamma_{(2),(2)}=0$ since their labels do not occur. Jacobi–Trudi determinant attached to the integer sequence
$\gamma[n]=(n-|\gamma|,\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\dots)$, equal to $0$ or $\pm1$ times

([[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]],

=\sum_\gamma \bar g^\gamma_{\alpha,\beta}\,
\langle s_{\gamma[n]},s_\delta\rangle_H,$$

straightening ([[thm-schur-functions-form-an-orthonormal-integral-basis]]).

$$\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)=N:=|\alpha|+|\beta|+\alpha_1+\beta_1,$$

finite support of $\bar g^\bullet_{\alpha,\beta}$ are ordinary partitions, the

exactly one input is empty, $N$ is already the least ordinary input rank, and

sharpness for an individual coefficient is claimed.

Let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety, i.e. a classical
algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), regarded as
a topological space with its analytic topology
([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]), and
let $k$ be a field. Write $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ for the category of sheaves
of $k$-vector spaces and $k$-linear morphisms
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]],
[[def-presheaf-of-groups-rings-modules]], [[def-module-on-ringed-space]]); it is
an abelian category ([[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]]), so its
bounded derived category $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is defined with the
conventions of [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]], under the
standing smallness hypothesis recorded there.

The category $D_c^b(X;k)$ is the full subcategory of
$D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ consisting of the complexes $A$ satisfying:

1. $A$ is **cohomologically bounded**: $H^j(A)=0$ for $|j|$ sufficiently large;
   and
2. $A$ is **algebraically constructible**: there exists a finite smooth
   algebraic stratification with the frontier condition $\mathfrak S$ of $X$
   ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]) such
   that for every stratum $S\in\mathfrak S$ and every integer $j$ the
   restriction $H^j(A)|_S$ is locally constant of finite rank
   ([[def-locally-constant-sheaf-of-finite-rank]]).

These are topological constructible sheaves, not coherent or quasi-coherent
sheaves. We use the shift convention of
[[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]: $H^j(A[m])=H^{j+m}(A)$. A
groupoid local system is identified with a locally constant sheaf only through
an explicit local comparison, which is not made here.

Constructibility is a condition on the cohomology sheaves of a complex, and it
is quantified existentially over finite smooth algebraic frontier
stratifications: no stratification is fixed, and no existence or
common-refinement theorem for stratifications is asserted by this definition.
Shifting replaces $H^j$ by $H^{j+m}$, which preserves cohomological boundedness
and shifts a witnessing stratification nowhere, so the class is closed under
shifts and under isomorphisms in $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$. No choice
principle is used.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a topological
space and let $k$ be a field. The category $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ of sheaves
of $k$-vector spaces is the category of modules over the ringed space
$(X,k_X)$ with constant structure sheaf $k_X$
([[def-locally-ringed-space]], [[def-module-on-ringed-space]]); it is a locally
small Grothendieck category and carries a functorial injective embedding, and
iterating that embedding on cokernels yields for every $k$-sheaf one specific
injective resolution
([[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]). These resolutions are
bounded-below injective replacements, so with the dependent choice supplied by
AC ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]) the bounded-below
injective complexes model the bounded derived category:
$K^+(\operatorname{Inj}\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))\to
D^+(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is an equivalence, and morphisms of the bounded
derived category are computed by these replacements
([[thm-injective-complexes-model-the-bounded-below-derived-category]]).

Now let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety and let
$\mathfrak S$ be a finite smooth algebraic stratification with the frontier
condition of $X$
([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). Let
$D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ be the full subcategory of
$D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ of complexes whose cohomology sheaves are bounded
and constructible with respect to $\mathfrak S$
([[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]]). Then
$D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ is a triangulated subcategory: it is closed under
shifts, isomorphisms and mapping cones. More generally, if two bounded
algebraically constructible complexes are constructible with respect to one
common finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification, then their cone is
bounded and constructible with respect to that stratification.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace
([[def-topological-space]]) with closed complement $Z=X\setminus U$, let
$i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of the subspace
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]), and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups
on $X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]]).
Write $\mathcal F|_U:=j^{-1}\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal F|_Z:=i^{-1}\mathcal F$ for
the restrictions ([[def-restriction-sheaf-open-subspace]]). Then:

1. the adjoint transpose of the identity of $\mathcal F|_U$ under the adjunction
   of [[thm-extension-by-zero-adjunction-exactness]] and the unit of the
   adjunction ([[thm-inverse-direct-image-adjunction]]) fit into a short exact
   sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on $X$
   $$0\to j_!(\mathcal F|_U)\to\mathcal F\to i_*(\mathcal F|_Z)\to0,$$
   where $j_!$ is extension by zero ([[def-extension-by-zero-abelian-sheaf]]) and
   $i_*$ is the direct image ([[def-direct-image-sheaf]],
   [[lem-direct-image-is-sheaf]]); exactness is that of
   [[def-exact-sequence-sheaves]];
2. if $\mathcal F=\mathbb Z_X$ is the constant sheaf with value $\mathbb Z$ on
   $X$, then $\mathcal F|_U$ is canonically isomorphic to the constant sheaf
   $\mathbb Z_U$ on $U$, so the sequence of clause 1 reads
   $0\to j_!(\mathbb Z_U)\to\mathbb Z_X\to i_*(\mathcal F|_Z)\to0$ up to that
   canonical isomorphism.

Let $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of a closed subset
$Z\subseteq X$ carrying the subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]), and
let $\mathcal G$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]])
whose stalks vanish off $Z$, that is $\mathcal G_x=0$ for every $x\in X\setminus Z$
([[def-stalk-of-presheaf]]). Then the unit
$$\eta:\mathcal G\longrightarrow i_*i^{-1}\mathcal G$$
of the adjunction ([[thm-inverse-direct-image-adjunction]]) between inverse image
and direct image ([[def-direct-image-sheaf]], [[lem-direct-image-is-sheaf]]) is an
isomorphism of sheaves of abelian groups; equivalently
$\mathcal G\cong i_*(\mathcal G|_Z)$ under the identification
$\mathcal G|_Z=i^{-1}\mathcal G$ ([[def-restriction-sheaf-open-subspace]]).

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace.

1. For every sheaf of abelian groups $\mathcal F$ on $U$ and every sheaf of
   abelian groups $\mathcal G$ on $X$, there is a natural bijection
   $$\operatorname{Hom}_X(j_!\mathcal F,\mathcal G) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_U(\mathcal F,j^{-1}\mathcal G).$$
2. The functor $j_!$ is exact on sheaves of abelian groups.

Let $f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ be a chain map in an additive category. The
**mapping cone** of $f$ is the chain complex $\operatorname{Cone}(f)_\bullet$
whose degree-$n$ term is
$$\operatorname{Cone}(f)_n:=D_n\oplus C[1]_n=D_n\oplus C_{n-1},$$
and whose differential is
$$d_n^{\operatorname{Cone}(f)}(y,x):=(d_n^D(y)+f_{n-1}(x),-d_{n-1}^C(x)).$$

Thus $\operatorname{Cone}(f)$ is the direct sum of $D$ and the shift $C[1]$ as
a graded object, with the off-diagonal term given by $f$.

The derived category, with shift $[1]$ and distinguished triangles the isomorphic images of cone triangles, is triangulated. The localization functor $Q$ is exact. Every such triangle gives a long exact cohomology sequence $\cdots\to H^n(X)\to H^n(Y)\to H^n(Z)\to H^{n+1}(X)\to\cdots$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: A sheaf on the one-point space is its vector space of global sections, so a bounded complex of $k$-sheaves on the point is a bounded complex of $k$-vector spaces, and the unique finite smooth stratification of the point makes constructibility with respect to it exactly the condition that every cohomology space be finite-dimensional by [F1]. A bounded complex whose cohomology is finite-dimensional is isomorphic in the derived category to a bounded complex of finite-dimensional vector spaces: truncate to the finite interval between the lowest and highest degrees in which cohomology is nonzero, and split the resulting bounded complex into the direct sum of its cohomology spaces placed in their degrees, using that every short exact sequence of vector spaces splits. Both sides are therefore equivalent to the bounded derived category of finite-dimensional vector spaces, with morphisms computed by the injective models of [F2].

On the point inverse and direct image of the identity are exact identity functors, and every section has compact support, so the proper-support functor is also the exact identity. Their derived functors are therefore identities. In the exceptional candidate of [[def-derived-operations-on-analytic-sheaves-over-locally-compact-spaces]], the fibre opens are only the point and the empty set; compact sections are exact, giving dimension bound $d=0$, and the constant sheaf $k$ is itself $c$-soft, so take $K=k[0]$. For a bounded finite-dimensional complex $B$ every term is injective over $k$, and the candidate has sections $\operatorname{Hom}_k^\bullet(k,B)=B$ on the point and zero on the empty set. Thus $f^!$ is the identity with its ordinary evaluation adjunction, and $\omega_{\operatorname{pt}}=a_{\operatorname{pt}}^!k=k[0]$. The ordinary-operations lemma [[lem-bounded-analytic-field-sheaves-have-derived-tensor-hom-and-pullback-pushforward-adjunctions]] identifies tensor and internal Hom with the finite signed complexes: $(A\otimes B)^n=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}A^p\otimes_kB^q$, with $d(a\otimes b)=d_Aa\otimes b+(-1)^pa\otimes d_Bb$, and $\mathcal Hom^n(A,B)=\prod_p\operatorname{Hom}_k(A^p,B^{p+n})$, with $d\varphi=d_B\varphi-(-1)^n\varphi d_A$. Their terms and amplitudes are finite, so they belong to the category identified in step 1.1. Here $f_*$ and $f_!$ in the Example denote their derived operations, which coincide with their exact underived functors in this case.

Apply [F3] to the constant sheaf $\mathcal F=k_{\mathbb C}$ on $X=\mathbb C$, with $U=\mathbb C^*$ and $Z=\{0\}$: the restriction $k_{\mathbb C}|_{\mathbb C^*}$ is the constant sheaf $k_{\mathbb C^*}$, the restriction to the closed point is $k$, and the sequence reads $0\to j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}\to k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k\to0$, the terms being computed by [F5] for the extension by zero. Stalkwise the middle sheaf is exact: at $x\neq0$ the stalk of $j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}$ is $k$ and the stalk of $i_*k$ is $0$, while at $0$ the first stalk is $0$ and the last is $k$; the quotient of $k_{\mathbb C}$ by $j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}$ has no stalks off $\{0\}$, and by [F4] it is canonically the pushforward $i_*k$ of its restriction to the closed point. All maps are $k$-linear, since they are obtained from the canonical adjunction units of [F5] applied to $k$-sheaves.

View $k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k$ as a chain map of complexes concentrated in degree $0$, and let $C$ be its mapping cone with the convention of [F6], so $C^{-1}=k_{\mathbb C}$, $C^0=i_*k$ and the differential $C^{-1}\to C^0$ is the map of step 2.2. Its cohomology is $H^{-1}(C)=\ker(k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k)=j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}$ by the exactness of step 2.2 and $H^0(C)=\operatorname{coker}(k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k)=0$, so $C$ is quasi-isomorphic to $j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}[1]$, since the two complexes have the same single nonzero cohomology sheaf in degree $-1$. By the rotation property of cone triangles in [F7], the triangle $k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k\to C\to k_{\mathbb C}[1]$ is isomorphic to the distinguished triangle $j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}\to k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k\to j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}[1]$, the ordinary localization triangle of the open subset $\mathbb C^*$; all three sheaves are constructible for the two-stratum stratification $\{\mathbb C^*,\{0\}\}$ of the line, so the triangle lies in $D_c^b(\mathbb C;k)$ by [F1].

citations.quote: For $n\geq1$ and $\eta\in\Omega_c^{n-1}(\mathbb R^n)$, with the standard orientation, $\int_{\mathbb R^n}d\eta=0$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For a smooth manifold $M^n$, with boundary allowed, the **density bundle** is $DM=\coprod_{p\in M}D(T_pM)$. In coordinates $x$, let $|dx|=|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ be the density taking value one on the coordinate frame. On overlaps,
$$|dy|=|\det D_x y|\,|dx|.$$
A smooth density is a section with smooth real coefficient in these frames. Its support is the closure of its nonzero locus. The absolute determinants are positive smooth transition functions and satisfy the cocycle identities by the chain rule. A countable atlas and [[thm-vector-bundle-construction-from-a-smooth-cocycle]] therefore give a smooth line bundle. For boundary charts the same gluing proof uses half-space product charts; smoothness of transitions follows from their local extensions, and Hausdorffness and second countability follow as for the supplied cocycle construction. The fibers are lines by [[prop-one-densities-form-a-one-dimensional-vector-space]]. When $n=0$ the empty frame trivializes $DM=M\times\mathbb R$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $\delta$ be a compactly supported smooth density on $M^n$, with boundary allowed. Choose a chart partition $(\rho_i)$ and write $\rho_i\delta=f_i|dx_i|$. For $n\geq1$ define
$$\int_M\delta=\sum_i\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widetilde f_i(x_i)\,dx_i.$$
The zero extensions are Riemann integrable, including at genuine faces, by [[lem-chart-supported-coefficients-have-well-defined-riemann-integrable-half-space-extensions]]. The compact-support/local-finiteness argument of [[lem-a-locally-finite-sum-is-finite-near-the-compact-support-of-a-form]] applies to density supports as closed sets, so the sum is finite. For $n=0$ sum the scalar density values over the finite support, without orientation signs. Empty support gives zero. Choice independence is discharged by [[thm-density-integration-is-defined-without-an-orientation]].

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

Let $E\to M$ be a smooth vector bundle. A **smooth bundle metric** on $E$ is a
choice of inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_p$ on each fibre $E_p$ such
that, for every pair of smooth local sections $s,t$, the function

$$p\mapsto\langle s(p),t(p)\rangle_p$$

is smooth on the common domain of $s$ and $t$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $K\subseteq M$ be compact, and let $W\subseteq M$ be open with $K\subseteq W$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:M\to [0,1]$ that equals $1$ on an open neighbourhood of $K$ and satisfies $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq W$.

Let $M$ be a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold without boundary of
dimension $n\ge2$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]), let $\mu$ be a smooth positive
density on $M$ ([[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]), and let $E\to M$ be
a finite-rank smooth vector bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-bundle-rank-fibre-and-trivial-bundle]]) over
$\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ carrying a smooth bundle metric
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ ([[def-smooth-bundle-metric]]), Euclidean in the
real case and Hermitian, linear in the first variable, in the complex case; in
the complex case the fibres are complex vector spaces through a smooth complex
structure on $E$
([[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]]). Write $\Gamma(E)$
for the smooth sections ([[def-smooth-section-local-section-and-support]]).

A $\mathbb K$-linear map $P:\Gamma(E)\to\Gamma(E)$ is a **linear differential
operator of order at most two** on $E$ when, on every chart domain $\Omega$ of
$M$ with coordinates $x=(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ and in every local frame of $E$ over
$\Omega$ in which a section is written $s\leftrightarrow u=(u^1,\ldots,u^r)$
and its image as $Ps\leftrightarrow((Ps)_1,\ldots,(Ps)_r)$,
$$(Ps)_\lambda=-\sum_{i,j=1}^na^{ij}_{\lambda\mu}(x)\,\partial_i\partial_ju^\mu(x)+\sum_{j=1}^nb^j_{\lambda\mu}(x)\,\partial_ju^\mu(x)+c_{\lambda\mu}(x)u^\mu(x),\qquad1\le\lambda\le r,$$
with smooth coefficient functions on $\Omega$ and summation over the repeated
index $\mu$ (and over $i,j$). Such an operator is **Laplace type** when in
addition, in every such chart and frame, its second-order coefficients are
scalar multiples of the identity, $a^{ij}_{\lambda\mu}=a^{ij}\delta_{\lambda\mu}$,
with $a^{ij}$ smooth real functions for which the matrix $(a^{ij}(x))$ is
symmetric and positive definite at every $x\in\Omega$. Its **principal symbol**
is the smooth section $\sigma_2(P)$ of $\mathrm{Sym}^2T^*M$
([[def-smooth-tensor-field]]) given on such a chart by
$\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)=a^{ij}(x)\xi_i\xi_j$ for $\xi\in T_x^*M$; equivalently
$\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)=a_x(\xi,\xi)\,\mathrm{id}_{E_x}$ for a smooth field of
positive-definite quadratic forms $a_x$ on $T_x^*M$, so that
$\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)>0$ whenever $\xi\ne0$.

$P$ is **formally symmetric** for $(\mu,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ when
$$\int_M\langle Ps,t\rangle\,d\mu=\int_M\langle s,Pt\rangle\,d\mu$$
for all compactly supported smooth sections $s,t\in\Gamma_c(E)$
([[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-smooth-density]]).

**Well-definedness.** The definition is local. On a fixed chart and frame the
displayed assignment is a $\mathbb K$-linear map on components with smooth
coefficients, and the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]])
computes the transition to another chart and frame on the overlap: the
second-order coefficients transform by the symmetric tensor rule
$a'^{kl}=a^{ij}\frac{\partial x'^k}{\partial x^i}\frac{\partial x'^l}{\partial x^j}$
together with conjugation by the frame-change matrix, while the terms produced
by the second derivatives of the coordinate change are absorbed into the
first-order coefficients. Hence a single operator that admits a local
expression on one cover admits a local expression on every chart and frame, and
the two hypotheses placed on the leading coefficient are invariant: scalar-ness
is preserved by frame conjugation and by the coordinate rule for a field of
symmetric matrices, and symmetric positive definiteness is preserved by both.
The principal symbol is therefore independent of the chart and frame, since two
local expressions of the same operator differ by an operator of order at most
one; it is smooth in $(x,\xi)$ because the $a^{ij}$ are smooth, and it is
positive on nonzero covectors exactly when $(a^{ij})$ is positive definite.
Formal symmetry is an identity between integrals of compactly supported smooth
sections and therefore depends only on the operator, the density and the
metric.

derivations.claim:
We first record the scalar one-derivative identity on an open set of $\mathbb R^n$. Let $a,b$ be compactly supported smooth functions and let $h$ be a smooth function, all on $\mathbb R^n$. Applying [F1] to the compactly supported $(n-1)$-form $\eta=(-1)^{i-1}abh\,dx^1\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat{dx^i}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^n$ gives $\int_{\mathbb R^n}\partial_i(abh)\,dx=0$; the product rule [F2] splits this into $\int(\partial_ia)\,bh\,dx+\int a\,\partial_i(bh)\,dx=0$. Taking $h=\gamma$ and rearranging, integration against the density $\gamma\,dx$ transposes $\partial_i$ to the operator $b\mapsto-\gamma^{-1}\partial_i(\gamma b)$, because $\partial_i(\overline b\gamma)=\gamma\,\overline{\gamma^{-1}\partial_i(\gamma b)}$:
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}(\partial_ia)\,\overline{b}\,\gamma\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R^n}a\,\overline{\bigl(-\gamma^{-1}\partial_i(\gamma b)\bigr)}\,\gamma\,dx,$$
and in the real case the same identity without conjugations. The opposite signs in the two boundary-free terms are the only content.

Iterating step 1.1 and inserting the matrix coefficients gives the local formula of the Statement, so $P^\star$ exists locally. For a multi-index $\alpha$ and a matrix coefficient $a=a(x)$, the transpose of $aD^\alpha$ against the fibre pairing is the operator $v\mapsto(-1)^{|\alpha|}\gamma^{-1}D^\alpha(\gamma a^*v)$: each single derivative contributes the factor $-\gamma^{-1}\circ\partial_i\circ\gamma$, the matrix acts by the fibre adjoint $a^*$, and [F2] expands $D^\alpha(\gamma a^*v)$ with top term $\gamma\,a^*D^\alpha v$ and lower-order terms, exactly as in the displayed formula. Summing over $|\alpha|\le2$ gives a smooth operator of order at most two on the chart.

Vanishing on a chart. Let $Q$ be a smooth operator on a chart domain with $\int\langle u,Qv\rangle\,d\mu=0$ for all compactly supported smooth $u,v$ there, and fix $v$. If $Qv$ did not vanish at a point $p$, then in an orthonormal frame of [F4] some component $(Qv)_\lambda$ would be nonzero at $p$; choose a nonnegative smooth cutoff $\chi$ supported in the open set where $(Qv)_\lambda\ne0$ and equal to $1$ at $p$, and set $u=\chi\,\overline{(Qv)_\lambda}\,e_\lambda$ in that frame, a compactly supported smooth section. Then $\langle u,Qv\rangle=\chi\lvert(Qv)_\lambda\rvert^2$ is nonnegative and positive near $p$, so its density integral is nonzero by [F3], contradicting the vanishing hypothesis. Hence $Qv=0$ for every $v$, so $Q=0$. In particular two local operators satisfying the local adjoint identity against $P$ on a common chart domain coincide, since their difference is annihilated against every pair of compactly supported tests there.

Leading coefficients. In a chart with orthonormal frames, write the local coefficients of $P$ as $a_\alpha$, $|\alpha|\le2$. By [F2] the coefficient of $D^\alpha v$ in $\gamma^{-1}D^\alpha(\gamma a_\alpha^*v)$ is $a_\alpha^*$, and all other terms contributed by $\gamma^{-1}D^\alpha(\gamma\,\cdot\,)$ have order at most $|\alpha|-1$; terms with $|\alpha|<2$ have order at most one. Hence the order-$\delta$ leading coefficients of $P^\star$ are $(-1)^\delta a_\alpha^*$.

Gluing. The local operators of step 2.1 on the members of a chart cover whose frames are orthonormal by [F4] agree on every overlap by step 3.1, so they patch to one global smooth linear operator $P^\star:\Gamma(F)\to\Gamma(E)$ of order at most two; on a chart, $P^\star$ is the local construction there.

Global adjoint identity. Let $u,v\in\Gamma_c$ be compactly supported smooth sections. Cover the compact set $\operatorname{supp}u$ by finitely many chart domains $U_1,\ldots,U_N$ carrying orthonormal frames. For each $i$ choose by [F5] a nonnegative smooth $\rho_i$ equal to $1$ near a compact subset $K_i\subseteq U_i$, with the $K_i$ chosen inside the respective charts so that $\bigcup_iK_i\supseteq\operatorname{supp}u$, and with $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i\subseteq U_i$; replacing $\rho_i$ by $\rho_i(\rho_1+\cdots+\rho_N)^{-1}$ makes $\sum_i\rho_i=1$ on a neighbourhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$. Then $u=\sum_i\rho_iu$, so linearity of $P$ gives $\int\langle Pu,v\rangle\,d\mu=\sum_i\int\langle P(\rho_iu),v\rangle\,d\mu$. Fix $i$: the section $\rho_iu$ is compactly supported in $U_i$, so by [F5] again choose a bump $\theta_i$ supported in $U_i$ and equal to $1$ near $\operatorname{supp}(\rho_iu)\cap\operatorname{supp}v$. Since $P$ and $P^\star$ are differential operators with the local expressions of step 2.1 and step 4.1, the pointwise identities $\langle P(\rho_iu),v\rangle=\langle P(\rho_iu),\theta_iv\rangle$ and $\langle\rho_iu,P^\star(\theta_iv)\rangle=\langle\rho_iu,P^\star v\rangle$ hold: the two sides differ only by products of a section with a section whose jet vanishes wherever the other factor is nonzero. Therefore the local adjoint identity of step 2.1 on the chart $U_i$ yields $\int\langle P(\rho_iu),v\rangle\,d\mu=\int\langle\rho_iu,P^\star v\rangle\,d\mu$, and summing over $i$ gives the global identity $\int\langle Pu,v\rangle\,d\mu=\int\langle u,P^\star v\rangle\,d\mu$.

Uniqueness. If a smooth operator $Q$ also satisfied the global adjoint identity, then $\int\langle u,(P^\star-Q)v\rangle\,d\mu=0$ for all compactly supported smooth $u,v$, so step 3.1 applied to $P^\star-Q$ on any chart gives $P^\star-Q=0$. Thus $P^\star$ is the unique such operator.

Consequences. For a Laplace-type $P$ the order-two coefficients are $a_{(i,j)}=-a^{ij}\delta_{\lambda\mu}$ with $(a^{ij})$ smooth symmetric positive definite, so those of $P^\star$ are $(-1)^2a_{(i,j)}^*=-a^{ij}\delta_{\lambda\mu}$, the same matrix; hence $P^\star$ is Laplace type and $\sigma_2(P^\star)=\sigma_2(P)$. Applying the defining identity twice and using step 6.1, $(P^\star)^\star=P$. Finally, with $E=F$, the difference of the defining identities for $P$ and $P^\star$ shows that $P$ is formally symmetric exactly when $\int\langle s,(P-P^\star)t\rangle\,d\mu=0$ for all compactly supported smooth $s,t$, which by step 3.1 holds exactly when $P=P^\star$. All three assertions follow.

boundaries.evidence: The identification is vacuous for the zero section and the empty test set; the uniqueness argument of step 6.1 covers it.
For the zero operator all coefficients vanish and the formula gives P^star=0; step 2.1 includes Qv=0 for every v.

boundaries.reason: No counting or dimension-one parameter occurs; rank-one bundles and order-one operators are ordinary cases of the local formula of step 2.1.

boundaries.evidence: Operators of order below two and vanishing leading coefficients are included: step 3.2 shows the adjoint has order at most that of P.

boundaries.reason: The manifold is boundaryless and all tests are compactly supported, so no boundary endpoint enters; step 1.1 records the boundary-free integration by parts.
The construction is choice-free: finite chart data, local integration by parts and uniqueness in step 3.1 require no selection.

boundaries.evidence: Item 3 forward direction: P=P^star inserted in the defining identity gives formal symmetry; step 7.1 states this direction.
Item 3 reverse direction: formal symmetry gives the vanishing of the pairing against (P-P^star), hence P=P^star by step 7.1 and step 3.1.
