Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M,E,P$ have exactly the compact, boundaryless, scalar-positive-symbol and formal symmetry hypotheses of [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]], with $\operatorname{dom}P=H^2(M,E)$. Write $\mathcal H=\ker P$.

Then $\mathcal H$ is finite dimensional and consists of smooth sections, $\operatorname{ran}P=\mathcal H^\perp$ is closed in $L^2$, and
$$L^2(M,E)=\mathcal H\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\operatorname{ran}P.$$
Let $\Pi$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal H$. There is a unique linear operator $G:L^2\to H^2\cap\mathcal H^\perp$ with
$$PG=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }L^2,\qquad GP=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }H^2,\qquad G\Pi=\Pi G=0.$$
It is bounded from $H^k$ to $H^{k+2}$ for every integer $k\ge0$, compact and selfadjoint on $L^2$, and preserves smooth sections. For all such $k$,
$$H^k=\mathcal H\oplus P(H^{k+2}),\qquad C^\infty(M,E)=\mathcal H\oplus P(C^\infty(M,E)),$$
where the second summands are the corresponding intersections with $\mathcal H^\perp$, and the decompositions are topological. The projection is smoothing: for every integer $r\ge0$, $\|\Pi f\|_{C^r}\le C_r\|f\|_2$. Consequently $G$ is a two-sided parametrix with finite-rank smoothing remainders. If additionally $(Pu,u)_2\ge0$ for smooth $u$, then $P$ and $G$ are nonnegative on their respective domains.

Let $(U,x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ be a smooth chart on a smooth manifold and
$\omega$ a smooth $k$-form on $U$, with $k\ge0$. Summing over increasing
$k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$
For every differential form $\omega$, $d(d\omega)=0$.

The real **de Rham cohomology** is $H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)=Z^k(M)/B^k(M)$, with $Z^k,B^k$ as in [[def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms]].

This is [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]] in real vector spaces. Only a closed form $\omega$ represents a class $[\omega]$. For closed forms $\omega,\omega\prime$, equality $[\omega]=[\omega\prime]$ means precisely $\omega\prime-\omega=d\eta$ for some $(k-1)$-form $\eta$. Addition and real scalar multiplication are induced by those of forms. All groups on the empty manifold are zero.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be open. Write $\Omega^k(U;\mathbb C)$ for smooth
complex-valued $k$-forms. For increasing multi-indices
$I=(i_1<\cdots<i_p)$ and $J=(j_1<\cdots<j_q)$, write
$dz^I=dz_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dz_{i_p}$ and
$d\bar z^J=d\bar z_{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge d\bar z_{j_q}$. The invertible
change of cotangent basis
$dz_j=dx_j+i\,dy_j$, $d\bar z_j=dx_j-i\,dy_j$ gives the direct sum
decomposition

$$\Omega^k(U;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\Omega^{p,q}(U),\qquad \Omega^{p,q}(U)=\left\{\sum_{I,J}a_{I,J}(z)\,dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J:a_{I,J}\in C^\infty(U;\mathbb C)\right\},$$

where $0\le p,q\le n$ and every sum is finite. On a $(p,q)$ form
$\eta=\sum_{I,J}a_{I,J}dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J$, define

$$\partial\eta=\sum_{I,J,j}(\partial_{z_j}a_{I,J})\,dz_j\wedge dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J,\qquad \bar\partial\eta=\sum_{I,J,j}(\partial_{\bar z_j}a_{I,J})\,d\bar z_j\wedge dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J.$$

Repeated differentials vanish by alternation; components outside the range
$0\le p,q\le n$ are zero. These operators are the components of $d$ of
bidegrees $(p+1,q)$ and $(p,q+1)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be open and let all forms below be smooth and
complex-valued. Then
$$d=\partial+\bar\partial,\qquad \partial^2=0,\qquad \bar\partial^2=0,\qquad \partial\bar\partial+\bar\partial\partial=0.$$
For $\eta\in\Omega^{p,q}(U)$ and $\theta\in\Omega^{r,s}(U)$,
$$\partial(\eta\wedge\theta)=\partial\eta\wedge\theta+(-1)^{p+q}\eta\wedge\partial\theta,\qquad \bar\partial(\eta\wedge\theta)=\bar\partial\eta\wedge\theta+(-1)^{p+q}\eta\wedge\bar\partial\theta.$$
The identities hold at bidegree endpoints as well, with components outside
$0\le p,q\le n$ interpreted as zero.

Let $X$ be a complex manifold of dimension $m\ge1$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]) with a Hermitian
metric $g$, and let $E\to X$ be a holomorphic vector bundle of rank $r$ with a
Hermitian metric $h$ ([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]).
Fix integers $p,q\ge0$. In a holomorphic chart with coordinates
$z=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)$ and a holomorphic frame of $E$, an **$E$-valued
$(p,q)$-form** is an expression
$$s=\sum_{|I|=p}\sum_{|J|=q}s_{IJ}\otimes dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J,$$
with $s_{IJ}$ smooth local sections of $E$ and increasing multi-indices $I,J$
([[def-bigraded-complex-differential-forms]]); such expressions agree on
overlaps because holomorphic changes of coordinates preserve bidegree and
holomorphic frame changes are complex-linear. The resulting smooth global
sections of the bundle $\Lambda^{p,q}T^*X\otimes E$ are denoted
$\mathcal A^{p,q}(X,E)$; the bundle is zero, and so is
$\mathcal A^{p,q}(X,E)$, when $p>m$ or $q>m$.

The **Dolbeault operator** is the first-order operator
$$\bar\partial_E:\mathcal A^{p,q}(X,E)\to\mathcal A^{p,q+1}(X,E),\qquad \bar\partial_E s=\sum_{I,J}\sum_{k=1}^m \bar\partial_{z_k}s_{IJ}\otimes d\bar z_k\wedge dz^I\wedge d\bar z^J,$$
with the Wirtinger operators $\bar\partial_{z_k}$
([[def-wirtinger-operators-in-several-complex-variables]],
[[def-bigraded-complex-differential-forms]]) acting componentwise on the local
sections $s_{IJ}$. It is independent of the holomorphic chart and frame, and
$\bar\partial_E^2=0$
([[thm-d-dbar-decomposition-and-identities]]); both assertions are proved
below.

Equip $\Lambda^{p,q}T^*X\otimes E$ with the Hermitian metric induced by $g$ and
$h$ ([[prop-riemannian-metrics-induce-metrics-on-dual-tensor-and-exterior-bundles]]
and [[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]). For compactly
supported smooth $s,t\in\mathcal A^{p,q}(X,E)$ the **$L^2$ pairing**
$$\langle s,t\rangle_{L^2}=\int_X\langle s,t\rangle\,d\mu_g$$
uses the Riemannian volume density $\mu_g$
([[def-riemannian-volume-density]],
[[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-smooth-density]]) and is a complex
inner product in the first-variable-linear convention
([[def-complex-l-two-inner-product]]); its completion
$L^2(X,\Lambda^{p,q}T^*X\otimes E)$ is a complex Hilbert space
([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]],
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]]). By
[[lem-formal-adjoints-of-differential-operators-exist-and-are-unique]] the
operator $\bar\partial_E$ has a **formal adjoint**
$\bar\partial_E^*:\mathcal A^{p,q+1}(X,E)\to\mathcal A^{p,q}(X,E)$, the unique
smooth first-order operator with
$$\langle\bar\partial_Es,t\rangle_{L^2}=\langle s,\bar\partial_E^*t\rangle_{L^2}$$
for all compactly supported smooth forms.

The **Dolbeault Laplacian**
$\Delta_{\bar\partial_E}=\bar\partial_E\bar\partial_E^*+\bar\partial_E^*\bar\partial_E$
is a formally symmetric Laplace-type second-order operator
([[def-second-order-laplace-type-operators-on-vector-bundles]]) preserving each
bidegree $(p,q)$, with
$$\langle\Delta_{\bar\partial_E}s,s\rangle_{L^2}=\|\bar\partial_Es\|_2^2+\|\bar\partial_E^*s\|_2^2\ge0$$
for compactly supported smooth $s$. Its principal symbol is
$\sigma_2(\Delta_{\bar\partial_E})(x,\xi)=|\xi^{0,1}|_g^2\,\mathrm{id}$, where
$\xi^{0,1}$ is the $(0,1)$-part of $\xi\in T_x^*X$; in particular the principal
form is smooth, and it is positive definite on nonzero real covectors.

Let $M$ be a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold without boundary,
$\mu$ a smooth positive density on $M$, and $E,F\to M$ finite-rank smooth vector
bundles over $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ with smooth bundle metrics,
Hermitian (first-variable-linear) in the complex case, with the conventions of
[[def-second-order-laplace-type-operators-on-vector-bundles]]. Let
$P:\Gamma(E)\to\Gamma(F)$ be a linear differential operator of order at most two
(the target-$F$ version of the local description in
[[def-second-order-laplace-type-operators-on-vector-bundles]]).

Then there is a unique linear differential operator $P^\star:\Gamma(F)\to\Gamma(E)$
of order at most two such that
$$\int_M\langle Pu,v\rangle_F\,d\mu=\int_M\langle u,P^\star v\rangle_E\,d\mu$$
for all compactly supported smooth sections $u\in\Gamma_c(E)$ and
$v\in\Gamma_c(F)$; it is the **formal adjoint** of $P$. It is given locally as
follows: in a chart with coordinates $x$, with density coefficient $\gamma>0$
defined by $\mu=\gamma\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$
([[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]), with frames of $E$ and $F$
orthonormal for the metrics (equivalently unitary in the complex case; such
frames exist locally by applying Gram–Schmidt to any local frame,
[[thm-gram-schmidt-orthonormalisation]]), and with local coefficients
$Pu=\sum_{|\alpha|\le2}a_\alpha D^\alpha u$,
$$P^\star v=\sum_{|\alpha|\le2}(-1)^{|\alpha|}\gamma^{-1}D^\alpha\bigl(\gamma\,a_\alpha^*v\bigr),$$
where $a_\alpha^*$ is the fibre adjoint. Consequently:
1. if the leading coefficients of $P$ of order $\delta\in\{0,1,2\}$ are the
   matrices $a_\alpha$, $|\alpha|=\delta$, then those of $P^\star$ are
   $(-1)^\delta a_\alpha^*$, computed in the same orthonormal frames; in
   particular the formal adjoint of a Laplace-type operator is again Laplace
   type and its principal symbol is unchanged,
   $\sigma_2(P^\star)=\sigma_2(P)$;
2. $(P^\star)^\star=P$;
3. if $E=F$, then $P$ is formally symmetric in the sense of
   [[def-second-order-laplace-type-operators-on-vector-bundles]] exactly when
   $P=P^\star$.

Let $M$ be a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold without boundary of
dimension $n\ge2$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]), let $\mu$ be a smooth positive
density on $M$ ([[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]), and let $E\to M$ be
a finite-rank smooth vector bundle
([[def-smooth-vector-bundle-rank-fibre-and-trivial-bundle]]) over
$\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ carrying a smooth bundle metric
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ ([[def-smooth-bundle-metric]]), Euclidean in the
real case and Hermitian, linear in the first variable, in the complex case; in
the complex case the fibres are complex vector spaces through a smooth complex
structure on $E$
([[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]]). Write $\Gamma(E)$
for the smooth sections ([[def-smooth-section-local-section-and-support]]).

A $\mathbb K$-linear map $P:\Gamma(E)\to\Gamma(E)$ is a **linear differential
operator of order at most two** on $E$ when, on every chart domain $\Omega$ of
$M$ with coordinates $x=(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ and in every local frame of $E$ over
$\Omega$ in which a section is written $s\leftrightarrow u=(u^1,\ldots,u^r)$
and its image as $Ps\leftrightarrow((Ps)_1,\ldots,(Ps)_r)$,
$$(Ps)_\lambda=-\sum_{i,j=1}^na^{ij}_{\lambda\mu}(x)\,\partial_i\partial_ju^\mu(x)+\sum_{j=1}^nb^j_{\lambda\mu}(x)\,\partial_ju^\mu(x)+c_{\lambda\mu}(x)u^\mu(x),\qquad1\le\lambda\le r,$$
with smooth coefficient functions on $\Omega$ and summation over the repeated
index $\mu$ (and over $i,j$). Such an operator is **Laplace type** when in
addition, in every such chart and frame, its second-order coefficients are
scalar multiples of the identity, $a^{ij}_{\lambda\mu}=a^{ij}\delta_{\lambda\mu}$,
with $a^{ij}$ smooth real functions for which the matrix $(a^{ij}(x))$ is
symmetric and positive definite at every $x\in\Omega$. Its **principal symbol**
is the smooth section $\sigma_2(P)$ of $\mathrm{Sym}^2T^*M$
([[def-smooth-tensor-field]]) given on such a chart by
$\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)=a^{ij}(x)\xi_i\xi_j$ for $\xi\in T_x^*M$; equivalently
$\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)=a_x(\xi,\xi)\,\mathrm{id}_{E_x}$ for a smooth field of
positive-definite quadratic forms $a_x$ on $T_x^*M$, so that
$\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)>0$ whenever $\xi\ne0$.

$P$ is **formally symmetric** for $(\mu,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ when
$$\int_M\langle Ps,t\rangle\,d\mu=\int_M\langle s,Pt\rangle\,d\mu$$
for all compactly supported smooth sections $s,t\in\Gamma_c(E)$
([[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-smooth-density]]).

**Well-definedness.** The definition is local. On a fixed chart and frame the
displayed assignment is a $\mathbb K$-linear map on components with smooth
coefficients, and the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]])
computes the transition to another chart and frame on the overlap: the
second-order coefficients transform by the symmetric tensor rule
$a'^{kl}=a^{ij}\frac{\partial x'^k}{\partial x^i}\frac{\partial x'^l}{\partial x^j}$
together with conjugation by the frame-change matrix, while the terms produced
by the second derivatives of the coordinate change are absorbed into the
first-order coefficients. Hence a single operator that admits a local
expression on one cover admits a local expression on every chart and frame, and
the two hypotheses placed on the leading coefficient are invariant: scalar-ness
is preserved by frame conjugation and by the coordinate rule for a field of
symmetric matrices, and symmetric positive definiteness is preserved by both.
The principal symbol is therefore independent of the chart and frame, since two
local expressions of the same operator differ by an operator of order at most
one; it is smooth in $(x,\xi)$ because the $a^{ij}$ are smooth, and it is
positive on nonzero covectors exactly when $(a^{ij})$ is positive definite.
Formal symmetry is an identity between integrals of compactly supported smooth
sections and therefore depends only on the operator, the density and the
metric.

A Riemannian metric induces smooth metrics on dual, tensor and exterior bundles. On decomposable covectors, $\langle\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k,\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_k\rangle=\det(\langle\alpha_i,\beta_j\rangle)$; increasing orthonormal wedge monomials have norm one.

The **Riemannian volume density** is $\mu_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in coordinates.

The matrix is that of [[prop-coordinate-criterion-for-a-riemannian-metric]], so its determinant is positive and smooth. The density frames and their absolute-Jacobian law are [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]. In dimension zero take the empty determinant to be one, giving weight one at every point, independently of orientation. The compatibility of these local formulas is proved in [[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]].

For a smooth manifold $M^n$, with boundary allowed, the **density bundle** is $DM=\coprod_{p\in M}D(T_pM)$. In coordinates $x$, let $|dx|=|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ be the density taking value one on the coordinate frame. On overlaps,
$$|dy|=|\det D_x y|\,|dx|.$$
A smooth density is a section with smooth real coefficient in these frames. Its support is the closure of its nonzero locus. The absolute determinants are positive smooth transition functions and satisfy the cocycle identities by the chain rule. A countable atlas and [[thm-vector-bundle-construction-from-a-smooth-cocycle]] therefore give a smooth line bundle. For boundary charts the same gluing proof uses half-space product charts; smoothness of transitions follows from their local extensions, and Hausdorffness and second countability follow as for the supplied cocycle construction. The fibers are lines by [[prop-one-densities-form-a-one-dimensional-vector-space]]. When $n=0$ the empty frame trivializes $DM=M\times\mathbb R$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $\delta$ be a compactly supported smooth density on $M^n$, with boundary allowed. Choose a chart partition $(\rho_i)$ and write $\rho_i\delta=f_i|dx_i|$. For $n\geq1$ define
$$\int_M\delta=\sum_i\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widetilde f_i(x_i)\,dx_i.$$
The zero extensions are Riemann integrable, including at genuine faces, by [[lem-chart-supported-coefficients-have-well-defined-riemann-integrable-half-space-extensions]]. The compact-support/local-finiteness argument of [[lem-a-locally-finite-sum-is-finite-near-the-compact-support-of-a-form]] applies to density supports as closed sets, so the sum is finite. For $n=0$ sum the scalar density values over the finite support, without orientation signs. Empty support gives zero. Choice independence is discharged by [[thm-density-integration-is-defined-without-an-orientation]].

Let $m\ge1$. A **chart** on a topological space $X$ is a homeomorphism
$\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ from an open set $U\subseteq X$ onto an open subset of
$\mathbb C^m$ with its usual topology ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]);
two charts $\varphi,\psi$ are **holomorphically compatible** when the
transition maps $\psi\circ\varphi^{-1}$ and $\varphi\circ\psi^{-1}$ are
holomorphic on the open sets where they are defined
([[def-holomorphic-function-in-several-complex-variables]]). A **holomorphic
atlas** is a family of pairwise compatible charts whose domains cover $X$. A
**complex manifold of dimension $m$** is a nonempty Hausdorff
([[def-hausdorff-space]]) second-countable ([[def-second-countable-space]])
topological space carrying a holomorphic atlas; the same maximal-atlas argument
as for [[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]] applies verbatim with
$\mathbb C^m$ in place of $\mathbb C$: the union of a holomorphic atlas with all
charts compatible with it is again a holomorphic atlas, so one passes to the
unique maximal atlas and calls its members holomorphic charts. Each chart is a
homeomorphism onto an open subset of $\mathbb C^m\cong\mathbb R^{2m}$, so $X$ is
a topological manifold without boundary of real dimension $2m$
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]), and for connected $X$ the case
$m=1$ recovers Riemann surfaces ([[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]]).

A **holomorphic map** $f:X\to Y$ between complex manifolds is a continuous map
whose expression in every pair of holomorphic charts is holomorphic
([[def-holomorphic-map-and-complex-jacobian]]); equivalently, composition with
$f$ preserves holomorphic functions.

**Induced smooth structure and complex structure.** Holomorphic functions on
open subsets of $\mathbb C^m$ are smooth
([[cor-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables-are-smooth]]), so every
holomorphic atlas is a smooth atlas ([[def-smooth-atlas]]) and $X$ is a smooth
manifold of real dimension $2m$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]) whose smooth charts
include the holomorphic ones. In holomorphic coordinates
$z_k=x_k+iy_k$ the **complex structure** is the endomorphism field $J$ of the
tangent bundle determined by $J\partial_{x_k}=\partial_{y_k}$ and
$J\partial_{y_k}=-\partial_{x_k}$; it satisfies $J^2=-\mathrm{id}$ and is
independent of the holomorphic chart, because a holomorphic transition map has
complex-linear differential ([[def-holomorphic-map-and-complex-jacobian]],
[[thm-chain-rule-for-holomorphic-maps-in-several-variables]]) and complex-linear
maps intertwine the two coordinate definitions of multiplication by $i$. A
**Hermitian metric** on $X$ is a Riemannian metric $g$
([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]) satisfying
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all tangent vectors $v,w$; its Riemannian volume density
is written $\mu_g$ ([[def-riemannian-volume-density]]). The complex structure
makes each tangent space a complex vector space, so the tangent bundle is a
smooth complex vector bundle in the sense of
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]].

**Holomorphic vector bundles and Hermitian bundle metrics.** A **holomorphic
vector bundle of rank $r$** on $X$ is a smooth complex vector bundle
$\pi:E\to X$ of rank $r$
([[def-smooth-vector-bundle-rank-fibre-and-trivial-bundle]],
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]]) together with an open
cover $(V_\alpha)$ of $X$ and smooth local trivializations
$\theta_\alpha:E|_{V_\alpha}\to V_\alpha\times\mathbb C^r$ whose transition
matrices $g_{\alpha\beta}:V_\alpha\cap V_\beta\to\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathbb C)$,
defined by $\theta_\alpha\theta_\beta^{-1}(p,v)=(p,g_{\alpha\beta}(p)v)$, are
holomorphic. A **holomorphic frame** over an open set $V$ is such a
trivialization. Changing holomorphic frame multiplies a local section by a
holomorphic matrix, hence a smooth local section is **holomorphic** exactly when
its representatives in holomorphic frames are holomorphic functions. A
**Hermitian metric** $h$ on $E$ is a smooth bundle metric
([[def-smooth-bundle-metric]]) whose fibre pairings are positive definite
Hermitian forms, linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the
second; the condition is frame-independent because the gauge freedom is
conjugation by a pointwise invertible matrix. Smooth sections are
$\Gamma(E)$ ([[def-smooth-section-local-section-and-support]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

A Riemannian metric induces smooth metrics on dual, tensor and exterior bundles. On decomposable covectors, $\langle\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_k,\beta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\beta_k\rangle=\det(\langle\alpha_i,\beta_j\rangle)$; increasing orthonormal wedge monomials have norm one.

derivations.claim: The de Rham Laplacian satisfies the hypotheses of [F1]. Let $D=d$ on real forms, or on their complexification, and $P=DD^*+D^*D$. The coordinate formula [F2] exhibits $D$ as a smooth first-order differential operator, so [F4] supplies its unique smooth first-order formal adjoint $D^*$. In an orthonormal basis of the cotangent space at a point ([F7]), the leading coefficient matrices of $D$ multiply, on a covector $\xi$, to exterior multiplication $\varepsilon(\xi)$, and those of $D^*$ are $(-1)^1$ times the metric adjoints, so they multiply to $-\varepsilon(\xi)^*$. The coefficient of $\partial_i\partial_j$ in $DD^*$ is therefore $\varepsilon(\xi)\bigl(-\varepsilon(\xi)^*\bigr)$ and in $D^*D$ it is $\bigl(-\varepsilon(\xi)^*\bigr)\varepsilon(\xi)$; by [F5] the second-order coefficient matrix of $P$ is $-(\varepsilon(\xi)\varepsilon(\xi)^*+\varepsilon(\xi)^*\varepsilon(\xi))$. The metric adjoint of $\varepsilon(\xi)$ is the contraction that deletes each factor of a wedge monomial pairing with $\xi$, with alternating signs, and deleting and reinserting the same factor on both sides gives the identity $\varepsilon(\xi)\varepsilon(\xi)^*+\varepsilon(\xi)^*\varepsilon(\xi)=|\xi|^2\mathrm{id}$; hence the second-order coefficient of $P$ is $-|\xi|^2\mathrm{id}$ and its principal symbol in the sense of [F5] is $\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)=|\xi|^2\mathrm{id}$, a smooth positive definite scalar form. Finally, for compactly supported smooth forms, $(Pu,v)_{L^2}=(D^*u,D^*v)_{L^2}+(Du,Dv)_{L^2}$ by [F4], which is conjugate-symmetric in $u,v$ and equals $\|Du\|_2^2+\|D^*u\|_2^2\ge0$ when $u=v$; so $P$ is formally symmetric and nonnegative. Thus [F1] applies to $P$ with domain $H^2$.

The Dolbeault Laplacian satisfies the hypotheses of [F1]. Fix $p$ and let $D=\bar\partial_E$ on the sum over $q$, $P=DD^*+D^*D$, with the operator and its adjoint as in [F3]; by that item $D$ is a smooth first-order operator and the Dolbeault Laplacian is the formally symmetric Laplace-type operator with $\sigma_2(P)(x,\xi)=|\xi^{0,1}|^2\mathrm{id}$, notation as in [F5]. The same computation as in step 1.1, now with $\eta=\xi^{0,1}$ and unitary frames ([F7]), gives the deletion identity $\varepsilon(\eta)\varepsilon(\eta)^*+\varepsilon(\eta)^*\varepsilon(\eta)=|\eta|^2\mathrm{id}$ including the holomorphic $p$-factors and the bundle factor, so the second-order coefficient is $-|\eta|^2\mathrm{id}$ and the principal symbol is $|\xi^{0,1}|^2\mathrm{id}$; for a nonzero real covector the $(0,1)$-part is nonzero, so the form is positive definite. The energy identity and formal symmetry are those established in [F3], and no K\"ahler hypothesis is used. Hence [F1] applies to this $P$ as well.

Consequences of $D^2=0$. Squaring $D^2=0$ and transposing the adjoint identity gives $(D^*)^2=0$, and expanding the two products gives $PD=DP$ and $PD^*=D^*P$. On smooth forms the energy identity of steps 1.1 and 2.1 shows $Pu=0$ exactly when $Du=0$ and $D^*u=0$; [F1] makes every $L^2$-harmonic element smooth, so this describes $\ker P$ on $H^2$ as well. Harmonic forms are orthogonal to the images of $D$ and $D^*$: for harmonic $h$, $(Dv,h)_{L^2}=(v,D^*h)_{L^2}=0$ and $(D^*v,h)_{L^2}=(v,Dh)_{L^2}=0$. Since $D$ raises the degree by one in the de Rham grading and the second bidegree by one in the Dolbeault bigrading, while $D^*$ lowers it, the operator $P$ preserves degrees, and the unique orthogonal solution defining $G$ in [F1] preserves degree: its other degree components solve the homogeneous equation and lie in the orthogonal complement of the kernel, hence vanish; the harmonic projection preserves degree as well.

Commutation identities. For smooth $u$, $P(DGu)=D(PGu)=D(u-\Pi u)=Du$ by step 3.1 and [F1]. The section $DGu$ is smooth and orthogonal to $\ker P$ by step 3.1, and $Du$ is orthogonal to $\ker P$ as well; by the uniqueness of the orthogonal solution in [F1], $DGu=GDu$. The same reasoning applied to $D^*$ gives $D^*G=GD^*$. Since $\Pi$ projects onto $\ker P$ and the images of $D$ and $D^*$ are orthogonal to it, $D\Pi=D^*\Pi=0$; taking adjoints and using that $\Pi$ is an orthogonal projection gives $\Pi D=\Pi D^*=0$. All identities are asserted on smooth forms, so no composition of unbounded Hilbert-space domains has been formed.

Decomposition and harmonic representatives. For smooth $u$, [F1] gives $u=\Pi u+(I-\Pi)u=\Pi u+DD^*Gu+D^*DGu$, and the three summands are pairwise orthogonal: the harmonic summand is orthogonal to both images by step 3.1, and $(Da,D^*b)_{L^2}=(D^2a,b)_{L^2}=0$ since $D^2=0$. Conversely a harmonic form or a form in the image of $D$ or $D^*$ lies in the displayed ambient degree, so this is the orthogonal smooth decomposition. If $u$ is closed, $Du=0$, then step 4.1 gives $DGu=GDu=0$ and the coexact term vanishes: $u=\Pi u+D(D^*Gu)$, a harmonic representative of the class. If a harmonic $h$ is exact, $h=Dv$, then $\|h\|_2^2=(Dv,h)_{L^2}=(v,D^*h)_{L^2}=0$ because $D^*h=0$ by step 3.1, so $h=0$; hence $h\mapsto[h]$ is injective, and the preceding formula makes it surjective. It is linear as the composition of a linear projection with a linear quotient map, and its domain is finite dimensional by [F1]; the same argument applies over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$.

Conclusion and endpoints. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 verified the exact scalar-positive-symbol, formal-symmetry and nonnegativity hypotheses for the de Rham and Dolbeault Laplacians, so [F1] gives genuine nonnegative selfadjoint realizations with domain $H^2$, finite smooth kernels, smoothing projections and smooth Green inverses; steps 3.1 through 5.1 proved the degree, commutation, orthogonal-decomposition and harmonic-representative assertions for both complexes. At the endpoint degrees the operators mapping outside the displayed range are zero by the degree convention of [F3], so the identities hold there as well. The trivial line bundle case gives the usual Dolbeault cohomology of complex-valued forms, and no sheaf comparison has been used or asserted.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold without boundary, of real dimension at least two. Its metric defines the $L^2$ pairing on forms by the Riemannian density; orientation is unnecessary. Let $d^*$ denote the formal adjoint of $d$, and $\Delta=dd^*+d^*d$ on total real forms, or on their complexification. With domain $H^2$ the operator is nonnegative and selfadjoint. Its degreewise smooth kernels $\mathcal H^k$ are finite dimensional, and there is an orthogonal smooth decomposition
$$\Omega^k(M)=\mathcal H^k\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}d\Omega^{k-1}(M)\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}d^*\Omega^{k+1}(M).$$
The map $h\mapsto[h]$ is an isomorphism $\mathcal H^k\to H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)$, over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ as appropriate.

More generally let $X$ be a compact complex manifold of complex dimension $m\ge1$ with a smooth Hermitian metric. Let $E$ be a holomorphic bundle of finite rank with a smooth Hermitian metric (meaning its local frames have holomorphic invertible transition matrices). On $E$-valued $(p,q)$ forms, define $\bar\partial_E$ by the coefficientwise Dolbeault operator in holomorphic bundle charts and let $\bar\partial_E^*$ be its formal adjoint. For each fixed $p$, $\Delta_{\bar\partial_E}=\bar\partial_E\bar\partial_E^*+\bar\partial_E^*\bar\partial_E$ on the sum over $q$ is nonnegative and selfadjoint on $H^2$; its smooth harmonic spaces $\mathcal H_E^{p,q}$ are finite dimensional and
$$\Omega^{p,q}(X,E)=\mathcal H_E^{p,q}\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\bar\partial_E\Omega^{p,q-1}(X,E)\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\bar\partial_E^*\Omega^{p,q+1}(X,E).$$
In particular harmonic forms represent the smooth Dolbeault quotient
$$H_{\bar\partial}^{p,q}(X,E):=\ker\bar\partial_E/\operatorname{im}\bar\partial_E$$
uniquely. Terms outside the degree range are zero. This asserts smooth Dolbeault cohomology; an identification with sheaf cohomology requires a separate Dolbeault-resolution comparison theorem.

For either complex write $D=d$ or $D=\bar\partial_E$, $P=DD^*+D^*D$, and let $\Pi,G$ be the preceding Green projection and inverse. They preserve degree, $G$ preserves smooth forms, and on smooth forms
$$DG=GD,\qquad D^*G=GD^*,\qquad D\Pi=\Pi D=D^*\Pi=\Pi D^*=0.$$
Every closed smooth $u$ satisfies $u=\Pi u+D(D^*Gu)$.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb Z^n\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be the integer lattice acting
on $\mathbb R^n$ by translations, and let $T^n=\mathbb R^n/\mathbb Z^n$ carry
the quotient topology with quotient map $q:\mathbb R^n\to T^n$. Then:

1. there is a Riemannian metric $g$ on $T^n$, unique, with
   $q^*g=\sum_{i=1}^n dx^i\otimes dx^i$; with this metric $T^n$ is a
   connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold and $q$ is a surjective local
   isometry;
2. $(T^n,g)$ is geodesically and metrically complete, and for $n\ge2$ it has
   vanishing sectional curvature: $K=0$ on every tangent two-plane;
3. the quotient charts of the proof identify $T_{[x]}T^n$ with $\mathbb R^n$,
   and under that identification the maximal geodesic with initial datum
   $v\in\mathbb R^n$ is
   $$t\mapsto[x+tv],\qquad t\in\mathbb R,$$
   so that the exponential map is defined on all of $T_{[x]}T^n$ and
   $\exp_{[x]}(v)=[x+v]$; in particular $\exp_{[x]}$ is not injective, since
   $\exp_{[x]}(0)=\exp_{[x]}(e_1)=[x]$ for the nonzero lattice vector
   $e_1\in\mathbb Z^n$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $k\ge 0$. A **smooth differential $k$-form**
on $M$ is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M\to M$. The space of such forms
is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, and $\Omega^0(M)=C^\infty(M)$.

Let $X:M\to TM$ be a smooth section of the tangent bundle, that is, a smooth
vector field on $M$, and let $\omega\in\Omega^k(M)$. The **interior product**
$\iota_X\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$ is defined pointwise by

$$ (\iota_X\omega)_p:=\iota_{X_p}\omega_p. $$

For $k=0$, adopt the formal convention $\Omega^{-1}(M):=\{0\}$ and set
$\iota_X\omega:=0$.

This pointwise field is smooth. Indeed, in local coordinates write
$X=\sum_jX^j\partial_j$ and expand $\omega$ in the smooth frame $dx^I$ as in
[[prop-local-coordinate-expression-for-a-differential-form]]. The coefficients
of $\iota_X\omega$ are signed finite sums of products $X^j\omega_I$, and are
therefore smooth.

derivations.claim: Write a smooth form uniquely as $u=\sum_Iu_I dx^I$ with periodic smooth coefficients on $\mathbb R^n$, using the global coframe and the descent along $q$ of [F2]. The constant metric gives $d=\sum_j\varepsilon(dx^j)\partial_j$ and $d^*=-\sum_j\iota_{\partial_j}\partial_j$; the wedge/contraction anticommutator recorded in [F1], applied in the orthonormal coframe, cancels the mixed terms, giving $\Delta u=-\sum_I\sum_j\partial_j^2u_I dx^I$. Integration over the unit cube, with opposite-face terms canceled by periodicity, yields $(\Delta u,u)_2=\sum_{I,j}\int_{[0,1]^n}|\partial_j u_I|^2$.

If $u$ is harmonic, the sum of nonnegative integrals in step 1.1 is zero. Each derivative is continuous, so a nonzero value would give a neighbourhood with positive integral; hence every $\partial_j u_I$ vanishes everywhere. Integration along line segments in $\mathbb R^n$ gives constant coefficients. Conversely constant coefficients give $\Delta u=0$ by step 1.1. The increasing wedge basis has $\binom nk$ members, and [F1] identifies this harmonic space with de Rham cohomology, proving the asserted representative and dimension claims.

The case k=1 is the ordinary one-degree computation of step 2.1; the binomial count includes one element in the endpoint cases.
The flat metric is positive definite by [F2] and no direction is degenerate; the zero form case is included in step 2.1.
The endpoint degrees k=0 and k=n are given by the same constant-coefficient argument in step 2.1.

citations.quote:
Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a Hausdorff topological space
([[def-hausdorff-space]], [[def-topological-space]]), with compact subsets as in
[[def-compact-space]]. Then:

1. **A point and a disjoint compact set are separated.** If $K \subseteq X$ is
   compact and $x \in X \setminus K$, there are $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ with
   $$x \in U, \qquad K \subseteq V, \qquad U \cap V = \varnothing .$$
2. **Two disjoint compact sets are separated.** If $K, L \subseteq X$ are compact
   and $K \cap L = \varnothing$, there are $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ with
   $$L \subseteq U, \qquad K \subseteq V, \qquad U \cap V = \varnothing .$$
3. **Compact implies closed.** Every compact subset of $X$ is closed in $X$.
4. **In a compact Hausdorff space the two classes coincide.** If in addition
   $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is compact, then a subset of $X$ is compact if and only if
   it is closed.

**The proof is written choice-free, and that is not a stylistic preference.** The
textbook argument says "for each $y \in K$ choose disjoint open $U_y, V_y$",
which is a selection over an arbitrary index set and therefore an appeal to the
full Axiom of Choice. What is done below instead is to take the family of **all**
open $V$ that admit some open $U \ni x$ disjoint from them — a family cut out by
a formula, with nothing selected — extract a finite subcover from it, and only
then make finitely many selections, which [[lem-finite-choice]] supplies as a
theorem of ZF.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). Then:

1. **A neighbourhood base of compact sets.** If $X$ is locally compact
   ([[def-locally-compact-space]]) and Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]), then
   every neighbourhood $N$ of a point $x \in X$ ([[def-neighbourhood-top]])
   contains a compact neighbourhood of $x$; so the compact neighbourhoods of $x$
   form a neighbourhood base at $x$.
2. **Heredity along open and closed subspaces.** If $X$ is locally compact and
   Hausdorff and $S \subseteq X$ is open, then the subspace $S$ is locally
   compact ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). If $X$ is locally compact and
   $F \subseteq X$ is closed, then the subspace $F$ is locally compact; no
   Hausdorff hypothesis is used for this half.
3. **Shrinking inside an open set.** If $X$ is locally compact and Hausdorff,
   $O \subseteq X$ is open and $x \in O$, there is an open $V$ with
   $$x \in V \subseteq \overline{V} \subseteq O$$
   and $\overline{V}$ a compact subset of $X$.
4. **Compact sets sit in open sets with compact closure.** If $X$ is locally
   compact and Hausdorff and $K \subseteq X$ is compact, there is an open
   $V \subseteq X$ with $K \subseteq V$ and $\overline{V}$ a compact subset of
   $X$ ([[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]]).

**No choice principle is used**; every cover produced below is defined by a
formula and thinned by [[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], which returns
members rather than indices.
The properties $T_0$, $T_1$, and Hausdorffness are hereditary in the sense of [[def-hereditary-property]].

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq X$. The **subspace topology** (also *relative topology*) on $S$ is

$$\mathcal{T}_S := \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\},$$

the family of **traces** on $S$ of the open sets of $X$. The pair
$(S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a **subspace** of $X$. A subset of $S$ that lies in
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is said to be **open in $S$**, and *relatively open* where the
ambient space needs emphasis.

**$\mathcal{T}_S$ is a topology, and this is discharged here.** (T1):
$\varnothing = \varnothing \cap S$ and $S = X \cap S$ are traces. (T2): if
$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of
$\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since
$U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical
such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying
$U' \cap S = W$ — and then
$\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in
$X$. (T3): $(U \cap S) \cap (V \cap S) = (U \cap V) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by
(T3) in $X$.

**Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set
$C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed
$F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and
$S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$
matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing.

**Bases and subbases trace as well.** If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then
$\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$
and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence
$x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$
shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with
unions.

**The inclusion is continuous.** The inclusion map $\iota : S \to X$,
$\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$,
so preimages of open sets are open and $\iota$ is continuous
([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b)). Moreover
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any
topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$.

**Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be
a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then

$$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$

*Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has
$(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is
continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous;
conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in
$S$ the set $g^{-1}[W] = (\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U]$ is open, so $g$ is continuous.
Both directions use only clause (b) of [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]].

**Restriction of a continuous map.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and
$S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since
$(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]).

**When relative and ambient agree.** If $S$ is open in $X$ then a subset of $S$
is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an
intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$
contained in $S$ is its own trace. The same statement with "closed" throughout
holds when $S$ is closed in $X$. Both are used in the pasting lemma of the next
item, and both fail without the hypothesis: $S$ itself is always open and closed
in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].

Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]) and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on
$X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]); this covers in particular every sheaf
of $k$-vector spaces over a field $k$, which is the case used by the
compact-support calculus, and for such a sheaf the groups below are $k$-vector
spaces and the maps $k$-linear. Global sections are written
$\Gamma(X,-)$ ([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]]). For a compact subset
$K\subseteq X$ ([[def-compact-space]]) let $i:K\hookrightarrow X$ be the
inclusion and consider the canonical restriction map
$$\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)\longrightarrow\Gamma(K,i^{-1}\mathcal F)=(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K),\qquad s\longmapsto s|_K,$$
which sends a global section ([[def-section-restriction-and-global-section]]) to
the section of the inverse image sheaf ([[def-inverse-image-presheaf-and-sheaf]])
that it induces on $K$. Then $\mathcal F$ is **c-soft**, also **soft for
compact supports**, when this map is surjective for every compact subset
$K\subseteq X$, that is: every section of $\mathcal F$ over a compact subset of
$X$ extends to a global section of $\mathcal F$. For sheaves of abelian groups
$\Gamma_c$ and $H^q_c$ of
[[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]] are the compactly supported
analogues of $\Gamma$ and $H^q$.

Two consistency facts hold; both are immediate from the definitions and from
the extension lemma for sections on a compact set, and they are recorded here
because the compact-support calculus uses the first constantly and the second
for injective sheaves.

1. **Neighbourhood formulation.** By
   [[lem-sections-near-a-compact-set-are-sections-on-that-set]], the source of
   the restriction map may be replaced by the defining colimit of the
   inverse-image presheaf,
   $(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K)=\varinjlim_{U\supseteq K}\mathcal F(U)$, so that
   $\mathcal F$ is c-soft if and only if for every compact $K$ and every open
   neighbourhood $U$ of $K$, every section $s\in\mathcal F(U)$ agrees with a
   global section of $\mathcal F$ on some open neighbourhood of $K$. It
   therefore suffices, for c-softness, to test the extended sections only
   locally near $K$.
2. **Flasque implies c-soft.** If $\mathcal F$ is flasque
   ([[def-flasque-sheaf]]) then $\mathcal F$ is c-soft: a class in
   $(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K)$ is represented by a section $s$ over an open
   neighbourhood $U$ of $K$, and flasqueness extends $s$ to a global section
   $t\in\mathcal F(X)$ with $t|_U=s$, so $t$ is a preimage of that class.

C-softness is a property of the pair $(X,\mathcal F)$ and not of the sheaf
alone: the compact subsets of the base space are part of the test. Nothing is
assumed about the support of the extended global sections, and c-softness is
not the same condition as flasqueness, only implied by it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space and
let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]); every clause applies in particular to
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces, and the tensor clause of (4) is stated only
there. Then:

1. if $\mathcal F$ is c-soft ([[def-c-soft-sheaf]]), every section of
   $\mathcal F$ over a compact subset $K\subseteq X$ extends to a compactly
   supported global section whose support is contained in any prescribed open
   neighbourhood of $K$;
2. every injective abelian sheaf on $X$ is c-soft;
3. if $\mathcal F$ is c-soft, then $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)=0$ for every $q>0$
   ([[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]]); when $X$ is compact this is
   the vanishing of the sheaf cohomology $H^q(X,\mathcal F)$
   ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]);
4. c-softness is preserved by restriction to open subsets, by restriction to
   closed subsets, by extension by zero along an open inclusion, and by finite
   direct sums of sheaves of abelian groups; for sheaves of $k$-vector spaces
   it is also preserved by tensor product with a constant $k$-vector space;
5. if $0\to\mathcal F'\xrightarrow{\alpha}\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\beta}\mathcal F''\to0$
   is a short exact sequence of sheaves of abelian groups and $\mathcal F'$ is
   c-soft, then every section of $\mathcal F''$ over a compact subset lifts to
   a section of $\mathcal F$ over an open neighbourhood of it, and the induced
   sequence
   $0\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F'')\to0$
   is exact; if $\mathcal F'$ and $\mathcal F$ are c-soft then
   $\mathcal F''$ is c-soft.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace, and let
$\mathcal F$ be a sheaf on $X$. The **restriction of $\mathcal F$ to $U$** is
the inverse image sheaf
$$
\mathcal F|_U:=j^{-1}\mathcal F.
$$

For an open set $W \subseteq U$, one may identify $(\mathcal F|_U)(W)$ with
$\mathcal F(W)$: because $U$ is open in $X$, the set $W$ is also open in $X$,
and in the neighbourhood-colimit defining $j^{-1}\mathcal F$ the open set $W$
itself is a neighbourhood of $j(W)=W$.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, and let $\mathcal G$ be a presheaf on $Y$.
The **inverse-image presheaf**
$$
f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G
$$
on $X$ is defined by
$$
(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U):=\varinjlim_{f(U)\subseteq V}\mathcal G(V),
$$
where $V$ runs over the open neighbourhoods of $f(U)$ in $Y$, ordered by
reverse inclusion. If $U' \subseteq U$, then every neighbourhood of $f(U)$ is a
neighbourhood of $f(U')$, so there is a natural restriction map
$(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U)\to(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U')$.

The **inverse image sheaf** of a sheaf $\mathcal G$ on $Y$ is the sheafification
of this presheaf:
$$
f^{-1}\mathcal G:=a(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G).
$$

When $U$ is open in $X$ and $V$ is an open set of $Y$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$,
there is a canonical map
$$
\mathcal G(V)\longrightarrow(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U)
$$
into the colimit class represented by $V$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space
([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-hausdorff-space]]) and let
$\mathcal E$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]); every clause applies in particular to
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces. Suppose that
$$H^1_c(V,\mathcal E|_V)=0\qquad\text{for every open subspace }V\subseteq X,$$
where $\mathcal E|_V$ is the restriction
([[def-restriction-sheaf-open-subspace]]) and $H^1_c$ is the first
compactly supported cohomology ([[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]]).
Then $\mathcal E$ is c-soft ([[def-c-soft-sheaf]]); more precisely, every
section of $\mathcal E$ over a compact subset $K\subseteq X$ extends to a
compactly supported global section of $\mathcal E$. Conversely, if
$\mathcal E$ is c-soft, then
$H^q_c(V,\mathcal E|_V)=0$ for every $q>0$ and every open subspace
$V\subseteq X$. Hence c-softness of $\mathcal E$ is equivalent to
$R\Gamma_c(V,\mathcal E|_V)$ being concentrated in degree $0$ for every open
subspace $V\subseteq X$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, and let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space. Then
the abelian category $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$ of $\mathcal O_X$-modules has
enough injectives: every $\mathcal O_X$-module embeds into an injective
$\mathcal O_X$-module, and the functorial injective embedding supplied by the
Grothendieck injective-embedding theorem for Grothendieck categories supplies,
by iteration of cokernels, one specific injective resolution
$$0\to\mathcal F\to I^0(\mathcal F)\to I^1(\mathcal F)\to\cdots$$
to each $\mathcal O_X$-module $\mathcal F$ with no further selection
([[def-injective-resolution-in-an-abelian-category]]). The Axiom of Choice
enters exactly through that embedding theorem applied to
$\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$; the category-theoretic verification below is
choice-free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, and let $X$ be a topological space. Then
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ has enough injectives, every abelian sheaf on $X$ admits an
injective resolution ([[def-injective-resolution-in-an-abelian-category]]), and
the embeddings below supply one injective resolution datum
([[def-supplied-injective-resolution-datum]]) on the whole category
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)$: for every abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ the datum assigns one
specific injective resolution
$$0\to\mathcal F\to I^0(\mathcal F)\to I^1(\mathcal F)\to\cdots,$$
built functorially from $\mathcal F$ with no further selection.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ be abelian categories, let $I$ be supplied
injective resolution data on all objects of $\mathcal A$, and let
$F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be an additive left exact functor. Then the additive functors
$$R_I^nF:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B,\qquad n\geq 0,$$
admit connecting maps that make them into a cohomological delta functor on
$\mathcal A$, and $R_I^0F$ is naturally isomorphic to $F$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a locally
compact Hausdorff space, let $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ be the category of sheaves of
abelian groups on $X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]) and let
$$\Gamma(X,-):\mathrm{Ab}(X)\longrightarrow\mathbf{Ab}$$
be the additive left exact global-sections functor
([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]],
[[def-section-restriction-and-global-section]]). For a sheaf $\mathcal F$ on
$X$ define the **compactly supported global sections** of $\mathcal F$ to be the
subgroup
$$\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F):=\{\,s\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal F):\operatorname{Supp}(s)\ \text{is a compact subset of }X\,\}\subseteq\Gamma(X,\mathcal F),$$
where the support of a section is the set of points at which its germ is
nonzero ([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]], [[def-germ-of-section]],
[[def-compact-space]]). A morphism $\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian
sheaves induces a map $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ by restriction of
$\Gamma(X,\varphi)$, and this makes $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ an additive functor
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)\to\mathbf{Ab}$ ([[def-additive-functor]],
[[def-morphism-of-presheaves]]). Six consistency facts hold; all are immediate
from the definitions, and they record the interface used by the compact-support
calculus.

1. **Well-definedness of $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$.** If $x\notin
   \operatorname{Supp}(s)$ then $s_x=0$ in the stalk $\mathcal F_x$
   ([[def-stalk-of-presheaf]]), and since the stalk maps of a morphism commute
   with the germ maps, $\varphi(s)_x=\varphi_x(s_x)=0$, so
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi(s))\subseteq\operatorname{Supp}(s)$. A support
   $\operatorname{Supp}(t)$ is closed in $X$: if $x\notin
   \operatorname{Supp}(t)$ then $t$ agrees with the zero section on some open
   neighbourhood of $x$, by the description of equality of germs
   ([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]]). Hence
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi(s))$ is a closed subset of $X$ contained in the
   compact set $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$; being closed in $X$ it is closed in the
   subspace $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$, so it is a compact subset of that compact
   space ([[thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]) and therefore
   a compact subset of $X$ ([[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]]), and
   $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ maps $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$ into
   $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal G)$. Composites and identities are computed
   componentwise, so $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is a functor; it is additive because
   $\Gamma(X,-)$ is.
2. **Sheaves of $k$-vector spaces.** If $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of
   $k$-vector spaces, then $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$ is a $k$-vector subspace of
   $\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$: the support of $c\cdot s$ is
   $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ for $c\ne0$ and $\varnothing$ for $c=0$, and the
   zero section has empty support. For a morphism $\varphi$ of sheaves of
   $k$-vector spaces the map $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ is $k$-linear, since
   $\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ is. The higher derived functors below are computed from
   an injective resolution datum on abelian sheaves, so they are abelian
   groups; the degree-zero part is the $k$-vector space
   $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$.
3. **Left exactness.** For every short exact sequence
   $0\to\mathcal F'\xrightarrow{\varphi'}\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathcal F''\to0$
   of abelian sheaves the sequence
   $$0\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')\xrightarrow{\Gamma_c(\varphi')}\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)\xrightarrow{\Gamma_c(\varphi)}\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F'')$$
   is exact. Injectivity: a monomorphism of sheaves has injective stalk maps
   ([[thm-exactness-of-sheaves-stalkwise]]), so
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi'(s'))=\operatorname{Supp}(s')$ and a section
   killed by $\varphi'$ has all germs zero, hence is zero. Exactness at the
   middle: the kernel of $\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ is the image of
   $\Gamma(X,\varphi')$ by left exactness of global sections
   ([[lem-global-sections-left-exact]]); if $s=\varphi'(s')$ has compact
   support, then $s'$ has the same support,
   $\operatorname{Supp}(s')=\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi'(s'))=
   \operatorname{Supp}(s)$, because $\varphi'$ is stalk-injective, so $s'$ lies
   in $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')$, and the reverse inclusion is immediate from
   $\varphi\circ\varphi'=0$. Thus $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is an additive left exact
   functor on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ ([[def-left-exact-and-right-exact-functor]]).
4. **The derived functors.** Abelian sheaves on $X$ have enough injectives, and
   the embeddings of [[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]] supply one
   functorial injective resolution datum $\mathcal F\mapsto I^\bullet(\mathcal F)$
   on the whole category $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, under the Axiom of Choice
   ([[def-right-derived-object-relative-to-injective-resolution-data]]). The
   **compactly supported cohomology** of $\mathcal F$ is
   $$H^q_c(X,\mathcal F):=R^q\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F):=H^q\bigl(\Gamma_c(X,I^\bullet(\mathcal F)_{\mathrm{del}})\bigr)\qquad(q\ge0),\qquad H^q_c(X,\mathcal F):=0\quad(q<0),$$
   the cohomology of the deleted resolution, as in the pattern of
   [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]; for a morphism $\varphi$ we
   write $H^q_c(X,\varphi):=R^q\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ for the induced map.
5. **Independence of the datum.** If $J$ is another supplied injective
   resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, then $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$ computed from
   $J$ is naturally isomorphic to $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$ computed from $I$
   ([[thm-right-derived-functors-from-two-supplied-injective-resolution-data-are-naturally-isomorphic]]);
   the Axiom of Dependent Choice needed for that comparison follows from AC
   ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]). The notation
   $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)$ therefore does not depend on the datum up to this
   canonical natural isomorphism.
6. **Delta functor and the compact case.** Since $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is additive
   and left exact and the datum is defined on all of $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, the
   functors $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$, $q\ge0$, carry connecting maps that make them a
   cohomological delta functor with $R^0\Gamma_c(X,-)\cong\Gamma_c(X,-)$, and
   every short exact sequence of abelian sheaves has a long exact
   compact-support cohomology sequence, natural in the sequence
   ([[thm-right-derived-functors-form-a-cohomological-delta-functor]]). If $X$
   is compact, then for every global section $s$ its support is closed in $X$ by
   fact 1, hence a closed subset of the compact space $X$ and therefore
   compact, so every global section is compactly supported; hence
   $\Gamma_c(X,-)=\Gamma(X,-)$ and
   $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)=H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ for every $q$, where $H^q(X,-)$ is
   the sheaf cohomology of [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]
   computed from the same datum.

Let $X$ be a topological space. A sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on $X$
is **exact** when it is exact in the abelian category of
[[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]], equivalently in the sense of
[[def-exact-sequence-and-short-exact-sequence-in-an-abelian-category]].

Thus a sequence
$$
\cdots\to \mathcal F_{i-1}\to \mathcal F_i\to \mathcal F_{i+1}\to\cdots
$$
is exact at $\mathcal F_i$ when the image sheaf of the first morphism equals
the kernel sheaf of the second.

The same language applies to $\mathcal O_X$-modules on a ringed space.

Let
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{i-1}\xrightarrow{d_{i-1}}\mathcal F_i\xrightarrow{d_i}\mathcal F_{i+1}\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
be a sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space $X$. Then the
sequence is exact if and only if, for every point $x\in X$, the stalk sequence
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow (\mathcal F_{i-1})_x\xrightarrow{(d_{i-1})_x}(\mathcal F_i)_x\xrightarrow{(d_i)_x}(\mathcal F_{i+1})_x\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
is exact.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Fix an open $U\subseteq X$, write $\mathcal O_U=\mathcal O_X|_U$ and $G_U:=j_{U!}\mathcal O_U$, the extension by zero of the structure sheaf restricted to $U$ [F5]. Its sections are $G_U(V)=\{a\in\mathcal O_X(V\cap U):\operatorname{Supp}(a)\text{ closed in }V\}$, and multiplication by $b\in\mathcal O_X(V)$ is $(b|_{V\cap U})a$; its support remains inside $\operatorname{Supp}(a)$, so this makes $G_U$ an $\mathcal O_X$-module. For $s\in\mathcal F(U)$ and $a\in G_U(V)$, the product $a\,s|_{V\cap U}$ is a section of $\mathcal F$ on $V\cap U$. On the open complement $V\setminus\operatorname{Supp}(a)$ take the zero section. The two sections agree on their overlap because $a$ vanishes there, so they glue uniquely to a section $\varphi_V(a)\in\mathcal F(V)$. This construction commutes with restriction and is $\mathcal O_X$-linear, hence defines $\varphi:G_U\to\mathcal F$ with $\varphi_U(1_U)=s$. Conversely, on $V\cap U$ any $\mathcal O_X$-linear morphism with this value sends $a$ to $a\,s|_{V\cap U}$, while on $V\setminus\operatorname{Supp}(a)$ it sends the zero section to zero; the same open cover therefore makes it unique. Thus $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)}(G_U,\mathcal F)\cong\mathcal F(U)$.

derivations.claim: **Fibres are locally compact Hausdorff.** For $y\in Y$ the fibre $F=f^{-1}(y)$ is closed in $X$ because $\{y\}$ is closed in the Hausdorff space $Y$ and $f$ is continuous [F1], so $F$ is a closed subspace of the locally compact space $X$ and is locally compact, and it is Hausdorff as a subspace of a Hausdorff space [F1]; the same holds for every open subspace $V\subseteq F$ [F1]. Consequently, for every sheaf $\mathcal G$ on $X$ that is c-soft on $X$, the restriction $\mathcal G|_F$ is c-soft on $F$ and its further restriction $\mathcal G|_V$ is c-soft on $V$, by the closed- and open-restriction clauses of [F2]; if $\mathcal G$ is injective on $X$ it is c-soft on $X$ by the injectivity clause of [F2].

**The resolution and its terms.** Fix the supplied functorial injective resolution datum on $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ of [F4] (on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ for the abelian case) and let $0\to\mathcal A\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots$ be the injective resolution it assigns to $\mathcal A$. Each $I^j$ is injective in the chosen sheaf category, hence flasque and c-soft on $X$ by [F2], hence restricts to a c-soft sheaf $I^j|_F$ on every fibre $F$ and to a c-soft sheaf $I^j|_V$ on every open $V$ of a fibre, by [step 1.1]; in particular each $I^j$ is fibrewise c-soft.

**Dimension shifting on an open subspace of a fibre.** Let $V\subseteq F$ be open in a fibre $F=f^{-1}(y)$ and define the syzygies $Z^0:=\mathcal A$ and, for $j\ge0$, $Z^{j+1}:=\operatorname{coker}(Z^j\to I^j)$, so that $0\to Z^j\to I^j\to Z^{j+1}\to0$ is a short exact sequence of sheaves on $X$. Restricting to the open subspace $V$ preserves exactness and cokernels, so $0\to Z^j|_V\to I^j|_V\to Z^{j+1}|_V\to0$ is a short exact sequence of sheaves on the locally compact Hausdorff space $V$ [F5] whose middle term is c-soft, hence acyclic [F2]; the long exact compactly supported cohomology sequence of [F5] therefore gives isomorphisms $H^p_c(V,Z^{j+1}|_V)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^{p+1}_c(V,Z^j|_V)$ for every $p\ge1$, because the two adjacent groups of the c-soft sheaf $I^j|_V$ vanish in positive degrees. Iterating these isomorphisms for $j=0,1,\dots,d-1$ with $p=1,2,\dots,d$ gives $H^1_c(V,Z^d|_V)\cong H^{d+1}_c(V,\mathcal A|_V)=0$, the last group vanishing by the dimension hypothesis of the statement because $d+1>d$ and $V$ is an open subspace of a fibre.

**The cokernel after $d$ steps is fibrewise c-soft.** Let $F=f^{-1}(y)$ be any fibre and let $V\subseteq F$ be open; by [step 3.1] one has $H^1_c(V,Z^d|_V)=0$ for every such $V$, so the vanishing criterion [F3] applied to the locally compact Hausdorff space $Z=F$ and the sheaf $\mathcal E=Z^d|_F$ shows that $Z^d|_F$ is c-soft on $F$. Since $y$ was arbitrary, $Z^d$ restricts to a c-soft sheaf on every fibre. Concatenating the short exact sequences $0\to Z^j\to I^j\to Z^{j+1}\to0$ for $j=0,\dots,d-1$ gives the exact sequence $0\to\mathcal A\to I^0\to I^1\to\cdots\to I^{d-1}\to Z^d\to0$, a bounded resolution of $\mathcal A$ entirely by $k$-linear maps and $k$-sheaves (by abelian maps and sheaves in the abelian case), whose terms $I^0,\dots,I^{d-1}$ are fibrewise c-soft by [step 2.1] and whose last term $Z^d$ is fibrewise c-soft by the preceding argument; when $d=0$ the construction stops at $Z^0=\mathcal A$ and the isomorphism $H^1_c(V,\mathcal A|_V)\cong H^{d+1}_c(V,\mathcal A|_V)=0$ of [step 3.1] with $d=0$ gives the c-softness of $\mathcal A$ on every fibre directly by [F3].

**Conclusion.** The displayed bounded resolution of the statement is [step 4.1], and taking $\mathcal A=k_X$ gives the instance of the constant sheaf. The Axiom of Choice is used only through the injective resolution datum of [F4] and the delta-functor and comparison statements of [F5], whose connecting maps use dependent choice, a consequence of AC [F6]; the fibre-by-fibre dimension count of [step 3.1] is finite.

For the zero sheaf the construction of steps 2.1 to 4.1 gives the zero resolution with zero terms, which are c-soft on every fibre.

citations.quote:
Let $\mathcal C$ be a category with specified zero morphisms
([[def-category-with-zero-morphisms]]), and let $f:A\to B$.

The **kernel** of $f$ is an equalizer

$$\ker(f)\xrightarrow{k}A\mathrel{\substack{\xrightarrow{f}\\[-0.6ex] \xrightarrow[0_{A,B}]{} }}B.$$

The **cokernel** of $f$ is a coequalizer

$$A\mathrel{\substack{\xrightarrow{f}\\[-0.6ex] \xrightarrow[0_{A,B}]{} }}B\xrightarrow{q}\operatorname{coker}(f).$$

in the sense of [[def-equalizers-and-coequalizers]]. Thus $fk=0$ and every
$h$ with $fh=0$ factors uniquely through $k$; dually, $qf=0$ and every $h$
with $hf=0$ factors uniquely through $q$.

Let $f:A\to B$ be a morphism in a category with kernels and cokernels
([[def-kernels-and-cokernels-as-equalizers-and-coequalizers]]).

The **image** of $f$ is the kernel of a cokernel of $f$:

$$\operatorname{im}(f):=\ker(\operatorname{coker}(f)).$$

The **coimage** of $f$ is the cokernel of a kernel of $f$:

$$\operatorname{coim}(f):=\operatorname{coker}(\ker(f)).$$

This page uses the object notation $\operatorname{im}(f)$ and
$\operatorname{coim}(f)$. Their defining arrows are the corresponding kernel and
cokernel maps.

For morphisms
$$0\to A\xrightarrow{i}B\xrightarrow{p}C\to 0$$
in an abelian category, the following are equivalent:

1. the sequence is short exact;
2. $i$ is a kernel of $p$ and $p$ is a cokernel of $i$.

A sequence of morphisms in an abelian category is **exact** when it is exact at
every interior object in the sense of [[def-exactness-at-a-node]].

In particular, a composable triple
$$0\to A\xrightarrow{i}B\xrightarrow{p}C\to 0$$
is a **short exact sequence** when it is exact at $A$, at $B$, and at $C$.

This page uses the sequence language literally: the definition names exactness
of displayed chains of morphisms, not chain complexes as objects.

In an abelian category, every monomorphism is the kernel of its cokernel, and
dually every epimorphism is the cokernel of its kernel.

Let
$$0\to A\xrightarrow{i}B\xrightarrow{p}C\to 0$$
be a short exact sequence in an abelian category.

1. If $s:C\to B$ satisfies $p s = 1_C$, then there is a unique morphism
   $\pi:B\to A$ such that
   $$\pi i = 1_A,\qquad i \pi + s p = 1_B.$$
2. If $\pi:B\to A$ satisfies $\pi i = 1_A$, then there is a unique morphism
   $s:C\to B$ such that
   $$p s = 1_C,\qquad i \pi + s p = 1_B.$$

In either case the sequence is split.

A short exact sequence
$$0\to A\xrightarrow{i}B\xrightarrow{p}C\to 0$$
in an abelian category is **split** when there exist morphisms
$$s:C\to B,\qquad \pi:B\to A$$
such that
$$p s = 1_C,\qquad \pi i = 1_A,\qquad i \pi + s p = 1_B.$$

Equivalently, the five-tuple $(B,i,s,\pi,p)$ is the biproduct diagram of $A$
and $C$ in the sense of [[def-biproduct]]. The point of the definition is the
displayed compatible structure, not merely an abstract isomorphism
$B \cong A \oplus C$.

A finite family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ in a category with zero morphisms has a
**biproduct** when both its coproduct and its product exist and the canonical morphism from the
coproduct to the product is an isomorphism
([[def-canonical-morphism-from-a-finite-coproduct-to-a-finite-product]]).

When this happens, either object may be written

$$\bigoplus_{i\in I}A_i,$$

since the canonical comparison identifies them uniquely. For two objects one
writes $A\oplus B$, and for the empty family one speaks of the **empty
biproduct**.

Transporting the product structure across the canonical comparison to the
coproduct object makes that comparison the identity. The resulting common
object, injections, and projections form the associated **biproduct diagram**;
this is the convention used whenever both kinds of structure maps are written
on one displayed object.

In an abelian category, every monomorphism is the kernel of its cokernel, and
dually every epimorphism is the cokernel of its kernel.

derivations.claim: For every $m\ge2$ the map $L:H^{-m}\to H^{-m+2}$ is a monomorphism, because $L^m=L^{m-1}L$ is an isomorphism: if $Lu=0$ then $L^mu=L^{m-1}Lu=0$, hence $u=0$.

For every $r\ge0$ the map $p:=L^{r+1}:H^{-r}\to H^{r+2}$ is an epimorphism and $s:=L(L^{r+2})^{-1}:H^{r+2}\to H^{-r}$ satisfies $ps=1_{H^{r+2}}$, because $pL=L^{r+2}$ is an isomorphism: if $vp=0$ then $vL^{r+2}=vpL=0$, hence $v=0$, and $ps=L^{r+1}L(L^{r+2})^{-1}=L^{r+2}(L^{r+2})^{-1}=1$.

Fix $r\ge0$ and let $i:P^{-r}\to H^{-r}$ be the kernel inclusion of $p=L^{r+1}$. By step 1.2 the map $p$ is an epimorphism, so it is a cokernel of its kernel $i$ by [F2], and the sequence $0\to P^{-r}\xrightarrow{i}H^{-r}\xrightarrow{p}H^{r+2}\to0$ is short exact by [F2]. Since $ps=1$ by step 1.2, the splitting lemma [F3] supplies the unique $\pi:H^{-r}\to P^{-r}$ with $\pi i=1_{P^{-r}}$ and $i\pi+sp=1_{H^{-r}}$, so $(H^{-r},i,s,\pi,p)$ is the biproduct diagram of $P^{-r}$ and $H^{r+2}$. The second inclusion $s$ is a monomorphism with left inverse $p$ and has image $\operatorname{im}(L)$: it is contained there because $s=L(L^{r+2})^{-1}$, and conversely $Lu=s(L^{r+2}u)$ for every $u\in H^{-r-2}$. Write $j:\operatorname{im}(L)\to H^{-r}$ for the image inclusion and $s=j\bar s$ for the corestriction $\bar s:H^{r+2}\to\operatorname{im}(L)$, an isomorphism because $s$ is a monomorphism; then $pj\bar s=ps=1$, so $pj=\bar s^{-1}$. With $e:=sp=L(L^{r+2})^{-1}L^{r+1}$ the identities $\pi i=1$, $ej=s\bar s^{-1}=j$, hence $ej=1_{\operatorname{im}(L)}$ by monicity of $j$, $ei=spi=0$, $\pi j=0$ (compose the identity $i\pi j=(1-sp)j=j-s\bar s^{-1}=0$ with the monomorphism $i$), and $i\pi+je=i\pi+sp=1_{H^{-r}}$ all hold, so $(H^{-r},i,j,\pi,e)$ is the biproduct diagram of the subobjects $P^{-r}$ and $LH^{-r-2}$: the decomposition is $H^{-r}=P^{-r}\oplus LH^{-r-2}$ with second projection $e$ and first projection $\pi=1-e$.

Base of the induction: for $j=0$ the object $H^{-r}$ is the biproduct of $P^{-r}=L^0P^{-r}$ and $L^1H^{-r-2}=LH^{-r-2}$. This is exactly the decomposition of step 2.1, so the assertion holds for $j=0$.

Induction hypothesis: fix $j\ge0$ and assume the assertion for this $j$, that is, $H^{-r}$ is the biproduct of $P^{-r},LP^{-r-2},\dots,L^jP^{-r-2j}$ and $L^{j+1}H^{-r-2j-2}$; we must derive it for $j+1$.

Applying step 2.1 with $r$ replaced by $r+2j+2$ gives the biproduct decomposition $H^{-r-2j-2}=P^{-r-2j-2}\oplus LH^{-r-2j-4}$. The map $L^{j+1}:H^{-r-2j-2}\to H^{-r}$ is a monomorphism, being a composite of the monomorphisms of step 1.1; by [F4] it carries this biproduct diagram to the biproduct diagram of its image, $\operatorname{im}(L^{j+1})=L^{j+1}P^{-r-2j-2}\oplus L^{j+1}(LH^{-r-2j-4})=L^{j+1}P^{-r-2j-2}\oplus L^{j+2}H^{-r-2j-4}$. Substituting this into the biproduct of the induction hypothesis (step 3.2) gives that $H^{-r}$ is the biproduct of $P^{-r},LP^{-r-2},\dots,L^{j+1}P^{-r-2j-2}$ and $L^{j+2}H^{-r-2j-4}$, which is the assertion for $j+1$.

By induction (steps 3.1, 3.2 and 4.1) the biproduct decomposition of step 3.2 holds for every $j\ge0$. Since $H^n=0$ for all sufficiently negative $n$, choose $J$ with $H^{-r-2J-2}=0$; then the tail $L^{J+1}H^{-r-2J-2}$ vanishes, and $H^{-r}$ is the biproduct of $P^{-r},LP^{-r-2},\dots,L^JP^{-r-2J}$, i.e. the finite direct sum decomposition $H^{-r}=\bigoplus_{j\ge0}L^jP^{-r-2j}$ of the Statement. Each restricted power $L^j|_{P^{-r-2j}}$ is a monomorphism, being for $j\ge1$ a composite of the monomorphisms of step 1.1 and for $j=0$ an identity.

Applying the isomorphism $L^r:H^{-r}\to H^r$ to the decomposition of step 5.1 carries the biproduct decomposition of $H^{-r}$ to a biproduct decomposition of $H^r$ with summands $L^r(L^jP^{-r-2j})=L^{r+j}P^{-r-2j}$, giving $H^r=\bigoplus_{j\ge0}L^{r+j}P^{-r-2j}$. Each restricted power $L^{r+j}|_{P^{-r-2j}}=L^r\circ\bigl(L^j|_{P^{-r-2j}}\bigr)$ is a monomorphism, being the composite of an isomorphism with the monomorphism of step 5.1.

Naturality. Let $\varphi_j:H^j\to H'^{\,j}$ be a morphism of graded objects into another such family $(H'^{\,j},L'^{\,j})$ with $L'\varphi_j=\varphi_{j+2}L$ for all $j$. Then $\varphi$ commutes with every iterate: $L'^{\,r}\varphi_{-r}=\varphi_rL^r$, hence $(L'^{\,r+2})^{-1}\varphi_{r+2}=\varphi_{-r-2}(L^{r+2})^{-1}$; consequently $\varphi_{-r}$ carries $P^{-r}=\ker L^{r+1}$ into $P'^{\,-r}=\ker L'^{\,r+1}$, because $L'^{\,r+1}\varphi_{-r}i=\varphi_{r+2}L^{r+1}i=0$ and the kernel inclusion of $L'^{\,r+1}$ has the universal property of [F1]. The comparison $\pi'\varphi_{-r}=\varphi^P\pi$ of the projections holds because both sides become equal after composition with the monomorphism $i'$, where $\varphi^P:P^{-r}\to P'^{\,r}$ is the factorization of $\varphi_{-r}i$ through $i'$; and $\varphi_{-r}s=s'\varphi_{r+2}$ holds by the displayed commutation with the inverses of $L^{r+2},L'^{\,r+2}$. So $\varphi$ preserves the decomposition of step 2.1, and by the same chain of identities at the parameter $r+2j+2$ it maps each summand $L^jP^{-r-2j}$ into $L'^{\,j}P'^{\,-r-2j}$ and intertwines the two finite decompositions of step 5.1; the second decompositions, obtained in step 6.1 from the first by the isomorphisms $L^r,L'^{\,r}$, are intertwined as well.

The base case of step 3.1 and the induction step of step 4.1 establish the hypothesis of step 3.2 for every $j\ge0$, so step 5.1 gives the first displayed decomposition for every $r\ge0$, and steps 6.1 and 7.1 give the second decomposition, the monomorphism clause and naturality; the degenerate cases are included, since a zero object has all its summands zero and every argument above is an identity between finitely many morphisms.

boundaries.evidence: step 5.1 terminates the peeling once $H^{-r-2J-2}=0$, leaving finitely many primitive summands and a vanishing tail; step 8.1 records that a zero object has all its summands zero.
step 8.1: the degenerate cases are included because a zero object has all summands zero and every argument in the proof is an identity between finitely many morphisms.
step 3.1 peels the first summand: $H^{-r}$ is the biproduct of the single primitive piece $P^{-r}$ and the tail $LH^{-r-2}$.
step 5.1 handles the case of a vanishing tail by choosing $J$ with $H^{-r-2J-2}=0$, so the decomposition stops after finitely many displayed summands.
step 3.1 opens the induction at $j=0$ and step 5.1 closes it at the finite $J$; step 4.1 re-peels the tail at the parameter $r+2j+2$.

boundaries.reason: All structure used is supplied by kernels, their universal property and the biproduct components of the splitting lemma, so nothing is selected from a family of sets.
The claim consists of direct sum decompositions, monomorphism clauses and naturality, not of a biconditional, so no forward implication of an equivalence is at issue.
No converse is asserted: the decompositions are constructed from the hypothesis $L^r:H^{-r}\to H^r$ an isomorphism, rather than characterised by it.

citations.quote: Every nilpotent endomorphism $N$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ has an ordered basis that is the concatenation of Jordan strings for $N$ at $0$. For $V=0$, this is the empty basis and the empty family of strings.

Let $H^j$, $j\in\mathbb Z$, be objects of an abelian category, zero for all but finitely many $j$, and let $L^j:H^j\to H^{j+2}$ be morphisms whose iterates give isomorphisms $L^r:H^{-r}\to H^r$ for every $r\ge0$, with $L^0=1_{H^0}$. Put $P^{-r}:=\ker\bigl(L^{r+1}:H^{-r}\to H^{r+2}\bigr)$ for $r\ge0$, and $P^{-r}=0$ for $r<0$. Then for every $r\ge0$ the powers of $L$ induce finite direct sum decompositions
$$H^{-r}=\bigoplus_{j\ge0}L^jP^{-r-2j},\qquad H^{r}=\bigoplus_{j\ge0}L^{r+j}P^{-r-2j},$$
where $L^jP^{-r-2j}$ denotes the image of the restriction of $L^j$ to the subobject $P^{-r-2j}\subseteq H^{-r-2j}$, and likewise for $L^{r+j}P^{-r-2j}$. Each displayed power $L^j$ or $L^{r+j}$ restricts to a monomorphism on its primitive source, and both decompositions are natural for morphisms commuting with $L$. This is a decomposition statement for graded objects in an abelian category; it does not identify primitive objects with classes annihilated by an untruncated map on a derived splitting of a complex.

For every ring $R$, the category $R\text{-}\mathbf{Mod}$ of left $R$-modules is
an abelian category.
If $B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)$ is a basis of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space $V$, then its dual family $B^*=(b_1^*,\ldots,b_n^*)$ is a basis of $V^*$. Consequently $\dim V^*=\dim V=n$.
