citations.quote:
A **rational mixed Hodge structure** consists of a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space $H$
with a finite basis ([[def-linear-basis]]) together with

- a finite increasing filtration $W$ of $H$, the **weight filtration**, and
- a finite decreasing filtration $F$ of
  $H_{\mathbb C}:=H\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$, the **Hodge filtration**
  ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),

such that the following opposition condition holds on every weight-graded
piece. Here a filtration is **finite** when $W_aH=0$ for all sufficiently
negative $a$ and $W_aH=H$ for all sufficiently positive $a$, and dually
$F^aH_{\mathbb C}=H_{\mathbb C}$ for $a\ll0$ and $F^aH_{\mathbb C}=0$ for
$a\gg0$ ([[def-increasing-and-decreasing-filtration-of-an-object]]).

**Conjugation.** The $\mathbb{Q}$-linear involution $\sigma$ of
$H_{\mathbb C}$, defined on generators by
$\sigma(h\otimes z)=h\otimes\bar z$ and extended $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly,
satisfies $\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $\sigma(cz)=\bar c\,\sigma(z)$ for
$c\in\mathbb C$ ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). It preserves the
subspace $W_aH_{\mathbb C}:=(W_aH)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$ for every $a$,
so it descends to each graded piece
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_aH_{\mathbb C}:=W_aH_{\mathbb C}/W_{a-1}H_{\mathbb C}$
([[def-associated-graded-object-of-a-filtered-object]]). The **conjugate
Hodge filtration** is $\bar F^q:=\sigma(F^q)$, a finite decreasing filtration
of $H_{\mathbb C}$.

**Opposition.** Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb C$-vector space with
finite decreasing filtrations $F$ and $\bar F$, and let $n$ be an integer. The
two filtrations are **$n$-opposed** when the natural map
$$\bigoplus_{p+q=n}\bigl(F^pV\cap\bar F^qV\bigr)\longrightarrow V,\qquad (v_{p,q})_{p+q=n}\longmapsto\sum_{p+q=n}v_{p,q},$$
is an isomorphism. Applied to $V=\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ this
condition is required for every $n$, with the *induced* filtrations: $F^p$
acts on $\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ through the image of
$F^p\cap W_nH_{\mathbb C}$, and $\bar F^q$ through the image of
$\bar F^q\cap W_nH_{\mathbb C}$. Writing
$$H^{p,q}_n:=F^p\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}\cap \bar F^q\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C},$$
the requirement is therefore the direct sum decomposition
$$\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}_n \qquad\text{for every }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Since $\sigma$ interchanges the induced filtrations $F^p$ and $\bar F^p$ and
preserves $W$, it maps $H^{p,q}_n$ onto $H^{q,p}_n$, so
$\overline{H^{p,q}_n}=H^{q,p}_n$. Equivalently, the opposition condition requires both
$F^pV\cap\bar F^qV=0$ whenever $p+q>n$ and
$F^pV+\bar F^{n+1-p}V=V$ for every $p$, on
$V=\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$. The conjunction, rather than either
condition alone, is equivalent to the displayed decomposition: the spanning
condition and the modular law give
$F^pV=F^{p+1}V+(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$, and the vanishing condition makes
this sum direct; descending induction through the finite filtration gives
$F^pV=\bigoplus_{a\ge p}(F^aV\cap\bar F^{n-a}V)$ and then the decomposition
of $V$. Conversely, the decomposition gives these two conditions by grouping
its summands by the first and second indices.

**Morphisms.** A morphism $f\colon H\to K$ of rational mixed Hodge structures
is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear map with $f(W_aH)\subseteq W_aK$ for all $a$ and
$f_{\mathbb C}(F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq F^pK_{\mathbb C}$ for all $p$, where
$f_{\mathbb C}=f\otimes\mathrm{id}$. Such an $f$ commutes with the
conjugations $\sigma$, hence also satisfies
$f_{\mathbb C}(\bar F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq\bar F^pK_{\mathbb C}$.

**Substructures, pure structures, Tate.** A subspace $H'\subseteq H$ with the
induced filtrations $W_aH'=H'\cap W_aH$ and
$F^pH'_{\mathbb C}=H'_{\mathbb C}\cap F^pH_{\mathbb C}$ is a **substructure**
when the induced filtrations again satisfy the opposition condition on every
graded piece, and a quotient $H\to Q$ with the quotient filtrations is a
**quotient structure** under the same requirement; that the kernel, image and
cokernel of a morphism do carry such structures is not part of the definition
and is proved in the strictness lemma below. A structure is **pure of weight
$n$** when $W_{n-1}H=0$ and $W_nH=H$; the opposition condition then says that
$H_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}$ with
$H^{p,q}=F^p\cap\bar F^q$, and $\overline{H^{p,q}}=H^{q,p}$. The **Tate
structure** $\mathbb Q(r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, is the pure structure of
weight $-2r$ with $\mathbb Q(r)_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C$ concentrated in type
$(-r,-r)$, that is $H^{-r,-r}=\mathbb C$ and $H^{p,q}=0$ for
$(p,q)\ne(-r,-r)$.

**Tensor and dual conventions.** The tensor product $H\otimes K$ carries
$$W_a(H\otimes K)=\sum_{b+c=a}W_bH\otimes W_cK,\qquad F^p(H\otimes K)_{\mathbb C}=\sum_{b+c=p}F^bH_{\mathbb C}\otimes F^cK_{\mathbb C},$$
where the sums of subspaces are those of the complexifications, and the dual
$H^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(H,\mathbb Q)$ carries
$$W_aH^*=\{u:u(W_{-a-1}H)=0\},\qquad F^pH^*_{\mathbb C}=\{u:u(F^{1-p}H_{\mathbb C})=0\}.$$

**Polarizability.** A pure rational Hodge structure $H$ of weight $n$ is
**polarizable** when it carries a rational bilinear form $Q$ of parity
$(-1)^n$ that pairs only complementary Hodge types, i.e.
$Q(H^{p,q},H^{p',q'})=0$ unless $p'=n-p$ and $q'=n-q$, and whose
Weil-operator Hermitian form $h(u,v):=Q(Cu,\bar v)$, where the Weil operator
$C$ acts as $i^{p-q}$ on $H^{p,q}$, is positive definite.

No mixed structure in this definition is assumed to split over $\mathbb R$ or
over $\mathbb Q$; the Deligne splitting constructed below is a decomposition
over $\mathbb C$ only.

For an increasing filtration, the **associated graded object** is the indexed family
$$\operatorname{gr}^F_pA=\operatorname{coker}(F_{p-1}A\hookrightarrow F_pA)=F_pA/F_{p-1}A\quad(p\in\mathbb Z).$$
For a decreasing filtration it is $\operatorname{gr}^p_FA=F^pA/F^{p+1}A$. Here the inclusions come from [[def-increasing-and-decreasing-filtration-of-an-object]], and quotient means [[def-the-quotient-of-an-object-by-a-subobject]]. This definition uses a family; it assumes no infinite direct sum. With $F^p=F_{-p}$, the decreasing piece at $p$ is the increasing piece at $-p$.

A **rational mixed Hodge structure** consists of a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space $H$
with a finite basis ([[def-linear-basis]]) together with

- a finite increasing filtration $W$ of $H$, the **weight filtration**, and
- a finite decreasing filtration $F$ of
  $H_{\mathbb C}:=H\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$, the **Hodge filtration**
  ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),

such that the following opposition condition holds on every weight-graded
piece. Here a filtration is **finite** when $W_aH=0$ for all sufficiently
negative $a$ and $W_aH=H$ for all sufficiently positive $a$, and dually
$F^aH_{\mathbb C}=H_{\mathbb C}$ for $a\ll0$ and $F^aH_{\mathbb C}=0$ for
$a\gg0$ ([[def-increasing-and-decreasing-filtration-of-an-object]]).

**Conjugation.** The $\mathbb{Q}$-linear involution $\sigma$ of
$H_{\mathbb C}$, defined on generators by
$\sigma(h\otimes z)=h\otimes\bar z$ and extended $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly,
satisfies $\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $\sigma(cz)=\bar c\,\sigma(z)$ for
$c\in\mathbb C$ ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). It preserves the
subspace $W_aH_{\mathbb C}:=(W_aH)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$ for every $a$,
so it descends to each graded piece
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_aH_{\mathbb C}:=W_aH_{\mathbb C}/W_{a-1}H_{\mathbb C}$
([[def-associated-graded-object-of-a-filtered-object]]). The **conjugate
Hodge filtration** is $\bar F^q:=\sigma(F^q)$, a finite decreasing filtration
of $H_{\mathbb C}$.

**Opposition.** Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb C$-vector space with
finite decreasing filtrations $F$ and $\bar F$, and let $n$ be an integer. The
two filtrations are **$n$-opposed** when the natural map
$$\bigoplus_{p+q=n}\bigl(F^pV\cap\bar F^qV\bigr)\longrightarrow V,\qquad (v_{p,q})_{p+q=n}\longmapsto\sum_{p+q=n}v_{p,q},$$
is an isomorphism. Applied to $V=\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ this
condition is required for every $n$, with the *induced* filtrations: $F^p$
acts on $\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ through the image of
$F^p\cap W_nH_{\mathbb C}$, and $\bar F^q$ through the image of
$\bar F^q\cap W_nH_{\mathbb C}$. Writing
$$H^{p,q}_n:=F^p\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}\cap \bar F^q\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C},$$
the requirement is therefore the direct sum decomposition
$$\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}_n \qquad\text{for every }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Since $\sigma$ interchanges the induced filtrations $F^p$ and $\bar F^p$ and
preserves $W$, it maps $H^{p,q}_n$ onto $H^{q,p}_n$, so
$\overline{H^{p,q}_n}=H^{q,p}_n$. Equivalently, the opposition condition requires both
$F^pV\cap\bar F^qV=0$ whenever $p+q>n$ and
$F^pV+\bar F^{n+1-p}V=V$ for every $p$, on
$V=\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$. The conjunction, rather than either
condition alone, is equivalent to the displayed decomposition: the spanning
condition and the modular law give
$F^pV=F^{p+1}V+(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$, and the vanishing condition makes
this sum direct; descending induction through the finite filtration gives
$F^pV=\bigoplus_{a\ge p}(F^aV\cap\bar F^{n-a}V)$ and then the decomposition
of $V$. Conversely, the decomposition gives these two conditions by grouping
its summands by the first and second indices.

**Morphisms.** A morphism $f\colon H\to K$ of rational mixed Hodge structures
is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear map with $f(W_aH)\subseteq W_aK$ for all $a$ and
$f_{\mathbb C}(F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq F^pK_{\mathbb C}$ for all $p$, where
$f_{\mathbb C}=f\otimes\mathrm{id}$. Such an $f$ commutes with the
conjugations $\sigma$, hence also satisfies
$f_{\mathbb C}(\bar F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq\bar F^pK_{\mathbb C}$.

**Substructures, pure structures, Tate.** A subspace $H'\subseteq H$ with the
induced filtrations $W_aH'=H'\cap W_aH$ and
$F^pH'_{\mathbb C}=H'_{\mathbb C}\cap F^pH_{\mathbb C}$ is a **substructure**
when the induced filtrations again satisfy the opposition condition on every
graded piece, and a quotient $H\to Q$ with the quotient filtrations is a
**quotient structure** under the same requirement; that the kernel, image and
cokernel of a morphism do carry such structures is not part of the definition
and is proved in the strictness lemma below. A structure is **pure of weight
$n$** when $W_{n-1}H=0$ and $W_nH=H$; the opposition condition then says that
$H_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}$ with
$H^{p,q}=F^p\cap\bar F^q$, and $\overline{H^{p,q}}=H^{q,p}$. The **Tate
structure** $\mathbb Q(r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, is the pure structure of
weight $-2r$ with $\mathbb Q(r)_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C$ concentrated in type
$(-r,-r)$, that is $H^{-r,-r}=\mathbb C$ and $H^{p,q}=0$ for
$(p,q)\ne(-r,-r)$.

**Tensor and dual conventions.** The tensor product $H\otimes K$ carries
$$W_a(H\otimes K)=\sum_{b+c=a}W_bH\otimes W_cK,\qquad F^p(H\otimes K)_{\mathbb C}=\sum_{b+c=p}F^bH_{\mathbb C}\otimes F^cK_{\mathbb C},$$
where the sums of subspaces are those of the complexifications, and the dual
$H^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(H,\mathbb Q)$ carries
$$W_aH^*=\{u:u(W_{-a-1}H)=0\},\qquad F^pH^*_{\mathbb C}=\{u:u(F^{1-p}H_{\mathbb C})=0\}.$$

**Polarizability.** A pure rational Hodge structure $H$ of weight $n$ is
**polarizable** when it carries a rational bilinear form $Q$ of parity
$(-1)^n$ that pairs only complementary Hodge types, i.e.
$Q(H^{p,q},H^{p',q'})=0$ unless $p'=n-p$ and $q'=n-q$, and whose
Weil-operator Hermitian form $h(u,v):=Q(Cu,\bar v)$, where the Weil operator
$C$ acts as $i^{p-q}$ on $H^{p,q}$, is positive definite.

No mixed structure in this definition is assumed to split over $\mathbb R$ or
over $\mathbb Q$; the Deligne splitting constructed below is a decomposition
over $\mathbb C$ only.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $U$ be a finite family of linear subspaces $U_i$ of
$V$ indexed by $i < n$ ([[def-linear-subspace]],
[[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]]); as everywhere on this page the index runs over
the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]).

**The sum of the other summands.** The set $\{0_V\}$ is a linear subspace of $V$:
it contains $0_V$, it is closed under addition since $0_V + 0_V = 0_V$, and it is
closed under scalar multiplication since $\lambda 0_V = 0_V$
([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]). So for each $j < n$ the family
$U^{(j)}$ defined by

$$U^{(j)}_i := U_i \quad (i \ne j), \qquad U^{(j)}_j := \{0_V\}$$

is again a finite family of linear subspaces of $V$ indexed by $i < n$, and we
write

$$\sum_{i \ne j} U_i \;:=\; \sum_{i<n} U^{(j)}_i ,$$

a linear subspace of $V$ by [[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]]. Replacing the
$j$-th summand by $\{0_V\}$, rather than re-indexing over a smaller set, keeps
every family on this page indexed by a natural number.

**The definition.** $V$ is the **internal direct sum** of the family $U$, written

$$V \;=\; \bigoplus_{i<n} U_i ,$$

when both of the following hold:

- **(D1)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i<n} U_i = V$;
- **(D2)** for every $j < n$,
  $\displaystyle U_j \cap \sum_{i \ne j} U_i = \{0_V\}$.

In (D2) the inclusion $\supseteq$ is automatic, since $U_j$ and
$\sum_{i \ne j} U_i$ are linear subspaces and each therefore contains $0_V$; the
content of (D2) is the inclusion $\subseteq$, that no nonzero vector of $U_j$ is
a sum of vectors drawn from the other summands.

### Two summands

Take $n = 2$ and write $U := U_0$, $W := U_1$. For $j = 0$ the family $U^{(0)}$ is
$\{0_V\}, W$, so $\sum_{i \ne 0} U_i = \{\, 0_V + w : w \in W \,\} = W$; for
$j = 1$ it is $U$ in the same way. So (D2) reduces to the single condition
$U \cap W = \{0_V\}$, and

$$V = U \oplus W \quad\text{means}\quad U + W = V \ \text{ and } \ U \cap W = \{0_V\}.$$

For two summands, therefore, (D2) and the pairwise condition coincide; this is
the familiar form of the definition.

### Three or more summands: (D2) is not the pairwise condition

For $n \ge 3$ the condition (D2) is **strictly stronger** than requiring
$U_i \cap U_j = \{0_V\}$ for all $i \ne j$.

That (D2) implies the pairwise condition is immediate: for $i \ne j$ with
$i, j < n$ we have $U_i = U^{(j)}_i \subseteq \sum_{i \ne j} U_i$, since a sum of
a family contains each of its summands ([[lem-sum-is-span-of-union]]), so
$U_j \cap U_i \subseteq U_j \cap \sum_{i \ne j} U_i = \{0_V\}$, and the reverse
inclusion holds because both are linear subspaces.

The converse fails, and it fails already for three summands: a family can satisfy
(D1) and have all its pairwise intersections trivial while (D2) is false, so that
decompositions are not unique. The companion examples page records a witness. A
definition stated with the pairwise condition in place of (D2) would therefore be
a different, and weaker, notion, and the characterisation by unique decomposition
([[lem-direct-sum-criterion]]) would be false for it.

### The empty family

$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, so $n = 0$ is a genuine case. Then
$\sum_{i<0} U_i = \{0_V\}$ ([[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]]) and (D2) is vacuous,
there being no $j < 0$. So $V = \bigoplus_{i<0} U_i$ holds exactly when
$V = \{0_V\}$: the zero space is the direct sum of the empty family, and no other
space is.

derivations.claim: (Two-filtration lemma, spanning and partial sums.) Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb C$-vector space with finite decreasing filtrations $F$ and $\bar F$ such that $V=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}(F^pV\cap\bar F^qV)$ for an integer $n$. Then (i) $F^aV+\bar F^{n+1-a}V=V$ for every $a$, and (ii) $F^aV=\bigoplus_{p\ge a}(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$, with the conjugate formula $\bar F^bV=\bigoplus_{q\ge b}(F^{n-q}V\cap\bar F^qV)$. For (i), write $v=\sum_{p+q=n}v_{p,q}$; the terms with $p\ge a$ sum into $F^aV$, and each remaining term has $p<a$, hence $q=n-p>n-a$, that is $q\ge n+1-a$, so their sum lies in $\bar F^{n+1-a}V$. For (ii), prove $F^aV\subseteq\sum_{p\ge a}(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$ by descending induction on $a$: the claim is trivial when $F^aV=0$, and otherwise (i) with $a+1$ gives $V=F^{a+1}V+\bar F^{n-a}V$, so the modular law applied to $F^{a+1}V\subseteq F^aV\subseteq V$ yields $F^aV=F^{a+1}V+(F^aV\cap\bar F^{n-a}V)$, in which the induction hypothesis places $F^{a+1}V$ inside $\sum_{p\ge a+1}(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$ while $F^aV\cap\bar F^{n-a}V$ is the term with $p=a$; the reverse inclusion is clear, and the sum is direct because the pieces $F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V$ are independent by the decomposition hypothesis, which is symmetric in the two filtrations, so the same argument with $F$ and $\bar F$ interchanged gives the formula for $\bar F^bV$.

(Two-filtration lemma, vanishing.) Under the hypothesis of step 1.1, $F^aV\cap\bar F^bV=0$ whenever $a+b>n$. Indeed, let $x\in F^aV\cap\bar F^bV$ and let $x=\sum_{p+q=n}x_{p,q}$ be its unique decomposition with $x_{p,q}\in F^pV\cap\bar F^qV$. Since $x\in F^aV$, its decomposition lies in $\bigoplus_{p\ge a}(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$ by step 1.1 (ii), so $x_{p,n-p}=0$ for every $p<a$; since $x\in\bar F^bV$, the conjugate half of step 1.1 (ii) gives $x_{n-q,q}=0$ for every $q<b$. If $x\ne0$, some $x_{p,n-p}$ is nonzero, and it satisfies $p\ge a$ and $n-p\ge b$, whence $n=p+(n-p)\ge a+b>n$, a contradiction; so $x=0$.

(Lifting.) Let $m=p+q$. Every $d\in W_{m-1}$ can be written as $d=z+g$ with $z\in F^p\cap W_{m-1}$ and $g\in(\bar F^q\cap W_{m-1})+\sum_{j\ge1}(\bar F^{q-j}\cap W_{m-j-1})$. To see this, construct elements $d_1,d_2,\dots$ and vectors $f_j,g_j$ as follows. Put $d_1=d$, and suppose $d_j\in W_{m-j}$ has been constructed for some $j\ge1$. By [F1] the induced filtrations on $\operatorname{Gr}^W_{m-j}$ are $(m-j)$-opposed, and step 1.1 (i) applied there with the pair $(p,q-j+1)$, whose indices sum to $m-j+1$, shows that the images of $F^p\cap W_{m-j}$ and $\bar F^{q-j+1}\cap W_{m-j}$ generate $\operatorname{Gr}^W_{m-j}$; choose $f_j\in F^p\cap W_{m-j}$ and $g_j\in\bar F^{q-j+1}\cap W_{m-j}$ whose classes sum to the class of $d_j$, and put $d_{j+1}:=d_j-f_j-g_j\in W_{m-j-1}$. By [F2] there is $J$ with $W_{m-J}=0$; the recursion stops there, and summing the identities $d_{j+1}=d_j-f_j-g_j$ gives $d=\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}(f_j+g_j)$. Each $f_j$ lies in $F^p\cap W_{m-j}\subseteq F^p\cap W_{m-1}$; $g_1$ lies in $\bar F^q\cap W_{m-1}$ and, for $j\ge2$, $g_j$ lies in $\bar F^{q-(j-1)}\cap W_{m-(j-1)-1}$. Hence $z:=\sum_jf_j$ and $g:=\sum_jg_j$ have the required properties.

(Surjectivity onto the graded summand.) Let $\xi\in H^{p,q}_m$. Since $H^{p,q}_m\subseteq F^p\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$ is the image of $F^p\cap W_m$, choose $x_0\in F^p\cap W_m$ representing $\xi$; since $H^{p,q}_m\subseteq\bar F^q\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$ is the image of $\bar F^q\cap W_m$, choose $y_0\in\bar F^q\cap W_m$ also representing $\xi$. Then $d:=x_0-y_0$ lies in $W_{m-1}$, so step 2.2 gives $d=z+g$ with $z\in F^p\cap W_{m-1}$ and $g$ in the displayed sum. Put $x:=x_0-z=y_0+g$. Then $x\in F^p\cap W_m$, and $x\in(\bar F^q\cap W_m)+\sum_{j\ge1}(\bar F^{q-j}\cap W_{m-j-1})$ because $y_0$ lies in the first summand and $g$ in the sum; so $x\in I^{p,q}$. Finally $x-x_0=-z\in W_{m-1}$, so $x$ and $x_0$ have the same class $\xi$ in $\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$. Hence the projection maps $I^{p,q}$ onto $H^{p,q}_m$, and $I^{p,q}\subseteq W_m\cap F^p$ holds by definition.

(Injectivity modulo the lower weight.) Suppose $0\ne x\in I^{p,q}\cap W_{m-1}$, and choose its least weight index $r$, so $x\in W_r\setminus W_{r-1}$ and $r<m$. Write $x=y+\sum_{j\ge1}g_j$ as in the defining formula, with $y\in\bar F^q\cap W_m$ and $g_j\in\bar F^{q-j}\cap W_{m-j-1}$; only finitely many terms are needed because $W$ is finite. Put $J=m-r-1\ge0$. The sum $\sum_{j>J}g_j$ lies in $W_{r-1}$, while $h:=y+\sum_{1\le j\le J}g_j$ lies in $\bar F^{q-J}$ and also in $W_r$, because $h=x-\sum_{j>J}g_j$. Thus the nonzero class of $x$ in $\operatorname{Gr}^W_r$ belongs to $F^p\operatorname{Gr}^W_r\cap\bar F^{q-J}\operatorname{Gr}^W_r$. But $p+q-J=r+1>r$, so step 2.1 makes that intersection zero, a contradiction. Together with step 3.1 this proves the projection isomorphism in (a).

(The weight decomposition and the direct-sum identity.) For every $m$ the projection restricts to an isomorphism $\bigoplus_{p+q=m}I^{p,q}\to\operatorname{Gr}^W_mH_{\mathbb C}$: by steps 3.1 and 4.1 each $I^{p,q}$ maps isomorphically onto $H^{p,q}_m$, and by [F1] the summands $H^{p,q}_m$ are independent with sum $\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$. In particular $\dim I^{p,q}=\dim H^{p,q}_m$, so $\sum_{p+q=m}\dim I^{p,q}=\dim\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$ for every $m$. The sum map $\psi_m\colon\bigoplus_{p+q\le m}I^{p,q}\to W_m$ is injective: if a finite sum $\sum_{m'\le m}\sum_{p+q=m'}x_{p,q}$ vanishes, its class in $\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$ is the sum of the classes of the top pieces $x_{p,m-p}$, which vanishes only if each of those pieces is zero because the restricted projection is an isomorphism; subtracting them leaves a vanishing sum over $m'\le m-1$, and induction on $m$ (with $W_m=0$ for all sufficiently negative $m$) finishes the argument. Its image therefore has dimension $\sum_{m'\le m}\dim\operatorname{Gr}^W_{m'}=\dim W_m$, the finite telescoping identity for the finite filtration $W$; an injective map between spaces of equal dimension is an isomorphism, so $W_mH_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q\le m}I^{p,q}$. Taking $m$ large gives $H_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p,q}I^{p,q}$.

(Conjugation modulo lower weights.) Work in $U=W_m/W_{m-2}$ with the images of $F^p\cap W_m$ and $\bar F^q\cap W_m$. Their intersection $T$ maps injectively to $\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$: its intersection with $W_{m-1}/W_{m-2}$ is $F^p\operatorname{Gr}^W_{m-1}\cap\bar F^q\operatorname{Gr}^W_{m-1}=0$ by step 2.1, since $p+q=m>m-1$. The formula for $I^{p,q}$ shows its image in $U$ lies in $T$, since every tail term has weight at most $m-2$. Step 3.1 shows this image maps onto $H^{p,q}_m$; the image of $T$ also lies in $H^{p,q}_m$, so injectivity makes the image of $I^{p,q}$ exactly $T$. Conjugating the same argument for $I^{q,p}$ shows that $\sigma(I^{q,p})$ has this same image $T$ in $U$. Therefore $I^{p,q}+W_{m-2}=\sigma(I^{q,p})+W_{m-2}$.

(The Hodge decomposition.) For all $a,m$ one has $F^a\cap W_m=\bigoplus_{p\ge a,\ p+q\le m}I^{p,q}$. Indeed, decompose $x\in F^a\cap W_m$ by step 5.1. Its class in $\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$ lies in $\bigoplus_{p\ge a}H^{p,m-p}_m$ by step 1.1, so its top components with $p<a$ vanish by the projection isomorphism. Subtracting the remaining top components leaves an element of $F^a\cap W_{m-1}$, and induction through the finite $W$ proves the assertion. Taking $m$ large proves $F^a=\bigoplus_{p\ge a}I^{p,q}$. Conjugating this identity gives $\bar F^b=\bigoplus_{q\ge b}\sigma(I^{q,p})$; it does not assert a decomposition of $\bar F$ by the original $I^{p,q}$.

(Functoriality.) Let $f\colon H\to K$ be a morphism of rational mixed Hodge structures. Since $f$ is defined over $\mathbb Q$, $f_{\mathbb C}$ commutes with the conjugations, so $f_{\mathbb C}(\bar F^qH_{\mathbb C})=\overline{f_{\mathbb C}(F^qH_{\mathbb C})}\subseteq\bar F^qK_{\mathbb C}$; it also satisfies $f_{\mathbb C}(F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq F^pK_{\mathbb C}$ and $f_{\mathbb C}(W_aH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq W_aK_{\mathbb C}$ by definition. Applying $f_{\mathbb C}$ to the two intersections and the sum defining $I^{p,q}(H)$ therefore produces an element of the corresponding intersection of $F^pK_{\mathbb C}$ with the sum of the $\bar F$-terms for $K$, and $W$-membership is preserved term by term; hence $f_{\mathbb C}(I^{p,q}(H))\subseteq I^{p,q}(K)$.

citations.quote:
Let $(H,W,F)$ be a rational mixed Hodge structure
([[def-rational-mixed-hodge-structure]]) with complex conjugation $\sigma$ on
$H_{\mathbb C}=H\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$, and write
$\bar F^a=\sigma(F^a)$ for the conjugate Hodge filtration; all weight spaces
below are the complexifications $W_aH_{\mathbb C}$. For integers $p,q$ put
$m=p+q$ and
$$I^{p,q}=\bigl(F^p\cap W_m\bigr)\cap\Bigl(\bigl(\bar F^q\cap W_m\bigr)+\sum_{j\ge1}\bigl(\bar F^{q-j}\cap W_{m-j-1}\bigr)\Bigr),$$
the intersections and the sum taken in $H_{\mathbb C}$. Then:

(a) $I^{p,q}\subseteq W_m\cap F^p$, the intersection $I^{p,q}\cap W_{m-1}$ is
zero, and the projection $W_m\to\operatorname{Gr}^W_mH_{\mathbb C}$ maps
$I^{p,q}$ isomorphically onto the summand $H^{p,q}_m$ of the mixed Hodge
definition;

(b) $W_mH_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q\le m}I^{p,q}$,
$F^aH_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p\ge a}I^{p,q}$ for all integers $a,m$; in
particular $H_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p,q}I^{p,q}$;

(c) every morphism $f\colon H\to K$ of rational mixed Hodge structures
satisfies $f_{\mathbb C}(I^{p,q}(H))\subseteq I^{p,q}(K)$.

The construction satisfies
$I^{p,q}+W_{m-2}=\sigma(I^{q,p})+W_{m-2}$ inside $W_m$.
It need not satisfy $\sigma(I^{p,q})=I^{q,p}$, and the same splitting need
not split $\bar F$: its conjugate gives
$\bar F^bH_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{q\ge b}\sigma(I^{q,p})$. The splitting is
the one pinned down in the sources by the displayed formula, not an arbitrary
direct-sum decomposition.

A **rational mixed Hodge structure** consists of a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space $H$
with a finite basis ([[def-linear-basis]]) together with

- a finite increasing filtration $W$ of $H$, the **weight filtration**, and
- a finite decreasing filtration $F$ of
  $H_{\mathbb C}:=H\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$, the **Hodge filtration**
  ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),

such that the following opposition condition holds on every weight-graded
piece. Here a filtration is **finite** when $W_aH=0$ for all sufficiently
negative $a$ and $W_aH=H$ for all sufficiently positive $a$, and dually
$F^aH_{\mathbb C}=H_{\mathbb C}$ for $a\ll0$ and $F^aH_{\mathbb C}=0$ for
$a\gg0$ ([[def-increasing-and-decreasing-filtration-of-an-object]]).

**Conjugation.** The $\mathbb{Q}$-linear involution $\sigma$ of
$H_{\mathbb C}$, defined on generators by
$\sigma(h\otimes z)=h\otimes\bar z$ and extended $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly,
satisfies $\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $\sigma(cz)=\bar c\,\sigma(z)$ for
$c\in\mathbb C$ ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). It preserves the
subspace $W_aH_{\mathbb C}:=(W_aH)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$ for every $a$,
so it descends to each graded piece
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_aH_{\mathbb C}:=W_aH_{\mathbb C}/W_{a-1}H_{\mathbb C}$
([[def-associated-graded-object-of-a-filtered-object]]). The **conjugate
Hodge filtration** is $\bar F^q:=\sigma(F^q)$, a finite decreasing filtration
of $H_{\mathbb C}$.

**Opposition.** Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb C$-vector space with
finite decreasing filtrations $F$ and $\bar F$, and let $n$ be an integer. The
two filtrations are **$n$-opposed** when the natural map
$$\bigoplus_{p+q=n}\bigl(F^pV\cap\bar F^qV\bigr)\longrightarrow V,\qquad (v_{p,q})_{p+q=n}\longmapsto\sum_{p+q=n}v_{p,q},$$
is an isomorphism. Applied to $V=\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ this
condition is required for every $n$, with the *induced* filtrations: $F^p$
acts on $\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ through the image of
$F^p\cap W_nH_{\mathbb C}$, and $\bar F^q$ through the image of
$\bar F^q\cap W_nH_{\mathbb C}$. Writing
$$H^{p,q}_n:=F^p\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}\cap \bar F^q\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C},$$
the requirement is therefore the direct sum decomposition
$$\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}_n \qquad\text{for every }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Since $\sigma$ interchanges the induced filtrations $F^p$ and $\bar F^p$ and
preserves $W$, it maps $H^{p,q}_n$ onto $H^{q,p}_n$, so
$\overline{H^{p,q}_n}=H^{q,p}_n$. Equivalently, the opposition condition requires both
$F^pV\cap\bar F^qV=0$ whenever $p+q>n$ and
$F^pV+\bar F^{n+1-p}V=V$ for every $p$, on
$V=\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$. The conjunction, rather than either
condition alone, is equivalent to the displayed decomposition: the spanning
condition and the modular law give
$F^pV=F^{p+1}V+(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$, and the vanishing condition makes
this sum direct; descending induction through the finite filtration gives
$F^pV=\bigoplus_{a\ge p}(F^aV\cap\bar F^{n-a}V)$ and then the decomposition
of $V$. Conversely, the decomposition gives these two conditions by grouping
its summands by the first and second indices.

**Morphisms.** A morphism $f\colon H\to K$ of rational mixed Hodge structures
is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear map with $f(W_aH)\subseteq W_aK$ for all $a$ and
$f_{\mathbb C}(F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq F^pK_{\mathbb C}$ for all $p$, where
$f_{\mathbb C}=f\otimes\mathrm{id}$. Such an $f$ commutes with the
conjugations $\sigma$, hence also satisfies
$f_{\mathbb C}(\bar F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq\bar F^pK_{\mathbb C}$.

**Substructures, pure structures, Tate.** A subspace $H'\subseteq H$ with the
induced filtrations $W_aH'=H'\cap W_aH$ and
$F^pH'_{\mathbb C}=H'_{\mathbb C}\cap F^pH_{\mathbb C}$ is a **substructure**
when the induced filtrations again satisfy the opposition condition on every
graded piece, and a quotient $H\to Q$ with the quotient filtrations is a
**quotient structure** under the same requirement; that the kernel, image and
cokernel of a morphism do carry such structures is not part of the definition
and is proved in the strictness lemma below. A structure is **pure of weight
$n$** when $W_{n-1}H=0$ and $W_nH=H$; the opposition condition then says that
$H_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}$ with
$H^{p,q}=F^p\cap\bar F^q$, and $\overline{H^{p,q}}=H^{q,p}$. The **Tate
structure** $\mathbb Q(r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, is the pure structure of
weight $-2r$ with $\mathbb Q(r)_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C$ concentrated in type
$(-r,-r)$, that is $H^{-r,-r}=\mathbb C$ and $H^{p,q}=0$ for
$(p,q)\ne(-r,-r)$.

**Tensor and dual conventions.** The tensor product $H\otimes K$ carries
$$W_a(H\otimes K)=\sum_{b+c=a}W_bH\otimes W_cK,\qquad F^p(H\otimes K)_{\mathbb C}=\sum_{b+c=p}F^bH_{\mathbb C}\otimes F^cK_{\mathbb C},$$
where the sums of subspaces are those of the complexifications, and the dual
$H^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(H,\mathbb Q)$ carries
$$W_aH^*=\{u:u(W_{-a-1}H)=0\},\qquad F^pH^*_{\mathbb C}=\{u:u(F^{1-p}H_{\mathbb C})=0\}.$$

**Polarizability.** A pure rational Hodge structure $H$ of weight $n$ is
**polarizable** when it carries a rational bilinear form $Q$ of parity
$(-1)^n$ that pairs only complementary Hodge types, i.e.
$Q(H^{p,q},H^{p',q'})=0$ unless $p'=n-p$ and $q'=n-q$, and whose
Weil-operator Hermitian form $h(u,v):=Q(Cu,\bar v)$, where the Weil operator
$C$ acts as $i^{p-q}$ on $H^{p,q}$, is positive definite.

No mixed structure in this definition is assumed to split over $\mathbb R$ or
over $\mathbb Q$; the Deligne splitting constructed below is a decomposition
over $\mathbb C$ only.

derivations.claim: (Weight strictness.) Let $y=f(x)\in f(H)\cap W_nK$ and decompose $x=\sum_{p,q}x^{p,q}$ along the splitting of $H_{\mathbb C}$; then $y=\sum_{p,q}f_{\mathbb C}(x^{p,q})$ with $f_{\mathbb C}(x^{p,q})\in I^{p,q}(K)$ by [F1]. Since $y\in W_nK=\bigoplus_{p+q\le n}I^{p,q}(K)$ and the sum is direct, all components with $p+q>n$ vanish: $f_{\mathbb C}(x^{p,q})=0$ whenever $p+q>n$. Hence $x':=\sum_{p+q\le n}x^{p,q}$ lies in $W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ and satisfies $f_{\mathbb C}(x')=y$, so $y\in f_{\mathbb C}(W_nH_{\mathbb C})$. The reverse inclusion $f(W_nH)\subseteq f(H)\cap W_nK$ is the preservation of $W$ by $f$.

(Hodge strictness.) The same computation with the condition $p<a$ instead of $p+q>n$: if $y=f_{\mathbb C}(x)\in f(H_{\mathbb C})\cap F^aK_{\mathbb C}$, decompose $x$ and use $F^aK_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p\ge a}I^{p,q}(K)$ to conclude that $f_{\mathbb C}(x^{p,q})=0$ for $p<a$, so $x'=\sum_{p\ge a}x^{p,q}$ lies in $F^aH_{\mathbb C}$ and maps to $y$.

(Rational descent.) Step 1.1 gives equality of the complexifications of the rational subspaces $A=f(W_nH)$ and $B=f(H)\cap W_nK$. Images and intersections commute with extension from $\mathbb Q$ to $\mathbb C$: in finite rational coordinates they are kernels or images of matrices, whose rank is unchanged on extension since the same nonzero rational minors remain nonzero. To descend $A_{\mathbb C}=B_{\mathbb C}$, map $A$ into the rational quotient $K/B$. Its complexification is zero, hence the rational map is zero (a nonzero rational coordinate remains nonzero over $\mathbb C$), so $A\subseteq B$; interchanging them gives equality. Together with step 1.2 this proves the stated rational $W$ strictness and complex $F$ strictness. Complex conjugation fixes the real scalar extension of a rational space and is not used to recover rational vectors.

(Exactness of $\operatorname{Gr}^W_n$.) Let $0\to A\xrightarrow{i}B\xrightarrow{p}C\to 0$ be a short exact sequence of mixed Hodge structures. By [F1] the splitting identifies $\operatorname{Gr}^W_nA$, $\operatorname{Gr}^W_nB$, $\operatorname{Gr}^W_nC$ with $\bigoplus_{p+q=n}I^{p,q}(A)$ and its analogues, and the maps $\operatorname{Gr}^W_n i$, $\operatorname{Gr}^W_n p$ with the direct sums of the maps induced by $i$ and $p$ between the pieces $I^{p,q}$. Each piecewise sequence $0\to I^{p,q}(A)\to I^{p,q}(B)\to I^{p,q}(C)\to 0$ is exact: the middle arrows are the restrictions of the injective $i$ and of the surjective $p$, and an element $b\in I^{p,q}(B)$ lies in $\ker p$ precisely when $b=i(a)$ for some $a\in A$, and decomposing $a$ into its $I$-pieces shows that all other pieces map to zero; since $i$ is injective, they vanish and $a\in I^{p,q}(A)$. A direct sum of short exact sequences is short exact, so $0\to\operatorname{Gr}^W_nA\to\operatorname{Gr}^W_nB\to\operatorname{Gr}^W_nC\to0$ is exact; a morphism is strict for $W$ precisely when it induces such exact sequences, so this recovers step 1.1 independently.

(Kernel, image and cokernel.) The functorial splitting [F1] makes $f_{\mathbb C}$ a direct sum of maps $I^{p,q}(H)\to I^{p,q}(K)$. Thus its kernel, image and cokernel decompose into the respective kernels, images and cokernels of these maps, and their induced or quotient $W$ and $F$ are the partial sums by $p+q\le n$ and $p\ge a$. The projection isomorphisms in [F1] identify their weight-$n$ pieces, with these induced $F$ filtrations, with the kernel, image and cokernel of $\operatorname{Gr}^W_n f$, computed componentwise in the pure decompositions $H^{p,q}_n,K^{p,q}_n$. These identifications are the canonical rational graded maps: for a kernel this follows from $W$ strictness, since if $f(x)\in W_{n-1}K$ with $x\in W_nH$, choose $y\in W_{n-1}H$ with $f(y)=f(x)$ and replace $x$ by $x-y$; the image and cokernel follow by the same induced/quotient description. The graded rational map commutes with conjugation and preserves $F$, hence also $\bar F$; between equal-weight pure structures it preserves each type $F^p\cap\bar F^q$ with $p+q=n$. Consequently its pure kernels, images and cokernels have conjugation exchanging their $(p,q)$ and $(q,p)$ pieces. Their $F$ partial sums and their conjugates are therefore $n$-opposed. Every weight-graded piece of the three rational filtered spaces satisfies the mixed Hodge axiom, proving the claim. This argument requires no exact conjugate decomposition on the mixed vector space.

(Pure image.) Now suppose $W_{n-1}H=0$ and $W_nK=K$. By step 3.1 the image is a mixed Hodge structure with the induced filtration, and step 1.1 gives $W_{n-1}(\operatorname{im}f)=f(W_{n-1}H)=0$ and $W_n(\operatorname{im}f)=f(H)\cap W_nK=f(H)=\operatorname{im}f$; hence the image is pure of weight $n$.

boundaries.evidence: The zero map has $\ker f=H$, $\operatorname{im}f=0$ and $\operatorname{coker}f=K$, for which the equalities of steps 1.1 and 2.1 read $0=0$.
The zero vector lies on both sides of each displayed equality, and step 2.1 shows the equalities of subspaces descend from the complexification.
Steps 1.1 and 1.2 apply to a single-weight structure as well as mixed structures.
Step 4.1 handles the pure-image weight bounds W_{n-1}H=0 and W_nK=K, including zero image.
The equalities are proved for all integers $n,p$ in steps 1.1, 1.2 and 2.1, including endpoint levels where one side is zero or all of the space.

citations.quote:
Let K be a cochain complex with decreasing filtration by subcomplexes. Set $C_n=K^{-n}$, $F_pC_n=F^{-p}K^{-n}$ and $d_n=d_K^{-n}$. Then
$$E_r^{p,q}(K)=E^r_{-p,-q}(C),\qquad d_r:E_r^{p,q}\to E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}.$$
The construction gives $E_0^{p,q}=\operatorname{gr}^p K^{p+q}$ and $E_1^{p,q}\cong H^{p+q}(\operatorname{gr}^p K)$. With degreewise finite filtration it naturally abuts to the decreasing image filtration on $H^{p+q}(K)$, with $E_\infty^{p,q}\cong\operatorname{gr}^pH^{p+q}(K)$.

Every morphism $f\colon H\to K$ of rational mixed Hodge structures is strict for
$W$ and for $F$:
$$f(W_nH)=f(H)\cap W_nK,\qquad f(F^pH_{\mathbb C})=f(H_{\mathbb C})\cap F^pK_{\mathbb C}$$
for all $n,p$. Its kernel, image and cokernel, with the induced or quotient
filtrations, are mixed Hodge structures; the functor $\operatorname{Gr}^W_n$ is
exact; and a morphism from a structure of weights at least $n$ (that is
$W_{n-1}H=0$) to a structure of weights at most $n$ (that is $W_nK=K$) has
pure image of weight $n$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category. A **cochain complex in $\mathcal A$**
is a family of objects $(C^n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ together with morphisms
$$d^n:C^n\to C^{n+1}$$
such that
$$d^{n+1}\circ d^n=0$$
for every $n\in\mathbb Z$.

This page uses the reindexing convention that a cochain complex $C^\bullet$ may
also be read as the chain complex with $(C^\sharp)_n:=C^{-n}$ and
$d^\sharp_n:=d^{-n}$, so that lower and upper indices differ only by the sign
of the grading.

A **rational cohomological mixed Hodge complex** consists of

(a) a bounded-below cochain complex $K_{\mathbb Q}$ of $\mathbb Q$-vector
spaces with an increasing filtration $W$ by subcomplexes, finite on each
cochain group;

(b) a cochain complex $K_{\mathbb C}$ of $\mathbb C$-vector spaces with an
increasing filtration $W$ by subcomplexes and a decreasing filtration $F$ by
subcomplexes, again finite on each cochain group;

(c) a morphism of complexes
$\alpha\colon K_{\mathbb Q}\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C\to K_{\mathbb C}$
compatible with the weight filtrations, such that for every $w$ the induced map
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_w\alpha$ is a quasi-isomorphism,

subject to the following axiom: for every integer $w$ the weight-graded
complex $\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK$ has finite-dimensional cohomology, its
differential (induced by $d_K$) is strict for the induced filtration $F$, and
for every $r$ the induced filtration $F$ on
$H^r(\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK_{\mathbb C})$, together with the induced rational
comparison
$H^r(\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK_{\mathbb Q})\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C\to
H^r(\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK_{\mathbb C})$, is a pure Hodge structure of weight
$r+w$ ([[def-rational-mixed-hodge-structure]]).

Here a cochain complex is a complex in the sense of
[[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]], a filtration by subcomplexes is
a filtered complex in the sense of [[def-filtered-chain-complex]], a morphism
compatible with the weight filtrations is a filtered chain map in the sense of
[[def-filtered-chain-map]], quasi-isomorphism means
[[def-quasi-isomorphism]], and finiteness on a cochain group $K^n$ means
$W_aK^n=0$ for all sufficiently negative $a$ and $W_aK^n=K^n$ for all
sufficiently positive $a$, with bounds depending on $n$; dually $F^pK^n=K^n$
for $p\ll0$ and $F^pK^n=0$ for $p\gg0$.

**The weight filtration on cohomology** is the shifted image filtration
$$W_mH^n(K):=\operatorname{im}\bigl(H^n(W_{m-n}K)\to H^n(K)\bigr).$$
The shift is essential: it is what makes the axiom's weight $r+w$ on the graded
complexes compatible with the weight of $H^n$, and pole-count weight on a
logarithmic complex is not the weight on its cohomology. The differential
strictness in the axiom is Deligne's condition (GH1); the equivalent
formulation that the $F$-spectral sequence of the graded complex degenerates at
its first page is recorded in the sources but is neither asserted nor used
here, so no degeneration theorem enters this definition.

**Morphisms and the sheaf case.** A morphism of cohomological mixed Hodge
complexes is a pair of chain maps $K_{\mathbb Q}\to L_{\mathbb Q}$ and
$K_{\mathbb C}\to L_{\mathbb C}$ compatible with both filtrations and with the
comparisons; compatible filtered homotopies are permitted. The same
definitions apply to bounded-below complexes of sheaves on a topological space
when the complexes are replaced by their derived global sections and the
resolutions used preserve the graded pieces; the existence of such resolutions
for the concrete complexes used later is proved where those complexes are
constructed, not here.

derivations.claim: (First page and pure strictness.) Put $G^p=W_{-p}$ and apply [F1] over $\mathbb Q$ and $\mathbb C$. Then $E_0^{p,q}=\operatorname{Gr}^p_GK^{p+q}$, $E_1^{p,q}=H^{p+q}(\operatorname{Gr}^W_{-p}K)$ and $E_\infty^{p,q}=\operatorname{Gr}^p_GH^{p+q}(K)$ for the image filtration. The axiom gives $E_1^{p,q}$ a pure rational Hodge structure of weight $q$. We will use the following explicit pure case of [F2]: a rational map preserving $F$ also preserves $\bar F$; between pure structures of the same weight it therefore preserves each type $F^a\cap\bar F^b$, so it is strict for $F$, and its kernels, images and cokernels have the induced pure structures. If the source has weight $q$ and the target has weight $q'<q$, it is zero: a source vector of type $(a,b)$ with $a+b=q$ maps into $F^a\cap\bar F^b$ of the target, which is zero because no target type of total $q'$ has both indices at least $a,b$. Thus no mixed Hodge structure on the abutment is being assumed.

(Strict representative correction.) For a complex $C$ with decreasing filtration $T$ by subcomplexes and $T$-strict differential, the sequence $0\to H^n(T^aC)\to H^n(C)\to H^n(C/T^aC)\to0$ is exact for every $a,n$. For injectivity, a cycle $x\in T^aC$ that is a boundary $dy$ in $C$ equals $dy'$ for some $y'\in T^aC$ by strictness. For surjectivity, a quotient cycle lifts to $x\in C$ with $dx\in T^aC$; strictness gives $y\in T^aC$ with $dy=dx$, so $x-y$ is a cycle with the same quotient class. If a cycle maps to a quotient boundary, subtract a lift of that boundary to obtain a cycle in $T^aC$, proving exactness at the middle. In particular $H(T^aC)$ identifies with the filtration induced on $H(C)$ by $T^a$. These corrections use only strictness of the differential on $C$.

(Exact filtered pages through $E_2$.) Fix a Hodge index $a$, and apply [F1] with the intersection and quotient $G$ filtrations to $A=F^aK_{\mathbb C}$, $B=K_{\mathbb C}$ and $C=B/A$. Their $E_0$ complexes form a short exact sequence $0\to E_0(A)\to E_0(B)\to E_0(C)\to0$: the first image in $G^pB/G^{p+1}B$ is $(F^aB\cap G^pB+G^{p+1}B)/G^{p+1}B$, exactly $F^aE_0(B)$, and the last term is its quotient. The mixed Hodge complex axiom says $d_0$ on $E_0(B)=\operatorname{Gr}^GK_{\mathbb C}$ is $F$-strict. Step 1.2 therefore gives a short exact sequence on $E_1$, with first image exactly $F^aE_1(B)$. Naturality of the page maps shows $d_1$ preserves this image for every $a$; its rational form then makes $d_1:E_1^{p,q}\to E_1^{p+1,q}$ a map of pure Hodge structures of weight $q$, strict by step 1.1. Apply step 1.2 again to the $E_1$ complexes to obtain exactness on $E_2$, with $E_2(A)$ identifying with the filtration induced on $E_2(B)=H(E_1(B),d_1)$. Denote this recursively induced filtration by $F_{\mathrm{rec}}$. The pure type decomposition of $E_1$ descends through its type-preserving $d_1$, so $E_2^{p,q}(B)$ with $F_{\mathrm{rec}}$ is pure of weight $q$.

(Higher differentials and exact stable pages.) Suppose the three page complexes are exact at page $r\ge2$, with $E_r(A)$ identifying with $F^a_{\mathrm{rec}}E_r(B)$ for every $a$, and $E_r^{p,q}(B)$ pure of weight $q$. Naturality shows $d_r$ preserves these images, hence $F_{\mathrm{rec}}$; it also preserves the rational structures. Its target $E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}$ has lower weight, so step 1.1 forces $d_r=0$. This zero map is strict, and step 1.2 applied to the exact triple of $E_r$ complexes gives exactness at $E_{r+1}$ and the recursive filtration identification. Since $d_r(B)=0$, injectivity of $E_r(A)\to E_r(B)$ and surjectivity onto $E_r(C)$ also give $d_r(A)=d_r(C)=0$. Starting from step 2.1 proves this induction for all $r\ge2$. Thus the weight sequence degenerates at $E_2$, and the three sequences for $A,B,C$ stabilize there; $E_\infty^{p,q}(B)=E_2^{p,q}(B)$ is pure of weight $q$ for the recurrent filtration.

(Recurrent filtration equals the abutment filtration.) By convergence and naturality [F1], the injective stable-page map $E_\infty(A)\to E_\infty(B)$ is $\operatorname{Gr}_G H(A)\to\operatorname{Gr}_G H(B)$ for the image $G$ filtrations on cohomology. A filtered linear map between finite filtered spaces whose graded map is injective is injective and strict: for any nonzero $x$, choose its largest decreasing-filtration index $p$; its nonzero graded class has nonzero image, so the image has this same index. This proves injectivity and, if the image of $x$ belongs to $G^p$, forces $x\in G^p$, which is strictness. The cohomology $G$ filtrations here are finite in each degree because $G$ is finite on the degree-$n$ cochain group, so the argument applies to $H^n(F^aK)\to H^n(K)$. Consequently its graded image is the induced filtration of the subspace $F^aH^n(K)=\operatorname{im}(H^n(F^aK)\to H^n(K))$ on $\operatorname{Gr}_GH^n(K)$: in filtration degree $p$ the numerator is $(F^aH^n(K)\cap G^pH^n(K))+G^{p+1}H^n(K)$. By steps 2.1 and 3.1 that same image on $E_\infty$ is $F^a_{\mathrm{rec}}$. This proves exactly the recurrent-to-abutment comparison needed here, with the strict representative correction supplied in step 1.2.

(Mixed Hodge structure and shifted weights.) Write $W_mH^n(K)=\operatorname{im}(H^n(W_{m-n}K)\to H^n(K))$. Substitution $p=n-m$, $q=m$ in [F1] and step 3.1 gives $\operatorname{Gr}^W_mH^n(K)=\operatorname{Gr}^{n-m}_GH^n(K)\cong E_2^{n-m,m}$. Step 4.1 makes this identification compatible with the Hodge filtration induced by $F$ on cohomology; the right side is pure of weight $m$ by step 2.1. The rational comparison is an isomorphism on $E_1$ by the graded quasi-isomorphism axiom and hence on the stable pages; finite filtered leading-term descent makes it an isomorphism on cohomology as well. The finitely many nonzero stable terms in degree $n$ are finite-dimensional, so $H^n(K_{\mathbb Q})$ is finite-dimensional. The induced $W$ and $F$ are finite, and every $\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$ with its induced $F$ is pure of weight $m$, precisely the mixed Hodge axiom.

(Functoriality.) A morphism of cohomological mixed Hodge complexes induces rational and complex cohomology maps compatible with the comparisons. It maps $W_{m-n}K$ to $W_{m-n}L$ and $F^aK_{\mathbb C}$ to $F^aL_{\mathbb C}$, hence preserves the cohomology image filtrations $W_m$ and $F^a$. These maps are therefore morphisms of the mixed Hodge structures of step 5.1. Naturality of [F1] and of the exact-page construction makes the graded-piece identifications compatible with these maps and their Hodge filtrations.

(The cosimplicial case.) Form $sK^n=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}K^{p,q}$ with the standard total differential. The cosimplicial identities, commutation with the internal differential and the usual total sign give $d^2=0$. The filtration $L_\ell sK^n=\bigoplus_{i\ge-\ell}K^{i,n-i}$ is increasing, by subcomplexes, and finite on each degree because $0\le i\le n$. Its graded piece is $\operatorname{Gr}^L_\ell sK\cong K^{-\ell}[\ell]$, so $H^r(\operatorname{Gr}^L_\ell sK)=H^{r+\ell}(K^{-\ell})$ is pure of weight $r+\ell$, and its internal differential is strict for $F$ by the Hodge complex hypothesis. Levelwise rational comparisons and filtration-preserving coface maps assemble to the total comparison, which is a graded quasi-isomorphism; the total complex is bounded below and its $F$ filtration is degreewise finite because each diagonal is finite. Thus $sK$ is a rational cohomological mixed Hodge complex for $L$. Applying steps 1.1-6.1 gives $E_1^{p,q}=H^{p+q}(\operatorname{Gr}^L_{-p}sK)=H^q(K^p)$, degeneration at $E_2$ and $\operatorname{Gr}^W_qH^n(sK)=\operatorname{Gr}^L_{q-n}H^n(sK)\cong E_2^{n-q,q}$, with its induced Hodge filtration and functorial mixed structure. Here $W_qH^n=L_{q-n}H^n$ is the shifted cohomology filtration, not the unshifted $L$.

(Weights at most the degree.) Since the cosimplicial degree is nonnegative, $E_1^{p,q}=0$ for $p<0$, hence $E_2^{n-q,q}=0$ when $q>n$. Step 7.1 gives $\operatorname{Gr}^W_qH^n(sK)=0$ for all $q>n$; finiteness of the weight filtration then gives $W_nH^n(sK)=H^n(sK)$, proving the stated bound.

boundaries.evidence: Step 8.1 uses vanishing cosimplicial entries with p<0.
Step 1.1 treats zero graded cohomology through the stated purity axiom, and steps 2.1 and 3.1 carry the exact page comparisons.
Step 5.1 identifies every individual Gr^W_m H^n with E_2^{n-m,m}, including a single nonzero weight.
Step 3.1 proves d_r=0 for every r>=2, including pages with vanishing terms.
Steps 7.1 and 8.1 use the exact total-degree and weight indices, including q=n.

citations.quote:
A **rational mixed Hodge structure** consists of a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space $H$
with a finite basis ([[def-linear-basis]]) together with

- a finite increasing filtration $W$ of $H$, the **weight filtration**, and

derivations.claim: The weight filtration is finite with $\operatorname{Gr}^W_{-2}=\mathbb Q e_1$, $\operatorname{Gr}^W_{-1}=0$ and $\operatorname{Gr}^W_0=H/\mathbb Q e_1\cong\mathbb Q e_0$. On $\operatorname{Gr}^W_{-2}$ the induced $F$ has $F^0=0$ and $F^{-1}=\operatorname{Gr}^W_{-2}$, since $F^0\cap W_{-2}=\mathbb C(e_0+ie_1)\cap\mathbb C e_1=0$; the conjugate filtration satisfies $\bar F^{-1}=\operatorname{Gr}^W_{-2}$ and $\bar F^0=0$ for the same reason, so the pieces are $H^{-1,-1}=\operatorname{Gr}^W_{-2}$ and nothing else, and $H^{-1,-1}$ is spanned by the image of $e_1$, which is rational. On $\operatorname{Gr}^W_0$ the image of $F^0\cap W_0=\mathbb C(e_0+ie_1)$ is all of $\operatorname{Gr}^W_0$ because $e_0+ie_1\mapsto e_0\ne0$, and $F^1=0$; the conjugate $\bar F^0=\sigma(F^0)=\mathbb C(e_0-ie_1)$ likewise has image all of $\operatorname{Gr}^W_0$, so the pieces are $H^{0,0}=\operatorname{Gr}^W_0$ and nothing else. Both graded pieces are therefore $n$-opposed, with the rational structure of $e_1$ and $e_0$ respectively, so $(H,W,F)$ is a rational mixed Hodge structure; its graded pieces are $\mathbb Q(1)$ and $\mathbb Q(0)$ in the convention [F2].

Let $\iota\colon\mathbb Q(1)\to H$ be the inclusion $\mathbb C\to H_{\mathbb C}$ sending $1$ to $e_1$ and let $\pi\colon H\to\mathbb Q(0)$ be the $\mathbb Q$-linear map $e_0\mapsto1$, $e_1\mapsto0$. Both preserve the filtrations: $\iota$ sends the weight-$(-2)$ structure into $W_{-2}H=\mathbb Q e_1$ and $F^{-1}\mathbb Q(1)_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C$ into $F^{-1}H_{\mathbb C}=H_{\mathbb C}$, while $F^0\mathbb Q(1)_{\mathbb C}=0$; and $\pi$ satisfies $\pi(W_{-1}H)=0=W_{-1}\mathbb Q(0)$ and $\pi(W_0H)=\mathbb Q(0)=W_0\mathbb Q(0)$, $\pi(F^0H_{\mathbb C})\subseteq\mathbb C=F^0\mathbb Q(0)_{\mathbb C}$ and $\pi(F^1H_{\mathbb C})=0$. Hence $0\to\mathbb Q(1)\xrightarrow{\iota}H\xrightarrow{\pi}\mathbb Q(0)\to0$ is a short exact sequence of rational mixed Hodge structures, with $\ker\pi=\mathbb Q e_1$.

Every $\mathbb Q$-linear section $s$ of $\pi$ satisfies $s(1)=e_0+q e_1$ with $q\in\mathbb Q$, because $\pi(e_0+q e_1)=1$ and $\pi(e_1)=0$. If $s$ were a morphism of mixed Hodge structures, it would satisfy $s_{\mathbb C}(F^0\mathbb Q(0)_{\mathbb C})\subseteq F^0H_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C(e_0+ie_1)$; since $F^0\mathbb Q(0)_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C$ and $s_{\mathbb C}(1)=e_0+qe_1$, there would be $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ with $e_0+qe_1=\lambda(e_0+ie_1)$. Comparing the coefficients of $e_0$ and $e_1$ in the basis $(e_0,e_1)$ gives $\lambda=1$ and $q=i$, which is impossible for $q\in\mathbb Q$. Hence the extension does not split in the category of rational mixed Hodge structures. The obstruction is visible directly in the $(0,0)$-direction: $F^0H_{\mathbb C}\cap\bar F^0H_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C(e_0+ie_1)\cap\mathbb C(e_0-ie_1)=0$, while a rational section must send $1$ into a rational vector of $F^0$, which is then also fixed by conjugation and hence would have to lie in this zero intersection.

citations.quote:
Let $V$ be an oriented finite-dimensional real inner product space of dimension $n$, with Gram pairings on the exterior powers of [[def-gram-inner-product-on-kth-exterior-power]] and oriented unit volume form $\omega$ of [[def-oriented-unit-volume-form]]. For each degree $k$ with $0\le k\le n$, the **Hodge star**

$$\star:\Lambda^kV\longrightarrow\Lambda^{n-k}V$$

is the linear map characterized by

$$\alpha\wedge\star\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle\,\omega\qquad\text{for all }\alpha,\beta\in\Lambda^kV.$$

Existence and uniqueness of $\star$ for every degree $0\le k\le n$ are proved in [[thm-hodge-star-exists-uniquely-and-has-the-orthonormal-basis-formula]], which discharges the well-definedness obligation recorded above.

Let $V$ be an oriented finite-dimensional real inner product space of dimension $n$. For every degree $0\le k\le n$ there is a unique linear map $\star:\Lambda^kV\to\Lambda^{n-k}V$ satisfying

$$\alpha\wedge\star\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle\,\omega\qquad\text{for all }\alpha,\beta\in\Lambda^kV,$$

where $\omega$ is the oriented unit volume form of [[def-oriented-unit-volume-form]]. If $(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$ is a positively oriented orthonormal basis and $I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_k\}$ has complement $I^c=\{i^c_1<\cdots<i^c_{n-k}\}$, let $\varepsilon_I$ be the sign of the permutation $(i_1,\ldots,i_k,i^c_1,\ldots,i^c_{n-k})\mapsto(1,\ldots,n)$; then

$$\star e_I=\varepsilon_I\,e_{I^c}.$$

On $\Lambda^kV$ of an oriented $n$-dimensional real inner product space, the Hodge star preserves the Gram pairing,

$$\langle\star\alpha,\star\beta\rangle=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle,$$

and satisfies

$$\star\circ\star=(-1)^{k(n-k)}\operatorname{id}_{\Lambda^kV}.$$

derivations.claim: Suppose $n=1$. Choose a unit vector $e_1$ and put $e_2=-Je_1$; then $g(e_1,e_2)=0$, $g(e_2,e_2)=1$, $Je_1=-e_2$, $Je_2=e_1$, and $\omega(e_1,e_2)=-g(Je_1,e_2)=g(e_2,e_2)=1$, so $\omega=e_1\wedge e_2$ is the positive unit volume form and $(e_1,e_2)$ is positively oriented. The basis $1,e_1,e_2,\omega$ of $\bigwedge^\bullet V_{\mathbb C}$ is orthonormal for $h$, and [F1] gives the star table $\star1=\omega$, $\star e_1=e_2$, $\star e_2=-e_1$, $\star\omega=1$. Hence $L(1)=\omega$ and $L$ kills $e_1,e_2,\omega$, while the adjoint $\Lambda$ satisfies $\Lambda\omega=1$ and kills $1,e_1,e_2$. Therefore $[L,\Lambda]=H$ is $-\mathrm{id}$, $0$, $0$, $\mathrm{id}$ on degrees $0,1,1,2$, that is $H=(k-1)\mathrm{id}$ on $\bigwedge^k$, and evaluating $HL-LH$ and $H\Lambda-\Lambda H$ on the four basis elements gives $[H,L]=2L$ and $[H,\Lambda]=-2\Lambda$. Evaluating the exponentials gives $W(1)=\omega$, $W(e_1)=e_1$, $W(e_2)=e_2$, $W(\omega)=-1$, while $J(1)=1$, $Je_1=-e_2$, $Je_2=e_1$, $J\omega=\omega$ give $\epsilon(0)J\star1=\omega$, $\epsilon(1)J\star e_1=e_1$, $\epsilon(1)J\star e_2=e_2$ and $\epsilon(2)J\star\omega=-1$; since both sides are complex linear, $W=\epsilon(k)J\star$ on $\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$ for $n=1$.

Let $V=V_1\oplus V_2$ with $V_1,V_2$ $g$-orthogonal and $J$-stable, oriented so that the positive volume form is $\operatorname{vol}_1\wedge\operatorname{vol}_2$; write $\omega_i=\omega|_{V_i}$, so $\omega=\omega_1+\omega_2$, and let $L_i,\Lambda_i,W_i,J_i$ be the corresponding operators on the factors. Under the linear isomorphism $\bigwedge^\bullet V_{1,\mathbb C}\otimes\bigwedge^\bullet V_{2,\mathbb C}\to\bigwedge^\bullet V_{\mathbb C}$, $a\otimes b\mapsto a\wedge b$, a check on orthonormal wedge bases gives the tensor rules $h(a\wedge b,a'\wedge b')=h_1(a,a')h_2(b,b')$, $\star(a\wedge b)=(-1)^{\deg a\deg b}(\star_1a)\wedge(\star_2b)$ and $J(a\wedge b)=J_1a\wedge J_2b$ for homogeneous $a,a'$ and $b,b'$, the middle one being forced by the characterizing property [F1] and consistent with the isometry property [F2]. Consequently $L=L_1+L_2$, $\Lambda=\Lambda_1+\Lambda_2$ (the adjoint of a sum of operators acting on the two tensor factors is the sum of the adjoints), $H=H_1+H_2$ where $H_i=(\deg-n_i)\mathrm{id}$ on the $i$-th factor with $n_i=\dim V_i/2$, and $W=W_1W_2$, $J=J_1J_2$, because operators on the two factors commute. If the three commutator relations and the identity $W=\epsilon(k)J\star$ hold on both factors, then they hold on $V$: the commutator relations split termwise, and for homogeneous $a,b$ the identity gives $W(a\wedge b)=\epsilon(\deg a)\epsilon(\deg b)(J_1\star_1a)\wedge(J_2\star_2b)$, which equals $\epsilon(\deg a+\deg b)J\star(a\wedge b)$ because $\epsilon(m+\ell)=(-1)^{m\ell}\epsilon(m)\epsilon(\ell)$ and the sign $(-1)^{\deg a\deg b}$ of the star rule cancels against $(-1)^{m\ell}$. Splitting off a two-plane $W=\mathrm{span}(e_1,-Je_1)$ with $V_2=W^\perp$ and iterating the base case 1.1 proves the three relations of part 1 and the identity of part 4 for every $n\ge0$: the degenerate factor $V_2=0$ has $\bigwedge^\bullet V_2=\mathbb C$ in degree zero, where all operators are the identity or zero and the relations are immediate, and for $n=0$ both sides of $W=\epsilon(k)J\star$ are the identity on this one-dimensional space.

Let $u
e0$ be primitive of degree $t$, so $\Lambda u=0$. From $[L,\Lambda]=H$ and $H=(t+2r-n)\mathrm{id}$ on degree $t+2r$ we get, by induction on $r\ge0$, the recurrence $\Lambda L^ru=r(n-t-r+1)L^{r-1}u$: indeed $\Lambda L^{r}u=L\Lambda L^{r-1}u-(t+2(r-1)-n)L^{r-1}u$ and substituting the induction hypothesis for $r-1$ gives the claim. Iterating gives the displayed factorial formula. Let $N$ be the largest index with $L^Nu
e0$, which exists because $L^ru=0$ once $t+2r>2n$. Then $L^{N+1}u=0$, so the recurrence with $r=N+1$ gives $0=\Lambda L^{N+1}u=(N+1)(n-t-N)L^Nu$; since $N+1
e0$ and $L^Nu
e0$, we get $N=n-t$. Hence $n-t\ge0$, so no nonzero primitive element has degree $t>n$; moreover $L^{n-t}u
e0$ and $L^{n-t+1}u=0$, and all coefficients in the factorial formula are nonzero for $0\le s\le r\le n-t$.

Let $\alpha\in\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$. Since $\Lambda=L^*$ on the finite-dimensional space $\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$, the image of $L:\bigwedge^{k-2}V_{\mathbb C}\to\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$ is the orthogonal complement of $\ker\Lambda$ on $\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}$, so $\alpha=u_0+L\alpha_1$ with $\Lambda u_0=0$ and $\alpha_1\in\bigwedge^{k-2}V_{\mathbb C}$. Inducting on $k$ (the cases $k=0$ and $k=1$ have no $L$-term) writes $\alpha=\sum_{r}L^ru_r$ with each $u_r$ primitive; terms with $\deg u_r>n$ are zero by step 3.1, which gives the stated range $r\ge\max(0,k-n)$. For uniqueness, suppose $\sum_{r=r_0}^{s}L^ru_r=0$ with each $u_r$ primitive and $u_s\ne0$. By the factorial formula $\Lambda^sL^su_s=s!u_s$ (note $L^su_s\ne0$ forces $s\le n-\deg u_s$), while for $r<s$ we get $\Lambda^sL^ru_r=\Lambda^{s-r}(\Lambda^rL^ru_r)=\Lambda^{s-r}(r!u_r)=0$ because $\Lambda u_r=0$; applying $\Lambda^s$ to the sum gives $s!u_s=0$, a contradiction. Finally, applying $\Lambda^s$ to a decomposed $\alpha$ shows $u_s=(s!)^{-1}\Lambda^s\alpha$ for the top index $s$, and subtracting $L^su_s$ and iterating computes each $u_r$ from $\alpha$ by a fixed rational polynomial in $L,\Lambda$; there are no choices at any step.

Choose a basis $(u_\alpha)$ of the direct sum $P=\bigoplus_jP^j$ of primitive spaces $P^j=\ker\Lambda\cap\bigwedge^jV_{\mathbb C}$, a finite direct sum of finite-dimensional spaces. By step 4.1 every element of $\bigwedge^\bullet V_{\mathbb C}$ has a unique expression as a finite sum of string elements $L^ru_\alpha$ with $0\le r\le n-\deg u_\alpha$; hence these string elements form a basis, and the string of $u_\alpha$ occupies each degree $t_\alpha,t_\alpha+2,\dots,2n-t_\alpha$. Fix $k\le n$ and let $t_\alpha=\deg u_\alpha$. Multiplication by $L^{n-k}$ sends the string element at position $r$ to position $r+n-k$, which is a valid position of the same string because $r+n-k\le n-t_\alpha$ follows from $k=t_\alpha+2r$; conversely position $r'$ of a degree-$2n-k$ element of the string is the image of $r=r'-(n-k)$ with $k=t_\alpha+2r\ge0$. On the direct sum of strings, $L^{n-k}$ is therefore a bijection from the degree-$k$ part onto the degree-$2n-k$ part, an isomorphism $L^{n-k}:\bigwedge^kV_{\mathbb C}\to\bigwedge^{2n-k}V_{\mathbb C}$. Similarly, $L^{n-k+1}L^ru_\alpha=L^{r+n-k+1}u_\alpha$ is zero exactly when $r=0$, and for $r\ge1$ it is a nonzero string element; expanding $u=\sum_{r\ge0,\alpha}c_{r,\alpha}L^ru_\alpha$ in degree $k$ and using basis independence, $L^{n-k+1}u=0$ forces $c_{r,\alpha}=0$ for every $r\ge1$, so $u=\sum_\alpha c_{0,\alpha}u_\alpha$ is primitive. The converse is step 3.1.

Since $J$ acts as $i$ on $V^{1,0}$ and $-i$ on $V^{0,1}$ and is multiplicative, $J=i^{p-q}$ on $\bigwedge^{p,q}V_{\mathbb C}$. Let $u\ne0$ be primitive of degree $k$ and type $(p,q)$, put $m=n-k\ge0$, and apply $W=\exp L\exp(-\Lambda)\exp L$ to $\exp(-L)u$: since $\Lambda u=0$ we get $W\exp(-L)u=\exp(L)\exp(-\Lambda)u=\exp(L)u$. Expanding $\exp(-L)u$ and comparing the components of degree $2n-k$, of which the left side has exactly $Wu$ (all other terms are mapped to lower degrees by $W$, which reverses the $H$-weight) and the right side exactly $L^mu/m!$, gives $Wu=L^mu/m!$. Substituting into the identity $Wu=\epsilon(k)J\star u$ of step 2.1 and applying $J^{-1}$, which acts on $L^mu$ by $i^{-(p-q)}=i^{q-p}$ because $L^mu$ has type $(p+m,q+m)$, gives $\star u=\epsilon(k)i^{q-p}L^mu/m!$, which is the displayed formula. For $n=0$ both sides are the identity and the formula is $*1=1$.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 disposes of the degenerate tensor factor V_2=0, whose exterior algebra is C in degree zero.
Steps 3.1 and 4.1 handle the zero element: its primitive decomposition is zero and the recurrence and coefficients vanish.
Step 1.1 is exactly the n=1 two-plane base case of the induction; step 2.1 also records the n=0 boundary.
Step 2.1 covers V_2=0 and the zero-dimensional space, and step 3.1 shows no nonzero primitive element has degree t>n.
Step 3.1 gives the degree bound t<=n and the vanishing L^{n-t+1}u=0, step 4.1 the range r>=max(0,k-n), and step 6.1 records the n=0 star identity.
The only selections are finite orthonormal bases in steps 1.1 and 2.1; the primitive decomposition and its projections are uniquely determined in step 4.1, so no choice principle is used.
Step 3.1: primitivity implies L^{n-t+1}u=0 and the degree bound.
Step 5.1: for k<=n, L^{n-k+1}u=0 implies u is primitive.

citations.quote:
For a smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, and $k\ge0$, define
$$I_M^k:\Omega^k(M)\longrightarrow C_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R),\qquad I_M^k(\omega)(\sigma)=\int_\sigma\omega.$$
On $c=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ this means $I_M^k(\omega)(c)=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\int_\sigma\omega$, a finite sum. In negative degrees $I_M^k$ is the zero map. Forms and the de Rham complex at a boundary use [[lem-the-de-rham-complex-and-pullback-extend-to-manifolds-with-boundary]]. No orientation of $M$ is required: the domain simplex has the specified orientation. The name integration cochain map is justified by [[thm-de-rham-integration-is-a-cochain-map]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, integration on smooth simplices followed by the inverse of restriction from continuous to smooth singular cohomology gives a natural isomorphism of unital graded real algebras
$$J_M:H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R).$$
The source product is wedge of form classes, the target product is the front/back singular cup product, and both stars denote direct sums of the homogeneous groups. Naturality is for smooth maps. No compactness assumption is imposed.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, the inclusion of smooth into continuous real singular chains induces an isomorphism
$$H_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)\longrightarrow H_k^{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R)$$
in every integer degree. This isomorphism is natural for smooth maps. The proof smooths only finitely many simplices at a time. For boundary targets it moves a finite compact set into the interior; it does not prescribe arbitrary boundary faces during smoothing.

Fix a space $X$, abelian group $G$ and integer $n\ge0$. For a singular cocycle $\varphi\in Z^n(X;G)$ and an integral singular cycle $c\in Z_n(X;\mathbb Z)$, define their **evaluation** to be $\varphi(c)\in G$, using [[def-singular-cohomology-with-coefficients]] and [[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]]. If $c=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ is its finite formal expansion, this value is $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)$.

The **Kronecker pairing** on quotient classes is the rule
$$\langle[\varphi],[c]\rangle=\varphi(c),\qquad H^n(X;G)\times H_n(X;\mathbb Z)\to G.$$
Its descent through both quotients, biadditivity and naturality are justified by the following lemma [[lem-the-kronecker-pairing-is-independent-of-cocycle-and-cycle-representatives]], before any use of the quotient pairing. It is not an assertion that evaluation gives an isomorphism to the full dual of homology.

For negative $n$, the two groups are zero and the pairing is the zero map. Empty $X$ and zero $G$ also give zero evaluation. When $G$ is an $R$-module, the cohomology variable is $R$-linear and the integral homology variable is additive; an $R$-bilinear pairing instead uses chains and homology over $R$ with $R$-linear cochains. No representative-selection function is included in the definition.

The Kronecker rule $\langle[\varphi],[c]\rangle=\varphi(c)$ is independent of both cocycle and cycle representatives and is additive in both variables. For a continuous $f:X\to Y$, $\alpha\in H^n(Y;G)$ and $z\in H_n(X;\mathbb Z)$, it satisfies
$$\langle f^*\alpha,z\rangle=\langle\alpha,f_*z\rangle.$$
For a coefficient homomorphism $u:G\to G'$, it satisfies $\langle u_*\alpha,z\rangle=u\langle\alpha,z\rangle$. The same representative-independence argument gives the $R$-bilinear pairing for $R$-linear cochains on chains over a commutative ring $R$.

Let $M$ be a compact boundaryless $n$-manifold with a specified $R$-orientation $\mu$, where $R$ is a commutative unital ring. Its **fundamental class** is
$$[M]=[M]_M\in H_n(M,M\setminus M;R)=H_n(M;R),$$
using [[lem-compatible-local-orientation-classes-exist-over-compact-subsets]] with the compact support $K=M$. The final equality holds at the chain-complex level: $C_*(\varnothing;R)=0$, so quotienting by it leaves $C_*(M;R)$. The cited lemma proves existence and uniqueness of this class with point restriction $\mu_x$ at every $x\in M$. Thus the notation denotes a class determined by the supplied orientation, not an arbitrary generator chosen afterward.

The same lemma gives finitely many open-and-closed components $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ and the restriction isomorphism
$$H_n(M;R)\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{j=1}^k H_n(M,M\setminus M_j;R).$$
The summand on the right identifies with $H_n(M_j;R)$: apply [[thm-excision-for-singular-homology]] to remove the closed set $M\setminus M_j$, which is the entire open relative subspace. The resulting pair is $(M_j,\varnothing)$. Under this identification $[M]$ corresponds to the finite tuple of the component fundamental classes.

If the orientation is negated on one component, its new fundamental-class summand is the negative of its old one. Indeed restriction is linear, so the negative class restricts to $-\mu_x$ at all points of that component, and uniqueness in the compact-set lemma identifies it with the new class. The other component summands are unchanged. In characteristic two this negation can leave the orientation and class unchanged; no distinction between $\mu$ and $-\mu$ is imposed when they are equal.

For empty $M$ the fundamental class is $0$ in the zero homology group, with an empty direct sum. For $R=0$ the unique orientation gives the zero class. A compact zero-manifold has finitely many singleton components, and its fundamental zero-cycle has at each point the coefficient prescribed by its local module generator. The definition requires a supplied orientation and uses no AC or simultaneous choice of one orientation per component.

Fix a dimension $n\ge1$ and one generator $e_n$ of $H_n(\mathbb R^n,\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\};\mathbb Z)$. A smooth orientation on a boundaryless $n$-manifold determines an integral local-homology orientation by requiring each positive chart centred at $p$ to send its local generator $\mu_p$ to $e_n$. This is independent of the positive chart and is a continuous generator section of the orientation local system. Use the same $e_n$ for all manifolds being compared.

If $F$ is smooth near $p$, $F(p)=q$, and $dF_p$ is invertible, its induced map on local integral homology carries $\mu_p$ to $\operatorname{sgn}(dF_p)\mu_q$. In dimension zero put $e_0=[\mathrm{point}]$; the smooth sign $\varepsilon(p)$ gives $\mu_p=\varepsilon(p)[p]$, and the local multiplier is the product of the source and target point signs. All assertions are choice-free. The local map is formed on a sufficiently small neighbourhood on which $p$ is the only preimage of $q$.

Let $F:M^n\to N^n$ be a smooth map of oriented smooth manifolds, and let $p$ be a regular preimage of $y$, so $F(p)=y$ and $dF_p:T_pM\to T_yN$ is an isomorphism. The **local orientation sign** $\operatorname{sgn}(dF_p)$ is $+1$ if the induced isomorphism of determinant lines carries the chosen ray of $T_pM$ to the chosen ray of $T_yN$, and $-1$ if it carries it to the other ray. For $n>0$ it is the sign of the derivative determinant in positively oriented bases. For $n=0$ it is $\varepsilon_M(p)\varepsilon_N(y)$, comparing the two specified rays directly; it need not be $+1$, although the empty determinant is one.

If $Z\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, then
inclusion $(X-Z,A-Z)\to(X,A)$ induces isomorphisms
$H_n(X-Z,A-Z;G)\cong H_n(X,A;G)$ for every $n$.

Let $m\ge0$, $n\ge1$, and $r\ge1$ be integers, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$
be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a $C^r$ map with

$$ r>\max\{m-n,0\}. $$

Then the critical value set of $f$ is a null subset of $\mathbb R^n$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a diffeomorphism of oriented smooth $n$-manifolds and
$\omega\in\Omega_c^n(N)$. If $F$ preserves orientation everywhere,
$\int_MF^*\omega=\int_N\omega$; if it reverses orientation everywhere,
$\int_MF^*\omega=-\int_N\omega$. If the sign varies between components,
apply the appropriate signed equality on each component and add. The
compact-support integrals are the choice-free finite-chart values, equal to
the global partition integrals whenever those are available.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For an oriented smooth manifold $M^n$, possibly with boundary, and $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$, choose a smooth partition $(\rho_i)$ subordinate to connected interior or boundary charts $(U_i,\phi_i)$. For $n\geq1$ set
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_i I_{\phi_i}(\rho_i\omega).$$
Each product has compact support in its chart and only finitely many are nonzero, by [[lem-a-locally-finite-sum-is-finite-near-the-compact-support-of-a-form]]. For $n=0$ set
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_{p\in\operatorname{supp}\omega}\varepsilon(p)\omega(p).$$
$\Lambda^0T_p^*M\cong\mathbb R$ has two orientations; define $\varepsilon(p)=+1$ when $1$ is positive in the chosen orientation and $\varepsilon(p)=-1$ when $-1$ is positive.
A zero-manifold is discrete; the singleton open cover of a compact subset has a finite subcover. Thus this sum too is finite. Empty support or empty $M$ gives zero. Independence of the choices is discharged by [[thm-global-form-integration-is-independent-of-the-atlas-partition-and-refinement]].

derivations.claim: Assume first that $\alpha$ is real and $m\ge1$. By [F2] choose a smooth singular cycle $z=\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\sigma_j$ representing the image of $[M]$ in $H_m(M;\mathbb R)$, and choose a continuous cocycle $\varphi$ representing the class $J_M[\alpha]=r_M^{-1}[I_M\alpha]$ with $r_M\varphi-I_M\alpha=\delta\psi$ for a smooth cochain $\psi$; evaluating on the smooth cycle $z$ gives $\langle J_M[\alpha],[M]\rangle=\varphi(z)=I_M\alpha(z)+\psi(\partial z)=I_M\alpha(z)=\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\int_{\Delta^m}\sigma_j^*\alpha$ by [F1] and the definition of $I_M$. It therefore remains to prove $\sum_ja_j\int_{\Delta^m}\sigma_j^*\alpha=\int_M\alpha$ for this smooth cycle.

Each $\sigma_j$ extends smoothly to an open neighbourhood of $\Delta^m$. Applying [F4] in finitely many charts covering the compact images, the critical values of all $\sigma_j$ and the images of all faces of all $\Delta^m$ form a set $N\subseteq M$ that is null in every smooth chart. For $y\notin N$ every preimage $x\in\sigma_j^{-1}(y)$ is an interior regular point of $\sigma_j$, and there are only finitely many of them, because a regular point has a neighbourhood on which $\sigma_j$ is injective and $\Delta^m$ is compact; put $\mu_j(y)=\sum_{x\in\sigma_j^{-1}(y)}\operatorname{sgn}(d\sigma_j(x))$ and $\mu(y)=\sum_ja_j\mu_j(y)$ for $y\notin N$.

Fix $y\notin N$ and a small closed ball $B\subseteq M$ around $y$. By [F3], excision identifies $H_m(M,M\setminus B;\mathbb R)$ with $H_m(B,B\setminus\{y\};\mathbb R)=\mathbb R\,\mu_y$, where $\mu_y$ is the local orientation class. The restriction of $[M]$ to this group is $\mu_y$ by the pointwise restriction property in [F3], and the restriction of the class of $z$ is $\mu(y)\mu_y$: subdividing the simplices of $z$ into pieces whose images lie either in $B$ or in $M\setminus B$, the pieces avoiding $B$ are killed in the relative quotient, while near each preimage of $y$ the germ of a regular $\sigma_j$ multiplies the local class $\mu_x$ by $\operatorname{sgn}(d\sigma_j(x))$ by [F3]. Since $z$ represents $[M]$, the two restrictions agree, and because $\mu_y$ generates an infinite cyclic group this forces $\mu(y)=1$. Hence $\mu=1$ on the complement of $N$.

Fix $j$. In a positively oriented chart at a regular point $x$, the coefficient of $\sigma_j^*\alpha$ is the coefficient of $\alpha$ at $\sigma_j(x)$ times $\det D\sigma_j(x)$, so the pullback coefficient vanishes identically on the critical set of $\sigma_j$, and $\int_{\Delta^m}\sigma_j^*\alpha=\int_{R_j}\sigma_j^*\alpha$ where $R_j$ is the set of regular points of $\sigma_j$ in the interior of $\Delta^m$. Cover $R_j$ by countably many connected open sets $V_i$ on which $\sigma_j$ restricts to a diffeomorphism onto its image, choose a subordinate locally finite smooth partition of unity $(\rho_i)$ using [F5], and let $\varepsilon_i\in\{\pm1\}$ be the sign of the differential on $V_i$. The change of variables theorem [F5] applied on each $V_i$ gives $\int_{R_j}\sigma_j^*\alpha=\sum_i\varepsilon_i\int_{\sigma_j(V_i)}\rho_i\alpha$, and monotone convergence [F5] applied to the positive and negative parts of the coefficient of $\alpha$ justifies exchanging this locally finite series with the integral: both sides are finite, the source integrand being continuous on the compact simplex. At a point $y\notin N$ with preimages $x_1,\dots,x_k$, the inner weight is $\sum_{l=1}^k\sum_{i:\,x_l\in V_i}\varepsilon_i\rho_i(x_l)=\sum_{l=1}^k\operatorname{sgn}(d\sigma_j(x_l))$ because $\sum_i\rho_i=1$ near each $x_l$ and $\varepsilon_i=\operatorname{sgn}(d\sigma_j(x_l))$ on each $V_i$ containing $x_l$. Therefore $\int_{\Delta^m}\sigma_j^*\alpha=\int_M\mu_j(y)\,\alpha(y)$, the null set $N$ being immaterial for the integral.

Summing the identity of step 2.2 with the coefficients $a_j$ and using $\mu=1$ outside $N$ from step 2.1 gives, for real $\alpha$ and $m\ge1$, $$\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\int_{\Delta^m}\sigma_j^*\alpha=\int_M\mu(y)\alpha(y)=\int_M\alpha(y),$$ which combined with step 1.1 proves $\langle J_M[\alpha],[M]\rangle=\int_M\alpha$. For complex $\alpha$ apply the real case to $\operatorname{Re}\alpha$ and $\operatorname{Im}\alpha$ and use real linearity of $J_M$, of the Kronecker pairing and of the integral. For $m=0$ the manifold is a finite set of points with orientation signs $\varepsilon(p)$, the fundamental class is $[M]=\sum_p\varepsilon(p)[p]$, the degree-zero comparison sends the class of a function $f$ to the evaluation classes $[f]=\sum_pf(p)[p]^*$, and both sides of the identity are $\sum_p\varepsilon(p)f(p)$ by the zero-dimensional convention in [F5]; the empty manifold gives $0=0$. The multiplicative consequence follows from the algebra isomorphism property of [F1] applied to the closed representatives. AC enters only through the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ recorded in the Given, which the de Rham comparison, the smooth partitions of unity and the smooth-chain comparison require; Sard, excision, change of variables, monotone convergence and the local multiplier computation are choice-free.

boundaries.evidence: The manifold is boundaryless in the statement and the singular cycle of step 1.1 has m>=1, so no boundary or empty-chain case arises.
Step 3.1 disposes of m=0 as a finite set of points with orientation signs and counting measure.
Steps 2.1-2.2 and 3.1 carry out the Sard-multiplicity computation for every m>=1, in particular m=1.
Step 1.2 shows the critical values and face images form a null set, so degenerate simplices contribute zero to the integral.
Step 3.1 handles m=0 and the top-degree endpoint, and step 1.1 pairs the top-degree fundamental class with the de Rham class.
Step 1.1 chooses a smooth cycle and cocycle representative under the item AC hypothesis; the Sard, excision and change-of-variables inputs are choice-free.
