Applying the acyclic-resolution theorem [F13] and the Künneth isomorphism of finite-dimensional vector-space complexes [F17] gives, for every $\sigma$, $H^q igl(\operatorname{pr}^{-1}\operatorname{St}_V(\sigma),\operatorname{pr}^*A igr)\cong H^q igl(I^ ullet_\sigma\otimes_k C^ ullet(F;k) igr)\cong igoplus_{p+r=q}H^p(I^ ullet_\sigma)\otimes_kH^r(F;k)\cong B_\sigma\otimes_kH^q(F;k)$, where $C^ ullet(F;k)$ denotes the finite model $\varprojlim_{\eta\in P_F}J^ ullet_\eta$ for $R\Gamma(F,k)$ supplied by [F10] and the last isomorphism uses that $I^ ullet_\sigma$ is a resolution of the vector space $B_\sigma$ concentrated in degree $0$.

**The direct image of a realized diagram.** For a diagram $V$, the sheaf $q_*q^{-1}V$ on $P$ has $q_*q^{-1}V(P_{\ge\sigma})=q^{-1}V(\operatorname{St}(\sigma))$, and I claim this equals $V_\sigma$; more precisely $q_*q^{-1}V\cong V$, where $V$ is regarded as the inverse-limit sheaf of step 1.2. Indeed, the comparison map $V\to q_*q^{-1}V$ has $\sigma$-component the canonical map $\varprojlim_{\tau\ge\sigma}V_\tau=V_\sigma\to q^{-1}V(\operatorname{St}(\sigma))$, namely the restriction of the canonical sections of $q^{-1}V$ to the star; for each $\sigma$ the composite $\varprojlim_{\tau\ge\sigma}V_\tau\to q^{-1}V(\operatorname{St}(\sigma))\to(q^{-1}V)_{b_\sigma}=V_\sigma$ is the projection of the limit, which is an isomorphism; step 4.1 independently identifies the star section group with $V_\sigma$, so the comparison itself is an isomorphism at every $\sigma$, and two sheaves on the Alexandrov space that agree on all principal opens are equal. Similarly, for each $j>0$ and each $\sigma$ one has $H^j(\operatorname{St}(\sigma),q^{-1}V)=0$ by step 4.1, and the assignment $U\mapsto H^j(q^{-1}U,q^{-1}V)$ is local on the base: on an open $U\subseteq P$ the restriction of $q_*$ to the opens below $U$ is direct image along the restricted map $q^{-1}U\to U$, so the sections of its derived functors over $U$ are computed by the same construction over $q^{-1}U$; since a sheaf on the finite Alexandrov space whose sections vanish over every principal open is zero, the higher derived sheaves $R^jq_*\bigl(q^{-1}V\bigr)$ vanish for $j>0$.

**The compact-support cochain model.** Apply the argument of steps 3.1 and 4.1 to the pair $(K,\varnothing)$, whose face poset is $P_K$ and whose realization is the compact space $|K|$: for a bounded complex $\widetilde V$ of finite-dimensional diagrams on $P_K$, choose a bounded injective resolution $\widetilde V\to J^\bullet$ with terms finite sums of standard injectives [F10], realize it, use the acyclicity of realized standard injectives for $\Gamma(|K|,-)$ from step 3.1, and apply the acyclic-resolution theorem [F13]; the outcome is that $R\Gamma\bigl(|K|,q_K^{-1}\widetilde V\bigr)$ is computed by the finite-dimensional bounded complex $\varprojlim_{\eta\in P_K}J^\bullet_\eta$, with the range bound of [F10] for the poset $P_K$ and its coefficient range. By step 2.2 this complex is a bounded finite cochain model for the compact-support cohomology $R\Gamma_c(X,q^{-1}V)$, and as in step 4.1 every map in the construction is $k$-linear between finite-dimensional spaces, so the model and hence the cohomology commute with every coefficient field extension by [F10].

**The comparison and its unit.** The realizability of the product diagrams together with the natural map $k\to J^\bullet$ of the fiber resolution and the identity of $B$ induce, on the models of step 4.2, a morphism $B\otimes_kC^\bullet(F;k)\to R\operatorname{pr}_*\operatorname{pr}^*A$ in $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(V))$, natural in $B$; here $C^\bullet(F;k)$ is the finite complex of $k$-vector spaces of step 4.2 and $B\otimes_kC^\bullet(F;k)$ denotes the tensor product of the realized diagram complex on $V$ with this finite complex of vector spaces, with the product differential. The morphism is obtained from the canonical maps $\Gamma(\operatorname{St}_V(\sigma),B)\otimes\Gamma(\eta,J^\bullet)\to\Gamma\bigl(\operatorname{St}_V(\sigma)\times\eta,q^{-1}(I^\bullet\boxtimes J^\bullet)\bigr)$ of the limit description of step 1.2, so it is compatible with restrictions to smaller stars. On each base star the source has $\Gamma\bigl(\operatorname{St}_V(\sigma),B\otimes_kC^\bullet(F;k)\bigr)=B_\sigma\otimes_kC^\bullet(F;k)$ up to canonical isomorphism by steps 1.2 and 4.1, while the target has $\Gamma\bigl(\operatorname{St}_V(\sigma),R\operatorname{pr}_*\operatorname{pr}^*A\bigr)=R\Gamma\bigl(\operatorname{pr}^{-1}\operatorname{St}_V(\sigma),\operatorname{pr}^*A\bigr)$, and on cohomology the comparison is the isomorphism computed in step 4.2; since the base stars form a basis and a morphism whose cohomology sheaves are isomorphisms on every member of a basis is an isomorphism, the comparison is an isomorphism. The unit of the adjunction between $\operatorname{pr}^*$ and $\operatorname{pr}_*$ sends $B$ to the image of $B\otimes(k\to C^\bullet(F;k))$ under this comparison, because the identity component of the tensor model is the identity of $B$ and the fiber unit is the inclusion of $k$ in degree $0$ given by the constant cocycle $1$.

**Full faithfulness.** Let $U,W$ be bounded complexes of finite-dimensional diagrams. Choose a bounded-above projective resolution $P^\bullet\to U$ as in step 1.5 and a bounded-below injective replacement $J^\bullet$ of $q^{-1}W$ in $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$, which is K-injective by [F11]; also fix a bounded injective model $I^\bullet$ of $W$ on the diagram side, which is K-injective as a bounded-below complex of injectives. Since $q^{-1}$ is exact, $q^{-1}P^\bullet\to q^{-1}U$ is a quasi-isomorphism, and since $U\to I^\bullet$ and $q^{-1}W\to J^\bullet$ are quasi-isomorphisms, the localization functors identify $\operatorname{Hom}_{D}\bigl(q^{-1}U,q^{-1}W\bigr)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{D}\bigl(q^{-1}P^\bullet,q^{-1}W\bigr)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_K\bigl(q^{-1}P^\bullet,J^\bullet\bigr)$, the last by [F11]. The adjunction of step 1.5's [F3] identifies the Hom complex of $q^{-1}P^\bullet$ and $J^\bullet$ with the Hom complex of $P^\bullet$ and $q_*J^\bullet$, levelwise and compatibly with the differentials, so $\operatorname{Hom}_K(q^{-1}P^\bullet,J^\bullet)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_K(P^\bullet,q_*J^\bullet)$. By step 5.1 the derived unit $W\to q_*J^\bullet$ is a quasi-isomorphism: apply the star-acyclic termwise model of step 4.1 to a bounded diagram representative of $W$, or build the comparison through its finitely many truncation triangles, so its cohomology is $H^j(W)$ in every degree. The complex $P^\bullet$ is a bounded-above complex of projectives, so it is K-projective by [F12], and therefore $\operatorname{Hom}_K(P^\bullet,q_*J^\bullet)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_D(P^\bullet,q_*J^\bullet)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_D(U,W)$, the first isomorphism by [F12] and the second because quasi-isomorphisms are inverted in both variables. Combining the chain of isomorphisms proves $\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(q^{-1}U,q^{-1}W)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(U,W)$; by [F14] the same holds for the bounded derived categories, so the realization functor is fully faithful.

**The cone bound.** If $H^r(F;k)=0$ for $1\le r\le R$ and $B$ lies in $D^{\ge b}$, then the cone of the unit $B\otimes(k\to C^\bullet(F;k))$ has cohomology concentrated in degrees $\ge b+R+1$: by [F17] the cohomology of $B\otimes_kC^\bullet(F;k)$ is $\bigoplus_{p+r=n}H^p(B)\otimes_kH^r(F;k)$, which for $n<b+R+1$ reduces to $H^n(B)\otimes_kH^0(F;k)$ and is identified with $H^n(B)$ by the unit, so the cone is acyclic below $b+R+1$. The comparison is local and uses only the supplied finite deleted-boundary models of the base and fiber; no global statement about bundles and no assertion that an arbitrary algebraic map is simplicial is made.

**Field extension of the Hom model.** In the computation of step 6.1 every object is a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space and every map is $k$-linear: the resolutions supplied by [F10] have finite-dimensional terms, the Hom complexes have finitely many finite-dimensional terms, and their cohomology computes the Hom groups in each degree by [F10]'s finite model. Extending scalars along an exact field extension $k\to K$ therefore replaces the diagrams by their termwise base changes and carries the finite matrices of the model to their base changes, so the cohomology of the model is the base change of the cohomology, and [F10] records this commutation for its models. This proves that ordinary Hom of bounded objects has bounded finite cochain models commuting with every coefficient field extension.

**The essential image.** First, if $V$ is a bounded complex of diagrams, then each cohomology sheaf of $q^{-1}V$ is $q^{-1}(H^jV)$ by exactness of $q^{-1}$, and its restriction to an open simplex in $P$ is constant of finite rank, so such complexes lie in the stated image and have bounded finite-rank locally constant cohomology on each open simplex. Conversely, let $A$ be a bounded complex on $X$ whose cohomology sheaves are finite-rank locally constant on every open simplex. By step 3.2 each $H^j(A)$ is isomorphic to $q^{-1}V_j$ for a finite-dimensional diagram $V_j$, and $V_j=0$ outside a finite range of degrees. We build $A$ inductively from its cohomology. If $A$ has at most one nonzero cohomology sheaf, then $A\cong H^n(A)[-n]\cong q^{-1}\bigl(V_n[-n]\bigr)$, using that $q^{-1}$ commutes with shifts up to canonical isomorphism because it is exact. Otherwise let $m$ be the least degree with $H^m(A)\neq0$; the canonical truncation triangle of [F14] reads $H^m(A)[-m]\to A\to\tau^{\ge m+1}A\to H^m(A)[-m+1]$. By induction on the number of nonzero cohomology degrees, $\tau^{\ge m+1}A\cong q^{-1}W$ for a bounded diagram complex $W$, and $H^m(A)[-m]\cong q^{-1}\bigl(V_m[-m]\bigr)$; by step 6.1 the connecting morphism $\delta:q^{-1}W\to q^{-1}(V_m[-m+1])$ is $q^{-1}(\delta_0)$ for a unique morphism $\delta_0$ of the diagram derived category. Completing $\delta_0$ to a distinguished triangle $V_m[-m]\to Y\to W\to V_m[-m+1]$ of [F14] and applying the exact functor $q^{-1}$ yields a triangle $q^{-1}(V_m[-m])\to q^{-1}Y\to q^{-1}W\to q^{-1}(V_m[-m+1])$ whose connecting morphism is $\delta$; two distinguished triangles with isomorphic first two objects and the same connecting morphism are isomorphic, so $A\cong q^{-1}Y$ and $A$ is realized. Hence the essential image is exactly the full subcategory of complexes with bounded finite-rank locally constant cohomology on each open simplex.

**Local models on an open simplex.** Let $x\in\sigma^\circ$, and let $\mathcal U$ be the cofinal family of open intrinsic balls $U\subseteq\operatorname{St}(\sigma)$ around $x$ with $U\cap\tau^\circ$ convex for every $\tau\supseteq\sigma$; every member of $\mathcal U$ meets exactly the open simplices $\tau^\circ$ with $\tau\supseteq\sigma$, so all members carry the restrictions of the same two diagrams, based on the principal filter $Q_\sigma=\{\tau\in P:\tau\supseteq\sigma\}$, and for $U'\subseteq U$ in $\mathcal U$ the diagram of $A|_{U'}$ is literally the diagram of $A|_U$ and the restriction is the identity on this data. The full-faithfulness computation of step 6.1 applies verbatim to each such $(U,Q_\sigma,q|_U)$, because the realizability and acyclicity inputs are the restrictions of the ones used there and every $U\cap\operatorname{St}(\tau)$ and $U\cap|\tau|$ for $\tau\in Q_\sigma$ is convex, nonempty for small $U$, and hence contractible with the metric hypothesis of [F7]; hence $\operatorname{Ext}^q_{D(U)}(A|_U,B|_U)\cong\operatorname{Ext}^q_{\operatorname{Diag}(Q_\sigma)}(V|_{Q_\sigma},W|_{Q_\sigma})$ for every $U\in\mathcal U$ where $A\cong q^{-1}V$, $B\cong q^{-1}W$, and these isomorphisms are compatible with the restriction maps, which become the identity. Consequently the restriction maps $\operatorname{Ext}^q_{D(U)}(A|_U,B|_U)\to\operatorname{Ext}^q_{D(U')}(A|_{U'},B|_{U'})$ are isomorphisms for nested members of $\mathcal U$, so the stalk colimit of step 1.6 stabilizes: the cohomology sheaves $R^q\mathcal{H}om(A,B)$ are locally constant of finite rank on each open simplex, with stalk $\operatorname{Ext}^q_{\operatorname{Diag}(Q_\sigma)}(V|_{Q_\sigma},W|_{Q_\sigma)}$ at every point of $\sigma^\circ$.

**Boundedness and field extension of internal Hom.** The models $\operatorname{Ext}^q_{\operatorname{Diag}(Q_\sigma)}(V|_{Q_\sigma},W|_{Q_\sigma})$ are finite-dimensional and vanish outside a range depending only on the internal amplitude of $V,W$ and the chain length of $Q_\sigma$, whose strict-chain length is at most that of $P$; since $P$ is finite and $Q_\sigma$ depends only on the simplex $\sigma$, the ranges are uniformly bounded over $\sigma$ and over points of $\sigma^\circ$, so $R\mathcal{H}om(A,B)$ is bounded with finite-rank locally constant cohomology. By [F10] the diagram Hom models commute with every field extension, and the identifications of step 7.3 use only the finite models, so extending scalars carries the internal-Hom models to the models of the extended objects. This proves the internal-Hom clause.

The ordinary equivalence is step 3.2; star acyclicity and the ordinary cohomology model are step 4.1; compact supports are steps 2.2 and 5.2; full faithfulness, its field compatibility and the essential image are steps 6.1, 7.1 and 7.2; internal derived Hom is steps 7.3 and 8.1; and the local product comparison with its unit and cone bound is steps 5.3 and 6.2. AC is consumed through the injective replacements, the acyclic-resolution theorem and the model suppliers of [F10] and [F11], and the statement asserts no finite-dimensionality of arbitrary sections, no simpliciality of arbitrary algebraic maps, and no injectivity of realized diagrams among all analytic sheaves.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement allows the empty retained poset when D=K; step 1.1 defines its empty carrier and step 3.2 gives the resulting zero-category equivalence. Step 3.1 treats empty intersections of relatively closed cell supports with stars.
The zero diagram realizes to the zero sheaf by step 1.2; standard injectives with zero coefficient space vanish in step 1.4, and the ordinary finite cochain construction of step 4.1 is then zero.
Step 1.4 includes the coefficient space k in a standard injective. The constant fibre unit and its comparison are realized in step 5.3, with the product pair supplied in step 2.3.

The finite strict-face-chain resolutions in steps 1.5 and 6.1 admit chains of length zero; repeated vertices contribute no strict-chain term. Step 4.1 uses the bounded injective resolution without a positive-length assumption.
Step 1.1 permits D=K, giving empty X and P. Step 5.2 explicitly applies the compact model (K,empty) for the compact-support comparison, covering the other deleted-boundary endpoint.

The Statement assumes AC; steps 4.1 and 5.2 use the declared injective and support-acyclicity suppliers. The ordinary finite diagram operations remain the actual finite models described in the Facts and Statement.
Step 7.2 proves that a realized bounded diagram complex has bounded finite-rank locally constant cohomology on the retained open simplices.
Step 7.2 proves the converse essential-image clause by ordinary truncation induction using full faithfulness from step 6.1.

Let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on a topological space $X$. We say that
$\mathcal F$ is a **sheaf** if for every open set $U \subseteq X$ and every
open cover $U=\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i$, including the empty cover of
$\varnothing$, the following two conditions hold.

**Locality.** If $s,t\in\mathcal F(U)$ satisfy
$$s|_{U_i}=t|_{U_i}\qquad\text{for all }i\in I,$$
then $s=t$.

**Gluing.** If sections $s_i\in\mathcal F(U_i)$ satisfy
$$s_i|_{U_i\cap U_j}=s_j|_{U_i\cap U_j}\qquad\text{for all }i,j\in I,$$
then there exists $s\in\mathcal F(U)$ such that
$$s|_{U_i}=s_i\qquad\text{for all }i\in I.$$

By locality, such a section $s$ is automatically unique. Thus a sheaf is
exactly a presheaf whose compatible local sections glue uniquely.

Let $X$ be a topological space.
Fix a ring $R$ when modules are under discussion.

A **presheaf of groups** on $X$ is a presheaf $\mathcal F$ such that every
$\mathcal F(U)$ is a group and every restriction map
$\rho^U_V:\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal F(V)$ is a group homomorphism
([[prop-groups-and-homomorphisms-form-category-grp]]).

A **presheaf of rings** on $X$ is defined the same way with rings and ring
homomorphisms ([[prop-rings-and-homomorphisms-form-category-ring]]).

A **presheaf of left $R$-modules** on $X$ is defined the same way with left
$R$-modules and $R$-linear maps
([[prop-modules-and-homomorphisms-form-category-rmod]]).

A **sheaf of groups**, **sheaf of rings**, or **sheaf of left $R$-modules** is
such a presheaf whose underlying set-valued presheaf is a sheaf.

In particular, each sheaf of groups has a distinguished identity section on
every open set; in additive notation this section is written $0$, and all
restrictions preserve the algebraic operations.

Let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space.

An **$\mathcal O_X$-module** is a sheaf $\mathcal F$ of abelian groups on $X$
such that for every open set $U \subseteq X$ the section group $\mathcal F(U)$
is an $\mathcal O_X(U)$-module, and for every inclusion $V \subseteq U$ the
restriction map
$$
\mathcal F(U)\longrightarrow\mathcal F(V)
$$
is $\mathcal O_X(U)$-linear after restricting scalars along
$\mathcal O_X(U)\to\mathcal O_X(V)$.

A **morphism of $\mathcal O_X$-modules** is a morphism of the underlying sheaves
of abelian groups whose components are $\mathcal O_X(U)$-linear on every open
set $U$.

Let $X$ be a topological space.

1. The category of sheaves of abelian groups on $X$ is an abelian category.
2. If $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ is a ringed space, then the category of
   $\mathcal O_X$-modules is also an abelian category.

Let
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{i-1}\xrightarrow{d_{i-1}}\mathcal F_i\xrightarrow{d_i}\mathcal F_{i+1}\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
be a sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space $X$. Then the
sequence is exact if and only if, for every point $x\in X$, the stalk sequence
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow (\mathcal F_{i-1})_x\xrightarrow{(d_{i-1})_x}(\mathcal F_i)_x\xrightarrow{(d_i)_x}(\mathcal F_{i+1})_x\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
is exact.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, and let $\mathcal G$ be a presheaf on $Y$.
The **inverse-image presheaf**
$$
f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G
$$
on $X$ is defined by
$$
(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U):=\varinjlim_{f(U)\subseteq V}\mathcal G(V),
$$
where $V$ runs over the open neighbourhoods of $f(U)$ in $Y$, ordered by
reverse inclusion. If $U' \subseteq U$, then every neighbourhood of $f(U)$ is a
neighbourhood of $f(U')$, so there is a natural restriction map
$(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U)\to(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U')$.

The **inverse image sheaf** of a sheaf $\mathcal G$ on $Y$ is the sheafification
of this presheaf:
$$
f^{-1}\mathcal G:=a(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G).
$$

When $U$ is open in $X$ and $V$ is an open set of $Y$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$,
there is a canonical map
$$
\mathcal G(V)\longrightarrow(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U)
$$
into the colimit class represented by $V$.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, and let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on $X$.
The **direct image presheaf**
$$f_*\mathcal F$$
on $Y$ is defined on an open set $V \subseteq Y$ by
$$
(f_*\mathcal F)(V):=\mathcal F(f^{-1}(V)).
$$
If $V' \subseteq V$, the restriction map
$$
(f_*\mathcal F)(V)\longrightarrow(f_*\mathcal F)(V')
$$
is the restriction map of $\mathcal F$ for the inclusion
$f^{-1}(V') \subseteq f^{-1}(V)$.

Thus direct image is just precomposition of the presheaf with the inverse-image
map on open sets.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map.

1. If $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf on $X$, then $f_*\mathcal F$ is a sheaf on $Y$.
2. If $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of groups, rings, or modules on $X$, then
   $f_*\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of the same kind on $Y$.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, let $\mathcal G$ be a sheaf on $Y$, and let
$\mathcal F$ be a sheaf on $X$. Then there is a natural bijection
$$\operatorname{Hom}_X(f^{-1}\mathcal G,\mathcal F) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_Y(\mathcal G,f_*\mathcal F).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a topological
space and let $k$ be a field. The category $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ of sheaves
of $k$-vector spaces is the category of modules over the ringed space
$(X,k_X)$ with constant structure sheaf $k_X$
([[def-locally-ringed-space]], [[def-module-on-ringed-space]]); it is a locally
small Grothendieck category and carries a functorial injective embedding, and
iterating that embedding on cokernels yields for every $k$-sheaf one specific
injective resolution
([[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]). These resolutions are
bounded-below injective replacements, so with the dependent choice supplied by
AC ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]) the bounded-below
injective complexes model the bounded derived category:
$K^+(\operatorname{Inj}\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))\to
D^+(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is an equivalence, and morphisms of the bounded
derived category are computed by these replacements
([[thm-injective-complexes-model-the-bounded-below-derived-category]]).

Now let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety and let
$\mathfrak S$ be a finite smooth algebraic stratification with the frontier
condition of $X$
([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). Let
$D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ be the full subcategory of
$D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ of complexes whose cohomology sheaves are bounded
and constructible with respect to $\mathfrak S$
([[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]]). Then
$D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ is a triangulated subcategory: it is closed under
shifts, isomorphisms and mapping cones. More generally, if two bounded
algebraically constructible complexes are constructible with respect to one
common finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification, then their cone is
bounded and constructible with respect to that stratification.

With supplied bounded-below injective replacements $j_X:X\to I_X$ (and DC or supplied homotopy extensions), $K^+(\operatorname{Inj}\mathcal A)\to D^+(\mathcal A)$ is an equivalence of triangulated categories. For a bounded-below complex $I$, K-injectivity can be tested using only bounded-below acyclic inputs.
A bounded-below cochain complex $I$ of injective objects is K-injective. Assume dependent choice for the countable successive homotopy extensions, or supply those extensions as data.

A cochain complex $I$ is **homotopically injective**, or **K-injective**, if $\operatorname{Hom}_K(A,I[r])=0$ for every acyclic cochain complex $A$ and every integer $r$. Equivalently, $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(A,I)$ is acyclic. This uses the Hom complex and shifted Hom identification fixed in [[def-homotopically-projective-bounded-above-complex]]. A **bounded-below K-injective complex** additionally has $I^n=0$ for all sufficiently negative $n$. The K-injective property itself neither assumes boundedness nor means termwise injectivity.

For a K-injective complex $I$ and any complex $X$, $Q:\operatorname{Hom}_K(X,I)\to\operatorname{Hom}_D(X,I)$ is bijective. Moreover, if $s:I\to J$ is a quasi-isomorphism, its cone triangle is split in $K$: $J\cong I\oplus\operatorname{Cone}(s)$ with $s$ corresponding to the inclusion.

Assume an abelian category satisfies AB3 and AB3*.

1. Every finite coproduct of projective objects is projective, and every finite
   product of injective objects is injective.
2. For an arbitrary small family, the same conclusion holds provided one may
   choose one lift or one extension for each index in each lifting problem; in
   particular it holds under the Axiom of Choice.

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category. A **cochain complex in $\mathcal A$**
is a family of objects $(C^n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ together with morphisms
$$d^n:C^n\to C^{n+1}$$
such that
$$d^{n+1}\circ d^n=0$$
for every $n\in\mathbb Z$.

This page uses the reindexing convention that a cochain complex $C^\bullet$ may
also be read as the chain complex with $(C^\sharp)_n:=C^{-n}$ and
$d^\sharp_n:=d^{-n}$, so that lower and upper indices differ only by the sign
of the grading.

Let $C$ be a [[def-homological-double-complex|homological double complex]] in
an abelian category. Suppose that for every integer $n$ the diagonal
[[def-products-and-coproducts|coproduct]] below exists, and write its injections
as $\iota^n_{p,q}$:
$$T_n=\operatorname{Tot}^{\oplus}_n(C)=\coprod_{p+q=n}C_{p,q}.$$
Define $d_n:T_n\to T_{n-1}$ to be the unique arrow with
$$d_n\iota^n_{p,q}=\iota^{n-1}_{p-1,q}h_{p,q}+\iota^{n-1}_{p,q-1}v_{p,q}\quad(p+q=n).$$
Each right-hand side is the sum of two morphisms with the same source and
target. The coproduct universal property supplies a unique $d_n$ from this
family; no infinite sum in a morphism group is required.

The resulting **direct-sum total complex** has differential of degree $-1$.
Its chain condition is established in
[[lem-the-total-differential-squares-to-zero]]. A diagonal with only zero
objects has zero coproduct: every family of maps from its objects is the
unique zero family. A diagonal with exactly one nonzero object has that
object as coproduct. For general infinite diagonals existence is a hypothesis,
not an implication of being an abelian category. No choices of elements or
representatives enter this construction.

For the direct-sum totalisation of an anticommuting homological double
complex, $d_{n-1}d_n=0$ for every integer $n$.

Let K be a cochain complex with decreasing filtration by subcomplexes. Set $C_n=K^{-n}$, $F_pC_n=F^{-p}K^{-n}$ and $d_n=d_K^{-n}$. Then
$$E_r^{p,q}(K)=E^r_{-p,-q}(C),\qquad d_r:E_r^{p,q}\to E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}.$$
The construction gives $E_0^{p,q}=\operatorname{gr}^p K^{p+q}$ and $E_1^{p,q}\cong H^{p+q}(\operatorname{gr}^p K)$. With degreewise finite filtration it naturally abuts to the decreasing image filtration on $H^{p+q}(K)$, with $E_\infty^{p,q}\cong\operatorname{gr}^pH^{p+q}(K)$.

For a cochain complex $X$, define the **canonical truncations** by

$$ (\tau^{\leq n}X)^i=\begin{cases}X^i&i<n,\\\ker d_X^n&i=n,\\0&i>n,\end{cases}\qquad (\tau^{\geq n}X)^i=\begin{cases}0&i<n,\\\operatorname{coker}d_X^{n-1}&i=n,\\X^i&i>n.\end{cases} $$

The differential into $\ker d_X^n$ is the factorization of $d_X^{n-1}$; the differential out of $\operatorname{coker}d_X^{n-1}$ is induced by $d_X^n$. All other retained differentials are those of $X$. There are natural maps $\tau^{\leq n}X\to X\to\tau^{\geq n}X$. Unlike [[def-brutal-truncation-of-a-complex]], these constructions correct the boundary using the cycle and boundary objects of [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]].

Every short exact sequence $0\to A\xrightarrow iB\xrightarrow qC\to0$ of cochain complexes gives a natural distinguished triangle $A\to B\to C\to A[1]$ in $D(\mathcal A)$. In particular, for every integer $n$ there are canonical distinguished triangles

$$\tau^{\leq n}X\to X\to\tau^{\geq n+1}X\to(\tau^{\leq n}X)[1],$$

$$\tau^{\leq n}X\to\tau^{\leq n+1}X\to H^{n+1}(X)[-n-1]\to(\tau^{\leq n}X)[1],$$

$$H^n(X)[-n]\to\tau^{\geq n}X\to\tau^{\geq n+1}X\to H^n(X)[-n+1].$$

The derived category, with shift $[1]$ and distinguished triangles the isomorphic images of cone triangles, is triangulated. The localization functor $Q$ is exact. Every such triangle gives a long exact cohomology sequence $\cdots\to H^n(X)\to H^n(Y)\to H^n(Z)\to H^{n+1}(X)\to\cdots$.

The canonical functors $D^-(\mathcal A),D^+(\mathcal A),D^b(\mathcal A)\to D(\mathcal A)$ are fully faithful and exact. Their essential images consist exactly of complexes with cohomology respectively bounded above, bounded below, or bounded on both sides.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety, i.e. a classical
algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), regarded as
a topological space with its analytic topology
([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]), and
let $k$ be a field. Write $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ for the category of sheaves
of $k$-vector spaces and $k$-linear morphisms
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]],
[[def-presheaf-of-groups-rings-modules]], [[def-module-on-ringed-space]]); it is
an abelian category ([[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]]), so its
bounded derived category $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is defined with the
conventions of [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]], under the
standing smallness hypothesis recorded there.

The category $D_c^b(X;k)$ is the full subcategory of
$D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ consisting of the complexes $A$ satisfying:

1. $A$ is **cohomologically bounded**: $H^j(A)=0$ for $|j|$ sufficiently large;
   and
2. $A$ is **algebraically constructible**: there exists a finite smooth
   algebraic stratification with the frontier condition $\mathfrak S$ of $X$
   ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]) such
   that for every stratum $S\in\mathfrak S$ and every integer $j$ the
   restriction $H^j(A)|_S$ is locally constant of finite rank
   ([[def-locally-constant-sheaf-of-finite-rank]]).

These are topological constructible sheaves, not coherent or quasi-coherent
sheaves. We use the shift convention of
[[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]: $H^j(A[m])=H^{j+m}(A)$. A
groupoid local system is identified with a locally constant sheaf only through
an explicit local comparison, which is not made here.

Constructibility is a condition on the cohomology sheaves of a complex, and it
is quantified existentially over finite smooth algebraic frontier
stratifications: no stratification is fixed, and no existence or
common-refinement theorem for stratifications is asserted by this definition.
Shifting replaces $H^j$ by $H^{j+m}$, which preserves cohomological boundedness
and shifts a witnessing stratification nowhere, so the class is closed under
shifts and under isomorphisms in $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$. No choice
principle is used.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace.

1. For every sheaf of abelian groups $\mathcal F$ on $U$ and every sheaf of
   abelian groups $\mathcal G$ on $X$, there is a natural bijection
   $$\operatorname{Hom}_X(j_!\mathcal F,\mathcal G) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_U(\mathcal F,j^{-1}\mathcal G).$$
2. The functor $j_!$ is exact on sheaves of abelian groups.

derivations.claim: **The simplicial sheaf category.** A simplicial analytic $k$-sheaf on $Z_\bullet$ is a family $F=(F_p)_{p\ge0}$ with $F_p\in\operatorname{Sh}_k(Z_p)$ and structure maps $Z_\alpha^{-1}F_p\to F_m$ for every monotone $\alpha:[p]\to[m]$, satisfying the identity and composition identities for composable simplicial operators; a morphism is a levelwise family of $k$-linear maps commuting with these structure maps. The category $\operatorname{Sh}_k(Z_\bullet)$ is abelian: kernels and cokernels are formed levelwise (cokernels after sheafification of the presheaf cokernel), and exactness is checked levelwise by [F1]; arbitrary products and coproducts are computed levelwise, so AB3 and AB3* hold; the category is locally small because each $\operatorname{Sh}_k(Z_p)$ is.

**Coinduction and explicit injective resolutions.** For $p\ge0$ and $I\in\operatorname{Sh}_k(Z_p)$ define the coinduced object $N_pI$ by $(N_pI)_m:=\prod_{\alpha:[m]\to[p]}(Z_\alpha)_*I$, the product over all monotone maps, with structure maps induced by composition of simplicial operators; then $\operatorname{Hom}(F,N_pI)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{Z_p}(F_p,I)$ naturally, because the component at $\alpha=\mathrm{id}_{[p]}$ is a bijection onto the data and every other component is determined from it by the structure maps of $F$. Hence $N_p$ is right adjoint to evaluation at $p$, which is exact, so $N_pI$ is injective for injective $I$; explicitly, $\operatorname{Hom}(-,N_pI)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{Z_p}((-)_p,I)$ is exact. Given $F$, choose functorial injective embeddings $F_p\rightarrowtail I_p$ by [F3]; the components give a morphism $F\to\prod_pN_pI_p$ that is a monomorphism because at level $m$ its component $p=m$, $\alpha=\mathrm{id}$ is the chosen embedding, and the product of injectives is injective by [F4] under AC. Iterating this embedding on cokernels and totalizing along the bounded-below index produces for every bounded-below complex of simplicial sheaves one explicit coinduced injective resolution.

**Acyclicity of coinduced injectives.** Let $J=N_pI$. For every $m$ the component at a fixed vertex $\alpha_0:Z_m\to Z_p$ of $q_{m*}J_m=\prod_{\alpha:[m]\to[p]}q_{p*}I$ is $q_{p*}I$, because $q_m\circ Z_\alpha=q_p$; thus $q_{m*}J_m$ is a product of copies of $q_{p*}I$ indexed by the monotone maps $[m]\to[p]$, that is, by the $m$-simplices of the standard $p$-simplex. On the normalized complex whose degree-$m$ term is this product and whose differential is the alternating sum of the maps that delete one vertex (the pullback-and-structure maps associated to the coordinate-deletion operators, which raise the cochain degree from $m$ to $m+1$), inserting a fixed vertex $0$ at the start of every tuple defines a contraction: the internal deletions cancel pairwise and the top deletion composes with the insertion to the identity, so $dh+hd=\mathrm{id}$ on the normalized complex, the augmented term being $q_{p*}I$, identified with the value at the identity tuple. A general injective $J$ is a retract of a product of coinduced injectives by the embedding of step 1.2, and a retract of a contractible complex is contractible, so for every injective $J$ the normalized augmented complex is contractible: $R^jq_*J=0$ for $j>0$ and $q_*J$ is its degree-$0$ part, the equalizer of $q_{0*}J_0\rightrightarrows q_{1*}J_1$. The normalized complex computes the right derived functors of the limit functor because normalization changes no cohomology, and it is contractible, so injective simplicial sheaves are acyclic for $q_*$.

**The derived augmentation model.** Let $F$ be a bounded-below complex of simplicial sheaves with $F^n=0$ for $n<a$, and let $F\to J^\bullet$ be the explicit coinduced injective resolution of step 1.2, chosen with $J^q=0$ for $q<a$. Form the double complex $D^{p,q}:=q_{p*}J^q_p$ for $p\ge0$, $q\ge a$, with $q$-differential the resolution differential and $p$-differential the alternating sum of the vertex-deletion maps of step 2.1 applied to $J^q$ (these are the maps $D^{p,q}\to D^{p+1,q}$ induced by the structure maps of $J^q$ at the face operators, and their squares vanish by the simplicial identities and [F5]). Since $J^q_p$ is injective in $\operatorname{Sh}_k(Z_p)$ by step 2.1, the cohomology in the internal resolution direction is $H^q(D^{p,\bullet})\cong R^qq_{p*}(F_p)$ by [F3]; since $J^q$ is injective in the simplicial category, each column is contractible by step 2.1, so the total complex is quasi-isomorphic to the augmented complex $q_*J^\bullet$, that is, to $Rq_*F$, and the spectral sequence of the filtration by $q$, whose convergence is supplied by [F5], has first page $R^qq_{p*}F_p$ with the alternating face differential. A common internal lower bound makes every diagonal finite: $J^q=0$ for $q<a$, so in total degree $n$ only $0\le p\le n-a$ occurs, each diagonal is a finite sum of complexes of sheaves, and no completion hypothesis is needed. The bisimplicial case is the same argument with two simplicial indices: coinduction is indexed by pairs of operators, the two vertex insertions give the two contractions, finite diagonals follow from the common bound, and iterated and simultaneous totalizations agree on finite diagonals by [F5]. For a composition of augmentations $Z_\bullet\to Y_\bullet\to S$ with exact inverse images, resolving first along $Z_\bullet\to Y_\bullet$ and then along $Y_\bullet\to S$ and totalizing gives a double complex whose two spectral sequences are the two compositions; the comparison maps of the adjunctions compose by naturality of units and counits, and both totalizations have the same finite diagonals, so $R(gf)_*\cong Rg_*\circ Rf_*$ with the models compatible.

**Locally split Čech nerves: the local contraction.** Let $q:P\to S$ admit local sections and let $Z_\bullet$ be its Čech nerve, $Z_p$ the $(p+1)$-fold fibre product of $P$ over $S$ with $q_p$ the projection. A section $s:V\to P$ over an open $V\subseteq S$ gives, for every $p$, the map $e_p:Z_p|_V\to Z_{p+1}|_V$, $(z_0,\dots,z_p)\mapsto(s(q(z_0)),z_0,\dots,z_p)$, which satisfies $d^0e_p=\mathrm{id}$, $d^{i+1}e_p=e_{p-1}d^i$, $\sigma^0e_p=e_{p+1}\sigma^0$ and $\sigma^{i+1}e_p=e_{p-1}\sigma^i$; so $Z_\bullet|_V\to V$ is a split augmented simplicial space. Fix $B\in D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(S))$ and put $F:=q_\bullet^*B$, so that $F_p=q_p^{-1}B$ and every map between the $Z_p$ that is compatible with the projections to $S$ induces a canonical isomorphism between the corresponding pullbacks of $B$, in particular the maps $e_p$ do. Therefore over $V$ the normalized augmented complex of step 2.1 receives contraction maps built from the $e_p$, and the vertex-insertion identity of step 2.1 applies verbatim: the complex is contractible, its degree-$0$ part is $B|_V$, and $R^jq_*(q_\bullet^*B)|_V=0$ for $j>0$. As the section domains $V$ cover $S$, this proves $Rq_*(q_\bullet^*B)\cong B$ and vanishing of the higher derived functors, with the unit of the adjunction $q_\bullet^*\dashv Rq_*$ an isomorphism.

**Full faithfulness and the essential image.** The derived adjunction between $q_\bullet^*$ and $Rq_*$ gives for bounded complexes $A,B$ on $S$ that $\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(q_\bullet^*A,q_\bullet^*B)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(A,Rq_*q_\bullet^*B)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{D}(A,B)$, the second isomorphism by step 3.2 applied to $B$ and naturality of the comparison; by [F6] the same holds in the bounded derived categories, so $q_\bullet^*$ is fully faithful. Its essential image is the full derived subcategory of objects with Cartesian cohomology. Every $q_\bullet^*B$ with $B$ bounded has Cartesian cohomology: the structure maps of $q_\bullet^*B$ are the canonical isomorphisms $Z_\alpha^{-1}q_p^{-1}B\to q_m^{-1}B$ and the same holds after taking cohomology, shifts and cones. Conversely let $F$ be a bounded complex of simplicial sheaves whose cohomology sheaves are Cartesian. Ordinary descent: on a local section domain $V$ the Cartesian structure isomorphisms identify each $F_p|_V$ with the pullback of $F_0|_V$ along any chosen vertex projection, and the simplicial identity for the two composites over overlaps is exactly the cocycle condition, so the local sheaves $F_0|_V$ and their gluing isomorphisms descend to a sheaf $B^j$ on $S$ with $q_\bullet^*B^j\cong H^j(F)$ for each $j$; for the complex, the canonical truncation triangles of [F6] build $F$ from the shifted $H^j(F)$, and full faithfulness lifts each connecting morphism from the descended truncations; induction on the number of nonzero cohomology degrees then realizes $F$ as $q_\bullet^*$ of a bounded complex on $S$.

**Algebraic principal bundles.** When $P\to S$ is an algebraic principal $\mathrm{GL}$-bundle, the fibre products and the structure maps of the Čech nerve are algebraic, the local sections may be taken over an algebraic trivializing cover, and the descent isomorphisms of step 4.1 are algebraic transition functions. Algebraic constructibility of a bounded complex is checked after pullback to a finite algebraic cover by [F8], and the descended cohomology sheaves are glued from the finitely many local models along those transition functions, so they are locally constant of finite rank on the strata of a finite smooth algebraic stratification refining the trivializing cover; hence both directions of the equivalence restrict to the algebraically constructible subcategories. No claim is made about a naive equivariant category for a nonfree action, and no proper-descent statement is used.

**Conclusion and caveats.** Step 1.2 gives the explicit coinduced injective resolutions; step 3.1 gives the derived augmentation model with first page $R^jq_{p*}F_p$, finite diagonals, the bisimplicial case and composition compatibility; steps 3.2, 4.1 and 5.1 give the locally split Čech descent equivalence with Cartesian cohomology and its restriction to the algebraically constructible subcategories. AC enters only through the injective replacements and the products of injectives of [F3] and [F4]; the construction is otherwise formal and uses no proper-hypercover theorem. The declared extension-by-zero input [F9] is retained as ambient data; it is not visibly loaded by the present route, and no statement here depends on it beyond its availability for an explicit open-subspace model.

boundaries.evidence: The empty-index cases are handled by the product conventions of steps 1.2 and 2.1: a product over no monotone maps is the terminal value, and the normalized augmented complex of a coinduced injective still has the augmentation q_{p*}I in degree zero.
The zero simplicial sheaf has the zero coinduced resolution in step 1.2, and its derived augmentation vanishes; the zero complex case of the double complex is treated in step 3.1.
The one-term simplicial diagram (p=0 only) reduces to the ordinary sheaf case in steps 1.2 and 3.1, and the one-section Čech nerve is step 3.2 where the extra degeneracy collapses the complex.

Degenerate simplicial operators are quotiented out in the normalized complex of step 2.1, whose contraction cancels exactly the internal deletions; degeneracies in the extra splitting are used in step 3.2.

The Statement assumes that the map admits local sections in its descent clause. Step 3.2 proves the contraction on each section domain and glues it; it does not assert descent for maps with no local sections.
AC is assumed and used only through the injective replacements and products of injectives of steps 1.2 and 2.1, as declared in the item's axiom_use and facts [F3], [F4] and [F7].
One direction of the descent equivalence is step 4.1: q^* of a bounded complex has Cartesian cohomology, preserved under shifts and cones.
The converse direction is also step 4.1: a bounded complex with Cartesian cohomology is realized by q^* after ordinary descent and truncation induction.

citations.quote: Assume AC. Let $K$ be a finite simplicial complex, $D$ a subcomplex and $X=|K|\setminus|D|$. Let $P$ be the face poset of the open simplices of $K$ not in $D$, ordered by inclusion of faces. The exact realization of finite-dimensional covariant $k$-diagrams on $P$ induces a fully faithful functor into $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$, with essential image the complexes having bounded finite-rank locally constant cohomology on each open simplex. Ordinary and compact-support cohomology, ordinary Hom and internal derived Hom have bounded finite cochain models and commute with every coefficient field extension. For a local product projection $\operatorname{pr}:V\times F\to V$ with supplied finite deleted-boundary models, there is a natural local comparison $R\operatorname{pr}_*\operatorname{pr}^*B\simeq B\otimes_k C^*(F;k)$, taking the unit to $B\otimes(k\to C^*(F;k))$. This does not assert that an arbitrary algebraic map is simplicial.

Let $X$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let $A$ be a
set. A function $f:U\to A$ on an open subset $U\subseteq X$ is **locally
constant** when every $x\in U$ has an open neighbourhood $V\subseteq U$ with
$x\in V$ on which $f$ is constant. Let $A_{\mathrm{pt}}$ be the **constant
presheaf** with value $A$, $A_{\mathrm{pt}}(U)=A$ for every open $U$ with all
restriction maps the identity ([[def-presheaf-on-topological-space]]), and let
$$A_X:=aA_{\mathrm{pt}}$$
be its sheafification ([[def-sheafification]]), the **constant sheaf** with
value $A$ on $X$. Then:

1. the assignment $\underline A_{\mathrm{loc}}(U):=\{f:U\to A\text{ locally
   constant}\}$, with the usual restriction maps, is a sheaf of sets on $X$, and
   for every $x\in X$ evaluation at $x$ is a canonical bijection
   $\underline A_{\mathrm{loc},x}\cong A$
   ([[lem-locally-constant-functions-form-a-sheaf]]);
2. there is a canonical isomorphism of sheaves of sets
   $$\theta:A_X\longrightarrow\underline A_{\mathrm{loc}}$$
   such that for every open $U\subseteq X$ and every $a\in A$ the section
   $\theta_U(\eta_{U}(a))$ is the constant function with value $a$, where
   $\eta:A_{\mathrm{pt}}\to A_X$ is the sheafification map;
3. if $A$ is an abelian group, then $A_{\mathrm{pt}}$ with its group operation is
   a presheaf of abelian groups ([[def-presheaf-of-groups-rings-modules]]) and
   $\underline A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with pointwise addition is a sheaf of abelian
   groups ([[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]]); the maps
   $a\mapsto\text{the constant function with value }a$ are group homomorphisms,
   and the group structures transported along the bijections $\theta_U$ make
   $A_X$ a sheaf of abelian groups for which every $\eta_U$ and every $\theta_U$
   is a group homomorphism.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace, and let
$\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $U$.

For an open set $V \subseteq X$, define
$$(j_!\mathcal F)(V) := \left\{ s\in \mathcal F(V\cap U): \operatorname{Supp}(s)\text{ is closed in }V \right\}.$$
Equivalently, $s$ lies in $(j_!\mathcal F)(V)$ exactly when for every
$x\in V\setminus U$ there exists an open neighbourhood $W_x \subseteq V$ with
$$
s|_{W_x\cap U}=0.
$$

Restriction maps are inherited from $\mathcal F$, so $j_!\mathcal F$ is a
subsheaf of $j_*\mathcal F$. When $V \subseteq U$, the support condition is
vacuous and
$$
(j_!\mathcal F)(V)=\mathcal F(V).
$$

This is the **extension by zero** of $\mathcal F$ along $j$. It is distinct in
general from the ordinary direct image $j_*\mathcal F$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The face poset is $P=\{v_0,v_1,e\}$ with $v_0\le e$ and $v_1\le e$, and every strict chain has length at most one. The incidence cochain model for the derived inverse limit of the diagram $(V_0,V_1,V_e,u_0,u_1)$ is the two-term complex with $C^0=V_0\oplus V_1\oplus V_e$, $C^1=V_e\oplus V_e$ and differential $d(v_0,v_1,w)=(w-u_0v_0,\,w-u_1v_1)$; by [F1] the cohomology of this complex is the actual derived global sections of $F$, so $R^i\Gamma(X,F)$ vanishes outside degrees $0$ and $1$.

Change coordinates invertibly in the source by $t:=w-u_1v_1$ and in the target by $(u,v):=(\text{first output}-\text{second output},\ \text{second output})$. In the new coordinates the differential is $d(t,v_0,v_1)=(u_1v_1-u_0v_0,\,t)$, which is the direct sum of the identity map $C\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}C$ and the two-term complex $[V_0\oplus V_1\xrightarrow{u_0-u_1}V_e]$ up to the harmless sign in the last coordinate. The identity summand is contractible, so $R^i\Gamma(X,F)\cong H^i[V_0\oplus V_1\xrightarrow{u_0-u_1}V_e]$ in degrees $0$ and $1$ and is zero in all other degrees.

For the constant sheaf $F=k_X$ we have $V_0=V_1=V_e=k$ with both generization maps the identity by [F2], so the difference map $k\oplus k\to k$ is surjective with kernel the diagonal copy of $k$; hence $H^0=k$ and $H^1=0$, and all higher cohomology vanishes by step 2.1. For $F=j_!k_{(0,1)}$ the diagram is $V_0=V_1=0$, $V_e=k$ with zero maps by [F3], so the two-term complex reduces to a single copy of $k$ in degree $1$; hence $H^1=k$, $H^0=0$ and all other cohomology vanishes. This proves both stated computations, and no step selects from a family, so no choice beyond the inherited AC is used by the computation.

boundaries.evidence: The empty-summand case does not arise: the face poset of the 1-simplex is nonempty, and step 1.1 exhibits all three open simplices; the empty open-edge case is excluded by the hypothesis that the sheaf is given on the closed interval.
Step 3.1 computes the zero endpoint spaces of the extension-by-zero sheaf j_!k_(0,1), whose diagram is V_0=V_1=0, V_e=k with zero maps.
The rank-one constant sheaf is computed in step 3.1: V_0=V_1=V_e=k with identity generization maps, giving H^0=k and H^1=0.
The degenerate strict chain of length zero and the length-one chains v_0<e, v_1<e are enumerated in step 1.1, so the two-term model is complete.
The two endpoints of the interval are the boundary case computed in steps 1.1 and 3.1; the open edge is the remaining simplex and is handled by the extension-by-zero computation.
The computation is finite linear algebra; AC is inherited from the incidence lemma cited in step 1.1 and no further selection occurs, as recorded in fact [F4].
The forward reading of the two stated computations is step 3.1: the constant sheaf gives k in degree zero, and the extension by zero gives k in degree one.
The vanishing halves are also step 3.1: H^1=0 for the constant sheaf and H^0=0 for the extension by zero, with all higher cohomology vanishing by the two-term model of step 2.1.

The Definition admits the empty variety with the empty finite stratification, and clause (e) with $D=K=arnothing$ presents the empty deleted-boundary model; no clause requires a stratum or simplex to exist.

boundaries.reason: The Definition asserts no count or quotient; clause (b) requires $ho_R^{-1}(0)=R$, which is a defining condition rather than a boundary case to discharge.
The clauses are stated for arbitrary finite stratifications and finite complexes, so no singleton restriction or one-stratum hypothesis occurs.

boundaries.evidence: Clause (d) permits an empty link, whose cone is a single apex by convention, so the minimal-stratum conical chart is admissible under the Definition itself.

boundaries.reason: Tubes may be shrunk and radial data reparametrized, but no limiting endpoint is asserted; local properness is stated over compact slices instead of at a boundary value.

boundaries.evidence: The Definition records that no choice principle is used: tube maps, radii, links and triangulations are supplied data, and the conical chart is a given homeomorphism rather than a selected one.

boundaries.reason: Clauses (a)-(e) introduce terminology; none asserts an implication between independent conditions, so no forward direction exists to discharge.
No converse is owed: the Definition does not characterize structures already defined elsewhere by an equivalent condition.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:X\to S$ be a finite morphism of schemes. Then every ring map $A\to B$ induced by $f$ on an affine chart $U=\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq S$ with $f^{-1}(U)=\operatorname{Spec}B$ is integral. Moreover $f$ is universally closed: for every morphism $T\to S$ the base-changed projection $X\times_ST\to T$ is a closed map, so the image of $X\times_ST$ and of every closed subset of it is closed in $|T|$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:A\to B$ be an integral ring map, and let $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(A)$ with $\ker f\subseteq\mathfrak p$. Then there exists a prime ideal $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}(B)$ such that $f^{-1}(\mathfrak q)=\mathfrak p$.

Let $k$ be a field and let $A$ be a nonzero finite-type $k$-algebra. Then there exist algebraically independent elements $z_1,\ldots,z_d\in A$ such that $A$ is a module-finite algebra over the polynomial ring $k[z_1,\ldots,z_d]$.

If $X$ is an irreducible classical variety, then $\dim X=\operatorname{trdeg}_k k(X)<\infty$. Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. u\colon C^{\mathrm{nu}}	o C$ with the following properties: 1. $C^{\mathrm{nu}}$ is regular of dimension one (equivalently normal: all local rings are discrete valuation rings or fields); 2. $
u$ is an isomorphism over the regular locus of $C$ and is birational on each irreducible component; 3. on an affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $C$, $
u$ is the morphism corresponding to the integral closure of $A$ in its total ring of fractions; 4. $
u$ is unique up to a unique $C$-isomorphism, and $
u_*\mathcal O_{C^{\mathrm{nu}}}$ is a coherent $\mathcal O_C$-module. No separability or perfectness hypothesis on $k$ is needed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a perfect field and let $X$ be a finite-type $k$-scheme. Here **regular** means that $X$ is locally Noetherian and every local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is regular local; **smooth over $k$** means that $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth under the local-standard-smooth convention of [[def-smooth-morphism-classical]]. Then $$X\text{ is regular}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X\to\operatorname{Spec}k\text{ is smooth}.$$ No reducedness, irreducibility, or closed-point restriction is imposed.

Let $C$ be a complex algebraic curve, meaning a one-dimensional algebraic set over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-affine-algebraic-set]]), and let $p\in C$ lie either in $\mathbb C^N$ (affine case) or in a standard affine chart of $\mathbb{CP}^N$ with its coordinates $(\zeta_1/\zeta_i,\dots)$ (projective case, [[def-projective-space-points]]). Assume that near $p$ the curve is the common zero set of holomorphic functions $f_1,\dots,f_{N-1}$ on a neighbourhood of $p$, and that their complex Jacobian matrix at $p$ has rank $N-1$. Here the matrix $J_F(p)=(\partial f_i/\partial t_j(p))$ uses the equation-row and coordinate-column convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-affine-algebraic-set]], extended directly to the stated local holomorphic functions by their complex partial derivatives; this hypothesis is the **Jacobian-rank sense** of nonsingularity used in this pair. Then there are an index $j$, a plane domain $A\subseteq\mathbb C$ and a holomorphic map $\phi:A\to\mathbb C^{N-1}$ such that, after permuting the coordinates so that the $j$-th coordinate comes first, $C$ agrees near $p$ with the graph $\{(z,\phi(z)):z\in A\}$, and the projection $(z,\phi(z))\mapsto z$ is a homeomorphism of that neighbourhood of $p$ in $C$ onto the plane domain $A$ whose inverse $z\mapsto(z,\phi(z))$ is holomorphic: one free ambient coordinate is a local parameter. Moreover, if two such local parameters $z$ and $w$ are defined on overlapping pieces, coming from the same ambient chart or from two standard affine charts, then the transition $z\mapsto w$ is holomorphic wherever both are defined.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$. Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible: $$\det\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial w_k}(a,b)\right)_{1\le j,k\le n}\ne0.$$ Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique holomorphic map $\varphi:A\to B$, such that $$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$ and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed, $$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

Let $k$ be any field, let $n\geq0$ be finite, let $I$ be an ideal of $k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$, and put $$X=\operatorname{Spec}(k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]/I).$$ Let $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in X(k)$, and let $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ be any finite generating list of the actual ideal $I$. Then the coordinate-velocity map gives a canonical $k$-linear isomorphism $$T_aX\cong\ker\!\left(J_{(f_1,\ldots,f_r)}(a):k^n\longrightarrow k^r\right).$$ The kernel is independent of the chosen finite generating list of $I$. No reducedness, perfectness, or characteristic hypothesis is needed. Finiteness of the list is available for every finite $n$ by the finite-variable polynomial Noetherian result cited below.

Let $X$ be a locally Noetherian scheme and $x\in X$. Write $R=\mathcal O_{X,x}$, let $\mathfrak m_x$ be its maximal ideal, and set $\kappa(x)=R/\mathfrak m_x$. The point $x$ is **regular** when $R$ is a regular local ring, with regularity defined by $\operatorname{edim}R=\dim R$. Then the intrinsic tangent space $T_xX$ is finite-dimensional over $\kappa(x)$, and $$x\text{ is regular}\Longleftrightarrow\dim_{\kappa(x)}T_xX=\dim\mathcal O_{X,x}.$$ This is absolute regularity of the local ring; it asserts no smoothness over a base field.
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every nonzero commutative Noetherian local ring $R$ satisfies $\dim R\le\operatorname{edim}R<\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). A regular local ring $R$ of dimension $d$ is a domain and Cohen–Macaulay. For every regular system $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$, the tuple is $R$-regular and $R/(x_1,\ldots,x_c)$ is regular local of dimension $d-c$ for all $0\le c\le d$.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring. Then the polynomial ring $R[x]$ is a Noetherian commutative ring. No hypothesis beyond Noetherianity is placed on $R$: it may have zero divisors, and it may be the zero ring.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function > ([[def-choice-function]]). Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty, there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for all $S \in \mathcal{F}$. An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if $X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$. Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that $f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

citations.quote: Let $X$ be a reduced quasi-projective complex algebraic variety, regarded as a classical variety over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]) with its analytic topology, its smooth points (regular local rings) and its finite smooth algebraic frontier stratifications ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). (a) **Whitney conditions.** Let $X=\coprod_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha$ be a finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification whose strata are pure-dimensional, and let $R\subseteq\overline S\setminus S$ be incident strata. In local analytic charts of an ambient smooth manifold, the pair $(S,R)$ satisfies **Whitney (a)** at $y\in R$ if for every sequence $x_n\in S$ with $x_n\to y$ whose tangent planes $T_{x_n}S$ converge to a plane $T$, one has $T_yR\subseteq T$; it satisfies **Whitney (b)** at $y$ if additionally, whenever $y_n\in R$ with $y_n\to y$ and the real secant lines through $x_n,y_n$ converge to a line $\ell$, one has $\ell\subseteq T$. A **finite complex algebraic Whitney stratification** of $X$ is a finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification satisfying (a) and (b) at every point of every incident pair. Coordinate independence of the limits and the implication (b)$\Rightarrow$(a), commonly used in the literature, are not assumed as proved here; requiring both conditions makes the intended interface explicit. (b) **Tube control data.** A system of **tube control data** on the analytic stratified space $X$ consists of an open neighbourhood $T_R$ of each stratum $R$, a continuous retraction $\pi_R:T_R\to R$ and a continuous radius $\rho_R:T_R\to[0,\infty)$ such that $\rho_R^{-1}(0)=R$, both maps are smooth on each stratum, and for every incident upper stratum $S$ the pair $(\pi_R,\rho_R)$ restricts to a submersion $S\cap T_R\to R\times(0,\infty)$. On the overlap neighbourhoods where the compositions are defined one requires $\pi_R\pi_S=\pi_R$ and $\rho_R\pi_S=\rho_R$ for $R<S$; every compatibility assertion must name the common domain on which the composition is defined. Tubes may be shrunk. For local conical constructions one requires local properness over compact base slices: sufficiently small closed radius ranges over a compact neighbourhood in $R$ have compact inverse image inside the tube. (c) **$f$-compatible tubes and controlled lifts.** Let $f:W\to B$ be a stratified submersion onto a smooth manifold. A tube system is **$f$-compatible** if $f\pi_R=f$ on the tubes used. A **controlled lift** of a smooth base field $v$ on $B$ is a field $V$ that is smooth on each stratum and satisfies $df(V)=v\circ f$, $d\pi_R(V)=V|_R\circ\pi_R$ and $d\rho_R(V)=0$ on specified controlled tube neighbourhoods. **Locally bounded** means the ambient norm is bounded on a neighbourhood of every point; this is an additional hypothesis, not a consequence of the definition. **Radial controlled lifts** instead satisfy $d\rho_R(V)=\rho_R$ with fixed $\pi_R$ together with the appropriate annular overlap controls. (d) **Conical product neighbourhoods.** A **conical product neighbourhood along $R$** is a stratum-preserving homeomorphism from a neighbourhood of a point of $R$ to $B^{2\dim_{\mathbb C}R}\times c(L)$ carrying $R$ to the ball times the cone apex, with compact finitely Whitney-stratified $L$. The radial and tangential transports must be compatible with the actual coefficient data when cohomological local systems are deduced; topological existence alone does not supply canonical derived-sheaf transport. (e) **Finite triangulation of a noncompact space.** In the compactification convention used here, a **finite triangulation** of a noncompact space $X$ consists of finite simplicial complexes $D\subseteq K$ together with a homeomorphism $|K|\setminus|D|\to X$; compatibility with prescribed subsets means they are unions of interiors of retained simplices. This does not assert that algebraic morphisms become simplicial, and real simplicial dimensions do not replace the complex dimensions of the algebraic strata.

For a dominant morphism $f:X\to Y$ between irreducible classical varieties, there is a nonempty open $U\subseteq Y$, contained in $f(X)$, such that every $X_y$ with $y\in U$ is nonempty and has pure dimension $r=\dim X-\dim Y$. Let $V$ be an irreducible complex algebraic variety of positive dimension ([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), let $O\subseteq V$ be a nonempty Zariski open subset and let $z\in V$. There is an irreducible algebraic curve $C\subseteq V$ through $z$ not contained in $V\setminus O$. There is also a holomorphic map $\gamma:\Delta\to V$ from a sufficiently small complex disk, with $\gamma(0)=z$ and $\gamma(s)\in O$ for all $s\ne0$; here $\Delta$ is a disk centred at $0$ and a map into $V$ is holomorphic when its coordinate functions in an affine model containing its image are holomorphic. The arc can be obtained by analytically parametrizing a point over $z$ in the finite normalization of $C$.

Let $k$ be any field, let $n\geq0$ be finite, let $I$ be an ideal of $k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$, and put $$X=\operatorname{Spec}(k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]/I).$$ Let $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in X(k)$, and let $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ be any finite generating list of the actual ideal $I$. Then the coordinate-velocity map gives a canonical $k$-linear isomorphism $$T_aX\cong\ker\!\left(J_{(f_1,\ldots,f_r)}(a):k^n\longrightarrow k^r\right).$$ The kernel is independent of the chosen finite generating list of $I$. For every $r$-subset $I$ of a basis of an $n$-dimensional $V$, the locus $p_I\ne0$ in $\operatorname{Gr}(r,V)$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf A_k^{r(n-r)}$; these loci cover the Grassmannian and have regular transition maps.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A **standard smooth presentation** of an $R$-algebra $S$ consists of integers $n\ge c\ge0$, elements $f_1,\dots,f_c$ of the polynomial ring $P=R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ ([[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]]) and an element $g\in P$ such that $$S\cong\bigl(R[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(f_1,\dots,f_c)\bigr)_g$$ as $R$-algebras, and such that the Jacobian matrix of ([[lem-ag-polynomial-quotient-differentials]]) $$\Bigl(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial x_i}\Bigr)_{\substack{1\le j\le c\\1\le i\le n}}$$ has a $c\times c$ minor whose image in $S$ is a unit, that is, an invertible element. The integer $n-c\ge0$ is the **relative dimension** of the presentation. The case $c=0$ is allowed and is exactly a localisation of a polynomial ring, $S\cong(R[x_1,\dots,x_n])_g$; the case $n=c=0$ presents $S=R[\,]_g$ for $g\in R$, that is a localisation of $R$ itself. For a homomorphism $R\to S$ of commutative rings that is finitely presented as an $R$-algebra ([[def-finitely-presented-module-and-algebra]]) and a prime $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$, the map is **standard smooth at $\mathfrak q$**, or has a standard smooth presentation at $\mathfrak q$, when there is $h\in S\smallsetminus\mathfrak q$ such that $S_h$ admits a standard smooth presentation over $R$. It is **locally standard smooth** when this holds at every prime of $S$; equivalently, when every point of $\operatorname{Spec}S$ has an affine open neighbourhood on which $S$ is presented by a single standard smooth presentation. Two conventions are part of the definition. First, the invertible minor may be assumed to sit in the first $c$ columns: if a minor on columns $i_1<\dots<i_c$ is a unit, the automorphism of $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ permuting the variables so that these become the first $c$ variables carries the presentation to one whose minor in the first $c$ columns is that unit, and the relative dimension $n-c$ is unchanged. Second, a further principal localisation can be absorbed into the presentation: adjoining a variable $z$ with the single equation $zg-1$ to a presentation produces a standard smooth presentation of the localisation, the new equation contributing a diagonal entry that keeps a block minor invertible, and it changes $n$ and $c$ by the same amount, so that the relative dimension is again unchanged.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$. Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible: $$\det\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial w_k}(a,b)\right)_{1\le j,k\le n}\ne0.$$ Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique holomorphic map $\varphi:A\to B$, such that $$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$ and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed, $$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a perfect field and let $X$ be a finite-type $k$-scheme. Here **regular** means that $X$ is locally Noetherian and every local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is regular local; **smooth over $k$** means that $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth under the local-standard-smooth convention of [[def-smooth-morphism-classical]]. Then $$X\text{ is regular}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X\to\operatorname{Spec}k\text{ is smooth}.$$ No reducedness, irreducibility, or closed-point restriction is imposed.

Fix an algebraically closed field $k$. The affine models used here are polynomial zero sets $Z\subseteq k^n$, including empty and reducible sets. Their closed subsets are common zero loci of polynomial families, relative to $Z$. Intersections combine equations, and finite unions use products of equations, so these are the closed sets of a topology. For an open $U\subseteq Z$, let $\mathcal O_Z(U)$ consist of functions $U\to k$ locally equal to $a/b$ for polynomials $a,b$ with $b$ nonvanishing on the chosen neighbourhood. Pointwise operations and restriction make these sets a sheaf of $k$-algebras: quotient expressions persist on restriction, and functions that agree locally glue uniquely with the same local quotient property. At a point z its stalk is the ring of germs of such functions. Evaluation at z maps it onto k, with kernel the germs vanishing at z. A germ nonzero at z is invertible: shrink to where its numerator and denominator are both nonzero and interchange them. Thus the kernel is the unique maximal ideal. These affine models are locally ringed spaces in the sense of [[def-locally-ringed-space]], with residue fields canonically k. A **classical algebraic prevariety** over k is a quasi-compact locally ringed space with a structure sheaf of k-algebras, covered by open subspaces isomorphic over k to these affine models. Here quasi-compact means every open cover has a finite subcover. Equivalently it admits a finite affine-model cover. To justify the converse, each affine model is quasi-compact: polynomial principal opens $D_Z(h)=\{z:h(z)\ne0\}$ form a basis. Given an open cover, take all h whose principal opens lie in a member. Their principal opens cover Z. The ideal generated by these h in $k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$ is finitely generated by [[thm-hilbert-basis-theorem]], iterated from the field k. Express finitely many generators using finitely many of the original h. Those finitely many h have the same common zero locus as the whole ideal, hence their principal opens still cover Z and yield a finite subcover. The empty model has the empty subcover. A finite union of quasi-compact subspaces is quasi-compact. A map is **regular** when it is a morphism of locally ringed spaces as in [[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]] whose sheaf maps respect k. For these function sheaves its sheaf map is necessarily pullback of functions: the local stalk map induces a k-map between residue fields k, hence the identity, so the value of a pulled-back section at x is its value at the image of x. Conversely, continuous pullback of local regular functions gives a local stalk map because a function vanishing at the image vanishes after pullback. Regularity can therefore be checked on affine charts: near every source point choose a target affine chart containing its image and an open neighbourhood in a source affine chart mapped into it; the target coordinate functions must pull back to locally polynomial quotients. This condition also implies continuity. Indeed zero sets of locally polynomial quotients are locally polynomial zero sets, hence closed; pulling back polynomial equations consequently gives closed sets. Substitution then pulls every local quotient on the target back to a local quotient on the source, using this continuity to restrict to its domain and its nonvanishing denominator. Thus the chart condition and the locally ringed-space definition agree. A prevariety is **separated** when the equalizer of every pair of regular maps into it, from any classical prevariety, is closed. A **classical algebraic variety** is a separated prevariety. Here varieties may be reducible or empty; an **irreducible classical variety** is nonempty and irreducible in the sense of [[def-irreducible-topological-space-and-subset]]. These definitions and the local verifications above use no Axiom of Choice.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if $X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$. Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that $f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
