boundaries.reason: No zero value or vanishing count occurs; the statements are conditional on properness.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.3 records that a one-point space is compact and therefore fibres are compact, and step 1.1 uses the one-point base in the closed-inclusion case.

boundaries.reason: There is no degenerate parameter; the six claims are structural and hold for arbitrary topological spaces under their stated hypotheses.
No interval or limiting endpoint occurs.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 records that no choice principle is used: the compactness and closedness arguments are finite or reduce to closedness of compact subsets in Hausdorff spaces.

boundaries.reason: Only the six stated stability implications are asserted, and none of them is a biconditional, so no forward direction of an equivalence is owed.
Each clause is a sufficient stability condition on proper maps; none asserts the converse of the others.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, and let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space. Then
the abelian category $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$ of $\mathcal O_X$-modules has
enough injectives: every $\mathcal O_X$-module embeds into an injective
$\mathcal O_X$-module, and the functorial injective embedding supplied by the
Grothendieck injective-embedding theorem for Grothendieck categories supplies,
by iteration of cokernels, one specific injective resolution
$$0\to\mathcal F\to I^0(\mathcal F)\to I^1(\mathcal F)\to\cdots$$
to each $\mathcal O_X$-module $\mathcal F$ with no further selection
([[def-injective-resolution-in-an-abelian-category]]). The Axiom of Choice
enters exactly through that embedding theorem applied to
$\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$; the category-theoretic verification below is
choice-free.

Let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on a topological space $X$. We say that
$\mathcal F$ is a **sheaf** if for every open set $U \subseteq X$ and every
open cover $U=\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i$, including the empty cover of
$\varnothing$, the following two conditions hold.

**Locality.** If $s,t\in\mathcal F(U)$ satisfy
$$s|_{U_i}=t|_{U_i}\qquad\text{for all }i\in I,$$
then $s=t$.

**Gluing.** If sections $s_i\in\mathcal F(U_i)$ satisfy
$$s_i|_{U_i\cap U_j}=s_j|_{U_i\cap U_j}\qquad\text{for all }i,j\in I,$$
then there exists $s\in\mathcal F(U)$ such that
$$s|_{U_i}=s_i\qquad\text{for all }i\in I.$$

By locality, such a section $s$ is automatically unique. Thus a sheaf is
exactly a presheaf whose compatible local sections glue uniquely.

If $\mathcal A$ has enough injectives and $X^n=0$ for $n<a$, there is a termwise monic quasi-isomorphism $j:X\to I$ with each $I^n$ injective and $I^n=0$ for $n<a$. Assume DC for the successive objectwise choices, or supply the successive injective monomorphisms. If only $H^n(X)=0$ for $n<a$, a quasi-isomorphism to such an $I$ still exists, without the termwise-monic assertion.

With supplied bounded-below injective replacements $j_X:X\to I_X$ (and DC or supplied homotopy extensions), $K^+(\operatorname{Inj}\mathcal A)\to D^+(\mathcal A)$ is an equivalence of triangulated categories. For a bounded-below complex $I$, K-injectivity can be tested using only bounded-below acyclic inputs.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, let $\mathcal G$ be a sheaf on $Y$, and let
$x\in X$. Then there is a canonical isomorphism
$$
(f^{-1}\mathcal G)_x\cong \mathcal G_{f(x)}.
$$

Let
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{i-1}\xrightarrow{d_{i-1}}\mathcal F_i\xrightarrow{d_i}\mathcal F_{i+1}\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
be a sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space $X$. Then the
sequence is exact if and only if, for every point $x\in X$, the stalk sequence
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow (\mathcal F_{i-1})_x\xrightarrow{(d_{i-1})_x}(\mathcal F_i)_x\xrightarrow{(d_i)_x}(\mathcal F_{i+1})_x\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
is exact.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, let $\mathcal G$ be a sheaf on $Y$, and let
$\mathcal F$ be a sheaf on $X$. Then there is a natural bijection
$$\operatorname{Hom}_X(f^{-1}\mathcal G,\mathcal F) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_Y(\mathcal G,f_*\mathcal F).$$

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, and let $\mathcal G$ be a presheaf on $Y$.
The **inverse-image presheaf**
$$
f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G
$$
on $X$ is defined by
$$
(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U):=\varinjlim_{f(U)\subseteq V}\mathcal G(V),
$$
where $V$ runs over the open neighbourhoods of $f(U)$ in $Y$, ordered by
reverse inclusion. If $U' \subseteq U$, then every neighbourhood of $f(U)$ is a
neighbourhood of $f(U')$, so there is a natural restriction map
$(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U)\to(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U')$.

The **inverse image sheaf** of a sheaf $\mathcal G$ on $Y$ is the sheafification
of this presheaf:
$$
f^{-1}\mathcal G:=a(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G).
$$

When $U$ is open in $X$ and $V$ is an open set of $Y$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$,
there is a canonical map
$$
\mathcal G(V)\longrightarrow(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U)
$$
into the colimit class represented by $V$.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, and let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on $X$.
The **direct image presheaf**
$$f_*\mathcal F$$
on $Y$ is defined on an open set $V \subseteq Y$ by
$$
(f_*\mathcal F)(V):=\mathcal F(f^{-1}(V)).
$$
If $V' \subseteq V$, the restriction map
$$
(f_*\mathcal F)(V)\longrightarrow(f_*\mathcal F)(V')
$$
is the restriction map of $\mathcal F$ for the inclusion
$f^{-1}(V') \subseteq f^{-1}(V)$.

Thus direct image is just precomposition of the presheaf with the inverse-image
map on open sets.

Let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space, and let $\mathcal F,\mathcal G$ be
$\mathcal O_X$-modules. The **tensor-product presheaf**
$$
\mathcal F\otimes_{p,\mathcal O_X}\mathcal G
$$
is defined by
$$(\mathcal F\otimes_{p,\mathcal O_X}\mathcal G)(U) := \mathcal F(U)\otimes_{\mathcal O_X(U)}\mathcal G(U)$$
for each open set $U \subseteq X$, with restriction induced from the
restriction maps of $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal G$.

The **tensor-product sheaf** is the sheafification of this presheaf:
$$\mathcal F\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}\mathcal G := a(\mathcal F\otimes_{p,\mathcal O_X}\mathcal G).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space, and let $\mathcal F,\mathcal G$ be
$\mathcal O_X$-modules. The **internal Hom sheaf**
$$
\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal F,\mathcal G)
$$
is the sheaf on $X$ defined by
$$U\longmapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_X|_U}(\mathcal F|_U,\mathcal G|_U)$$
for each open set $U \subseteq X$.

Restriction to a smaller open set $V \subseteq U$ sends a morphism
$\mathcal F|_U\to\mathcal G|_U$ to its restriction
$\mathcal F|_V\to\mathcal G|_V$. Multiplication by a local section
$a\in \mathcal O_X(U)$ acts on a morphism $\varphi$ by either pre- or
post-composition with multiplication by $a$, giving
$\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal F,\mathcal G)$ the structure of an
$\mathcal O_X$-module.

Let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on a topological space $X$. For every $x\in X$,
the sheafification map induces a bijection
$$\eta_{\mathcal F,x}:\mathcal F_x\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }(a\mathcal F)_x.$$

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace.

1. For every sheaf of abelian groups $\mathcal F$ on $U$ and every sheaf of
   abelian groups $\mathcal G$ on $X$, there is a natural bijection
   $$\operatorname{Hom}_X(j_!\mathcal F,\mathcal G) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_U(\mathcal F,j^{-1}\mathcal G).$$
2. The functor $j_!$ is exact on sheaves of abelian groups.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace, and let
$\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $U$.

For an open set $V \subseteq X$, define
$$(j_!\mathcal F)(V) := \left\{ s\in \mathcal F(V\cap U): \operatorname{Supp}(s)\text{ is closed in }V \right\}.$$
Equivalently, $s$ lies in $(j_!\mathcal F)(V)$ exactly when for every
$x\in V\setminus U$ there exists an open neighbourhood $W_x \subseteq V$ with
$$
s|_{W_x\cap U}=0.
$$

Restriction maps are inherited from $\mathcal F$, so $j_!\mathcal F$ is a
subsheaf of $j_*\mathcal F$. When $V \subseteq U$, the support condition is
vacuous and
$$
(j_!\mathcal F)(V)=\mathcal F(V).
$$

This is the **extension by zero** of $\mathcal F$ along $j$. It is distinct in
general from the ordinary direct image $j_*\mathcal F$.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ be abelian categories, let $I$ be supplied
injective resolution data on all objects of $\mathcal A$, and let
$F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be an additive left exact functor. Then the additive functors
$$R_I^nF:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B,\qquad n\geq 0,$$
admit connecting maps that make them into a cohomological delta functor on
$\mathcal A$, and $R_I^0F$ is naturally isomorphic to $F$.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $I$ be a supplied injective resolution datum on a class $\mathcal D$ and
$F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ an additive functor between abelian categories.
If $J\in\mathcal D$ is an injective object, then for every $n>0$,
$$R_I^nF(J)=0.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a topological space $X$, let
$$\Gamma(X,-):\mathrm{Ab}(X)\to\mathbf{Ab}$$
be the additive left exact global-sections functor
([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]]), and let $I$ be the supplied
functorial injective resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ of
[[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]]: it assigns to every abelian
sheaf $\mathcal F$ one specific injective resolution
$0\to\mathcal F\to I^\bullet(\mathcal F)$
([[def-right-derived-object-relative-to-injective-resolution-data]]).

For every $q\ge0$ and every abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$ define the
**$q$-th sheaf cohomology group of $\mathcal F$** to be the right derived
object of $\Gamma(X,-)$ relative to $I$:
$$H^q(X,\mathcal F):=R_I^q\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)=H^q\bigl(\Gamma(X,I^\bullet(\mathcal F)_{\mathrm{del}})\bigr),$$
the cohomology object of the complex
$\Gamma(X,I^0(\mathcal F))\to\Gamma(X,I^1(\mathcal F))\to\cdots$ of abelian
groups obtained from the deleted resolution
([[def-deleted-resolution]], [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]]).
We also set $H^q(X,\mathcal F):=0$ for $q<0$.

Because $I$ is a fixed supplied datum, the group $H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ is a
specific group for each pair $(X,\mathcal F)$, and for a morphism
$\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian sheaves we write
$H^q(X,\varphi):=R_I^q\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ for the induced map; it is the map on
cohomology induced by $\Gamma(X,-)$ applied to the cochain maps supplied with
the datum, and it is additive in $\varphi$.

If $J$ is another supplied injective resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ then
$R_I^q\Gamma(X,-)$ and $R_J^q\Gamma(X,-)$ are naturally isomorphic, so the
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ computed from $J$ agree with the ones above up to a
canonical natural isomorphism; the Axiom of Dependent Choice needed for that
comparison follows from AC
([[thm-right-derived-functors-from-two-supplied-injective-resolution-data-are-naturally-isomorphic]],
[[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]). The notation
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ therefore does not depend on the datum used, up to this
canonical isomorphism, and we call $q$ the **cohomological degree**.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a topological space and let
$$0\to\mathcal F\to\mathcal G\xrightarrow{\ \varphi\ }\mathcal H\to0$$
be a short exact sequence of abelian sheaves on $X$
([[def-exact-sequence-sheaves]]) in which $\mathcal F$ is flasque
([[def-flasque-sheaf]]).

1. For every open subset $U\subseteq X$ the map
   $\varphi_U:\mathcal G(U)\to\mathcal H(U)$ is surjective.
2. If moreover $\mathcal G$ is flasque, then $\mathcal H$ is flasque.

The Axiom of Choice is used exactly once, to apply Zorn's lemma in part 1
([[thm-zorn]], [[cor-ac-iff-zorn]]).

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian
groups on $X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]],
[[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]]). For open subsets
$U\subseteq V\subseteq X$ write
$$\rho^V_U:\mathcal F(V)\longrightarrow\mathcal F(U)$$
for the restriction map of $\mathcal F$
([[def-section-restriction-and-global-section]]).

Then $\mathcal F$ is **flasque**, also called **flabby**, when each of these
restriction maps is surjective: for all open $U\subseteq V\subseteq X$ the map
$\rho^V_U$ is onto. Equivalently, $\mathcal F$ is flasque when every section of
$\mathcal F$ over an open subset $U$ extends to every larger open subset $V$,
that is, when for every $s\in\mathcal F(U)$ there is $t\in\mathcal F(V)$ with
$t|_U=s$.

The same condition on restriction maps defines flasque sheaves of sets and
flasque sheaves of modules over a sheaf of rings; on this page the notion is
used for sheaves of abelian groups.

For a chain map $f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$, the cone $\operatorname{Cone}(f)$ is
acyclic if and only if $f$ is a quasi-isomorphism. This is exactly the same
criterion already recorded on the mapping-cone page.

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category. We use cochains as in [[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]], with $X[k]^n=X^{n+k}$ and $d_{X[k]}^n=(-1)^kd_X^{n+k}$. Thus $H^n(X[k])=H^{n+k}(X)$. The cochain category $K(\mathcal A)$ is the reindexed published homotopy category. Put

$$D(\mathcal A)=K(\mathcal A)[\mathrm{qis}^{-1}],\qquad Q:K(\mathcal A)\longrightarrow D(\mathcal A).$$

Likewise $D^-,D^+,D^b$ initially mean the localizations of the termwise bounded variants of [[def-bounded-bounded-below-and-bounded-above-complex]]. Roof morphisms exist by [[lem-quasi-isomorphisms-admit-the-roof-calculus-in-the-homotopy-category]] and [[thm-the-calculus-of-fractions-constructs-the-localization]] under its standing size hypothesis: a small category of complexes, or supplied small cofinal denominator families. Every assertion of Hom sets is under that hypothesis. In the bounded module models, supplied replacements will separately exhibit those Hom sets. No general local-smallness theorem for unbounded $D(\mathcal A)$ is asserted.

The cone convention is $\operatorname{Cone}(f)^n=Y^n\oplus X^{n+1}$, $d(y,x)=(d_Yy+fx,-d_Xx)$, and its triangle ends in $X[1]$.

Let
$$0\to A^\bullet\to B^\bullet\to C^\bullet\to0$$
be a short exact sequence of cochain complexes in an abelian category. Then
there is a natural exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H^n(A)\to H^n(B)\to H^n(C)\xrightarrow{\partial^n}H^{n+1}(A)\to H^{n+1}(B)\to H^{n+1}(C)\to\cdots.$$

Let $K^{p,q}$ be a first-quadrant double cochain complex whose signed total
complex uses finite direct sums on every diagonal. Suppose a cochain complex
$C^\bullet$ maps to the bottom edge so that, for every $p$, the augmented
column
$$0\longrightarrow C^p\longrightarrow K^{p,0}\xrightarrow{v}K^{p,1}\xrightarrow{v}K^{p,2}\longrightarrow\cdots$$
is exact and the augmentations commute with the horizontal maps. Then the
induced cochain map $C^\bullet\to\operatorname{Tot}K$ is a quasi-isomorphism.

derivations.claim: The inverse image $f^*=f^{-1}$ is exact and $f^*\dashv f_*$, and $f_*$ preserves injective objects. By [F4] there is a natural isomorphism $(f^{-1}G)_x\cong G_{f(x)}$ under which the stalk of $f^{-1}\varphi$ is $\varphi_{f(x)}$; since exactness is tested stalkwise, $f^{-1}$ preserves kernels, images and cokernels and is exact. The adjunction bijection of [F4] is $k$-linear, its two directions being given on sections by the canonical $k$-linear maps $G\to f_*f^{-1}G$ and $f^{-1}f_*F\to F$; hence $f^*$ is left adjoint to $f_*$ in $\operatorname{Sh}_k$. If $I$ is injective, then $\operatorname{Hom}_Y(-,f_*I)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_X(f^*(-),I)$ is a composite of the exact functor $f^*$ and the exact representable functor $\operatorname{Hom}_X(-,I)$, so $f_*I$ is injective.

The tensor product has the expected stalks, and tensoring is exact in each variable. Define $A\otimes_kB$ as the sheafification of the sectionwise tensor presheaf of [F5]. By [F5] sheafification preserves stalks, so $(A\otimes_kB)_x$ is the filtered colimit $\varinjlim_U A(U)\otimes_kB(U)$ over the open neighbourhoods of $x$; since tensor products of vector spaces commute with filtered colimits, this is $A_x\otimes_kB_x$, and the stalk of $A\otimes\varphi$ is $\operatorname{id}\otimes\varphi_x$. For fixed $B$, the functor $A\mapsto A\otimes_kB$ is therefore stalkwise $A_x\mapsto A_x\otimes_kB_x$, which is exact because every $k$-vector space is flat, and exactness is stalkwise by [F4]; the same holds in the other variable. The restriction to opens is the evident one, so all these maps are compatible with restriction, and no choice is used in this step.

Injective $k$-sheaves are flasque. Let $I$ be injective and let $U\subseteq V$ be open. The canonical map $j_{U!}k_U\to j_{V!}k_V$ of [F6] is a monomorphism of $k$-sheaves: on stalks it is the identity $k\to k$ on $U$, the monomorphism $0\to k$ on $V\setminus U$, and $0\to0$ elsewhere. By [F6], $\operatorname{Hom}_X(j_{U!}k_U,I)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_U(k_U,I|_U)\cong I(U)$ and similarly with $V$. Injectivity of $I$ extends every morphism $j_{U!}k_U\to I$, that is, every section over $U$, along this monomorphism to a morphism $j_{V!}k_V\to I$, that is, a section over $V$ restricting to it. Hence the restriction $I(V)\to I(U)$ is surjective, and $I$ is flasque by [F8].

The adjunction $f^*\dashv Rf_*$ holds on bounded-below derived categories. Let $F$ be a bounded-below complex on $X$ and let $j:F\to I_F$ be a bounded-below termwise injective replacement, supplied under DC by [F3]; declare $Rf_*F:=f_*I_F$, well defined up to canonical isomorphism because any two such replacements are homotopy equivalent by [F3] and $f_*$ preserves homotopy equivalences. Since $f_*$ preserves zero objects in each degree, $f_*I_F$ is bounded below, and it is termwise injective by step 1.1; hence it is K-injective by [F3], and for every bounded-below complex $G$ on $Y$ the localization identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_{D(Y)}(G,f_*I_F)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{K(Y)}(G,f_*I_F)$. The levelwise adjunction of [F4] identifies this with $\operatorname{Hom}_{K(X)}(f^*G,I_F)$, and because $I_F$ is K-injective and quasi-isomorphic to $F$, this is $\operatorname{Hom}_{D(X)}(f^*G,F)$. All identifications are natural and $k$-linear, and the triangle identities are the triangle identities of the levelwise adjunction, so $f^*\dashv Rf_*$ on $D^+$.

Flasque $k$-sheaves are acyclic for sections on every open set. Let $F$ be flasque and embed it into an injective $I$ using [F2], with quotient $Q$. Viewed as a short exact sequence of underlying abelian sheaves, the sequence $0\to F\to I\to Q\to0$ has flasque kernel $F$ and flasque middle term $I$ by step 1.3, so [F8] gives that $I(U)\to Q(U)$ is surjective for every open $U$ and that $Q$ is flasque. Write $H^q(U,-)$ for the right derived functors of the $k$-linear sections functor at $U$ formed with the functorial datum of [F2]; these are the groups compared with the published sheaf cohomology by [F7]. By [F7] the family $(H^q(U,-))_{q\ge0}$ is a cohomological delta functor, so the displayed short exact sequence yields a long exact sequence; by [F7] again $H^q(U,I)=0$ for $q>0$ because $I$ is injective. Hence $H^1(U,F)=0$ and, for every $n\ge1$, $H^{n+1}(U,F)\cong H^n(U,Q)$. Since $Q$ is again flasque, the same argument applies to $Q$, and induction on $n$ gives $H^n(U,F)=0$ for all $n\ge1$ and every open $U$, uniformly over all flasque sheaves.

Bounded complexes are K-flat, and the signed total tensor computes the derived tensor. Let $A$ be a bounded complex, say $A^p=0$ for $p\notin[a,b]$, and let $C$ be an acyclic bounded-below complex. Form the double cochain complex $K^{p,q}=A^p\otimes_kC^q$ with horizontal differential induced by $d_A$ and vertical differential $(-1)^p\operatorname{id}\otimes d_C$. After translating bidegrees it is first quadrant with finite diagonal sums, and for fixed $p$ its column is $A^p\otimes_kC^\bullet$, which is acyclic because tensoring with the sheaf $A^p$ is exact by step 1.2. By [F9] the total complex $\operatorname{Tot}(A\otimes_kC)$ is acyclic; this is the statement that bounded $A$ is K-flat. Now let $f:B\to B'$ be a quasi-isomorphism of bounded complexes with cone $\operatorname{Cone}(f)$ in the cochain convention of [def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category] ([[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]), so that $0\to B'\to\operatorname{Cone}(f)\to B[1]\to0$ is a short exact sequence of complexes. Tensoring with $A$ is termwise exact by step 1.2, so it carries this sequence to a short exact sequence of complexes of sheaves of $k$-vector spaces, and $\operatorname{Tot}(A\otimes_k\operatorname{Cone}(f))$ is acyclic by the K-flatness just proved because $\operatorname{Cone}(f)$ is acyclic by the cone criterion [F9] and bounded. The long exact cohomology sequence [F9] then shows that $\operatorname{Tot}(A\otimes_kB)\to\operatorname{Tot}(A\otimes_kB')$ is a quasi-isomorphism; by symmetry the same holds in the other variable. Therefore the signed total tensor of bounded representatives descends to a bifunctor $D^b\times D^b\to D$, independent of the chosen bounded representatives, and it represents the derived tensor $A\otimes_k^LB$.

The sheaf tensor–Hom adjunction holds on sections over each open. For $k_X$-modules $H,A,G$ there is a natural bijection $\operatorname{Hom}_X(H\otimes_kA,G)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_X(H,\mathcal Hom(A,G))$: on sections over an open $U$ it is the vector-space tensor–Hom transposition $g\mapsto(h\mapsto g(h\otimes-))$, with inverse $s\mapsto(h\otimes a\mapsto s(h)(a))$, and these sectionwise bijections are compatible with restriction to smaller opens and with the $k_X$-module structures because both constructions are built from restriction maps and scalar multiplication. Hence for fixed $A$ the functor $\mathcal Hom(A,-)$ is right adjoint to the exact functor $-\otimes_kA$ of step 1.2; consequently $\mathcal Hom(A,J)$ is injective whenever $J$ is injective, its representable functor being the composite of $-\otimes_kA$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_X(-,J)$. The bijection is natural in all three variables.

The internal derived Hom is computed by the injective model. Let $A$ be a bounded complex, let $B$ be a bounded-below complex, and let $j_B:B\to I_B$ be a bounded-below termwise injective replacement supplied by [F3]; the complex $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I_B)$ has degree-$n$ term the finite product over $p$ of the internal Hom sheaves $\mathcal Hom(A^p,I_B^{p+n})$ and differential $d\varphi=d_{I_B}\varphi-(-1)^n\varphi d_A$ in the convention of [[def-derived-hom-in-the-bounded-setting]]. Each term is injective by step 2.4, because $A^p$ is a sheaf and $-\otimes_kA^p$ is exact; the complex is bounded below because $A$ is bounded and $I_B$ is bounded below, and only finitely many $p$ contribute; hence it is K-injective by [F3]. Therefore $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I_B)$ computes $\operatorname{Hom}_D(-,B)$ without roofs, and we declare $R\mathcal Hom(A,B):=\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I_B)$; it is the actual internal derived Hom: its terms are internal Hom sheaves on $X$, not sectionwise Hom spaces of stalks, and its restriction to an open $U$ is the same construction over $U$.

Bounded-below flasque complexes are acyclic for derived sections. Let $C^\bullet$ be a bounded-below complex of flasque $k$-sheaves, with $C^n=0$ for $n<b$, let $\varphi:C^\bullet\to J^\bullet$ be a bounded-below termwise injective replacement supplied by [F3], and fix an open $U$. I first record a lemma: if $K^\bullet$ is an acyclic bounded-below complex whose every term is acyclic for the sections functor at $U$, then $\Gamma(U,K^\bullet)$ is acyclic. Indeed, put $Z^n=\ker(K^n\to K^{n+1})$; the complex is acyclic, so $0\to Z^n\to K^n\to Z^{n+1}\to0$ is a short exact sequence for every $n$, and $Z^n=0$ for $n<b$. If $Z^n$ is acyclic for sections at $U$, then the long exact sequence of [F7] for this sequence, together with the acyclicity of $K^n$, shows that $Z^{n+1}$ is again acyclic for sections at $U$; inducting on $n$ upward from $n<b$, every $Z^n$ is acyclic. With all $Z^n$ acyclic, the same sequences give short exact sequences $0\to\Gamma(U,Z^n)\to\Gamma(U,K^n)\to\Gamma(U,Z^{n+1})\to0$ on sections, so the kernel of $\Gamma(U,K^n)\to\Gamma(U,K^{n+1})$ equals the image of $\Gamma(U,K^{n-1})\to\Gamma(U,K^n)$: the former is the kernel of $\Gamma(U,K^n)\to\Gamma(U,Z^{n+1})$, which is the image of $\Gamma(U,Z^n)$ because $\Gamma$ of a short exact sequence is left exact and the sequence is right exact at the quotient, and $\Gamma(U,K^{n-1})\to\Gamma(U,Z^n)$ is surjective, so the two images agree. Hence $H^n(\Gamma(U,K^\bullet))=0$ for every $n$. Now apply this lemma to the cone $K^\bullet=\operatorname{Cone}(\varphi)$ of the cochain map $\varphi$ in the convention of [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]. Its terms $J^n\oplus C^{n+1}$ are direct sums of an injective term, acyclic for sections at $U$ by [F7], and a flasque term, acyclic by step 2.2; a direct sum of two acyclic objects is acyclic by the long exact sequence [F7] applied to $0\to J^n\to J^n\oplus C^{n+1}\to C^{n+1}\to0$. The cone is acyclic and bounded below, so the lemma gives that $\Gamma(U,\operatorname{Cone}(\varphi))$ is acyclic. The canonical identification of complexes $\Gamma(U,\operatorname{Cone}(\varphi))\cong\operatorname{Cone}(\Gamma(U,\varphi))$ holds because sections over $U$ preserve finite direct sums and the differentials are those of $\varphi$; by the cone criterion [F9] the map $\Gamma(U,C^\bullet)\to\Gamma(U,J^\bullet)$ is therefore a quasi-isomorphism for every open $U$. Since any two bounded-below injective replacements of $C^\bullet$ are homotopy equivalent by [F3], the ordinary section complex $\Gamma(U,C^\bullet)$ represents the derived sections $R\Gamma(U,C^\bullet)$ of the bounded-below flasque complex.

The internal derived Hom is well defined on the bounded derived categories. Let $A\to A'$ be a quasi-isomorphism of bounded complexes and let $I$ be a bounded-below complex of injectives. The canonical map $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A',I)\to\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I)$ has cone canonically identified with $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(\operatorname{Cone}(A\to A'),I)$, with the Koszul signs of the Hom complex; since $I$ is K-injective by [F3] and the cone of $A\to A'$ is acyclic and bounded below, $\mathcal Hom^\bullet$ of an acyclic bounded-below complex into $I$ is acyclic; hence the map is a quasi-isomorphism by the cone criterion. If $I\to I'$ is a homotopy equivalence of bounded-below complexes of injectives, then $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,-)$ carries it to a homotopy equivalence, hence a quasi-isomorphism; and any two bounded-below injective replacements of $B$ are homotopy equivalent by [F3]. Combining the two comparisons, $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I_B)$ depends only on the isomorphism classes of $A$ and $B$ in the derived categories, up to canonical quasi-isomorphism, and is natural in both variables.

The tensor–Hom adjunction and its coherence identities hold on the derived category. For a bounded complex $C$ and a bounded-below complex $I$ of injectives, the currying map $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A\otimes_kC,I)\to\mathcal Hom^\bullet(C,\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I))$, which sends a morphism $\varphi$ to $c\mapsto(a\mapsto(-1)^{|c||a|}\varphi(a\otimes c))$ on pure tensor sections and extends by linearity and gluing, is an isomorphism of complexes: over each open it is the vector-space tensor–Hom transposition of step 2.4, bijective on sections, and the Koszul sign makes both sides carry the single differential rule $d\psi=d_I\psi-(-1)^n\psi d_{\text{source}}$ of [[def-derived-hom-in-the-bounded-setting]], so it commutes with differentials and with restriction. Taking $I$ to be an injective replacement of the bounded-below complex $B$ and using that $C$ is K-flat and $I$, $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I)$ are K-injective, the $H^0$ transposition identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_D(C\otimes_k^LA,B)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_D(C,R\mathcal Hom(A,B))$ naturally in the bounded $C,A$ and bounded-below $B$; this is the tensor–Hom adjunction, with unit and counit the canonical currying maps. The associativity isomorphism $(A\otimes_kB)\otimes_kC\cong A\otimes_k(B\otimes_kC)$, the symmetry isomorphism $A\otimes_kB\cong B\otimes_kA$ with its Koszul sign, the evaluation morphism $R\mathcal Hom(A,B)\otimes_k^LA\to B$, and the currying bijection all hold on pure tensor sections, where they are the usual vector-space identities, and extend by linearity, gluing and the comparison maps of step 4.1; being defined on sections they are natural and compatible with restriction to opens, hence internal. The triangle identities are those of step 2.4 at chain level.

The claims are now assembled. Inverse image is exact and $f^*\dashv Rf_*$ on $D^+$ is step 2.1; the derived tensor of bounded complexes is the signed total tensor by step 2.3; the internal derived Hom is the injective model of step 3.1, well defined by step 4.1; flasque sheaves are acyclic for sections on every open set by step 2.2, and bounded-below flasque complexes compute their derived sections by step 3.2; the tensor–Hom adjunction and the dg associativity, symmetry, evaluation and currying identities are step 5.1. AC is assumed and consumed exactly as follows: AC yields DC by [F1], DC is used by the injective replacement suppliers of [F3] and the delta-functor and injective-acyclicity statements of [F7], the functorial injective resolutions of [F2] use the Grothendieck embedding theorem under AC, and the flasque section lifting of [F8] uses Zorn's lemma under AC; the stalk, tensor, Hom and adjunction verifications are choice-free. No bounded-constructibility claim for the internal Hom is made: that is supplied later on this page by the geometric finite conical and incidence models, which are not prerequisites of this lemma.
