Let $k$ be a field and let $X,Y$ be locally compact Hausdorff spaces
([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-hausdorff-space]]). Write
$\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ for the category of sheaves of $k$-vector spaces
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]])
viewed as modules over the constant ring sheaf $k_X$, and form derived
categories in those sheaves ([[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]).
For a continuous map $f:X\to Y$, set $f^*=f^{-1}$
([[def-inverse-image-presheaf-and-sheaf]]) and define $f_!F$ on an open
$V\subseteq Y$ to consist of the sections of $F$ on $f^{-1}(V)$ whose closed
support ([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]],
[[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]]) maps properly to $V$, properness
being that of [[def-proper-continuous-map]] together with its stability lemma
[[lem-proper-continuous-map-stability]]. Under AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]),
$Rf_*$ and $Rf_!$ are computed on bounded-below $k$-linear injective
replacements. Tensor means the signed total tensor over $k$
([[def-sheaf-tensor-product]]) and internal derived Hom is the injective
construction of
[[lem-bounded-analytic-field-sheaves-have-derived-tensor-hom-and-pullback-pushforward-adjunctions]]
([[def-sheaf-hom]]).

Suppose the uniform all-fibre-open cohomological dimension bound of
[[lem-finite-fibre-dimension-gives-bounded-fibrewise-soft-resolutions]] holds,
and choose its finite resolution $k_X\to K$; for an open $U\subseteq X$ put
$K_U=j_{U!}j_U^*K$ ([[def-extension-by-zero-abelian-sheaf]],
[[def-c-soft-sheaf]]). For a bounded-below injective complex $I$ on $Y$,
define the exceptional inverse-image candidate to be the sheaf complex with
open sections $\operatorname{Hom}_Y^\bullet(f_!K_U,I)$.
[[thm-compactly-supported-derived-pushforward-has-exceptional-inverse-image-adjoint]]
proves that this candidate is a sheaf complex and is independent of the chosen
resolution. Set $\omega_X=a_X^!k$ and $D_XA=R\mathcal Hom(A,\omega_X)$ when the
terminal map satisfies the same finite-dimensional hypotheses. Constructible
restriction is a separate geometric theorem; none of these definitions asserts
a generic six-functor axiom.

The prescriptions are those of Verdier's exposé: $f^*$ is the exact inverse
image, $f_!$ is the sheaf of sections whose closed support is proper over the
base — a presheaf by the local nature of properness, whose sheaf property on
bounded-below injective inputs is proved by the exceptional-adjoint theorem
recorded in `justified_by` — $Rf_*$ is derived from the direct image
[[def-direct-image-sheaf]] on bounded-below injective replacements, and the
terms of the chosen finite resolution are $c$-soft and hence acyclic for
compact support ([[lem-c-soft-field-sheaves-are-compact-support-acyclic]]).
The ordinary-operations lemma also supplies the flasque acyclicity
([[def-flasque-sheaf]]) used to compare resolutions. AC is used only for
injective replacements; the proper-support sections, extension by zero and the
exceptional candidate itself are choice-free constructions. Cohomological
shifts obey $H^i(A[r])=H^{i+r}(A)$ in the convention of
[[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]].

If $\mathcal A$ has enough injectives and $X^n=0$ for $n<a$, there is a termwise monic quasi-isomorphism $j:X\to I$ with each $I^n$ injective and $I^n=0$ for $n<a$. Assume DC for the successive objectwise choices, or supply the successive injective monomorphisms. If only $H^n(X)=0$ for $n<a$, a quasi-isomorphism to such an $I$ still exists, without the termwise-monic assertion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map of topological spaces and let $k$ be a field. Inverse image of sheaves of $k$-vector spaces ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[def-inverse-image-presheaf-and-sheaf]]) is exact and $f^*\dashv Rf_*$, where $Rf_*$ is computed on bounded-below $k$-linear injective replacements ([[lem-bounded-below-complexes-admit-injective-replacements]], [[thm-injective-complexes-model-the-bounded-below-derived-category]]). For bounded complexes $A,B$ ([[def-bounded-bounded-below-and-bounded-above-complex]]) the derived tensor over $k$ is their signed total tensor ([[def-sheaf-tensor-product]]), and for bounded $A$ and bounded-below $B$ the derived internal Hom $R\mathcal Hom(A,B)$ is computed by $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I_B)$ in a $k$-linear bounded-below injective model $B\to I_B$ ([[def-sheaf-hom]], [[def-derived-hom-in-the-bounded-setting]]). Flasque $k$-sheaves ([[def-flasque-sheaf]]) are acyclic for sections on every open set ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). The tensor-Hom adjunction and the dg associativity, evaluation and symmetry identities are natural. No bounded-constructibility claim for the internal Hom is made here; that requires the local geometric supplier of the later constructible items.

Let $K\subseteq X$ be a compact subset ([[def-compact-space]]) of a locally
compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-hausdorff-space]]),
let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of $k$-vector spaces on $X$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]) and let $i:K\hookrightarrow X$ be the
inclusion. Then the canonical map
$$\varinjlim_{U\supseteq K,\ U\ \text{open}}\mathcal F(U)\longrightarrow\Gamma(K,i^{-1}\mathcal F)=(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K)$$
is an isomorphism of $k$-vector spaces. Moreover, for pairwise disjoint compact
subsets $K_1,\dots,K_m\subseteq X$ and sections $s_j\in\mathcal F(U_j)$ over open
neighbourhoods $U_j$ of the respective $K_j$, there are an open neighbourhood $U$
of $K_1\cup\dots\cup K_m$ and a section $s\in\mathcal F(U)$, together with, for
every $j$, an open neighbourhood $W_j\subseteq U_j$ of $K_j$ with
$s|_{W_j}=s_j|_{W_j}$; in particular the zero section can be prescribed on any
compact set disjoint from the given one. The isomorphism is $k$-linear, and no
choice principle is used: every selection in the proof is made from finitely
many nonempty sets.

Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]) and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on
$X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]); this covers in particular every sheaf
of $k$-vector spaces over a field $k$, which is the case used by the
compact-support calculus, and for such a sheaf the groups below are $k$-vector
spaces and the maps $k$-linear. Global sections are written
$\Gamma(X,-)$ ([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]]). For a compact subset
$K\subseteq X$ ([[def-compact-space]]) let $i:K\hookrightarrow X$ be the
inclusion and consider the canonical restriction map
$$\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)\longrightarrow\Gamma(K,i^{-1}\mathcal F)=(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K),\qquad s\longmapsto s|_K,$$
which sends a global section ([[def-section-restriction-and-global-section]]) to
the section of the inverse image sheaf ([[def-inverse-image-presheaf-and-sheaf]])
that it induces on $K$. Then $\mathcal F$ is **c-soft**, also **soft for
compact supports**, when this map is surjective for every compact subset
$K\subseteq X$, that is: every section of $\mathcal F$ over a compact subset of
$X$ extends to a global section of $\mathcal F$. For sheaves of abelian groups
$\Gamma_c$ and $H^q_c$ of
[[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]] are the compactly supported
analogues of $\Gamma$ and $H^q$.

Two consistency facts hold; both are immediate from the definitions and from
the extension lemma for sections on a compact set, and they are recorded here
because the compact-support calculus uses the first constantly and the second
for injective sheaves.

1. **Neighbourhood formulation.** By
   [[lem-sections-near-a-compact-set-are-sections-on-that-set]], the source of
   the restriction map may be replaced by the defining colimit of the
   inverse-image presheaf,
   $(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K)=\varinjlim_{U\supseteq K}\mathcal F(U)$, so that
   $\mathcal F$ is c-soft if and only if for every compact $K$ and every open
   neighbourhood $U$ of $K$, every section $s\in\mathcal F(U)$ agrees with a
   global section of $\mathcal F$ on some open neighbourhood of $K$. It
   therefore suffices, for c-softness, to test the extended sections only
   locally near $K$.
2. **Flasque implies c-soft.** If $\mathcal F$ is flasque
   ([[def-flasque-sheaf]]) then $\mathcal F$ is c-soft: a class in
   $(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K)$ is represented by a section $s$ over an open
   neighbourhood $U$ of $K$, and flasqueness extends $s$ to a global section
   $t\in\mathcal F(X)$ with $t|_U=s$, so $t$ is a preimage of that class.

C-softness is a property of the pair $(X,\mathcal F)$ and not of the sheaf
alone: the compact subsets of the base space are part of the test. Nothing is
assumed about the support of the extended global sections, and c-softness is
not the same condition as flasqueness, only implied by it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space and
let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]); every clause applies in particular to
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces, and the tensor clause of (4) is stated only
there. Then:

1. if $\mathcal F$ is c-soft ([[def-c-soft-sheaf]]), every section of
   $\mathcal F$ over a compact subset $K\subseteq X$ extends to a compactly
   supported global section whose support is contained in any prescribed open
   neighbourhood of $K$;
2. every injective abelian sheaf on $X$ is c-soft;
3. if $\mathcal F$ is c-soft, then $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)=0$ for every $q>0$
   ([[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]]); when $X$ is compact this is
   the vanishing of the sheaf cohomology $H^q(X,\mathcal F)$
   ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]);
4. c-softness is preserved by restriction to open subsets, by restriction to
   closed subsets, by extension by zero along an open inclusion, and by finite
   direct sums of sheaves of abelian groups; for sheaves of $k$-vector spaces
   it is also preserved by tensor product with a constant $k$-vector space;
5. if $0\to\mathcal F'\xrightarrow{\alpha}\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\beta}\mathcal F''\to0$
   is a short exact sequence of sheaves of abelian groups and $\mathcal F'$ is
   c-soft, then every section of $\mathcal F''$ over a compact subset lifts to
   a section of $\mathcal F$ over an open neighbourhood of it, and the induced
   sequence
   $0\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F'')\to0$
   is exact; if $\mathcal F'$ and $\mathcal F$ are c-soft then
   $\mathcal F''$ is c-soft.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a locally
compact Hausdorff space, let $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ be the category of sheaves of
abelian groups on $X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]) and let
$$\Gamma(X,-):\mathrm{Ab}(X)\longrightarrow\mathbf{Ab}$$
be the additive left exact global-sections functor
([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]],
[[def-section-restriction-and-global-section]]). For a sheaf $\mathcal F$ on
$X$ define the **compactly supported global sections** of $\mathcal F$ to be the
subgroup
$$\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F):=\{\,s\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal F):\operatorname{Supp}(s)\ \text{is a compact subset of }X\,\}\subseteq\Gamma(X,\mathcal F),$$
where the support of a section is the set of points at which its germ is
nonzero ([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]], [[def-germ-of-section]],
[[def-compact-space]]). A morphism $\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian
sheaves induces a map $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ by restriction of
$\Gamma(X,\varphi)$, and this makes $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ an additive functor
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)\to\mathbf{Ab}$ ([[def-additive-functor]],
[[def-morphism-of-presheaves]]). Six consistency facts hold; all are immediate
from the definitions, and they record the interface used by the compact-support
calculus.

1. **Well-definedness of $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$.** If $x\notin
   \operatorname{Supp}(s)$ then $s_x=0$ in the stalk $\mathcal F_x$
   ([[def-stalk-of-presheaf]]), and since the stalk maps of a morphism commute
   with the germ maps, $\varphi(s)_x=\varphi_x(s_x)=0$, so
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi(s))\subseteq\operatorname{Supp}(s)$. A support
   $\operatorname{Supp}(t)$ is closed in $X$: if $x\notin
   \operatorname{Supp}(t)$ then $t$ agrees with the zero section on some open
   neighbourhood of $x$, by the description of equality of germs
   ([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]]). Hence
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi(s))$ is a closed subset of $X$ contained in the
   compact set $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$; being closed in $X$ it is closed in the
   subspace $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$, so it is a compact subset of that compact
   space ([[thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]) and therefore
   a compact subset of $X$ ([[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]]), and
   $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ maps $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$ into
   $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal G)$. Composites and identities are computed
   componentwise, so $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is a functor; it is additive because
   $\Gamma(X,-)$ is.
2. **Sheaves of $k$-vector spaces.** If $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of
   $k$-vector spaces, then $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$ is a $k$-vector subspace of
   $\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$: the support of $c\cdot s$ is
   $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ for $c\ne0$ and $\varnothing$ for $c=0$, and the
   zero section has empty support. For a morphism $\varphi$ of sheaves of
   $k$-vector spaces the map $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ is $k$-linear, since
   $\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ is. The higher derived functors below are computed from
   an injective resolution datum on abelian sheaves, so they are abelian
   groups; the degree-zero part is the $k$-vector space
   $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$.
3. **Left exactness.** For every short exact sequence
   $0\to\mathcal F'\xrightarrow{\varphi'}\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathcal F''\to0$
   of abelian sheaves the sequence
   $$0\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')\xrightarrow{\Gamma_c(\varphi')}\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)\xrightarrow{\Gamma_c(\varphi)}\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F'')$$
   is exact. Injectivity: a monomorphism of sheaves has injective stalk maps
   ([[thm-exactness-of-sheaves-stalkwise]]), so
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi'(s'))=\operatorname{Supp}(s')$ and a section
   killed by $\varphi'$ has all germs zero, hence is zero. Exactness at the
   middle: the kernel of $\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ is the image of
   $\Gamma(X,\varphi')$ by left exactness of global sections
   ([[lem-global-sections-left-exact]]); if $s=\varphi'(s')$ has compact
   support, then $s'$ has the same support,
   $\operatorname{Supp}(s')=\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi'(s'))=
   \operatorname{Supp}(s)$, because $\varphi'$ is stalk-injective, so $s'$ lies
   in $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')$, and the reverse inclusion is immediate from
   $\varphi\circ\varphi'=0$. Thus $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is an additive left exact
   functor on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ ([[def-left-exact-and-right-exact-functor]]).
4. **The derived functors.** Abelian sheaves on $X$ have enough injectives, and
   the embeddings of [[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]] supply one
   functorial injective resolution datum $\mathcal F\mapsto I^\bullet(\mathcal F)$
   on the whole category $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, under the Axiom of Choice
   ([[def-right-derived-object-relative-to-injective-resolution-data]]). The
   **compactly supported cohomology** of $\mathcal F$ is
   $$H^q_c(X,\mathcal F):=R^q\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F):=H^q\bigl(\Gamma_c(X,I^\bullet(\mathcal F)_{\mathrm{del}})\bigr)\qquad(q\ge0),\qquad H^q_c(X,\mathcal F):=0\quad(q<0),$$
   the cohomology of the deleted resolution, as in the pattern of
   [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]; for a morphism $\varphi$ we
   write $H^q_c(X,\varphi):=R^q\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ for the induced map.
5. **Independence of the datum.** If $J$ is another supplied injective
   resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, then $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$ computed from
   $J$ is naturally isomorphic to $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$ computed from $I$
   ([[thm-right-derived-functors-from-two-supplied-injective-resolution-data-are-naturally-isomorphic]]);
   the Axiom of Dependent Choice needed for that comparison follows from AC
   ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]). The notation
   $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)$ therefore does not depend on the datum up to this
   canonical natural isomorphism.
6. **Delta functor and the compact case.** Since $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is additive
   and left exact and the datum is defined on all of $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, the
   functors $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$, $q\ge0$, carry connecting maps that make them a
   cohomological delta functor with $R^0\Gamma_c(X,-)\cong\Gamma_c(X,-)$, and
   every short exact sequence of abelian sheaves has a long exact
   compact-support cohomology sequence, natural in the sequence
   ([[thm-right-derived-functors-form-a-cohomological-delta-functor]]). If $X$
   is compact, then for every global section $s$ its support is closed in $X$ by
   fact 1, hence a closed subset of the compact space $X$ and therefore
   compact, so every global section is compactly supported; hence
   $\Gamma_c(X,-)=\Gamma(X,-)$ and
   $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)=H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ for every $q$, where $H^q(X,-)$ is
   the sheaf cohomology of [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]
   computed from the same datum.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a locally
compact Hausdorff space, let $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ be the category of sheaves of
abelian groups on $X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]) and let
$$\Gamma(X,-):\mathrm{Ab}(X)\longrightarrow\mathbf{Ab}$$
be the additive left exact global-sections functor
([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]],
[[def-section-restriction-and-global-section]]). For a sheaf $\mathcal F$ on
$X$ define the **compactly supported global sections** of $\mathcal F$ to be the
subgroup
$$\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F):=\{\,s\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal F):\operatorname{Supp}(s)\ \text{is a compact subset of }X\,\}\subseteq\Gamma(X,\mathcal F),$$
where the support of a section is the set of points at which its germ is
nonzero ([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]], [[def-germ-of-section]],
[[def-compact-space]]). A morphism $\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian
sheaves induces a map $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ by restriction of
$\Gamma(X,\varphi)$, and this makes $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ an additive functor
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)\to\mathbf{Ab}$ ([[def-additive-functor]],
[[def-morphism-of-presheaves]]). Six consistency facts hold; all are immediate
from the definitions, and they record the interface used by the compact-support
calculus.

1. **Well-definedness of $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$.** If $x\notin
   \operatorname{Supp}(s)$ then $s_x=0$ in the stalk $\mathcal F_x$
   ([[def-stalk-of-presheaf]]), and since the stalk maps of a morphism commute
   with the germ maps, $\varphi(s)_x=\varphi_x(s_x)=0$, so
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi(s))\subseteq\operatorname{Supp}(s)$. A support
   $\operatorname{Supp}(t)$ is closed in $X$: if $x\notin
   \operatorname{Supp}(t)$ then $t$ agrees with the zero section on some open
   neighbourhood of $x$, by the description of equality of germs
   ([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]]). Hence
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi(s))$ is a closed subset of $X$ contained in the
   compact set $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$; being closed in $X$ it is closed in the
   subspace $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$, so it is a compact subset of that compact
   space ([[thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]) and therefore
   a compact subset of $X$ ([[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]]), and
   $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ maps $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$ into
   $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal G)$. Composites and identities are computed
   componentwise, so $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is a functor; it is additive because
   $\Gamma(X,-)$ is.
2. **Sheaves of $k$-vector spaces.** If $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of
   $k$-vector spaces, then $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$ is a $k$-vector subspace of
   $\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$: the support of $c\cdot s$ is
   $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ for $c\ne0$ and $\varnothing$ for $c=0$, and the
   zero section has empty support. For a morphism $\varphi$ of sheaves of
   $k$-vector spaces the map $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ is $k$-linear, since
   $\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ is. The higher derived functors below are computed from
   an injective resolution datum on abelian sheaves, so they are abelian
   groups; the degree-zero part is the $k$-vector space
   $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$.
3. **Left exactness.** For every short exact sequence
   $0\to\mathcal F'\xrightarrow{\varphi'}\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathcal F''\to0$
   of abelian sheaves the sequence
   $$0\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')\xrightarrow{\Gamma_c(\varphi')}\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)\xrightarrow{\Gamma_c(\varphi)}\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F'')$$
   is exact. Injectivity: a monomorphism of sheaves has injective stalk maps
   ([[thm-exactness-of-sheaves-stalkwise]]), so
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi'(s'))=\operatorname{Supp}(s')$ and a section
   killed by $\varphi'$ has all germs zero, hence is zero. Exactness at the
   middle: the kernel of $\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ is the image of
   $\Gamma(X,\varphi')$ by left exactness of global sections
   ([[lem-global-sections-left-exact]]); if $s=\varphi'(s')$ has compact
   support, then $s'$ has the same support,
   $\operatorname{Supp}(s')=\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi'(s'))=
   \operatorname{Supp}(s)$, because $\varphi'$ is stalk-injective, so $s'$ lies
   in $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')$, and the reverse inclusion is immediate from
   $\varphi\circ\varphi'=0$. Thus $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is an additive left exact
   functor on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ ([[def-left-exact-and-right-exact-functor]]).
4. **The derived functors.** Abelian sheaves on $X$ have enough injectives, and
   the embeddings of [[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]] supply one
   functorial injective resolution datum $\mathcal F\mapsto I^\bullet(\mathcal F)$
   on the whole category $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, under the Axiom of Choice
   ([[def-right-derived-object-relative-to-injective-resolution-data]]). The
   **compactly supported cohomology** of $\mathcal F$ is
   $$H^q_c(X,\mathcal F):=R^q\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F):=H^q\bigl(\Gamma_c(X,I^\bullet(\mathcal F)_{\mathrm{del}})\bigr)\qquad(q\ge0),\qquad H^q_c(X,\mathcal F):=0\quad(q<0),$$
   the cohomology of the deleted resolution, as in the pattern of
   [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]; for a morphism $\varphi$ we
   write $H^q_c(X,\varphi):=R^q\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ for the induced map.
5. **Independence of the datum.** If $J$ is another supplied injective
   resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, then $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$ computed from
   $J$ is naturally isomorphic to $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$ computed from $I$
   ([[thm-right-derived-functors-from-two-supplied-injective-resolution-data-are-naturally-isomorphic]]);
   the Axiom of Dependent Choice needed for that comparison follows from AC
   ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]). The notation
   $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)$ therefore does not depend on the datum up to this
   canonical natural isomorphism.
6. **Delta functor and the compact case.** Since $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is additive
   and left exact and the datum is defined on all of $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, the
   functors $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$, $q\ge0$, carry connecting maps that make them a
   cohomological delta functor with $R^0\Gamma_c(X,-)\cong\Gamma_c(X,-)$, and
   every short exact sequence of abelian sheaves has a long exact
   compact-support cohomology sequence, natural in the sequence
   ([[thm-right-derived-functors-form-a-cohomological-delta-functor]]). If $X$
   is compact, then for every global section $s$ its support is closed in $X$ by
   fact 1, hence a closed subset of the compact space $X$ and therefore
   compact, so every global section is compactly supported; hence
   $\Gamma_c(X,-)=\Gamma(X,-)$ and
   $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)=H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ for every $q$, where $H^q(X,-)$ is
   the sheaf cohomology of [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]
   computed from the same datum.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map between locally
compact Hausdorff spaces ([[def-locally-compact-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]) and let $d\ge0$ be an integer such that
$$H^q_c(V,\mathcal F)=0\qquad(q>d)$$
for every open subspace $V$ of every fibre $f^{-1}(y)$, $y\in Y$, and every
sheaf $\mathcal F$ of $k$-vector spaces on $V$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]],
[[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]]; the sheaves may equally be
sheaves of abelian groups). Then every sheaf $\mathcal A$ of $k$-vector spaces
on $X$ has a bounded resolution by fibrewise c-soft sheaves: there is an exact
sequence
$$0\longrightarrow\mathcal A\longrightarrow\mathcal K^0\longrightarrow\mathcal K^1\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow\mathcal K^d\longrightarrow0$$
in which each $\mathcal K^j$ restricts to a c-soft sheaf on every fibre
$f^{-1}(y)$ ([[def-c-soft-sheaf]]). For $d=0$ this says that every sheaf on
$X$ is already c-soft on every fibre. In particular the constant sheaf $k_X$
has such a resolution.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological spaces ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$f:X\to Y$ be continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]). Then $f$ is **proper**
when for every compact subset $K\subseteq Y$ ([[def-compact-space]]) its
preimage $f^{-1}(K)$ is a compact subset of $X$. Compactness of subsets is the
intrinsic condition of [[def-compact-space]], namely compactness of the
subspace $f^{-1}(K)$ with the subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]);
by [[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]] it is equivalent to the ambient
reading, so a subset is compact exactly when every cover by open subsets of the
ambient space has a finite subcover, and the two readings are used
interchangeably below without further comment.

This is the notion of properness used throughout the analytic six-operation
development on this page, where the spaces involved are locally compact
Hausdorff ([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-hausdorff-space]]). The
stability properties consumed by the later items — closed inclusions are
proper, composites of proper maps are proper, properness is preserved by base
change along a continuous map into a Hausdorff space, and fibres and closed
subspaces of a proper map inherit properness — are proved in the lemma
`lem-proper-continuous-map-stability` on this page. The definition involves no
choice principle: it quantifies over compact subsets and preimages only.

Let $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ be topological spaces ([[def-topological-space]]), with
properness as in [[def-proper-continuous-map]].

1. If $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ is the inclusion of a closed subset, then $i$ is
   proper.
2. If $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$ are proper continuous maps, then the composite
   $gf:X\to Z$ is proper.
3. If $f:X\to Y$ is proper, $Y$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and
   $u:Y'\to Y$ is continuous, then the pullback
   $$f':X\times_YY'\longrightarrow Y',\qquad X\times_YY'=\{(x,y')\in X\times Y': f(x)=u(y')\},$$
   the subset carrying the subspace topology of the product
   ([[def-product-topology]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]), is proper.
4. If $f:X\to Y$ is proper, then every fibre $f^{-1}(y)$ is a compact subset of
   $X$.
5. If $f:X\to Y$ is proper and $S\subseteq X$ is closed, then the restriction
   $f|_S:S\to Y$ is proper.
6. If $f:X\to Y$ is proper and $Y$ is locally compact Hausdorff
   ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), then $f$ is a closed map: the image of
   every closed subset of $X$ is closed in $Y$.

These are the stability properties consumed by the closed-support functor
$f_!$ on this page; no choice principle is used in any of them.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace.

1. For every sheaf of abelian groups $\mathcal F$ on $U$ and every sheaf of
   abelian groups $\mathcal G$ on $X$, there is a natural bijection
   $$\operatorname{Hom}_X(j_!\mathcal F,\mathcal G) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_U(\mathcal F,j^{-1}\mathcal G).$$
2. The functor $j_!$ is exact on sheaves of abelian groups.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace, and let
$\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $U$.

For an open set $V \subseteq X$, define
$$(j_!\mathcal F)(V) := \left\{ s\in \mathcal F(V\cap U): \operatorname{Supp}(s)\text{ is closed in }V \right\}.$$
Equivalently, $s$ lies in $(j_!\mathcal F)(V)$ exactly when for every
$x\in V\setminus U$ there exists an open neighbourhood $W_x \subseteq V$ with
$$
s|_{W_x\cap U}=0.
$$

Restriction maps are inherited from $\mathcal F$, so $j_!\mathcal F$ is a
subsheaf of $j_*\mathcal F$. When $V \subseteq U$, the support condition is
vacuous and
$$
(j_!\mathcal F)(V)=\mathcal F(V).
$$

This is the **extension by zero** of $\mathcal F$ along $j$. It is distinct in
general from the ordinary direct image $j_*\mathcal F$.

Let $X$ be a topological space, let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf of $k$-vector
spaces (or of abelian groups) on $X$
([[def-presheaf-on-topological-space]]), let $U\subseteq X$ be open and let
$s\in\mathcal F(U)$. The **support of $s$** is
$$\operatorname{Supp}(s):=\{\,x\in U: s_x\neq 0\,\}\subseteq U,$$
where $s_x\in\mathcal F_x$ denotes the germ of $s$ at $x$ in the stalk
$\mathcal F_x$ ([[def-stalk-of-presheaf]], [[def-germ-of-section]]). A section
$s\in\mathcal F(X)$ is **compactly supported** when its support is a compact
subspace of $X$ ([[def-compact-space]]). For a subspace $Z\subseteq X$ and a
presheaf $\mathcal G$ on $Z$, the support of $t\in\mathcal G(Z)$ is defined by
the same condition using the stalks of $\mathcal G$. The support is not assumed
closed in $X$ nor compact.

When $\mathcal F$ is a **sheaf** of $k$-vector spaces the following three
consistency facts hold; they are immediate consequences of the definitions
above and are recorded here because every later compact-support statement uses
them.

1. $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ is closed in $U$. Indeed, if $x\notin
   \operatorname{Supp}(s)$ then $s_x=0$ in the stalk; equality of germs means
   that $s$ and the zero section agree on some open neighbourhood $W\subseteq U$
   of $x$ ([[def-germ-of-section]]), so $s$ vanishes on the open neighbourhood
   $W$ of $x$, and $U\setminus\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ is therefore open in $U$.
2. $\operatorname{Supp}(s)=\varnothing$ if and only if $s=0$. If every germ of
   $s$ is zero then $s=0$ by the locality axiom of a sheaf applied to the cover
   of $U$ by its open subsets ([[lem-section-zero-if-all-germs-zero]]); the
   converse is immediate, since the zero section has zero germ at every point.
3. $\operatorname{Supp}(s|_V)=\operatorname{Supp}(s)\cap V$ for every open
   $V\subseteq U$. Restriction is compatible with the germ maps, so
   $(s|_V)_x=s_x$ for every $x\in V$ ([[def-germ-of-section]]).

Since $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ is closed in $U$ by fact 1, a section whose
support is contained in some compact subset of $X$ is compactly supported: a
closed subset of a compact space is compact. Fact 1 is closedness in $U$ only,
and nothing here asserts that the support is closed in $X$ or that $U$ is
closed. No choice principle is used anywhere: germs, stalks, supports and
restrictions are elementary.

Let $X$ be a topological space.

1. **(Flat resolutions.)** Let $\mathcal C^\bullet$ be a bounded-above cochain
   complex of abelian sheaves on $X$ ([[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]]),
   so that $\mathcal C^n=0$ for all $n\gg0$
   ([[def-bounded-bounded-below-and-bounded-above-complex]]); fix $a$ with
   $\mathcal C^n=0$ for $n>a$. Then there are a cochain complex
   $\mathcal P^\bullet$ of abelian sheaves with $\mathcal P^n$ flat for every
   $n$ ([[def-flat-abelian-sheaf]]) and $\mathcal P^n=0$ for every $n>a$, and a
   cochain map ([[def-cochain-map]]) $\alpha:\mathcal P^\bullet\to\mathcal C^\bullet$
   that is surjective on stalks in every degree and induces an isomorphism
   $H^n(\alpha):H^n(\mathcal P^\bullet)\to H^n(\mathcal C^\bullet)$ for every $n$
   ([[def-quasi-isomorphism]], [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]]):
   a bounded-above, termwise surjective quasi-isomorphism out of a bounded-above
   complex of flat sheaves. Moreover $\mathcal P^\bullet$ and $\alpha$ are
   canonically determined by $\mathcal C^\bullet$, being built from the canonical
   flat epimorphisms of [[lem-flatness-criteria-and-flat-covers-for-abelian-sheaves]]
   after discarding their zero-section summands. Explicitly use
   $G_{\mathrm{red}}(\mathcal E):=\bigoplus_{(U,s),\,s\ne0}j_{U!}\mathbb Z_U$,
   with its induced epimorphism to $\mathcal E$, in the recursion. Since
   $G_{\mathrm{red}}(0)=0$, increasing the initial bound adds only zero terms;
   the construction is independent of $a$. No choice principle is used.

2. **(Flat complexes are K-flat.)** If $\mathcal K^\bullet$ is a bounded-above
   complex of flat abelian sheaves on $X$, then $\mathcal K^\bullet$ is K-flat in
   the sense of [[def-k-flat-complex-of-abelian-sheaves]]: for every acyclic
   bounded-above complex $\mathcal F^\bullet$ of abelian sheaves
   ([[def-exactness-of-a-complex-at-a-degree-and-acyclic-complex]]) the
   tensor-product total complex
   $\operatorname{Tot}(\mathcal F^\bullet\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathcal K^\bullet)$
   of [[def-tensor-product-of-abelian-sheaves]] is acyclic. Consequently
   $\operatorname{Tot}(-\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathcal K^\bullet)$ preserves
   quasi-isomorphisms
   ([[lem-k-flat-abelian-sheaf-complexes-preserve-quasi-isomorphisms]]).

Let $M\in D^-(\mathcal A)$ and $N\in D^+(\mathcal A)$, with termwise bounded representatives. With supplied bounded-above projective models under [[thm-projective-complexes-model-the-bounded-above-derived-category]], define $\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}(M,N)=Q\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(P_M,N)$. Alternatively, with supplied bounded-below injective models under [[thm-injective-complexes-model-the-bounded-below-derived-category]], use $Q\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(M,I_N)$. The target is $D^+(\mathbf{Ab})$.

Here the cochain form of [[def-hom-complex-of-chain-complexes]] has degree-$r$ term $\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}(M^i,N^{i+r})$ and differential $du=d_Nu-(-1)^ru d_M$. If $M^i=0$ above $b$ and $N^j=0$ below $a$, nonzero factors require $a-r\leq i\leq b$, a finite interval, and the whole term is zero for $r<a-b$.

This construction is a bifunctor on the declared derived categories. Indeed homotopies in either variable induce Hom-complex homotopies. Replacing a projective model by a homotopy equivalent one therefore changes its Hom complex by a homotopy equivalence. A quasi-isomorphism in the target has acyclic cone, whose Hom from $P_M$ is acyclic by K-projectivity; hence the Hom map is a quasi-isomorphism. This also follows degree by degree from [[prop-morphisms-from-a-homotopically-projective-complex-need-no-roof]], which identifies each Hom-complex cohomology with the corresponding derived Hom. The injective argument uses [[prop-morphisms-into-a-homotopically-injective-complex-need-no-roof]] and reverses the roles of source and target. Thus both variables descend through localization. When both systems exist, the quasi-isomorphisms $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(P_M,N)\to\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(P_M,I_N)\leftarrow\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(M,I_N)$ give their natural identification. Either one-sided resolution hypothesis suffices.

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category. We use cochains as in [[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]], with $X[k]^n=X^{n+k}$ and $d_{X[k]}^n=(-1)^kd_X^{n+k}$. Thus $H^n(X[k])=H^{n+k}(X)$. The cochain category $K(\mathcal A)$ is the reindexed published homotopy category. Put

$$D(\mathcal A)=K(\mathcal A)[\mathrm{qis}^{-1}],\qquad Q:K(\mathcal A)\longrightarrow D(\mathcal A).$$

Likewise $D^-,D^+,D^b$ initially mean the localizations of the termwise bounded variants of [[def-bounded-bounded-below-and-bounded-above-complex]]. Roof morphisms exist by [[lem-quasi-isomorphisms-admit-the-roof-calculus-in-the-homotopy-category]] and [[thm-the-calculus-of-fractions-constructs-the-localization]] under its standing size hypothesis: a small category of complexes, or supplied small cofinal denominator families. Every assertion of Hom sets is under that hypothesis. In the bounded module models, supplied replacements will separately exhibit those Hom sets. No general local-smallness theorem for unbounded $D(\mathcal A)$ is asserted.

The cone convention is $\operatorname{Cone}(f)^n=Y^n\oplus X^{n+1}$, $d(y,x)=(d_Yy+fx,-d_Xx)$, and its triangle ends in $X[1]$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $X$ be a topological space and let
$\mathcal F$ be a flasque sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-flasque-sheaf]]). Then for every open subspace $U\subseteq X$ and every
integer $q>0$,
$$H^q(U,\mathcal F|_U)=0,$$
where $H^q(U,-)$ denotes sheaf cohomology on the space $U$
([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]) computed with the global
sections functor of $U$, and $\mathcal F|_U$ is the restriction of $\mathcal F$
to $U$. Equivalently, every restriction $\mathcal F|_U$ is $\Gamma$-acyclic
([[def-acyclic-sheaf-global-sections]]).

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian
groups on $X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]],
[[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]]). For open subsets
$U\subseteq V\subseteq X$ write
$$\rho^V_U:\mathcal F(V)\longrightarrow\mathcal F(U)$$
for the restriction map of $\mathcal F$
([[def-section-restriction-and-global-section]]).

Then $\mathcal F$ is **flasque**, also called **flabby**, when each of these
restriction maps is surjective: for all open $U\subseteq V\subseteq X$ the map
$\rho^V_U$ is onto. Equivalently, $\mathcal F$ is flasque when every section of
$\mathcal F$ over an open subset $U$ extends to every larger open subset $V$,
that is, when for every $s\in\mathcal F(U)$ there is $t\in\mathcal F(V)$ with
$t|_U=s$.

The same condition on restriction maps defines flasque sheaves of sets and
flasque sheaves of modules over a sheaf of rings; on this page the notion is
used for sheaves of abelian groups.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). Then:

1. **A neighbourhood base of compact sets.** If $X$ is locally compact
   ([[def-locally-compact-space]]) and Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]), then
   every neighbourhood $N$ of a point $x \in X$ ([[def-neighbourhood-top]])
   contains a compact neighbourhood of $x$; so the compact neighbourhoods of $x$
   form a neighbourhood base at $x$.
2. **Heredity along open and closed subspaces.** If $X$ is locally compact and
   Hausdorff and $S \subseteq X$ is open, then the subspace $S$ is locally
   compact ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). If $X$ is locally compact and
   $F \subseteq X$ is closed, then the subspace $F$ is locally compact; no
   Hausdorff hypothesis is used for this half.
3. **Shrinking inside an open set.** If $X$ is locally compact and Hausdorff,
   $O \subseteq X$ is open and $x \in O$, there is an open $V$ with
   $$x \in V \subseteq \overline{V} \subseteq O$$
   and $\overline{V}$ a compact subset of $X$.
4. **Compact sets sit in open sets with compact closure.** If $X$ is locally
   compact and Hausdorff and $K \subseteq X$ is compact, there is an open
   $V \subseteq X$ with $K \subseteq V$ and $\overline{V}$ a compact subset of
   $X$ ([[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]]).

**No choice principle is used**; every cover produced below is defined by a
formula and thinned by [[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], which returns
members rather than indices.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a Hausdorff topological space
([[def-hausdorff-space]], [[def-topological-space]]), with compact subsets as in
[[def-compact-space]]. Then:

1. **A point and a disjoint compact set are separated.** If $K \subseteq X$ is
   compact and $x \in X \setminus K$, there are $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ with
   $$x \in U, \qquad K \subseteq V, \qquad U \cap V = \varnothing .$$
2. **Two disjoint compact sets are separated.** If $K, L \subseteq X$ are compact
   and $K \cap L = \varnothing$, there are $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ with
   $$L \subseteq U, \qquad K \subseteq V, \qquad U \cap V = \varnothing .$$
3. **Compact implies closed.** Every compact subset of $X$ is closed in $X$.
4. **In a compact Hausdorff space the two classes coincide.** If in addition
   $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is compact, then a subset of $X$ is compact if and only if
   it is closed.

**The proof is written choice-free, and that is not a stylistic preference.** The
textbook argument says "for each $y \in K$ choose disjoint open $U_y, V_y$",
which is a selection over an arbitrary index set and therefore an appeal to the
full Axiom of Choice. What is done below instead is to take the family of **all**
open $V$ that admit some open $U \ni x$ disjoint from them — a family cut out by
a formula, with nothing selected — extract a finite subcover from it, and only
then make finitely many selections, which [[lem-finite-choice]] supplies as a
theorem of ZF.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), with
subspaces as in [[def-subspace-topology-top]] and compactness as in
[[def-compact-space]]. Then:

1. **Closed in compact is compact.** If $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is compact and
   $F \subseteq X$ is closed in $X$, then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$.
2. **Finite unions.** If $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $K_0, \dots, K_n$ are compact
   subsets of $X$, then $K_0 \cup \dots \cup K_n$ is a compact subset of $X$. The
   union of the empty list is $\varnothing$, which is a compact subset of every
   space.

Claim 1 needs $X$ to be compact and claim 2 does not; no hypothesis of any kind
is placed on $X$ in claim 2. **No choice principle is used**: claim 1 selects
nothing, taking a least index where a selection would be natural, and claim 2
makes finitely many selections through [[lem-finite-choice]], a theorem of ZF.

derivations.claim: The proper-support functor is a sheaf, additive and left exact; for proper $f$ it equals $f_*$, for an open inclusion it is extension by zero, and for a closed inclusion it is direct image. For a sheaf $A$ and open $V\subseteq Y$ let $f_!A(V)$ be the set of $s\in A(f^{-1}V)$ whose support maps properly to $V$, with restrictions inherited from $A$; these are well defined because for open $W\subseteq V$ the support of $s|$ is $\operatorname{Supp}(s)\cap f^{-1}W$ by [F9], and the preimage of a compact subset of $W$ under $\operatorname{Supp}(s)\cap f^{-1}W\to W$ is the corresponding preimage under the proper map $\operatorname{Supp}(s)\to V$. Additivity is evident from linearity of restriction and gluing. For the sheaf property let $V=\bigcup V_\alpha$ and let $s_\alpha$ be compatible sections; they glue to $s\in A(f^{-1}V)$ with $\operatorname{Supp}(s)\subseteq\bigcup_\alpha\operatorname{Supp}(s_\alpha)$ and $s|=s_\alpha$ over $f^{-1}V_\alpha$. If $L\subseteq V$ is compact, cover $L$ by finitely many open $W_1,\dots,W_n$ with compact closures $\overline{W_j}$ contained in some $V_{\alpha(j)}$, possible by [F12]; then $\operatorname{Supp}(s)\cap f^{-1}(L)\subseteq\bigcup_j\bigl(\operatorname{Supp}(s_{\alpha(j)})\cap f^{-1}(\overline{W_j})\bigr)$, a finite union of compact sets because $\overline{W_j}\subseteq V_{\alpha(j)}$ is compact and $\operatorname{Supp}(s_{\alpha(j)})\to V_{\alpha(j)}$ is proper; and $\operatorname{Supp}(s)\cap f^{-1}(L)$ is closed in $f^{-1}(L)$ by [F9], so it is a finite union of closed subsets of these compacta, hence compact by [F12]. Thus $f_!A$ is a sheaf. Kernels are computed sectionwise, so $(f_!\ker\varphi)(V)=\ker(f_!\varphi)(V)$ and $f_!$ is left exact. If $f$ is proper, every support map is proper by [F8], so $f_!=f_*$. If $f=j:U\hookrightarrow Y$ is an open inclusion, properness of $\operatorname{Supp}(s)\to V$ is equivalent to closedness of $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ in $V$ by [F8], which is exactly the extension-by-zero condition of [F9]; if $f=i:Z\hookrightarrow Y$ is a closed inclusion then $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ is closed in $V\cap Z$, hence in $V$, and $i_!=i_*$.

The comparison map to compactly supported fibre sections is injective. For $y\in Y$ and a sheaf $A$ on $X$, restriction of representatives defines $(f_!A)_y\to\Gamma_c(X_y,A|_{X_y})$: a germ represented by $s\in f_!A(V)$ restricts to the fibre $X_y$, its support there is $\operatorname{Supp}(s)\cap X_y$, compact because $f|_{\operatorname{Supp}(s)}$ is proper and $\{y\}$ is compact, and the class depends only on the germ. If it is zero, then $s$ vanishes near every point of $\operatorname{Supp}(s)\cap X_y$; since $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ is closed in $f^{-1}V$ and its fibre part is compact, [F3] and [F12] let us shrink $V$ around $y$ so that the support of $s$ over the shrunk base meets no point of $X_y$, and the remaining part of the support over the shrunk base is closed and differs from $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ by a closed set on which $s$ vanishes; hence the germ of $s$ at $y$ is zero.

The comparison map is surjective, hence an isomorphism. Let $t\in\Gamma_c(X_y,A|_{X_y})$ have compact support $Q$. By [F3], its restriction near $Q$ is represented by an ambient section $s_0$ on a neighbourhood $W$ of $Q$. Shrink $W$ so that $s_0|_{W\cap X_y}=t|_{W\cap X_y}$: equality holds near every point of $Q$ and its equality locus is open in the fibre, so an ambient neighbourhood of the compact $Q$ can be chosen inside it. By [F12] choose an open $W_0$ containing $Q$ with compact closure contained in $W$, and put $C=\overline{W_0}\setminus W_0$. Since $C\cap X_y$ is disjoint from $Q$, the germs of $s_0$ there are zero. Its zero locus is open, so choose an open $N\subseteq W$ containing $C\cap X_y$ on which $s_0=0$. The compact set $C\setminus N$ is disjoint from $X_y$; its continuous image is compact and hence closed in the Hausdorff $Y$, and does not contain $y$. Let $Y_0=Y\setminus f(C\setminus N)$, an open neighbourhood of $y$. Then $C\cap f^{-1}Y_0\subseteq N$. On $f^{-1}Y_0$ glue $s_0$ on $W_0\cap f^{-1}Y_0$ with zero outside $\overline{W_0}$, using the open vanishing neighbourhood $N\cap f^{-1}Y_0$ of the collar to cover and match across it. The resulting section $s$ restricts to $t$ on the fibre and has support contained in $\overline{W_0}\cap f^{-1}Y_0$. For every compact $L\subseteq Y_0$, $\operatorname{Supp}(s)\cap f^{-1}L$ is closed in the compact $\overline{W_0}$, so it is compact. Thus $s\in f_!A(Y_0)$ represents $t$. No extension of a section from $Q\cup(C\cap X_y)$ to all of $\overline{W_0}$ has been assumed. The comparisons are natural under restriction.

Fibrewise acyclicity and the fibre formula. If $A$ is injective then $A$ is $c$-soft by [F5], and restriction of a $c$-soft sheaf to a closed subspace is $c$-soft by [F4]; a fibre $X_y=f^{-1}(\{y\})$ is closed because $\{y\}$ is closed in $Y$, so $A|_{X_y}$ is $c$-soft and hence $\Gamma_c$-acyclic in positive degrees by [F5]. An injective resolution of $A$ on $X$ restricts to a $\Gamma_c$-acyclic resolution of $A|_{X_y}$, so $(Rf_!A)_y\simeq R\Gamma_c(X_y,A|_{X_y})$ by the fibre formula of step 1.3 and exactness of stalks, which evaluates the derived functor on the fibre. The uniform bound $d$ of [F7] makes every fibre $X_y$ have $H^q_c(X_y,-)=0$ for $q>d$, so $Rf_!$ has cohomological dimension at most $d$ fibrewise and maps $D^b(X)$ to $D^b(Y)$: a bounded complex has bounded fibrewise cohomology, and the fibre formula exhibits $Rf_!$ of it as fibrewise compact-support cohomology concentrated in bounded degrees. A fibrewise $c$-soft sheaf is $f_!$-acyclic by the same stalk computation.

The complex $H_K(I)$ is a termwise flasque sheaf complex with lower bound $\inf(I)-d$. Let $I$ be a bounded-below injective complex on $Y$ and $K$ the finite fibrewise-soft resolution of [F7] in degrees $0,\dots,d$, with $K_U=j_{U!}j_U^*K$ for open $U\subseteq X$. For an open cover $U=\bigcup U_i$ of an open $U$, the augmented extension-by-zero Čech complex of $K_U$ is exact on stalks: at a point $x\in U$, the simplex of indices $i$ with $x\in U_i$ has the elementary contracting homotopy that adds a fixed such index, and on $U$ the complex resolves $k_U$ columnwise. Each term is a direct sum of sheaves $j_{W!}(K|_W)$, which are fibrewise $c$-soft by [F4] because $K$ is, and hence $f_!$-acyclic by step 2.1. The cycles of the augmented complex are again $f_!$-acyclic: dimension shifting along its short exact cycle sequences identifies $R^qf_!$ of a cycle with $R^{q+r}f_!$ of an earlier cycle for every $r$, and choosing $r>d$ makes the latter vanish by step 2.1; consequently $f_!$ carries the resolution to an exact complex. Since each $I^q$ is injective, $\operatorname{Hom}_Y(-,I^q)$ preserves exactness, and the first three terms give the sheaf equalizer for the presheaf $U\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_Y(f_!K_U,I)$, so $H_K(I)$ is a sheaf complex. For $V\subseteq U$ the map $K_V\to K_U$ is monic and $f_!$ is left exact by step 1.1, so $f_!K_V\to f_!K_U$ is monic; injectivity of $I^q$ then makes the restriction maps of $H_K(I)$ surjective in every total degree, because $\operatorname{Hom}_Y(-,I^q)$ sends a monomorphism to a surjection and finite products over the finite $K$-degree preserve surjectivity. Thus $H_K(I)$ is termwise flasque. Its degree-$n$ term is a finite product of terms $\operatorname{Hom}_Y(f_!K_U,I^{p+n})$ with $p\in[0,d]$, so it vanishes for $n<\inf(I)-d$.

The generators $E_U=j_{U!}k_U$ are resolved by $K_U$ against $f_!$, and derived sections of $H_K(I)$ are computed by the ordinary section complex. By [F9] and [F1], $\operatorname{Hom}_X(E_U,H_K(I))=\operatorname{H}^0$ of the complex $\Gamma(U,H_K(I))=\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_Y(f_!K_U,I)$. The complex $K_U$ resolves $E_U$ by $f_!$-acyclic terms by step 3.1, so $f_!K_U$ represents $Rf_!E_U$ and the identity $\Gamma(U,H_K(I))=\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_Y(f_!K_U,I)$ represents the derived Hom $\operatorname{RHom}_Y(Rf_!E_U,I)$. Since $H_K(I)$ is a bounded-below flasque complex by step 3.1, its ordinary section complex computes its derived sections by [F2], so $\operatorname{RHom}_X(E_U,H_K(I))\simeq\Gamma(U,H_K(I))$ and the comparison is evaluation on generators, natural in $U$ and in morphisms of generators.

The generator resolution of a bounded complex and the derived comparison. Let $A$ be a bounded complex of $k$-sheaves. By [F10] the descending kernel recursion produces a bounded-above complex $M$ of direct sums of generators $E_U=j_{U!}k_U$, together with a stalk-surjective quasi-isomorphism $M\to A$; the recursion is $k$-linear, and each $M^n=\bigoplus E_U$ is a direct sum of generators. The bounded complex $K$ of [F7] is K-flat over $k$ by [F2], so $K\otimes_kM\to A$ is a resolution of $A$ whose terms are direct sums of the $K_U$ and hence $f_!$-acyclic by step 3.1; applying $f_!$ computes $Rf_!A$, using that an acyclic complex with $f_!$-acyclic terms has acyclic $f_!$-image by dimension shifting past the bound $d$, truncating below any prescribed degree before a comparison. Termwise evaluation on the generator summands and additivity of $f_!$ give the chain identity $\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_X(M,H_K(I))=\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_Y(f_!(K\otimes_kM),I)$: on a single generator $E_U$ this is the defining identity of [F1], and direct sums on the left correspond to direct sums of $f_!K_U$ on the right while $\operatorname{Hom}$ turns them into products, which are exact over a field. Let $J$ be a bounded-below injective replacement of $H_K(I)$. Since $M\to A$ is a quasi-isomorphism and $J$ is K-injective, $\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_X(A,J)\to\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_X(M,J)$ is a quasi-isomorphism; by [F2] each generator comparison $\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_X(E_U,H_K(I))\to\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_X(E_U,J)$ is a quasi-isomorphism, and products and direct sums over $k$-vector spaces preserve these; the Hom bicomplex has bounded diagonals because $M$ is bounded above and $H_K(I),J$ are bounded below, so row comparison proves the total comparison $\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_X(M,H_K(I))\to\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_X(M,J)$ is a quasi-isomorphism. Combining, $\operatorname{RHom}_X(A,H_K(I))\simeq\operatorname{RHom}_Y(Rf_!A,I)$ for bounded $A$ and bounded-below injective $I$.

The Hom transposition, the adjoint candidate and its lower bound. Taking $I=I_B$ a bounded-below injective replacement of a bounded-below complex $B$ with $I_B^n=0$ for $n<\inf(B)$ by [F1], step 5.1 gives $\operatorname{RHom}_X(A,H_K(I_B))\simeq\operatorname{RHom}_Y(Rf_!A,I_B)$, and $H^0$ yields the natural exceptional Hom transposition $\operatorname{Hom}(Rf_!A,B)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}(A,f^!B)$ for bounded $A$, with $f^!B$ represented by $H_K(I_B)$. By step 3.1 the representative has lower bound $\inf(I_B)-d=\inf(B)-d$, so $f^!$ has lower cohomological bound $\inf(B)-d$. The construction uses the chosen finite resolution and the chosen injective model; any two choices differ by the unique identity-transposition comparisons induced by the resolution comparisons of [F2], so the transposition is well defined.

The counit and the coherence laws on the bounded constructible specialization. For each closed $Q\subseteq f^{-1}V$ with $Q\to V$ proper, the complex of $Q$-supported sections of $H_K(I)$ is $\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_Y(f_!(K|_Q),I)$ by the exact open/closed support sequence and fibrewise acyclicity; since $Q\to V$ is proper, $f_!(K|_Q)=f_*(K|_Q)$ by [F8], and precomposing with $k_V\to f_*k_Q\to f_*(K|_Q)$, induced by the constant-section unit and the coaugmentation $k_X\to K$, gives a map to $I(V)$. These maps commute with enlargement of supports and with restriction, so they assemble to a morphism $f_!H_K(I)\to I$; the flasque terms of $H_K(I)$ are $f_!$-acyclic by step 3.1, so this is the derived counit and on every generator $E_U$ its induced Hom transposition is exactly the defining evaluation of step 4.1. When the later geometric theorem proves that $f^!$ preserves the bounded constructible subcategory, the Hom transposition becomes a genuine adjunction $Rf_!\dashv f^!$ on that specialization, and its two triangle identities follow by inverse transposition; in that category the unique identity-transposition comparisons between choices of $K$ and $I$ satisfy the identity and cocycle laws. The lemma does not infer an unrestricted $D^+$-source adjunction from this bounded-source generator argument.
