Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let
$G=\prod_i\operatorname{GL}_{n_i}(\mathbb C)$ be a finite product of complex
general linear groups with $n_i\ge1$
([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]), acting algebraically on a
separated finite-type complex algebraic variety $X$
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]],
[[def-algebraic-group-action-and-scheme-theoretic-stabilizer]]). For integers
$N_i\ge n_i+1$ put
$$U_N=\prod_i\operatorname{Inj}(\mathbb C^{n_i},\mathbb C^{N_i}),\qquad B_N=\prod_i\operatorname{Gr}(n_i,N_i),\qquad X_N=(U_N\times X)/G,$$
where $G$ acts on $U_N$ by precomposition of frames and on $U_N\times X$
diagonally, and set $r_N=2\min_i(N_i-n_i)$. Let
$p_N:G^\bullet\times P_N\to G^\bullet\times X$, with
$P_N=U_N\times X$ and $p_N=(\mathrm{id},\operatorname{pr}_X)$, be the
simplicial map of the two action nerves
([[def-equivariant-constructible-derived-category-for-complex-algebraic-varieties]]),
and let $Q_N:D^b_{G,c}(X;k)\to D_c^b(X_N;k)$ be the composite of $p_N^*$ with
the locally split Čech descent equivalence for the principal bundle
$P_N\to X_N$
([[lem-locally-split-cech-nerves-give-derived-cartesian-sheaf-descent]]).
Then, for bounded algebraically constructible $A,B$ in $D^b_{G,c}(X;k)$:

1. **Hom comparison.** If $A\in D_c^{\le a}$ and $B\in D_c^{\ge b}$, then
   pullback induces an isomorphism
   $\operatorname{Hom}_G(A,B[m])\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{X_N}(Q_N(A),Q_N(B)[m])$
   whenever $m\le b+r_N-a$;
2. **full faithfulness.** On an ordinary cohomological interval
   $D_c^{[b,a]}$ of width $a-b\le r_N$, the functor $Q_N$ is fully faithful;
3. **image.** On such an interval the image of $Q_N$ consists exactly of the
   objects $H$ whose principal-bundle pullback $q_N^*H$ lies in the image of
   $\operatorname{pr}_X^*:D_c^{[b,a]}(X;k)\to D_c^{[b,a]}(P_N;k)$, i.e. of
   the resolution triples whose frame-bundle pullback comes from $X$; the
   image is closed under retracts, and under extensions when
   $r_N\ge a-b+1$;
4. **coherence.** For two resolutions $N,M$, use the common product resolution
   $U_N\times U_M$ and its associated quotient
   $X_{N,M}=(U_N\times U_M\times X)/G$ with projections
   $\pi_N:X_{N,M}\to X_N$ and $\pi_M:X_{N,M}\to X_M$.
   The pullbacks $\pi_N^*Q_N(A)$ and $\pi_M^*Q_M(A)$ are canonically
   identified on intervals of width at most $\min(r_N,r_M)$, and their
   Hom comparisons commute with natural transformations and satisfy the
   cocycle identity after pullback to a triple product resolution.
   No identification of $U_N\times U_M$ with $U_{N+M}$ or direct
   isomorphism of functors with different target categories is asserted;
5. **trivial group.** If $G$ is trivial then $U_N$, $B_N$ and $X_N$ are $X$
   or a point, $r_N=\infty$, and $Q_N$ is the identity of $D_c^b(X;k)$.

No global tensor splitting
$Ra_{N*}a_N^*B\simeq B\otimes_kR\Gamma(U_N;k)$ is asserted for the
frame-bundle projection $a_N:P_N\to B_N$; the comparison is used only on the
nerve and through the finite local models.

For analytic algebraic maps on its proved constructible subcategory, the six operations $f^*,Rf_*,Rf_!,f^!,\otimes_k^L,R\mathcal Hom$ have their three adjunctions, composition and identity comparisons, ordinary proper and extraordinary proper base change, projection formula, support localization, dualizing transitivity and trace. The comparisons commute with Cartesian pasting, composition of maps, evaluation and trace, giving a coherent pull-push product calculus. For a locally trivial product projection with finite-type smooth fibre $F$, the actual finite product cochain model gives $R\mathrm{pr}_*\mathrm{pr}^*B\simeq B\otimes_k C^*(F;k)$, with its ordinary unit. Smooth base change for $Rf_*$ holds whenever a supplied factorization $f=p\circ j$ has $p$ proper and $j$ an open inclusion with the conical local models below; proper maps already satisfy it. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: **The dimension correction.** The projections $\operatorname{pr}_X:P_N\to X$ and $q_N:P_N\to X_N$ are smooth surjective algebraic maps of pure relative complex dimensions $u_N$ and $g$, and $\operatorname{pr}_X^*A_X\cong q_N^*Q_N(A)$ by [F3]. Since $s_N+g=u_N$, this gives $q_N^*(Q_N(A)[s_N])[g]\cong\operatorname{pr}_X^*A_X[u_N]$. The left side is the normalized object under the perverse-exact functor $q_N^*[g]$, and the right side is $A_X$ under the perverse-exact functor $\operatorname{pr}_X^*[u_N]$. Thus the comparison uses the unshifted base object $A_X$, without an extra shift by $u_N$ on $X$.

**Connected fibres and local systems.** Each $\operatorname{GL}_{n_i}(\mathbb C)$ is path connected: Gaussian elimination expresses an invertible matrix as a product of elementary matrices and nonzero diagonal matrices, each joined to the identity by a path. Each frame space $\operatorname{Inj}(\mathbb C^{n_i},\mathbb C^{N_i})$ is the continuous image of connected $\operatorname{GL}_{N_i}(\mathbb C)$ under its first-$n_i$-columns map, so $U_N$ is connected. A locally trivial bundle with connected fibre induces a surjection on fundamental groups: lift a base loop locally and join its endpoint to its initial point inside the fibre. Thus on a connected smooth invariant stratum $S$ both $q_N:U_N\times S\to S_N$ and $\operatorname{pr}_S:U_N\times S\to S$ induce surjective fundamental-group maps. Local trivializations define parallel transport by subdivision along paths; subdivision of a homotopy square proves homotopy invariance, and a sub-local-system is exactly a subspace of one stalk invariant under this loop transport, extended to all stalks by transport. Thus these pullbacks preserve and reflect irreducibility, since the full monodromy image is unchanged. If $L$ is an equivariant local system and $L_N=Q_NL$, any ordinary sub-local-system $M_N\subset L_N$ pulls back to a sub-local-system of $\operatorname{pr}_S^*L$. On the product the $U_N$ factor acts trivially on this monodromy representation and its subrepresentations, so $q_N^*M_N=\operatorname{pr}_S^*M$ for a local system $M$ on $S$. The actual resolution-image criterion in ordinary interval $[0,0]$ descends $M_N$ to an equivariant local system and the degree-zero Hom comparison lifts its injection. Hence $L$ is simple equivariantly if and only if $L_N$ is irreducible ordinarily, and by the connected-fibre pullbacks if and only if its underlying local system on $S$ is irreducible.

**Detection via restriction to $X$.** By [F1] the shifted pullbacks $\operatorname{pr}_X^*[u_N]$ and $q_N^*[g]$ are exact for the ordinary middle-perverse t-structures and commute with truncation; hence, for every $a$, $q_N^*\bigl(Q_N(A)[s_N]\bigr)[g]=\operatorname{pr}_X^*(A_X[u_N])$ lies in the perverse aisle ${}^pD^{\le a}$ of $P_N$ if and only if $A_X$ lies in ${}^pD^{\le a}$ of $X$, and by exactness of $q_N^*[g]$ this is equivalent to $Q_N(A)[s_N]\in{}^pD^{\le a}(X_N)$. The same computation for the dual aisle identifies the two inequalities, so the structure is detected by restriction to $X$ and by the normalized resolution simultaneously. Independence of the sufficiently large $N$ follows because the conditions are those of the fixed ordinary object $A_X$. This proves claim 1.

**Perverse exactness and conservativity.** Truncation in the equivariant category is transported through the equivalence of claim 1: the perverse truncation triangles of [F2] on $X$ and on $X_N$ correspond under the smooth pullbacks of [F1] because those commute with truncation and cohomology, and since pullback is a functor the correspondence preserves composition of morphisms. Hence $A\mapsto Q_N(A)[s_N]$ carries the perverse t-structure of $D^b_{G,c}$ detected in claim 1 to the ordinary perverse t-structure of $X_N$ and is exact. For conservativity, if $Q_N(A)=0$ then the Hom comparison of [F3] at $m=0$ gives $\operatorname{End}_G(A)\cong\operatorname{End}_{X_N}(0)=0$, so the identity of $A$ is zero and $A\cong0$; conversely $A=0$ clearly gives $Q_N(A)=0$. This proves claim 2.

**Truncation lifting.** Let $A\in D^b_{G,c}(X;k)$ have ordinary amplitude in $[b,a]$ and choose $N$ with $r_N$ at least the width of the ordinary amplitudes of $A$, its ordinary perverse truncations and their finitely many iterated perverse cohomology objects; the amplitude bookkeeping is finite because the ordinary perverse t-structure is bounded and the truncations of a fixed bounded object involve finitely many cohomological degrees. Put $T={}^p\tau^{\le a}\bigl(Q_N(A)[s_N]\bigr)$ in $D_c^b(X_N;k)$, an ordinary perverse truncation, and compute its normalized pullback: since $q_N^*[g]$ is perverse exact and $s_N+g=u_N$ with $\operatorname{pr}_X^*A_X\cong q_N^*Q_N(A)$, one has $q_N^*T[g]\cong{}^p\tau^{\le a}\bigl(\operatorname{pr}_X^*A_X[u_N]\bigr)$, which perverse exactness of $\operatorname{pr}_X^*[u_N]$ identifies with $\operatorname{pr}_X^*\bigl({}^p\tau^{\le a}A_X\bigr)[u_N]$, equivalently $q_N^*T\cong\operatorname{pr}_X^*\bigl({}^p\tau^{\le a}A_X\bigr)[s_N]$ up to canonical isomorphism: the smooth pullbacks commute with the perverse truncation. By the image criterion of [F3] applied to the frame bundle, $T[-s_N]$ lies in the finite-resolution image once $N$ is large enough that the unnormalized bounded amplitude of the truncation triangle fits into the comparison range; descents of $T[-s_N]$ and the correspondingly unshifted truncation triangle give an object ${}^p\tau_G^{\le a}A\in D^b_{G,c}(X;k)$ with the displayed compatibility, and the bounded fully faithful comparison of [F3] lifts the canonical image isomorphism uniquely between two such lifts. This proves claim 3.

**Projectors, concentration and simplicity.** Let $K\in D^b_{G,c}(X;k)$ have ordinary cohomology in $[b,a]$ with $a-b\le r_N$, so that the degree-zero ring comparison $\operatorname{End}_G(K)\cong\operatorname{End}_{X_N}(Q_NK)$ of [F3] is an isomorphism. A finite family of mutually orthogonal idempotents in $\operatorname{End}_{X_N}(Q_NK)$ summing to the identity pulls back to a finite family in $\operatorname{End}_G(K)$ with the same relations, and the idempotent splitting of [F3] splits each of them; the summands remain in $[b,a]$ because ordinary cohomology of a direct summand is a direct summand. By claims 1 and 2 the normalized functor is exact and conservative, so a nonzero proper equivariant subobject of a lift would give a nonzero proper ordinary subobject of the corresponding normalized object; this proves reflection of simplicity, which is the direction consumed by the semisimplicity application, as well as detection of perverse concentration. The preservation direction is proved below using the actual connected general linear group hypothesis and local-system descent. This proves claim 4.

**Underlying ordinary simplicity.** The equivariant truncations of step 4.1 and the localization adjunctions of [F4] define intermediate extension by the image of ${}^pH^0j_!\to{}^pH^0Rj_*$. A simple equivariant heart object $A$ has irreducible invariant support $Z$: the finite support components are permuted by connected $G$, hence individually invariant, and localization on a dense component would otherwise yield a nonzero proper subobject. Choose the invariant dense smooth open where its ordinary cohomology is locally constant; equivariance preserves this locus and algebraic constructibility gives a dense algebraic such open. The perverse inequalities force restriction there to be a local system $L[\dim Z]$. A proper equivariant sub-local-system yields a proper subobject by localization adjunction and perverse image, so $L$ is simple equivariantly. Absence of boundary subobjects and quotients identifies $A$ with $j_{!*}L[\dim Z]$ by the image and adjunction characterization of [F2]. Restriction is perverse exact by step 2.1 and commutes with localization in [F4], hence with that image. Step 1.2 makes $L$ irreducible ordinarily, so $A_X$ is the ordinary simple intersection complex of [F2].

**Preservation after normalization.** Smooth dimension-shifted pullback along a locally trivial map with connected smooth fibres preserves ordinary simple intersection complexes: the fundamental-group surjection preserves irreducibility on the dense smooth open, smooth local product comparison commutes with $j_!$ and $Rj_*$ on boundary charts, and perverse exactness carries their intermediate-extension image to the same image upstairs. Here the fibres are irreducible frame spaces, so the inverse image of an irreducible support is irreducible. Apply this to $\operatorname{pr}_X$, with fibre $U_N$. For simple equivariant $A$, step 5.1 makes $A_X$ simple, so $\operatorname{pr}_X^*A_X[u_N]$ is simple. By step 1.1 this is $q_N^*(Q_N(A)[s_N])[g]$. Any nonzero proper subobject of $Q_N(A)[s_N]$ would give one upstairs through exact conservative $q_N^*[g]$, a contradiction. Thus normalization preserves simplicity; reflection is step 4.2 and concentration is step 2.1. Both directions use the same $s_N=u_N-g$ and stated ring-comparison threshold, with the actual product of connected general linear groups.

**Conclusion.** Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 prove claims 1 and 2, step 4.1 claim 3, and steps 4.2, 5.1 and 6.1 claim 4. Let $J_0=\{a\in A:Ta=0\}\subseteq A$ be the kernel computed in $\mathbb Q$-coordinates, a rational subspace; then $J_0\otimes\mathbb C=J$, since a rational linear system has the same solutions after extension of scalars and its solution space over $\mathbb C$ is the complexification of its rational solution space. Since $J$ is a two-sided ideal of $B$, the intersection $J_0=J\cap A$ is a two-sided ideal of $A$, and $W=\{v\in V:J_0v=0\}$ is a rational $A$-submodule of $V$. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Identify $W_{\mathbb C}$ with the socle. Because $J_0\otimes\mathbb C=J$, one has $W_{\mathbb C}=\{v\in V_{\mathbb C}:Jv=0\}$. Hence the socle of $V_{\mathbb C}$ is contained in $\{v:Jv=0\}$. derivations.claim: 1.1 Let $A\subseteq\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q}(V)$ be the $\mathbb Q$-span of the monodromy matrices. It contains the identity and is closed under multiplication, because a product of monodromy matrices is a monodromy matrix, so it is a finite-dimensional unital $\mathbb Q$-algebra. For every field $E$ over $\mathbb Q$ the canonical map $A\otimes_{\mathbb Q}E\to\operatorname{End}_E(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}E)$ is injective: rationally independent matrices stay independent after extending scalars, as one sees by comparing coordinates in a rational basis of $V$. Its image is the $E$-span of the monodromy matrices, so submodules for this image are exactly the monodromy-invariant subspaces of $V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}E$; in particular the action of $A_{\mathbb C}=A\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$ on $V_{\mathbb C}$ is faithful. [given, algebra]

2.1 Assume $V_{\mathbb C}$ is semisimple. Let $J=J(A_{\mathbb C})$. If $T\subseteq V_{\mathbb C}$ is a simple submodule, then $JT$ is a submodule equal to $0$ or $T$, and $JT=T$ would give $J^kT=T$ for every $k\ge1$, contradicting the nilpotence of $J$ from [F1]. Hence $J$ kills every simple summand of $V_{\mathbb C}$ and therefore kills all of $V_{\mathbb C}$, since a semisimple module is a direct sum of simple submodules by [F4]. Faithfulness of the action, established in step 1.1, then forces $J=0$: an element of $J$ acts as zero on $V_{\mathbb C}$. Therefore $A_{\mathbb C}$ is semisimple. [F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Choose the rational basis $a_1,\dots,a_d$ of $A$ and let $T=(\operatorname{tr}(L_{a_ia_j}))_{i,j}$ be the Gram matrix of the regular trace form of $A$ in this basis. Its entries are rational: passing from $A$ to $A_{\mathbb C}$ extends the rational matrix of left multiplication by $a_ia_j$ to a complex matrix with the same trace. By step 2.1 and [F2] the regular trace form of $A_{\mathbb C}$ is nondegenerate, so $\det T\ne0$ as a complex number, and since $\det T\in\mathbb Q$ it is a nonzero rational number. For every field $k$ the scalar extension $\mathbb Q\hookrightarrow k$ therefore makes $T$, viewed over $k$, a nondegenerate matrix. No embedding of $k$ into $\mathbb C$ is used. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $k$ be any characteristic-zero field and put $A_k=A\otimes_{\mathbb Q}k$. For $x\in J(A_k)$ and $b\in A_k$ the product $xb$ lies in the nilpotent ideal $J(A_k)$ by [F1], so $(xb)^n=0$ for some $n$ and the endomorphism $L_{xb}$ of $A_k$ is nilpotent; by [F3] its trace vanishes. Nondegeneracy of the extended matrix $T$ from step 3.1 then forces $x=0$, so $J(A_k)=0$. By [F1] the quotient $A_k/J(A_k)=A_k$ is a semisimple ring. [F1, F3, step 3.1, algebra]

Hence $V_k$ is a sum of images of simple modules, each of which is simple or zero, and $V_k$ has finite length over $k$; by [F4] it is a finite direct sum of simple modules, that is, semisimple. By [F7] we may view $S$ as a finite-type separated integral scheme over $\mathbb C$; smoothness of the algebraic variety means every local ring is regular, so by the equivalence of [F7] the structure morphism $S\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$ is scheme-smooth. Applying the Jacobian criterion of [F7] to this morphism gives an affine neighbourhood of $x$ with a presentation $C_h\cong(\mathbb C[t_1,\dots,t_m]/(f_1,\dots,f_r))_g$ in which some $r\times r$ minor of the Jacobian matrix $(\partial f_j/\partial t_i)$ is invertible at $x$, and whose fibres have dimension $m-r$; here the fibre is the local variety itself, so $m-r=n=\dim S$. After relabelling the coordinates and applying the holomorphic implicit function theorem of [F7] to the holomorphic map $(f_1,\dots,f_r)$ near the image of $x$, the common zero locus is locally the graph of a holomorphic function of the remaining $m-r=n$ coordinates; the graph coordinate map identifies a neighbourhood of $x$ in the analytic topology with an open ball in $\mathbb C^n$, and this analytic topology is the one of [F7]. The same presentation and implicit-function argument applied to the reduced induced structure of a locally closed smooth complex subvariety exhibits its points as complex charts of dimension equal to its complex dimension. Consequently $S$, and every smooth locally closed complex subvariety of $S$, is a complex manifold for the analytic topology, hence in particular a smooth real manifold of twice its complex dimension; the chart balls are path-connected neighbourhoods, so $S$ and its open subsets are locally path connected. The family $\widetilde{\mathcal F}$ is a homotopy from $\gamma_2$ to $\widetilde{\mathcal F}_a$ through based loops, so $[\widetilde{\mathcal F}_a]=[\gamma_2]=[\gamma]$ in $\pi_1(S,s)$ by [F8], while $[\widetilde{\mathcal F}_a]$ lies in the image of $\pi_1(U,s)\to\pi_1(S,s)$ by [F8]. In the discarded case $K=\varnothing$ of step 2.2 the loop $\gamma_2$ itself already lies in $U$, so the same conclusion holds. Since every class in $\pi_1(S,s)$ has a continuous based loop representative, the map $\pi_1(U,s)\to\pi_1(S,s)$ is surjective. [F2, F6, F8, step 1.2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Path connectedness. Let $x,y\in U$. By step 1.1 the space $S$ is locally path connected, and it is connected by hypothesis, so [F9] makes $S$ path connected; choose a path in $S$ from $x$ to $y$, reparametrize it so that it is constant near $0$ and near $1$, and apply the relative approximation [F5] with the closed set $\{0,1\}$ (on which the reparametrized path is smooth because it is constant) to obtain a smooth path $\beta:[0,1]\to S$ from $x$ to $y$ that is constant near $0$ and $1$. Likewise choose a smooth path $\eta:[0,1]\to S$ from $y$ to $x$, constant near its endpoints. Glue these into a smooth based loop $\gamma:S^1\to S$: traverse $\beta$ on the first quarter of the circle, $\eta$ on the second quarter, and the constant loop at $x$ on the second half; the loops are constant near the three junction points and agree there, so $\gamma$ is smooth, and $\gamma$ is based at $x$. Its bad set $\gamma^{-1}(Z)$ is disjoint from a neighbourhood of the junction points, because $\gamma$ is constant with value $x$ or $y$, both in $U$, near those points. Apply the constructions of steps 2.2, 3.1 and 4.1 with this loop $\gamma$ in place of $\gamma_2$ and with the same finite family of pieces $Z_j$: the cutoff $\chi$ vanishes on a neighbourhood of the junction points and equals one near $\gamma^{-1}(Z)$, the truncated family is transverse to every piece, and a good parameter $a$ yields a smooth loop $\gamma'=\widetilde{\mathcal F}_a:S^1\to U$ that agrees with $\gamma$ on a neighbourhood of the junction points and is homotopic to $\gamma$ through based loops. Restricting $\gamma'$ to the first quarter of the circle gives a continuous path in $U$ from $\gamma'(0)=\gamma(0)=x$ to $\gamma'(1/4)=\gamma(1/4)=y$. As $x,y\in U$ were arbitrary, $U$ is path connected. [F9, F5, F4, F3, F2, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra] ∎

boundaries.evidence: If $n=0$ then $S$ is a point, $Z=\varnothing$ and $U=S$; the discarded case $K=\varnothing$ of step 4.1 proves surjectivity and step 5.1 the path-connectedness criterion (steps 4.1, 5.1).
Dimension zero and the empty complement are exactly the cases handled in step 4.1's $K=\varnothing$ branch and step 5.1; no positive-dimensional parameter count is needed there.
For a one-dimensional base $S$, $Z$ is finite and the strata of step 2.1 are points, of real codimension two in the surface $S$; steps 2.2-5.1 apply verbatim.

The complement $Z$ may be empty, reducible, singular or of mixed dimension; step 2.1 iterates the dimension descent using only generic smoothness of components, and step 4.1 discards the empty bad set.
The base point is kept fixed: the cutoff of step 2.2 vanishes at the base point and the slice is based for every parameter (step 3.1); no other endpoint occurs.

AC is assumed and used exactly through the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ suppliers invoked in steps 1.2, 2.2 and 4.1; the stratification and finitely many perturbations are otherwise choice-free (statement, step 1.2).

boundaries.reason: The lemma asserts path-connectedness and surjectivity, not a biconditional; no forward iff direction is owed.
No converse is asserted.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every projective morphism in the finite-dimensional
H-projective convention of this page is proper: if $f:X\to S$ factors over $S$
as
$$X\xrightarrow{i}\mathbb P^n_S\longrightarrow S$$
with $n\ge0$, $i$ a closed immersion and the second arrow the projection, then
$f$ is proper. The empty source, the empty base and the case $n=0$ are
included, and no Noetherian, field, reducedness or nonemptiness hypothesis is
imposed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
Jacobian-criterion, ample-powers, Chern-form and comparison suppliers below.
Let $X$ be a smooth projective complex scheme of pure dimension $n\ge0$.

Then the closed points of $X$ carry a structure of **complex manifold**
$X^{\mathrm{an}}$, its **analytification**: if $X\ne\varnothing$ and $n\ge1$
this is a compact Hausdorff second-countable smooth complex manifold of complex
dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]); if $n=0$ it is the
finite discrete set $X(\mathbb C)$ with its unique complex structure in the
convention of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]]; and if
$X=\varnothing$ then $X^{\mathrm{an}}=\varnothing$. Every standard smooth
algebraic chart of $X$ becomes a holomorphic chart of $X^{\mathrm{an}}$, and
every morphism of smooth complex schemes $X\to Y$ induces a holomorphic map
$X^{\mathrm{an}}\to Y^{\mathrm{an}}$.

Moreover, for every ample invertible sheaf $A$ on $X$ there is a smooth
positive closed real $(1,1)$-form $\eta_A$ on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$ whose de Rham
class is the real image of the topological first Chern class
$c_1(A):=c_1(A^{\mathrm{an}})\in H^2(X^{\mathrm{an}};\mathbb Z)$:
$$J_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}[\eta_A]=\rho_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}\bigl(c_1(A)\bigr),$$
where $J$ is the de Rham comparison and $\rho$ the change of coefficients
$\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$
([[lem-rational-cohomology-scalar-comparison-for-compact-smooth-manifolds]]).
In dimension $n=0$ and for $X=\varnothing$ every $2$-form and every degree-two
cohomology class is zero and $\eta_A=0$, so the identity holds trivially.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism locally of
finite presentation ([[def-locally-finite-presentation-morphism]]) and let
$x\in X$ with $s=f(x)$. Then $f$ is smooth at $x$
([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]]) if and only if there are affine open
neighbourhoods $U=\operatorname{Spec}C$ of $x$ and
$V=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $s$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$ and a presentation of
$C_h$, for some $h\in C\smallsetminus\mathfrak q$ with $\mathfrak q$ the prime
of $x$, as
$$C_h\;\cong\;\Bigl(A[t_1,\dots,t_m]/(f_1,\dots,f_r)\Bigr)_g,$$
in which some $r\times r$ minor of the Jacobian matrix
$\bigl(\partial f_j/\partial t_i\bigr)$ has image a unit of $C_h$. Such a chart
is flat over $A$ with geometrically regular fibres whose components have
dimension $m-r$; in the local-dimension convention of
[[def-relative-dimension-smooth-morphism]] it exhibits relative dimension
$m-r$ at $x$.

The criterion demands that *some* presentation have an invertible $r\times r$
minor; it does not demand this of an arbitrary redundant equation list, and
$r>m$ makes an invertible $r\times r$ minor impossible by definition of the
matrix shape.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m\times\mathbb C^n$ be open, let
$f:U\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic, and let $(a,b)\in U$ satisfy $f(a,b)=0$.
Assume the complex Jacobian with respect to the second block is invertible:

$$\det\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial w_k}(a,b)\right)_{1\le j,k\le n}\ne0.$$

Then there are neighbourhoods $A$ of $a$ and $B$ of $b$, and a unique
holomorphic map $\varphi:A\to B$, such that

$$f(z,\varphi(z))=0\qquad(z\in A),$$

and, after shrinking $A\times B$ if needed,

$$f(z,w)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w=\varphi(z).$$

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open and let
$F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth. For every base point $(t_0,x_0)\in D$ there are
$h>0$ and an open neighbourhood $W$ of $(t_0,x_0)$ such that each initial pair
$(s,y)\in W$ has a unique solution on $[s-h,s+h]$, and the resulting local
solution map is smooth in the initial time and initial state.

Let $F(t,x,\lambda)$ be jointly $C^\infty$ in $(t,x,\lambda)$ on an open time-state-parameter
domain. Near any base data $(t_0,x_0,\lambda_0)$ there are a compact time
interval $I$ and a neighbourhood $W$ of $(x_0,\lambda_0)$ such that, for every
$(y,\lambda)\in W$, the solution of

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t),\lambda),\qquad x(t_0)=y,$$

is defined on $I$, and the resulting solution map is smooth in the pair
$(y,\lambda)$.

Let $V:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a smooth vector field on an open set $U$, and for
each $x_0\in U$ let $x(\,\cdot\,;x_0)$ denote the unique maximal solution of
$x'=V(x)$ with $x(0)=x_0$. Then the maximal solution domain

$$\Omega:=\{(t,x_0)\in\mathbb R\times U:t\text{ lies in the maximal interval of }x(\,\cdot\,;x_0)\}$$

is open in $\mathbb R\times U$. On $\Omega$, the evaluation map
$\Phi(t,x_0):=x(t;x_0)$ is smooth in the state variable and continuous jointly in
$(t,x_0)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M$ be a closed smooth
manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Then $M$ has the homotopy type of a finite
CW complex ([[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]) having a neighbourhood basis of contractible open sets at
every point, and let $k$ be a field. Write $k_X$ for its constant sheaf. There
are natural isomorphisms
$$H^q(X,k_X)\cong H^q_{\operatorname{sing}}(X;k)$$
in every degree, where the left side is derived cohomology in the category of
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces (computed with the functorial $k$-linear injective
resolutions supplied by
[[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]; compare
[[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). The same assertion holds on
every open subset of $X$. In particular a nonempty contractible space with this
local property has constant-sheaf cohomology $k$ in degree zero and zero
otherwise. This applies to every finite-polyhedral open star and to its
nonempty intersection with a closed simplex.

Assume AC and the actual geometric and derived-incidence suppliers of the Verdier theorem. For analytic algebraic maps on its proved constructible subcategory, the six operations $f^*,Rf_*,Rf_!,f^!,\otimes_k^L,R\mathcal Hom$ have their three adjunctions, composition and identity comparisons, ordinary proper and extraordinary proper base change, projection formula, support localization, dualizing transitivity and trace. The comparisons commute with Cartesian pasting, composition of maps, evaluation and trace, giving a coherent pull-push product calculus. For a locally trivial product projection with finite-type smooth fibre $F$, the actual finite product cochain model gives $R\mathrm{pr}_*\mathrm{pr}^*B\simeq B\otimes_k C^*(F;k)$, with its ordinary unit. Smooth base change for $Rf_*$ holds whenever a supplied factorization $f=p\circ j$ has $p$ proper and $j$ an open inclusion with the conical local models below; proper maps already satisfy it. Their finite constructible models commute with extension of coefficient fields. Geometric output preservation is the exact geometric supplier, not an additional axiom.

Assume AC. For a compact Kähler manifold $X$ in the sense of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]], every de
Rham class has a unique smooth harmonic representative and
$$H^k(X;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}H^{p,q}(X),\qquad \overline{H^{p,q}(X)}=H^{q,p}(X).$$
Here $H^{p,q}(X)$ is precisely the set of classes with a $d$-closed smooth
representative of type $(p,q)$, so the decomposition is independent of the
Kähler metric. Writing $\Omega_X^p$ for the sheaf of holomorphic $p$-forms (the
kernel of $\bar\partial$ on the sheaf $\mathcal A^{p,0}$ of smooth $(p,0)$-forms),
$H^{p,q}(X)$ is isomorphic to $H^q(X,\Omega_X^p)$, the sheaf cohomology of
[[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]. The Hodge filtration
$F^a=\bigoplus_{p\ge a}H^{p,k-p}$ of $H^k(X;\mathbb C)$ equals the filtration
induced by the holomorphic-degree filtration of the de Rham complex, whose
spectral sequence has $E_1^{p,q}=H^q(X,\Omega_X^p)$ and degenerates at $E_1$.
Pullback by holomorphic maps of compact Kähler manifolds and cup product
preserve Hodge type, so $H^k(X;\mathbb Q)$ is a functorial rational pure Hodge
structure.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M,E,P$ have exactly the compact, boundaryless, scalar-positive-symbol and formal symmetry hypotheses of [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]], with $\operatorname{dom}P=H^2(M,E)$. Write $\mathcal H=\ker P$.

Then $\mathcal H$ is finite dimensional and consists of smooth sections, $\operatorname{ran}P=\mathcal H^\perp$ is closed in $L^2$, and
$$L^2(M,E)=\mathcal H\mathbin{\oplus^\perp}\operatorname{ran}P.$$
Let $\Pi$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal H$. There is a unique linear operator $G:L^2\to H^2\cap\mathcal H^\perp$ with
$$PG=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }L^2,\qquad GP=I-\Pi\quad\hbox{on }H^2,\qquad G\Pi=\Pi G=0.$$
It is bounded from $H^k$ to $H^{k+2}$ for every integer $k\ge0$, compact and selfadjoint on $L^2$, and preserves smooth sections. For all such $k$,
$$H^k=\mathcal H\oplus P(H^{k+2}),\qquad C^\infty(M,E)=\mathcal H\oplus P(C^\infty(M,E)),$$
where the second summands are the corresponding intersections with $\mathcal H^\perp$, and the decompositions are topological. The projection is smoothing: for every integer $r\ge0$, $\|\Pi f\|_{C^r}\le C_r\|f\|_2$. Consequently $G$ is a two-sided parametrix with finite-rank smoothing remainders. If additionally $(Pu,u)_2\ge0$ for smooth $u$, then $P$ and $G$ are nonnegative on their respective domains.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
analytic suppliers below. Let $X$ be a compact Kähler $n$-fold in the
conventions of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]], with
Kähler form $\omega$, and let $0\le k\le n$. On the primitive space $P^k$ put
$$Q_k(a,b)=\epsilon(k)\int_Xa\wedge b\wedge\omega^{n-k},$$
where $a,b$ are closed smooth representatives of the classes and the integral
is independent of the representatives. This form is $(-1)^k$-symmetric, pairs
$P^{p,q}$ only with $P^{q,p}$, and for nonzero $a\in P^{p,q}$ satisfies
$$i^{p-q}Q_k(a,\bar a)=(n-k)!\,\|a_{\mathrm{harm}}\|_{L^2}^2>0.$$
If $[\omega]=\ell\in H^2(X;\mathbb Q)$, then $Q_k$ is a rational polarization
of $P^k$, and full $H^k$ is polarized by the orthogonal direct sum form $S_k$
that on $L^rP^{k-2r}$ is $(-1)^rQ_k$, equivalently
$S_k(L^ru,L^rv)=Q_{k-2r}(u,v)$ for $u,v\in P^{k-2r}$; degrees $k>n$ are
polarized by transporting the polarization of $H^{2n-k}$ along $L^{k-n}$, with
Tate shift. For every real Kähler class the same positivity and nondegeneracy
statements hold, without rationality. In particular this applies to smooth
closed complex projective submanifolds of projective space with a hyperplane
polarization, hence to smooth projective complex varieties through their smooth
projective analytifications; more generally it applies to every real Kähler
class, including $\ell+\epsilon\eta$ when represented by a positive closed
form. For any continuous family of Kähler classes the primitive kernels (of
every fixed degree $0\le k\le n$) vary continuously as subspaces; rational
primitive spaces are asserted only at rational classes.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Assume AC. Let $R$ be a commutative PID and $X,Y$ spaces such that every $H_q(Y;R)$ is a finite free $R$-module. For every $n\ge0$ the additive singular cohomology cross product gives an isomorphism
$$\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^p(X;R)\otimes_RH^q(Y;R)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^n(X\times Y;R).$$
All indices are nonnegative. The symmetric assertion holds when every $H_p(X;R)$ is finite free instead. No bound on the number of nonzero homology degrees and no finite-rank hypothesis on the singular chain groups is required.

Fix a commutative unital ring $R$. A **left $R$-module local system** on a
space $X$ is a covariant functor
$$\mathcal L:\Pi_1(X)\longrightarrow R\text{-}\mathbf{Mod},$$
where the source is [[def-fundamental-groupoid-of-a-space]], functor means
[[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]], and the target is the category in
[[prop-modules-and-homomorphisms-form-category-rmod]]. Write
$\mathcal L_x$ for its value at $x$ and
$$T_\gamma=\mathcal L([\gamma]):\mathcal L_x\longrightarrow\mathcal L_y$$
for transport along a path $\gamma:x\to y$. Every arrow of the source has a
reversed inverse, so functoriality makes every $T_\gamma$ an isomorphism, with
$T_{\bar\gamma}=T_\gamma^{-1}$ and
$T_{\alpha*\beta}=T_\beta T_\alpha$.

A **morphism of local systems** $\eta:\mathcal L\to\mathcal K$ is a natural
transformation ([[def-natural-transformation]]): it is a family of
$R$-linear maps $\eta_x:\mathcal L_x\to\mathcal K_x$ satisfying
$$\eta_yT^\mathcal L_\gamma=T^\mathcal K_\gamma\eta_x$$
for every path $\gamma:x\to y$. Isomorphisms of local systems are natural
isomorphisms.

A continuous map $f:X\to Y$ induces a functor
$\Pi_1(f):\Pi_1(X)\to\Pi_1(Y)$ by $x\mapsto f(x)$ and
$[\gamma]\mapsto[f\gamma]$. Postcomposition preserves constants, reversals,
and concatenation, so this is well defined. The **pullback local system** is
$$f^*\mathcal K=\mathcal K\circ\Pi_1(f),\qquad (f^*\mathcal K)_x=\mathcal K_{f(x)},\qquad T^{f^*\mathcal K}_\gamma=T^\mathcal K_{f\gamma}.$$
Pullback of a coefficient morphism is defined componentwise. Thus
$(gf)^*=f^*g^*$ and $1_X^*$ are literal equalities of functors with these
conventions.

All definitions work independently on every path component. The empty space
has the unique empty local system. No basepoint, universal cover, common fiber,
or choice principle is required.

For later comparison with group rings, if $x$ is fixed and
$g=[\alpha]\in\pi_1(X,x)$, the base fiber is given the **left monodromy
convention**
$$g\cdot m:=T_{\bar\alpha}(m).$$
The reversal is essential: covariance and first-path-first multiplication give
$T_{\alpha*\beta}=T_\beta T_\alpha$, so
$T_{\overline{\alpha*\beta}}=T_{\bar\alpha}T_{\bar\beta}$, exactly the left
action law $(gh)m=g(hm)$.

derivations.claim: Local product structure. The analytification $f^{\mathrm{an}}$ is a proper holomorphic map, because $f$ is projective by hypothesis and projective morphisms are proper by [F1]; its fibres are closed complex submanifolds, compact by properness. At every point of $X$ the smooth algebraic morphism $f$ admits the presentation of [F2], and the holomorphic implicit function theorem of [F2] exhibits holomorphic charts in which $f^{\mathrm{an}}$ is the linear projection of a product of polydiscs; consequently each fibre is a compact complex manifold. In particular, for every $s\in S$ the fibre $f^{-1}(s)$ is compact and, by [F1] applied fibrewise, carries a Kähler structure.

Transport and the cohomology local systems. Choose a smooth horizontal complement to $\ker df^{\mathrm{an}}$ on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$ (locally the product charts of step 1.1 provide one; glue the local choices with a smooth partition of unity on the manifold $X^{\mathrm{an}}$ [F9]). For a path $\gamma:[0,1]\to S$ and a point $x\in f^{-1}(\gamma(0))$, the horizontal ODE $\dot x(t)\in H_{x(t)}$ with $f(x(t))=\gamma(t)$ has a unique maximal solution by [F3]; because $f$ is proper, the lifted solution stays in the compact set $f^{-1}(K)$ for a compact neighbourhood $K$ of $\gamma([0,1])$, so by the openness of the maximal solution domain in [F3] it exists on all of $[0,1]$. The resulting transport map $\tau_\gamma:f^{-1}(\gamma(0))\to f^{-1}(\gamma(1))$ is a diffeomorphism, smooth in the initial point by the smooth dependence on initial data in [F3], and an endpoint-fixed smooth homotopy of paths gives a homotopy of terminal diffeomorphisms by the parameter dependence in [F3]. The terminal point maps need not be identical, but their induced maps on cohomology are identical by homotopy invariance. Piecewise smooth representatives and homotopies suffice for the fundamental groupoid: subdividing a path or homotopy into finitely many parameter pieces lying in coordinate charts and using linear interpolation in smaller convex charts gives the usual piecewise smooth representatives without changing the endpoint-fixed homotopy class. Concatenation and reversal give composition and inverses of the cohomology transports. The assignments $x\mapsto H^m(f^{-1}(x);R)$ for $R=\mathbb Z,\mathbb Q$, together with the isomorphisms $\tau_\gamma^*$, therefore define functors on the fundamental groupoid of $S$, that is, $R$-module local systems in the sense of [F8]; this is the local system $R^mf^{\mathrm{an}}_*\underline R$ of the family.

Identification with the sheaves and integral lattices. On each fibre, and on each product chart of step 1.1, the space is a metric space with a neighbourhood basis of contractible open sets, so [F4] identifies singular cohomology with constant-sheaf cohomology there. The proper base change clause of [F5] identifies the sheaf $R^mf_*\mathbb Q$ with the fibrewise cohomology of the local system of step 2.1; the same identification for $\mathbb Z$-coefficients gives the local system $R^mf_*\mathbb Z$. Each fibre is a closed smooth manifold, so its integral cohomology is finitely generated by [F4]; hence the quotient of $H^m(f^{-1}(x);\mathbb Z)$ by its torsion group is a full finitely generated free lattice in $H^m(f^{-1}(x);\mathbb Q)$, and the transport isomorphisms of step 2.1 preserve the torsion subgroups and these lattices. Passing to the quotient by torsion therefore produces the full monodromy-stable integral lattice of the variation.

Continuous pure Hodge decomposition. Fix $s\in S$ and a smooth trivialization $B\times F\cong f^{-1}(B)$ near $s$ obtained by transporting the whole compact fibre along radial paths in a sufficiently small convex base chart using step 2.1, with $F$ the fibre over $s$. The restrictions of a smooth family of Kähler metrics — for instance the pullback along the projective embedding of the positive closed forms supplied in [F1] — give a smooth family $\Delta_t$, $t\in B$, of formally self-adjoint elliptic Laplacians on the fixed compact manifold $F$, with continuously varying uniformly elliptic coefficients on the fixed manifold; here the smooth family of metrics is obtained from the projective embedding into $S\times\mathbb P^N$ by restricting the Fubini-Study form, and the identification of the fibres with $F$ is the product chart. By the elliptic parametrix and Fredholm theory of [F6], the kernel of $\Delta_{t_0}$ is finite dimensional and the resolvent is bounded from $L^2$ to $H^2$; a fixed contour around $0$ separating the zero spectrum gives, for $t$ near $t_0$, convergent Neumann series for $(\Delta_t-\lambda)^{-1}$ and hence a continuously varying finite-rank projection onto the kernel of $\Delta_t$, compare [F6]. Its rank equals $\dim\ker\Delta_{t_0}$ for $t$ near $t_0$ and the kernel dimension is the constant Betti number of the fixed fibre by [F6], so no nonzero eigenspace can occur inside this contour projection; the projection is smoothing and therefore projects exactly onto the harmonic space; applying the same continuously varying projections to the type projections of the forms yields continuously varying subspaces $H^{p,q}_t$ of the harmonic representatives. Since the decomposition is independent of the metric and functorial by [F6], the resulting family of decompositions of $H^m(f^{-1}(t);\mathbb C)$ is a continuous pure Hodge decomposition of weight $m$ of the local system $R^mf_*\mathbb Q$ in the sense of the definition.

Flat Lefschetz operators and polarization. Let $L$ be a relatively ample line bundle on $X$. Its first Chern class lies in $H^2(X;\mathbb Q)$. Apply the positive Chern-metric construction of [F1] to the ample restriction on each compact fibre, extend that metric to a neighbourhood using the smooth trivialization of step 2.1, and shrink the base chart so vertical positivity persists by compactness. Relative to a fixed smooth reference metric on $L$, patch the logarithms of the local metric ratios with a smooth partition of unity pulled back from the base. On a fibre these base weights are constant, so the resulting Chern curvature is their positive convex combination; it is globally closed, represents $c_1(L)$ and restricts on every fibre to a Kähler form with rational class. No positivity in base directions is asserted. Then in the product chart the restrictions to the fibres induce one and the same class on the fixed model $F$ under the identifications $\tau_\gamma$ of step 2.1, because those identifications are induced by the homotopic family of inclusions of the fibres into $X$ and cohomology is homotopy invariant; explicitly, if $\psi_t:F\to f^{-1}(t)$ are the product-chart identifications, then the maps $(t,x)\mapsto\psi_t(x)$ exhibit the composites $i_t\circ\psi_t$ as homotopic to $i_s\circ\psi_s$, so $\psi_t^*(c_1(L)|_{f^{-1}(t)})=\psi_s^*(c_1(L)|_{f^{-1}(s)})$. Cup product and integration are compatible with the transport isomorphisms, so the map $a\mapsto c_1(L)\smile a$ is a flat Lefschetz operator, and the polarized Lefschetz decomposition supplied by [F7] is flat. The forms $Q_k$ of [F7] applied to the primitive pieces give a flat rational bilinear form, since their defining integrals involve only cup products, the flat powers of the Kähler class just described, and the constant sign $\epsilon(k)$; the positivity clause of [F7] holds on every fibre, and the full polarization is the sign-adjusted orthogonal sum along the flat Lefschetz decomposition, hence also flat, rational and positive. This supplies the flat rational polarization required in the definition.

Geometric closures and full lattices. All assertions are made over a fixed open piece of the base, and may be pulled back along a base change to any smooth $S'$ by change of the parameter. Products: for smooth projective $f_i:X_i\to S$, $i=1,2$, the product family $X_1\times_SX_2\to S$ is smooth projective, and the cohomological Künneth isomorphism of [F8] identifies $R^{m}(f_1\times_Sf_2)_*\mathbb Q$ with the direct sum of tensor products $R^pf_{1*}\mathbb Q\otimes R^{q}f_{2*}\mathbb Q$, $p+q=m$, compatible with Hodge type because pullback and wedge of $(p,q)$ forms preserve bidegree by [F6]; this rational comparison uses [F8] over the field $\mathbb Q$, where the finite-dimensional homology groups are free. The ambient product-family cohomology has a full stable integral lattice by step 3.1; intersecting it with each rational tensor summand gives a full monodromy-stable lattice in that summand, since a rational basis can be multiplied by common denominators into the ambient lattice. Thus products and their full lattices are geometric without assuming that the integral cohomology of every smooth projective fibre is torsion-free. Direct sums are realized by disjoint unions of families over $S$. The degree-two cohomology of the constant family $\mathbb P^1\times S\to S$ is $\mathbb Q(-1)$, of type $(1,1)$, and its rational Hodge dual is $\mathbb Q(1)$, of type $(-1,-1)$, by the dual and Tate conventions in the definition. For a realization $H|_U\subseteq\bigoplus_i R^{m_i}(f_i)_*\mathbb Q(r_i)$, twisting by any integer $r$ gives the realization inside $\bigoplus_i R^{m_i}(f_i)_*\mathbb Q(r_i+r)$, which is allowed directly by that definition; the same rational idempotent remains flat and preserves the shifted Hodge types. Thus all integer Tate twists have the stated geometric realizations, without identifying a positive twist with untwisted degree-two cohomology. For a pure variation of weight $w$, its flat rational nondegenerate polarization of step 4.1 gives $H^*\cong H(w)$ as Hodge variations, so the just-proved Tate realization also realizes the dual; the dual of a full stable lattice is again full and stable. Finite sums of pure weights are handled componentwise. Exterior powers are Hodge direct summands of tensor powers cut out by the rational alternating idempotent, which is flat and a Hodge morphism on every fibre; more generally a prescribed flat rational idempotent that is a Hodge morphism on every fibre cuts out a geometric Hodge direct summand of a realized variation. Intersecting such a rational direct summand with the full ambient lattice of step 3.1 gives its full monodromy-stable lattice: a rational basis of the summand can be cleared to integral vectors of the ambient lattice, and flatness of the summand makes the intersection monodromy-stable. Finally, for a morphism $g:X'\to X$ of smooth projective complex varieties, $g^*:H^m(X;\mathbb Q)\to H^m(X';\mathbb Q)$ preserves Hodge types by the pullback functoriality clause of [F6], so rational pullbacks between smooth projective fibres are morphisms of pure Hodge structures. This proves every closure and lattice clause of the statement concerning a single smooth projective family; the Gauss-Manin family itself is geometric and polarizable by steps 2.1-5.1.

Conclusion. Steps 2.1 and 3.1 produce the finite-rank rational and integral local systems with full monodromy-stable lattices, step 3.2 the continuous pure Hodge decomposition, step 4.1 the flat Lefschetz operators and the flat rational polarization, and step 5.1 the remaining closure, lattice and pullback clauses. Hence $R^mf_*\mathbb Q$ is a geometric polarizable rational Hodge variation in the sense of the definition, with the stated additional properties. No analytic-variation theorem or Gauss-Manin semisimplicity theorem is imported; the argument is the fibre-bundle, harmonic and Künneth construction of the family categories.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For a smooth projective morphism
$f:X\to S$ of smooth quasiprojective complex varieties, $R^mf_*\mathbb Q$ is a
finite-rank local system ([[def-local-system-of-r-modules-and-its-pullback]]),
with full monodromy-stable integral lattice obtained from
$R^mf_*\mathbb Z$ modulo torsion, and with a continuous pure Hodge
decomposition of weight $m$ ([[def-geometric-polarizable-hodge-variation]]). A
relatively ample line bundle supplies flat Lefschetz operators and a flat
rational polarization of this variation. Products, sums, Tate twists, exterior
powers and Hodge direct summands have the corresponding geometric realizations
and full integral lattices. Pullbacks of algebraic maps between smooth
projective fibers preserve rational Hodge structures.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a triangulated category with a bounded t-structure, with truncation functors and t-cohomology as in [[def-truncation-functors-and-cohomology-of-a-t-structure]] and [[lem-t-cohomology-is-additive-shift-compatible-and-detects-amplitude]]. Let $K\in\mathcal T$ and let $L:K\to K[2]$ be a morphism such that for every integer $j\ge0$ the map
$$H^{-j}_t(L^j):H^{-j}_t(K)\longrightarrow H^{-j}_t(K[2j])\cong H^j_t(K)$$
is an isomorphism, where $L^j:=L[2j-2]\circ\cdots\circ L[2]\circ L$ is the $j$-fold iterate (so $L^0=1_K$) and the identification is the shift isomorphism $H^j_t(K)\cong H^{-j}_t(K[2j])$ of that lemma. Then there is an isomorphism
$$K\cong\bigoplus_j H^j_t(K)[-j]$$
in $\mathcal T$; the sum is finite because the t-structure is bounded. The isomorphism is not asserted to be canonical, and no compatibility with primitive lifts is claimed: this is the abstract splitting criterion, not the stronger primitive-compatible decomposition used in the Hodge theory of projective maps. The degenerate case in which $H^{-n}_t(K)$ and $H^n_t(K)$ are both zero (they vanish together because $H^{-n}_t(L^n)$ is an isomorphism) is covered by the same formulas, all of which are then the zero maps between zero objects.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
analytic suppliers below. Let $X$ be a compact Kähler $n$-fold with Kähler form
$\omega$, in the conventions of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]], and put
$L=[\omega]\smile(-)$ on cohomology. Then the following hold.

- $L^{n-k}:H^k(X;\mathbb R)\to H^{2n-k}(X;\mathbb R)$ is an isomorphism for
  $0\le k\le n$.
- Harmonic representatives transport $(L,\Lambda,H)$ to an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$
  action: $L$ is cup product with $[\omega]$, $\Lambda$ on cohomology means
  applying $\Lambda$ to the harmonic representative and not to an arbitrary
  closed form, $H$ acts by $\deg-n$, and
  $[L,\Lambda]=H$, $[H,L]=2L$, $[H,\Lambda]=-2\Lambda$ hold on cohomology.
- Primitive cohomology is
  $P^k=\{a\in H^k(X;\mathbb R):\text{the harmonic representative of }a\text{ lies in }\ker\Lambda\}$,
  and for $0\le k\le n$ one has
  $P^k=\ker\bigl(L^{n-k+1}:H^k(X;\mathbb R)\to H^{2n-k+2}(X;\mathbb R)\bigr)$;
  for every $k$,
  $$H^k(X;\mathbb R)=\bigoplus_{r\ge\max(0,k-n)}L^rP^{k-2r},$$
  and a class of type $(p,q)$ has primitive components of type $(p-r,q-r)$.
- If $[\omega]$ is the real image of a rational class
  $\ell\in H^2(X;\mathbb Q)$, all these decompositions and $L$-isomorphisms are
  rational, and they remain isomorphisms after extension to every
  characteristic-zero field.

Assume AC. Let $U$ be smooth quasiprojective over $\mathbb C$, and choose an SNC smooth projective compactification $j:U\hookrightarrow X$, boundary $D$. The logarithmic de Rham complex with Hodge filtration by degree and pole-count weight filtration constructs a functorial rational mixed Hodge structure on $H^n(U,\mathbb Q)$, independent of the compactification. $$W_nH^n(U,\mathbb Q)=\operatorname{im}(H^n(X,\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow H^n(U,\mathbb Q)).$$

Given finitely many such compactifications, there is another dominating all of them and restricting to the identity on $U$. A morphism of smooth quasiprojective varieties extends to a morphism of such compactifications after modifying the source compactification outside its open variety.

Every morphism $f\colon H\to K$ of rational mixed Hodge structures is strict for
$W$ and for $F$:
$$f(W_nH)=f(H)\cap W_nK,\qquad f(F^pH_{\mathbb C})=f(H_{\mathbb C})\cap F^pK_{\mathbb C}$$
for all $n,p$. Its kernel, image and cokernel, with the induced or quotient

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). If $U$ is a nonempty
Zariski open subset of a connected smooth complex algebraic variety $S$, then
$U$ is path connected and $\pi_1(U,s)\to\pi_1(S,s)$ is surjective for every
$s\in U$ ([[def-fundamental-groupoid-of-a-space]]).

Assume AC and the actual geometric and derived-incidence suppliers of the Verdier theorem. For analytic algebraic maps on its proved constructible subcategory, the six operations $f^*,Rf_*,Rf_!,f^!,\otimes_k^L,R\mathcal Hom$ have their three adjunctions, composition and identity comparisons, ordinary proper and extraordinary proper base change, projection formula, support localization, dualizing transitivity and trace. The comparisons commute with Cartesian pasting, composition of maps, evaluation and trace, giving a coherent pull-push product calculus. derivations.claim: Leray edge map in the family case. Let $f:X\to S$ be smooth projective and put $H=R^mf_*\mathbb Q$. By [F3] choose an SNC smooth projective compactification $\overline X$ of $X$. A relatively ample line bundle exists because $f$ is projective, and by [F2] its class acts on the ordinary bounded t-structure by centered hard-Lefschetz isomorphisms, so [F2] splits $Rf_*\mathbb Q\cong\bigoplus_jR^jf_*\mathbb Q[-j]$ in the constructible derived category. Under the Leray identification $H^m(X;\mathbb Q)\cong H^m(S,Rf_*\mathbb Q)$ supplied by [F6], this decomposition expresses $H^m(X;\mathbb Q)$ as the direct sum of the groups $H^{m-j}(S,R^jf_*\mathbb Q)$; the edge map $H^m(X;\mathbb Q)\to H^0(S,R^mf_*\mathbb Q)$ is the projection onto the $j=m$ summand and is therefore surjective. The stalk of $R^mf_*\mathbb Q$ at $s$ is $H^m(X_s;\mathbb Q)$ by proper base change [F6], and evaluation at $s$ from the global flat sections $H^0(S,R^mf_*\mathbb Q)$ is injective because $S$ is connected; its image is exactly the monodromy-invariant subspace $H^m(X_s;\mathbb Q)^{\pi_1(S,s)}$. Consequently the composite $H^m(X;\mathbb Q)\to H^m(X_s;\mathbb Q)$ has image the invariant subspace.

Weights and strictness identify the invariant subspace. The space $H^m(X,\mathbb Q)$ carries the mixed Hodge structure of [F3], whose weights are at least $m$; the target $H^m(X_s,\mathbb Q)$ is pure of weight $m$, because $X_s$ is a smooth projective variety and the restriction $H^m(X,\mathbb Q)\to H^m(X_s,\mathbb Q)$ is a morphism of mixed Hodge structures by [F6] and [F1]. Strictness [F4] applied to this morphism, whose target has $W_{m-1}=0$ and $W_m=H$, gives that the image of $H^m(X,\mathbb Q)$ equals the image of its minimal weight part $W_mH^m(X,\mathbb Q)$; by [F3] that minimal weight part is the image of $H^m(\overline X,\mathbb Q)\to H^m(X,\mathbb Q)$. Combining with step 1.1, the image of $H^m(\overline X,\mathbb Q)\to H^m(X_s,\mathbb Q)$ equals the image of $H^m(X,\mathbb Q)\to H^m(X_s,\mathbb Q)$, which is the monodromy-invariant subspace. Since $H^m(\overline X,\mathbb Q)$ and $H^m(X_s,\mathbb Q)$ are pure of weight $m$ and the restriction is a Hodge morphism by [F1], its image is a Hodge substructure; this proves that the invariant subspace is a Hodge substructure in the family case.

Base-point independence and flatness of Hodge components in the family case. The restriction $H^m(\overline X,\mathbb Q)\to H^m(X_s,\mathbb Q)$ factors through the canonical map $E:H^m(\overline X,\mathbb Q)\to H^0(S,R^mf_*\mathbb Q)$ followed by evaluation at $s$, and $E$ is independent of $s$. Its kernel $K=\ker E$ is therefore one fixed rational subspace, and evaluation identifies $H^0(S,R^mf_*\mathbb Q)$ with the quotient $H^m(\overline X,\mathbb Q)/K$, carrying the quotient Hodge structure, at every base point simultaneously; this is the asserted one constant Hodge structure on the invariant spaces. Now let $v$ be a global flat section of $H$. Since the invariant space at $s$ is a Hodge substructure by step 2.1, the Hodge components of the value $v_s$ lie again in the invariant space, hence are values of global flat sections $w_1,\dots,w_r$; their sum $\sum_iw_i$ is a global flat section with the same value at $s$ as $v$, so it equals $v$ by connectedness. Since the Hodge decomposition of the invariant fibre is the fixed quotient structure of step 2.1, the section $w_i$ is the Hodge component of $v$ of the corresponding type at every fibre. This proves, in the family case, both that the invariant subspace is a Hodge substructure and that the Hodge components of global flat sections are global flat sections.

Reduction of a general geometric variation to the realization open. Let $U\subseteq S$ be a nonempty Zariski open on which $H$ has an algebraic realization: $H|_U$ is the image of a flat rational idempotent $p$ that is a Hodge morphism at every point, inside $A=\bigoplus_iR^{m_i}(f_i)_*\mathbb Q(r_i)$ for smooth projective $f_i:X_i\to U$; this is the definition of a geometric variation, and each summand is a finite direct sum of weight pieces. By steps 1.1-3.1 applied to each $f_i$ over $U$ (note $U$ is again connected smooth quasiprojective), the statement holds for every $R^{m_i}(f_i)_*\mathbb Q(r_i)$: its invariant part is a constant Hodge substructure and the Hodge components of its global flat sections are flat. Finite direct sums and Tate twists preserve both assertions, because monodromy acts componentwise and the twist changes only the weight; hence the statement holds for $A|_U$. Because $p$ is flat and a Hodge morphism, it commutes with monodromy and with the Hodge decompositions, so the invariant space of $H|_U$ is the image under $p$ of the invariant space of $A|_U$, and it inherits the constant Hodge structure; the Hodge components of a flat section of $H|_U$ are the images under $p$ of the components of a lift and are therefore flat. This proves the assertions for $H|_U$.

Extension from $U$ to $S$. The inclusion $U\hookrightarrow S$ induces a surjection $\pi_1(U,s)\to\pi_1(S,s)$ by [F5]. Therefore a vector of $H_s$ fixed by $\pi_1(U,s)$ is fixed by $\pi_1(S,s)$, so restriction of flat sections $H^0(S,H)\to H^0(U,H|_U)$ is an isomorphism: it is injective because $S$ is connected, and surjective by the preceding sentence. Given a global flat section $v$ of $H$, its restriction to $U$ has, by step 4.1, Hodge components that are flat sections of $H|_U$; each extends uniquely to a global flat section $w_i$ of $H$, and $v-\sum_iw_i$ is a global flat section vanishing on the dense open $U$, hence vanishes by continuity. For each type $(a,b)$, the corresponding $w_i$ takes its values in the continuous Hodge subbundle of that type on $U$. Membership in this subbundle is a closed condition: in a local trivialization its continuously varying projection has kernel describing the complement, and the difference between $w_i$ and its type projection is continuous. This difference vanishes on the dense open $U$, hence on all of $S$. Thus $w_i$ has the prescribed type everywhere; uniqueness of the fiber decomposition makes these global flat sections exactly the Hodge components of $v$. In particular the invariant space $H_s^{\pi_1(S,s)}$, the values of global flat sections, is stable under all Hodge type projections and is a Hodge substructure with the induced pure decomposition.

Independence of the base point for a general variation. Evaluation identifies the rational space $E=H^0(S,H)$ with each invariant fiber $H_s^{\pi_1(S,s)}$. Transport along a path identifies these invariant fibers through this one space $E$, since a global flat section is transported to its own value. Step 5.1 proves that the Hodge components of every global flat section are again global flat sections. On the realization open $U$, steps 3.1 and 4.1 identify these type decompositions with one fixed quotient Hodge structure on $E$, and the closed-membership argument of step 5.1 extends those same types to every point of $S$. Consequently evaluation gives one Hodge structure on $E$ independent of $s$, and transport restricted to the invariant fibers preserves that structure. This assertion concerns the invariant constant subsystem; it does not assume that transport on the full variation preserves the moving Hodge decomposition. Finite sums of pure weights are handled one weight at a time, proving every clause of the statement.

derivations.claim: 1.1 Rational descent of the socle and its lattice. Let $H$ be a nonzero pure geometric object of rank $r$ over the connected base $S$, and let $W_{\mathbb C}$ be the socle of the complex monodromy module $V_{s,\mathbb C}$, a nonzero finite-dimensional complex module by [F2]. By [F2] there is a rational flat subspace $W_{\mathbb Q}\subseteq V_s$ with $W_{\mathbb C}=W_{\mathbb Q}\otimes\mathbb C$; since it is monodromy-invariant it is the fibre at $s$ of a local subsystem of $H$, which we again call $W$. Let $H_{\mathbb Z}$ be the full monodromy-stable integral lattice of [F3] and put $W_{\mathbb Z}=W_{\mathbb Q}\cap H_{\mathbb Z}$; a rational basis of $W_{\mathbb Q}$ becomes integral after clearing denominators, so $W_{\mathbb Z}$ is a full lattice in $W_{\mathbb Q}$, and the monodromy preserves it and acts by invertible integral matrices. On the determinant line $\det W=\bigwedge^{e}W$, $e=\dim_{\mathbb Q}W_{\mathbb Q}$, the monodromy therefore acts by $\pm1$, so $(\det W)^{\otimes2}$ is a constant rank-one local subsystem of the geometric tensor object $\bigwedge^eH\otimes\bigwedge^eH$ of [F3], generated by a global horizontal section. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The determinant line of a simple summand and the torus images. Write $W_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{m}S_i$ as a direct sum of simple submodules, possible because the socle is a sum of simples and the module has finite length ([F4]). Fix one simple summand $T=S_1$ of dimension $d$ and let $T'=\bigoplus_{i\ge2}S_i$, a flat complement with $\dim T'=e-d$. The exterior algebra gives a canonical identification $\det W\cong\bigwedge^dT\otimes\bigwedge^{e-d}T'$, so $V:=\bigwedge^dT\otimes\bigwedge^{e-d}T'$ is a rank-one flat complex subsystem of the geometric tensor object $A:=\bigwedge^dH_{\mathbb C}\otimes\bigwedge^{e-d}H_{\mathbb C}$, and $V^{\otimes2}=(\det W)^{\otimes2}$ is constant by step 1.1; the fixed part of $A$ is a constant family of Hodge substructures by [F1]. For every $t\in\mathbb C^\times$ the line $tV=(t\bigwedge^dT)\otimes(t\bigwedge^{e-d}T')$ has square $(tV)^{\otimes2}=t(V^{\otimes2})$, a line inside the fixed part of $A$, hence a flat line: the torus acts on the fixed part, which is constant and consists of Hodge substructures, and every line of a constant subsystem is flat. Over a simply connected open $U$ on which the ambient tensor object is trivialized by a flat frame, let $\sigma$ be a nowhere zero local generator of $tV|_U$ and let $h$ be a horizontal generator of the flat line $(tV)^{\otimes2}|_U$; then $\sigma^{\otimes2}=g\cdot h$ for a nowhere zero smooth function $g$, so the projective class of $\sigma^{\otimes2}$ is the constant class of $h$. In the flat frame the coefficients of $\sigma^{\otimes2}$ are the quadratic monomials in the coefficients of $\sigma$, and this squaring map on projective classes is injective, as the Veronese embedding of a projective space is injective; hence the projective class of $\sigma$ is constant, $\sigma$ may be rescaled to a horizontal generator, and $tV$ is flat. Now a nonzero decomposable tensor $p\otimes q$, with $p$ a generator of $\bigwedge^d(tT)$ and $q$ a generator of $\bigwedge^{e-d}(tT')$, determines each factor line: its image under the canonical identification is the line spanned by $p$, and its kernel the hyperplane annihilating the line spanned by $q$, so a horizontal decomposable generator of the flat line $tV$ makes both factors locally constant. Therefore $\bigwedge^d(tT)$ and $\bigwedge^{e-d}(tT')$ are flat for every $t$. Finally the Plücker line of a subspace determines the subspace by $tT=\{v:v\wedge\bigwedge^d(tT)=0\}$, an identity that commutes with the transport of the tensor object, so $tT$ is a flat subspace of $H_{\mathbb C}$ for every $t\in\mathbb C^\times$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Openness of irreducibility and torus-stability of the socle. For $t$ near $1$ the flat subspace $tT$ is simple: were there $t_n\to1$ with $t_nT$ reducible, there would be, for each $n$, a proper nonzero flat subspace $U_n\subset t_nT$ of some fixed dimension $\varrho$, $1\le\varrho<d$; the invariance condition under the finitely many monodromy operators is closed in the Grassmannian, and the Grassmannian of $\varrho$-planes in a fixed finite-dimensional complex space is compact by [F5], so a subsequence of the $U_n$ converges to a $\varrho$-plane $U\subseteq T$ that is again flat, contradicting simplicity of $T$. Hence, for $t$ in a neighbourhood of $1$, each $tS_i$ is a simple flat subspace of $H_{\mathbb C}$, and every simple flat subspace is contained in the socle $W_{\mathbb C}$ by [F2]; summing over the finitely many $S_i$ gives $tW\subseteq W$, hence $tW=W$ by dimension. Thus the stabilizer of $W$ in $\mathbb C^\times$ contains a neighbourhood of the identity; a subgroup of a topological group with nonempty interior is open, and the connected group $\mathbb C^\times$ has no proper nonempty open subgroup, so $tW=W$ for every $t\in\mathbb C^\times$. Consequently $W_s$ is stable under the Hodge torus at every point $s$, so $W_{\mathbb Q}$ is a Hodge substructure of $H$ at every point; since it is already flat, it is a Hodge subvariation. [F2, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Polarization splitting and induction. Let $Q$ be a polarization of the pure object $H$. Its restriction to the Hodge subvariation $W$ is nondegenerate: if $v\in W_s$ were a nonzero radical vector, then with the Weil operator $C$ of the Hodge structure the vector $C\bar v$ lies in $W_{s,\mathbb C}$ because $W_s$ is a Hodge substructure, so the positivity of the Weil-operator Hermitian form $h(v,v)=\pm Q(v,C\bar v)$ would give the contradiction $0=Q(v,C\bar v)\ne0$. Hence the $Q$-orthogonal complement $W^\perp$ is a flat Hodge subvariation and $H=W\oplus W^\perp$; the orthogonal projection onto $W$ is a flat rational idempotent that is a Hodge morphism, so $W^\perp$ is a geometric direct summand of $H$ by [F3], of smaller rank unless $W=H$. The submodule $W_{\mathbb C}$ is a direct sum of simples by construction, and by induction over the rank the complex monodromy module of $W^\perp$ is semisimple; a direct sum of semisimple modules is semisimple, so the complex monodromy module of $H$ is semisimple. A non-pure object is a finite direct sum of pure weight pieces, handled one weight at a time, and the rank-zero case is the empty direct sum. [F3, F4, step 3.1, algebra]

On higher-dimensional layers the induction hypothesis already gives the upper perverse stalk bound, preserved by ordinary truncation; on $W_i$ truncation makes the degree at most $-i$. These are exactly the upper perverse bounds for $A$ on $U_i$, without any claim that $U_i$ has dimension $i$. Thus on each affine $V\subset U_i$, [F1] and the triangle $A\to K\to Q$ give $H^q(V,Q)=0$ for $q>0$. All ordinary cohomology sheaves of $Q$ are supported on the closed smooth layer $W_i\subset U_i$ and are local systems there.

If $Q$ is nonzero, let $b>-i$ be its largest nonzero cohomological degree and let $L=\mathcal H^b(Q)|_{W_i}$ be nonzero on a connected component. The finitely many smooth irreducible components of $W_i$ are disjoint and closed in $U_i$; remove the components where $L$ is zero and all but one nonzero component, and choose an affine open $V_0\subset U_i$ in the resulting open, meeting the retained component. Then $V_0\cap W_i$ is smooth affine and $L$ is a nonzero local system on it. Step 1.1 supplies a principal open of it with nonzero $H^i(L)$. Since $W_i\cap V_0$ is closed in the affine $V_0$, the defining function lifts from its coordinate-ring quotient to a function on $V_0$; localizing the latter gives an affine $V\subset U_i$ with $H^i(V\cap W_i,L)\ne0$. The closed embedding $e:V\cap W_i\hookrightarrow V$ has exact pushforward, and $Q|_V=e_*e^*Q|_V$ because all its cohomology is supported there. Thus $H^a(V,\mathcal H^t(Q))=H^a(V\cap W_i,\mathcal H^t(Q)|_{W_i})$. In the bounded spectral sequence $H^a(V\cap W_i,\mathcal H^t(Q)|_{W_i})\Rightarrow H^{a+t}(V,Q)$, [F1] gives $a\le i$ and maximality of $b$ gives $t\le b$. The nonzero term $(i,b)$ has no incoming differential, since those would start at a larger $t$, and no outgoing differential, since those would end at a larger $a$. It is the sole term in its total degree $i+b>0$, contradicting step 1.2. Hence $Q=0$, completing the descending dimension induction and the converse.

Let $P\in{}^pD^{\le0}_c(X)$. For every affine Zariski open $V\subset Y$ its inverse image under the affine morphism $u$ is affine, and derived composition with [F1] gives $H^q(V,Ru_*P)=H^q(u^{-1}V,P)=0$ for $q>0$; the characterization proved in step 2.1 therefore puts $Ru_*P$ in the upper perverse aisle. For $P$ in the lower aisle, apply this to $DP$ and dualize by [F2] to obtain the claimed lower-aisle preservation by $Ru_!$. All zero and empty cases follow from the same zero triangles.
